"'Where is he, where is he?' — crying thus, he ran here and there; that king of Saubha was indeed seeking battle with me in combat."
"'Today I shall send that sinful, vile, treacherous one — enraged over the slaying of Śiśupāla — to the realm of death.'"
"'He by whose sinful nature my kinsman, Śiśupāla, king of the earth, was struck down — him I shall slay upon this earth.'"
"'A kinsman, young, and a king at that — not slain at the forefront of battle but killed off-guard, a hero — I will slay that Janārdana.'"
"Lamenting in these and other words, O great king, he mounted to the sky in that wish-flying Saubha and hurled abuse at me, O joy of the Kurus."
"Upon returning, I heard how that very wicked one had behaved toward me, O Kaurava — that corrupt-souled king, the lord of Mārtikāvata."
"Then I too, O Kaurava, my eyes disturbed with rage, made up my mind firmly, O king, and set my heart on his destruction."
"The trampling of the Ānārta people, the insults against me personally, O Kaurava, and the swollen arrogance of that evil-deeded one —"
"— and so, O lord of the earth, I set out for the destruction of Saubha. He was sighted by me in a whirlpool of the ocean, as I sought him."
"Then, O king, I sounded the conch Pāñcajanya, born of the waters, and calling out Śālva, I took my stand ready for battle in the combat."
For a brief moment there was battle between me and those demons; all of them were brought under my control and cast down upon the earth.
This was the task, O mighty-armed one, on account of which I did not come then — hearing even of it, to Hāstinapura, and of the gambling that arose from that act of impropriety.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Vāsudeva, O mighty-armed one, O great-minded one, describe to me in full detail the slaying of Saubha — I am not yet satisfied with what has been told.
Vāsudeva said: Hearing that king Śrautaśrava had been slain by me, O mighty-armed one, O foremost of the Bhāratas, Śālva marched upon the city of Dvāravatī.
That exceedingly wicked soul Śālva besieged it on all sides, O son of Pāṇḍu; he arrayed his forces and took position, keeping that aerial city ready at hand.
Stationed there, that king assailed the city with his entire advancing force, and battle raged at that place.
The city was fully equipped on all sides — with banners and arched gateways, with wheels and palisade-stakes, with catapults and trenches.
It had platforms and covered ways, lofty watch-towers and gate-towers, devices for seizing hair and scalps, fire-brands, fire-tubes, and pestles.
It had corner-fortifications, O foremost of the Bhāratas, kettledrums and tabors, stores of fuel, grass and kuśa-grass, O king, along with śataghni-engines and plowshares.
It had bhuśuṇḍī-tubes, stone balls and clubs, all manner of weapons and axes, iron shields, and also fire and stakes with iron tips.
It was furnished, O bull of the Bhāratas, in accordance with the rules prescribed by the treatises, with many diverse materials — clubs and other offensive implements in abundance.
It was manned, O tiger of the Kurus, by warriors capable of repelling attack — heroes of renowned lineages and of proven valor in battle.
It was guarded by the central contingent, known as the Sārasa, and likewise by raised detachments, by cavalry, and by foot-soldiers.
A proclamation was made throughout the city that wine must not be drunk, and those guarding against negligence — Ugrasena, Uddhava and others — were on full alert.
"For Śālva, king of men, will strike when men are heedless" — with this in mind, all those Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas stood vigilant.
And all the Ānartas — actors, dancers, and singers — were all expelled outside the city by those who were protecting the accumulated wealth.
All the bridges were broken, boats were prohibited, and the moats too, O Kauravya, were made well-staked with iron spikes.
The wells, O best of the Kurus, and likewise the cooking pits, were secured; and for a distance of a krośa all around, the ground was made uneven and difficult.
Naturally difficult of access, naturally well-guarded, naturally equipped with weapons — that fortress was especially so at that time, O sinless one.
Well defended and well concealed, furnished with all weapons, that city, O foremost of the Bhāratas, was like the abode of Indra itself.
None without a seal could go out, and none without a seal could enter the city of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, O king, at that time when Saubha had arrived.
Along all the streets and at every crossroads, O Kaurava, O king of kings, there was a force, abundant in elephants and horses.
That army, O mighty-armed one, had been given their wages and provisions, had been furnished with weapons and equipment, and had already proven their valor.
Not one received an unjust wage, not one had wages delayed, not one was kept merely by patronage, and not one was of unproven valor.
Thus, O king, Dvārakā was excellently provided for by the liberal-handed ones, and well protected by king Āhuka, O lotus-eyed one.
Vāsudeva said: Having approached that city, O king of kings, Śālva the lord of Saubha then encamped with his large force of men and elephants.
That army, endowed with the four divisions of force, protected by king Śālva, encamped on level ground near an abundant water source.
Avoiding cremation grounds, temples of the gods, ant-hills, and sacred trees, that army encamped.
By the division of the regiments, six roads were made, and there were nine descending passages in Śālva's camp, O king.
Fully furnished with all weapons, skilled in all arms, crowded with chariots, elephants, and horses, swarming with foot-soldiers and banners —
Filled with contented and well-fed men, marked by the signs of heroes, with diverse banners and armor, with diverse chariots and bows —
Having thus encamped before Dvārakā, O Kauravya, O bull among men, he then launched his assault with the speed of the king of birds.
Seeing that army of Śālva's lord descending upon them, the young princes, sons of the Vṛṣṇis, sallied forth and fought.
Unable to tolerate that advance of king Śālva, O Kauravya — Cārudeṣṇa and Sāmba and Pradyumna the great chariot-fighter.
All of them clad in armor on their chariots, with diverse ornaments and banners, they engaged in close combat with the many bull-like warriors of king Śālva.
Taking up his bow, Sāmba, delighted, engaged in battle in that conflict with Śālva's minister, the army-commander Kṣemavṛddhi.
The son of Jāmbāvatī released a great shower of arrows upon him, O foremost of the Bhāratas, as the thousand-eyed Indra releases rain.
That army-commander Kṣemavṛddhi endured that tumultuous shower of arrows, O great king, as immovable as the Himālaya.
Then Kṣemavṛddhi in turn released upon Sāmba, O king of kings, a far greater net of arrows wrought by illusion.
Then Sāmba, tearing apart that illusion-made net by illusion itself, rained down a thousand arrows upon his chariot.
Then the army-commander Kṣemavṛddhi, pierced by Sāmba, fled on swift horses, sorely afflicted by Sāmba's arrows.
When that fierce army-commander of Śālva had fled, a mighty Daitya named Vegavān then rushed upon my son.
Attacked by him, O king of kings, Sāmba the ornament of the Vṛṣṇi clan, O king, stood firm, the hero checking the speed of Vegavān.
Then Sāmba, O son of Kuntī, the hero of true valor, swiftly hurled against Vegavān the swift mace, whirling it round.
Struck by it, O king, Vegavān fell to the earth like a great tree with decayed roots, broken by the wind.
When that great demon had fallen, struck down by the mace, my son entered the great army and fought on.
Engaged with Cārudeṣṇa was a Dānava named Vivindhya, recognized as a great chariot-fighter, O great king, a great archer.
Then a most tumultuous battle between Cārudeṣṇa and Vivindhya took place, O king, just as the primeval battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Both furious at one another, both roaring, they struck each other with arrows, O great king, like two mighty lions.
Then the son of Rukmiṇī took an arrow blazing like fire and sun, consecrated it with the great weapon-spell, and fitted it to the bow — the destroyer of enemies.
That great chariot-fighter, filled with rage, calling out to Vivindhya, hurled it — my son, O king — and Vivindhya fell lifeless.
Seeing Vivindhya slain and the army thrown into disorder, Śālva came again upon that place with the Saubha flying at will.
Then the entire force dwelling in Dvārakā was thrown into confusion on seeing Śālva, O mighty-armed one, aboard the Saubha which had now descended to earth.
Then sallying forth, O son of Kuntī, and steadying that force of the Ānartas, Pradyumna spoke these words, O great king.
"Let all of you stand firm; let all of you watch me in battle, as I repel by force the Saubha together with its king in this conflict."
"I shall today destroy the army of the lord of Saubha with iron shafts like serpents, released from the arm through the bow — O Yādavas!"
"Take courage — there is no cause for fear. The lord of Saubha perishes today; attacked by me, that wicked soul shall be destroyed along with his Saubha."
While Pradyumna was thus speaking joyfully, O son of Pāṇḍu, that force stood firm, O hero, and fought with ease.
Vāsudeva said: Having spoken thus to the Yādavas, O bull of the Bhāratas, the son of Rukmiṇī mounted his golden chariot yoked with armored horses.
Raising his makara banner with its wide-open mouth and ornaments, he pursued the enemies with those horses that seemed to fly through the sky.
Brandishing and making resound his finest bow, the mighty hero, bearing quiver and sword, with leather guard and finger-bracer bound on —
He, moving his bow with lightning speed from palm to palm, bewildered all the Daityas who dwelt in the Saubha.
No one could find an opening against him as he repeatedly drew and released his bow, repeatedly slaying enemies in battle.
His countenance showed no change; his limbs did not tremble; even as he roared like a lion, the world heard something wondrous and supreme.
The water-creature mounted on its golden pole — wide-mouthed, destroyer of all great fish — gleaming, terrifying, at the head of the chariot, his banner blazed at the forefront of Śālva's army.
Then Pradyumna, the afflicted of enemies, sallied forth swiftly and rushed straight at Śālva himself, intending to make war, O king.
But the advance of the hero Pradyumna in that great battle was not tolerated by Śālva, who grew furious, O ornament of the Kuru clan.
He, Śālva the conqueror of enemy cities, maddened with the intoxication of rage, descended from the sky-going vessel and engaged Pradyumna in battle.
The most tumultuous battle between those two champions — Śālva and the Vṛṣṇi hero — was witnessed by assembled people as if it were the battle between Bali and Vāsava.
His chariot, O hero, was fashioned by illusion, adorned with gold, bearing a banner and a flag, with a trailing train, furnished with a quiver.
He, the glorious one of great might, mounted that excellent chariot, O lord, and released arrows upon Pradyumna, O Kauravya.
Then Pradyumna released a shower of arrows swiftly in battle, with the speed of his arm, as if bewildering Śālva.
The lord of Saubha, struck by those in battle, did not endure it, and released arrows resembling blazing fire upon my son.
The son of Rukmiṇī, pierced by Śālva's arrows, O king of kings, swiftly released a vital-point-piercing arrow in battle.
That feathered shaft sent by my son quickly split his armor and pierced his heart; he fell and lost consciousness.
When that hero, king Śālva, had fallen unconscious, the great Dānavas ran away, cleaving the earth asunder in their flight.
A cry of lamentation arose from Śālva's army, O lord of the earth, O king, when the lord of Saubha had fallen insensible.
Then Śālva rose up, O Kauravya, and regaining consciousness, that mighty one swiftly released an arrow at Pradyumna.
Pierced by that arrow, the mighty-armed Pradyumna, standing in battle, the hero was sorely wounded in the collar-bone region and then sank down upon his chariot.
Having pierced him — the son of Rukmiṇī — O great king, Śālva roared a lion's roar, filling the earth with that sound.
Then, when stupor had overcome my son, O Bhārata, he swiftly released yet more arrows, difficult to withstand.
Struck by those many arrows and bewildered by him, Pradyumna lay motionless on the battlefield, O best of the Kauravas.
Vāsudeva said: When that Pradyumna, best among the mighty, was tormented by Śālva's arrows, the Vṛṣṇis who had come to battle trembled, their resolve broken.
The entire army of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas raised cries of grief when Pradyumna fell, O king, while the enemies rejoiced.
Seeing him thus bewildered, the trained charioteer Daruki swiftly carried him away from the battle with swift horses.
When the chariot had gone not too far, the driver of the best of chariots regained his senses, grasped his bow, and spoke these words to the charioteer.
"O charioteer, what is your intention? Why do you go with your back to the enemy? This is not declared the duty of the Vṛṣṇi heroes in battle.
"Is there no confusion in you, O charioteer, upon seeing Śālva in the great battle? Or depression upon seeing the combat? Tell me the truth.
The charioteer said: No confusion has entered me, O Janārdana, nor has fear taken hold of me. But I consider Śālva too heavy a burden for you, O son of Keśava.
"So I withdraw slowly, O hero — this evildoer is powerful, and a warrior who has been confused in battle must be protected by his charioteer.
"Long-lived one, you must always be protected by me, and I likewise must be protected by you — knowing that a warrior must always be guarded, I have withdrawn.
"You are alone, O mighty-armed one, while the Dānavas are many. Judging this battle as unequal, O Rukminiya's son, I have retreated.
Vāsudeva said: While the charioteer spoke thus, then the one whose banner bears the sea-monster, O Kauravya, said to the charioteer: "Turn the chariot back."
"O son of Dāruka, never do this again under any circumstance — retreat from battle, O charioteer, as long as I am alive, at any time.
"He is not born in the Vṛṣṇi clan who abandons battle, or who strikes down one who has fallen and says 'I am yours.'
"Likewise one who strikes a woman, or an old man, or a child, or one without a chariot, or one scattered in rout, or one whose weapons and arms are broken.
"And you are born in a charioteer's family, trained in the charioteer's craft, and you know dharma for the Vṛṣṇis even in battles, O Dāruka.
"Knowing fully the conduct of the Vṛṣṇis at the forefront of armies, do not make retreat again, O charioteer, under any circumstance.
"What will the elder brother of Gada, the formidable Mādhava, say to me who has retreated, been struck from behind, and fled the battle in fear?
"Or what will Balarama, the elder brother of Keśava, clad in blue, intoxicated with pride, the mighty-armed one, say when he comes?
"What will the grandson of Śini, the lion among men and great archer, say about my retreat from battle, O charioteer? And Sāmba, the victor in battle?
"And the formidable Cārudeṣṇa, and likewise Gada and Sāraṇa, and Akrūra the mighty-armed — what will they say to me, O charioteer?
"And the women of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, gathering together, what will they say to me who am considered brave, virtuous, and ever proud of manhood?
"'This Pradyumna comes back, frightened, having abandoned the great battle — shame on him!' they will say, and will not say 'well done.'
"Shame and mockery spoken in words, even for me or one like me, is worse than death, O charioteer. Therefore do not retreat again.
"For Hari, the slayer of Madhu, having entrusted his burden to me, has gone to the sacrifice of Pārtha the lion of Bhāratas, of immeasurable splendor.
"The hero Kṛtavarmā, as he was departing, was restrained by me: 'I will hold back Śālva — you stay,' I said. O son of the charioteer,
"And he, the son of Hridika, trusting me, turned back. Having met him after abandoning the battle, what shall I say to that great warrior?
"When the formidable one bearing conch, discus and mace — the lotus-eyed man, the mighty-armed one — comes back, what shall I say to him?
"And to Sātyaki and Balarama and those other Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis who constantly rival me — what indeed shall I say to them?
"Having abandoned this battle, struck from behind by arrows, carried away by you helplessly, O charioteer, I could not live under any circumstance.
"So turn the chariot back swiftly, O son of Dāruka. This must never be done thus, even in adversity.
"I would never value life, O charioteer, if I have retreated from battle in fear, struck from behind by arrows.
"When have you ever known me, O son of the charioteer, tormented by fear, abandoning the battlefield and retreating like a coward?
"It is not fitting for you to abandon the battle, O son of Dāruka, when I am so eager to fight. Go where the battle is."
Vāsudeva said: Thus addressed, O son of Kuntī, the charioteer's son then spoke to Pradyumna in battle these smooth and sweet words straightforwardly.
"I have no fear, O son of Rukmiṇī, in guiding the horses in battle, and I am skilled in warfare for the Vṛṣṇis — there is nothing other than that here.
"Long-lived one, the instruction in charioteering is remembered: the warrior must be protected in all circumstances. And you were greatly tormented.
"For you were struck hard by an arrow shot by Śālva and overcome by stupor, O hero — that is why I retreated.
"Now you, the foremost of the Sātvatas, have fortunately regained your senses. Watch my skill in guiding the horses, O son of Keśava's beloved.
"Born of Dāruka and trained properly by him, fearless I now enter this great army of Śālva."
Having spoken thus, O hero, he then urged the horses in battle and, taking up the reins, charged forward with speed.
He executed intricate circular maneuvers, paired and alternating ones, and various leftward and rightward ones on all sides.
Struck by the whip, O king, and gathered up by the reins, those finest horses appeared as if leaping into the sky.
Recognizing Dāruka as possessed of lightness of hand, O king, those horses then barely touched the ground with their hooves, as if on fire.
He circled Śālva's army counter-clockwise, O bull of the Bhāratas, with little effort — it seemed like a wonder.
Unable to endure being circled counter-clockwise by Pradyumna, that king of Saubha suddenly struck his charioteer with three arrows.
But the son of Dāruka, disregarding that onslaught of arrows, O mighty-armed one, continued onward in harmony with the horses.
Then that king of Saubha released many various arrows once more at my son, the heroic son of Rukmiṇī.
The son of Rukmiṇī, slayer of enemy heroes, cut down those arrows before they reached him with sharp arrows, smiling and displaying his lightness of hand.
Seeing those arrows cut down by Pradyumna, that king of Saubha resorted to a terrible demonic illusion and released arrows.
Recognizing the Daitya weapon being deployed, the mighty one countered it with the Brahmā weapon, cutting it apart, and released other arrows.
Those arrows swiftly dispelled that weapon and pierced him, feeding on blood — in his head, chest and face — and he swooned and fell.
When that wretched Śālva had fallen, tormented by arrows, the son of Rukmiṇī nocked another arrow, the destroyer of enemies.
Seeing that arrow, honored by all the Dāśārhas, blazing like the sun's fire, being drawn to the bowstring — cries of lamentation arose in the sky.
Then all the hosts of gods together with Indra and the lord of wealth dispatched Nārada and the mighty Wind-god.
Those two came to the son of Rukmiṇī and spoke the words of the gods: "This Śālva king must not be slain by you, O hero, under any circumstance.
"Withdraw the arrow again — this one is not to be killed by you in battle. For with this arrow of his in the field, there is no man anywhere who cannot be killed.
"His death in battle, O mighty-armed one, has been ordained by the Creator as Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī. Let that not prove false."
Then Pradyumna, exceedingly delighted, withdrew that finest arrow from the best of bows and placed it back in the quiver.
Then Śālva rose up, O king of kings, utterly despondent, and quickly withdrew with his army, tormented by Pradyumna's arrows.
That cruel one, harassed by the Vṛṣṇis, abandoned Dvārakā and, mounting the Saubha vessel, O king of kings, ascended to the sky.
Vāsudeva said: When the city of Anarta was freed, then I came back, after the great Rājasūya sacrifice of yours had concluded, O king.
And I saw Dvārakā, O great king, with its luster destroyed, bereft of Vedic recitation and vaṣaṭ calls, its noble women without ornaments.
Seeing the groves of Dvārakā in unrecognizable forms, filled with doubt, I asked the son of Hridika.
"This city of the Vṛṣṇis appears greatly ill at ease, its men and women unwell — what is this, O tiger among men? We wish to hear."
Thus addressed by me, the son of Hridika told me all this in detail — the siege and deliverance by Śālva, O best of kings.
Then I, O best of the Kauravas, having heard everything completely, there and then made up my mind for the destruction of King Śālva.
Then I, O best of the Bhāratas, having reassured the people of the city, King Āhuka and likewise Anakadundubhi and all the foremost Vṛṣṇi heroes, spoke these words gladly.
"Vigilance must always be maintained in the city, O bulls of the Yādavas. Know that I am setting forth for the destruction of King Śālva.

"I will not return to the city of Dvārakā without slaying him. Having slain Śālva together with his Saubha city, I shall see you again. Let this war-drum, terror to enemies, be struck with the three-sama beat."
Those heroes, duly reassured by me, O bull of the Bhāratas, all said to me joyfully: "Go, slay the enemies."
Blessed with benedictions by those heroes of gladdened souls, having caused the best of twice-born to recite blessings, and bowing my head to Āhuka,
With my chariot yoked to Sainya and Sugrīva, filling all directions with sound, I blew the foremost conch Pāñcajanya, O king.
I set forth, O tiger among men, surrounded by a great force — an organized four-limbed army shining with victory.
Passing through many lands, mountains with many trees, lakes and rivers, I reached Marttikavata.
There I heard, O tiger among men, that Śālva had set out from the city nearby, mounted on the Saubha vessel. I followed him from behind.
Then reaching the ocean, in the bosom of its great waves, Śālva, O enemy-slayer, mounted on the Saubha vessel, came to be at the navel of the sea.
He, spotting me from afar, smiling as it were, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that evil-souled one challenged me again and again to battle.
His city could not be reached by the many marrow-piercing arrows shot from Śārṅga — then anger entered me.
That evil-natured outcast of the demons, O king, formidable as he was, poured upon me torrents of arrows by the thousands.
He showered arrows upon my soldiers, my charioteer, and my horses; yet we fought on, O Bhārata, paying no heed to his shafts.
Then the warriors who followed Śālva's standard hurled upon me in battle hundreds of thousands of well-notched arrows.
Those demons covered my horses, my chariot, and Dāruka himself with arrows that pierced to the vital points.
O hero, neither the horses nor the chariot nor my charioteer Dāruka could be seen, hidden as they were beneath those arrows; nor could I myself be seen, nor my soldiers.
Then I too, O Kauravya, duly discharged with my divine bow many tens of thousands of arrows that had been consecrated with mantras.
But that Saubha, suspended in the sky, was out of reach of my army, O Bhārata — it hovered at a distance of barely a krośa.
Then all those onlookers, standing as though in an arena, cheered me loudly with lion-roars and clapping of hands.
The arrows discharged from my bow entered the bodies of the demons in that great battle, stained with blood, like locusts swarming in.
Then a great tumult arose within Saubha as those struck by my sharp arrows fell into the vast ocean.
Those demons, their arms and shoulders severed, looking like headless trunks, roaring fearful roars, fell down.
Then I filled with my breath the Pāñcajanya — that conch born of the waters, bright as cow's milk, white jasmine, the moon, lotus stalks, and silver.
Seeing them fallen, Śālva, the lord of Saubha, then began to fight against me in battle with a great magical warfare.
Then javelins, spears, tridents, battle-axes, double-edged swords, and fire-tubes rained down upon me ceaselessly.
I quickly countered all of those with my own magic and destroyed them; when that illusion was shattered, he fought me with mountain peaks.
Then it seemed like darkness, then again like dawn; it seemed a bad day, then a fair one; cold, then hot, O Bhārata.

Thus the enemy fought against me, deploying illusion after illusion; knowing all of it, I destroyed each illusion with my own, and then at the proper moment scattered him on all sides with arrows in direct combat.
Then the sky, O great king, appeared as if lit by a hundred suns, a hundred moons, and thousands upon ten-thousands of stars, O son of Kuntī.

Then neither day nor night could be distinguished, nor the directions; overcome with bewilderment, I applied the Prajñā weapon, and by means of that weapon the illusion was scattered like cotton by the wind.
Such was that tumultuous, hair-raising battle; and once light was restored, O lord of kings, I fought the enemy again.
Vāsudeva said: Thus fighting with me in battle, O tiger among men, Śālva, that great enemy of kings, once again rose into the sky.
Then Śālva, that dull-witted one, craving victory, hurled at me in fury, O great king, śataghnis, great maces, blazing tridents, pestles, and swords.
I quickly repelled those weapons as they came hurtling at me, and with arrows swiftly released I cut them in two and three pieces right there in the sky; then a great noise arose in the atmosphere.
Then with a hundred thousand well-notched arrows he covered Dāruka, the horses, and the chariot.
Then Dāruka spoke to me, O hero, seeming distressed: "I can barely hold my place here, tormented as I am by Śālva's arrows."
Hearing those pitiful words from my charioteer, I turned to look at him and saw him pierced and tormented by arrows.
O foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, I could see not a single spot on his chest, his head, his body, or his two arms that had not been struck by arrows.
From the torment of that arrow-shower, copious blood streamed from him, like a mountain rich with ochre ore drenched by clouds.
Seeing that charioteer, reins still in hand, sinking in battle, tormented by Śālva's arrows, I steadied him, O mighty-armed one.
Then a certain man from Dvārakā came hurrying to my chariot and spoke to me, as if out of friendship, O Bhārata.
He was an attendant of Āhuka, O hero, downcast and choked with sorrow — hear what he said, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
"The lord of Dvārakā, Āhuka, sends you this message, O hero — understand it well, O Keśava, hear what your father's friend says to you.
'Śālva has attacked Dvārakā today, O joy of the Vṛṣṇis; while you were engaged elsewhere, O invincible one, the son of Śūra has been slain by force.'
'Therefore, enough of this battle; turn back, O Janārdana; protect Dvārakā itself — that is the great duty before you now.'
Hearing those words of his, I became extremely distressed and could not settle on what was to be done or what was not.
Hearing those unwelcome words, O hero, I inwardly reproached Sātyaki, Balarama, and the great warrior Pradyumna in my mind.
For I had entrusted to them, O joy of the Kurus, the protection of Dvārakā and of my father before setting out to destroy Saubha.
'Does the mighty-armed Balarama, slayer of foes, still live? And Sātyaki? And Rukmiṇī's son? And the valiant Cārudeṣṇa? And Sāmba and the rest?' — thinking thus, I was overcome with deep grief.
For while these tiger-like men are alive, not even Indra himself, wielder of the thunderbolt, could slay the son of Śūra.
The son of Śūra must clearly be slain, and clearly Balarama and all the rest must also be dead — so my mind was convinced.
And I, repeatedly brooding over that total ruin, utterly shaken, O great king, fought Śālva again.
Then I saw, O great king, the son of Śūra falling down from Saubha, O hero; thereupon bewilderment seized me.
As he fell, the form of my father, O lord of men, was like that of Yayāti when his merit was exhausted and he fell from heaven to earth.
His turban fallen and disheveled, his garments and hair scattered, he appeared as he fell like a planet whose merit is spent.
Then the Śārṅga, best of bows, fell from my hands in that delusion, and overcome, O son of Kuntī, I sank down onto the floor of the chariot.
Then all my army cried out in dismay, losing their senses, seeing me slumped in the chariot-seat as if dead, O Bhārata.
Arms outstretched, feet outstretched as he fell — I saw that form of my father like a bird in flight falling down.
O mighty-armed one, those warriors, spears and swords in hand, striking him hard as he fell, caused my heart to tremble violently.
Then after a moment, regaining my senses, O hero, in that great tumult I could see neither Saubha nor the enemy nor Śālva — nor the aged form of my father.
Then my mind settled with certainty: this is illusion. Fully awakened, I once again scattered arrows by the hundreds.
Vāsudeva said: Then, O best of Bhāratas, grasping my splendid bow, I brought down with arrows the heads of those enemies of the gods from Saubha.
And I sent upward-flying arrows like venomous serpents, of fierce brilliance, released from the Śārṅga with full draw, toward the king Śālva.
Then Saubha was no longer visible, O foremost of the Kuru line — it had vanished by illusion; and I was filled with wonder.
Then those hosts of demons, with distorted faces and wild hair, screamed out, O great king, while I stood firm, O Bhārata.
Then I quickly applied in that great battle the weapon that tracks sound, for the purpose of killing them; thereupon the sound ceased.
All those demons who had raised that cry were slain by flaming arrows bright as the sun, guided by sound.
When that sound ceased, another cry arose from a different direction, O great king; there too I struck with arrows.
Thus the demons made their cries from all ten directions, sideways and upward too, O Bhārata — and all of them were slain by me.
Then Saubha, that city that moved at will, having gone to the east, appeared again, O hero, bewildering my eyes.
Then a demon of monkey-like form, a destroyer of worlds, suddenly overwhelmed me with a great shower of stones.
Struck on all sides by that shower of mountain rocks, O lord of kings, I became like an anthill heaped up with mountain stones.
Then I, with my horses, charioteer, and banner, buried under mountains, O king, became invisible, covered by those rocks.
Then those Vṛṣṇi heroes who were my soldiers, seized with terror, suddenly fled in all directions.
Then there arose a universal cry of dismay, O lord of peoples — heaven, earth, and sky all cried out when I became invisible.
Then my well-wishing friends, their hearts sunk with grief, O king, wept and wailed, overcome with pain and sorrow.
The enemies rejoiced, and even those who were not enemies felt anguish; so did things stand, O hero — I heard of all this afterward, O Acyuta.
Then, taking up my beloved Vajra weapon, the crusher of all stones, I shattered all those mountains to pieces.
Then my horses, crushed under the weight of those mountains, moved feebly with labored breath, O great king, trembling as it were.
Seeing me emerge like the sun rising and splitting apart a mass of clouds in the sky, all my kinsmen rejoiced again.
Then my charioteer, folding his hands and bowing, said to me, O king: 'Look well, O descendant of Vṛṣṇi — Śālva, the lord of Saubha, stands before you.'
'Enough of disdaining him, O Kṛṣṇa — apply yourself earnestly; abandon all gentleness and friendship toward Śālva today.'
'Slay Śālva, O mighty-armed one; do not let him live, O Keśava; with all your valor, O hero, the enemy is to be killed, O destroyer of foes.'
'An enemy must not be despised, even a weak one by the strong — how much less one who is standing firm in battle?'
'Therefore, O tiger among men, O master, O best of the Vṛṣṇi clan, slay him with all your efforts — do not let the right moment pass you by again.'
'He is not to be won over by gentleness, nor is he your friend — he who has fought you, O hero, and laid waste to Dvārakā.'
Hearing such words from my charioteer, O son of Kuntī, recognizing their truth, I fixed my mind firmly on battle.
For the slaying of king Śālva and the bringing down of Saubha, I said to Dāruka, O hero: 'Hold your position for a moment.'
Then the divine, irresistible, impenetrable, supremely powerful, beloved Āgneya weapon, bearer of all things, of great blazing splendor —
— that great weapon, the reducer to ash of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, demons, and wicked kings in battle —
— I consecrated with mantras the immaculate discus with razor edge, incomparable, the destroyer of enemies, like Yama the Ender of time itself.
"Destroy Saubha by your own valour, and also the enemies of mine who are here." Saying this, in anger I hurled it at him with the strength of my arms.
The form of Sudarśana as it flew through the sky was then like a second sun blazing at the end of an age.
Reaching that city Saubha and stripping it of its lustre, it split it down the middle as a saw splits a tall piece of timber.
Saubha was thus cleft in two and struck down by the power of Sudarśana; it fell as Tripura fell when shattered by the arrow of Maheśvara.
When Saubha had fallen, the discus returned to my hand; lifting it again with speed, I cried out: "Now for Śālva!"
Then Śālva, who was swinging his massive mace in that great battle, was suddenly cut in two, and the discus blazed with radiance.
When that hero fell, the Dānavas, terror-stricken in their hearts, fled crying "Alas!" in all directions, tormented by my arrows.
Then, having positioned my chariot near where Saubha had fallen, I blew my conch with joy and filled my friends with delight.
Seeing that city, shaped like the peak of Meru, with its battlements and gatehouses shattered, burning fiercely, the women fled in all directions.
Having thus slain Śālva in battle and brought down Saubha, I returned again to the Anarta land and brought joy to my friends.
It is for this reason, O king, that I did not come to the city named after the elephant; had I gone there, O slayer of enemy heroes, Suyodhana would not be alive today.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed best of men, Madhusūdana, the wise one, took leave of the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas and departed.
The mighty-armed one paid his respects to Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira and was smelled on the crown of the head by the king, and likewise by Bhīma of great arms.
Kṛṣṇa, honoured by the Pāṇḍavas, placed Subhadrā and Abhimanyu upon the golden chariot, then mounted it himself.
Kṛṣṇa departed for Dvārakā on a chariot yoked with Sainya and Sugrīva, blazing like the sun, having first consoled Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, after the descendant of the Dāśārhas had departed, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, son of Pṛṣata, also took the sons of Draupadī and went to his own city.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, king of the Cedis, also took his sister and, having bidden farewell to the Pāṇḍavas, departed for the lovely city of Śuktimatī.
The Kekayas too, permitted to leave by Kuntī's son of immeasurable might, took their leave of all the Pāṇḍavas and also departed, O Bhārata.
The brahmanas, the Vaiśyas, and the inhabitants of the provinces, though being dismissed, would not abandon the Pāṇḍavas.
That assembly of great souls in Kāmyaka was a wondrous spectacle to behold, O lord of kings, O bull of the Bhāratas.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, great-souled, having honoured those brahmanas, in due time ordered his men: "Yoke the chariots."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the lord of the Dāśārhas had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the twins, Kṛṣṇā, and the family priest mounted their excellent chariots yoked with the finest horses.

Those heroes, united, resplendent as lords of beings, set out together for the forest, having first given golden nishkas, garments, and cows to those versed in the teaching of sacred syllables and mantras.
Twenty armed retainers went ahead; and all of them, carrying bows, armour, yellow-tinted arrows, bowstrings, mechanical devices, and quivers, marched in the rear.
Then Indrasena, swiftly taking up the princess's garments, her nurses, her maidservants, and her ornaments, followed in the rear with his chariot.
Then the citizens, undaunted in spirit, approached the foremost of the Kurus and circumambulated him; the brahmanas greeted him warmly, as did all the leading men of the Kurujāṅgala region.
He in turn greeted them with kindness — Dharmarāja along with his brothers — and that great-souled lord stood there, gazing at the throng of people from Kurujāṅgala.
The great-souled bull of the Kurus felt toward them as a father feels toward his sons; and they in turn, toward that foremost of the Bhāratas, were then as sons toward a father.
Then the great multitude of people, approaching the foremost hero of the Kurus, stood surrounding him, crying "Alas, our lord! Alas, O Dharma!" — and all with tear-streaked faces from grief.
"Where has Dharmarāja gone, the best of the Kurus, the lord of his people, who, like a father abandoning his sons, has left us — these citizens and all the country folk?"
"Shame on the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, so cruel of mind, on Saubala, and on Karṇa of evil intent — those sinners who desire your misfortune, O lord of men, you who are ever steadfast in righteousness."
"Where has Dharmarāja gone, the great-souled one of unfailing deeds, who himself built that matchless great city, shining like the city of the gods, the city of Śatakratu, and then abandoned it?"
"Where has Dharmarāja gone, abandoning that incomparable assembly hall which Maya built for the great-souled one, bright as the hall of the gods, guarded by the gods like some divine illusion?"

Bībhatsu, of supreme valour and versed in dharma, pleasure, and artha, spoke to them all with a loud voice: "Having completed this sojourn in the forests, the king will strip his enemies of their glory."
"O foremost among the twice-born, you should go separately or together, approach the ascetics, propitiate those versed in dharma and artha, and speak so that our highest goal may be accomplished."
When Arjuna had spoken these words, O king, those brahmanas and people of all castes rejoiced together and circumambulated the foremost upholder of dharma.
Taking leave of Pārtha, Vṛkodara, Dhanañjaya, Yājñasenī, and the twins, and with Yudhiṣṭhira's permission, they departed for their respective homelands, their joy departed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, when they had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, true to his vows, virtuous of soul, addressed all his brothers.
"We must dwell in the lonely forest for these twelve years. Choose a region in the great wilderness that abounds in deer and birds."
"Rich in flowers and fruits, beautiful, auspicious, fit for holy people — a place where we may dwell comfortably through all these years."
When he had spoken thus, Dhanañjaya replied to Dharmarāja, honouring that guide of men as one honours a guru, respecting his noble spirit.
Arjuna said: You are yourself the attendant of the great sages and elders; there is nothing in the world of men that is unknown to you.
For you have always served the brahmanas, O bull of the Bhāratas — Dvaipāyana and the rest, and the great ascetic Nārada.
He who always travels self-controlled through the gates of all worlds — from the world of the gods to the world of Brahmā, and even to the realm of the Gandharvas and Apsaras.
You know all the paths of the brahmanas — there is no doubt. And you know the powers of all of them, O lord of the earth.
You alone, O king, know what is truly beneficial. Wherever you wish to dwell, O great king, there shall we go.
This lake called Dvaitavana is fit for holy people, rich in flowers and fruits, beautiful, and frequented by various birds.
"It pleases me that we spend these twelve years here — if it meets with your approval, O king, or what else does Your Honour think?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This is my view too, O Pārtha, what you have proposed. Let us go to the great and renowned lake of Dvaitavana, a holy place.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all the Pāṇḍavas, those walkers of the path of dharma, set out together with many brahmanas for the holy lake of Dvaitavana.
Brāhmaṇas who maintained the agnihotra fire, and those who did not; those devoted to recitation, wandering ascetics, those given to silent repetition, and forest dwellers —
— many brahmanas, ascetics of truthful nature and firm vows, by the hundreds surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira there.
The Pāṇḍavas, those bulls of the Bhāratas, went there and entered the holy, beautiful Dvaitavana together with many brahmanas.
The lord of the kingdom beheld that great forest filled at the end of the hot season with flowering shāla, palm, mango, madhūka, nīpa, kadamba, sarjā, arjuna, and karnikāra trees.
Perched on the tops of the great trees, uttering their charming calls, were flocks of peacocks, dātyūha birds, chakoras, and forest cuckoos throughout that woodland.
The lord of the kingdom beheld in that forest great herds of mighty elephants, steady as mountains, intoxicated with rut, together with their female consorts and the bull leaders of the herds.

Approaching that lovely and prosperous land, in that forest which was the abode of the upholders of dharma, he saw many groups of siddhas and sages, wearing bark garments and matted locks, firm in spirit.

Then that king, the foremost among the virtuous of soul, descended from his vehicle and, together with his brothers and retinue, entered that forest like Śakra of immeasurable might entering the third heaven.
Eager to behold him, that keeper of his word, groups of Cāraṇas and Siddhas converged upon him; and the forest-dwellers too stood surrounding that lion among kings, that noble-spirited one.

He there paid his respects to all the Siddhas; honoured in return as befits a king and as befits a god, the foremost upholder of dharma, his palms joined, entered together with all the leading twice-born.
That virtuous, great-souled king, fatherly in nature, was approached by ascetics devoted to dharma, and honoured by them, sat down at the foot of a great tree laden with flowers.

Bhīma, Kṛṣṇā, Dhanañjaya, the twins, and their attendants — those foremost of the Bhāratas — all dismounted from their conveyances, freed the horses, and stood in attendance upon the lord of men there.

That great tree, bent low with canopies of vines, graced by those five mighty-bowed great-souled Pāṇḍavas who had come to dwell beneath it, shone like a great mountain surrounded by elephant herd-lords.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having reached that forest, those sons of the lord of men, accustomed to comfort, having come to their arduous dwelling, sported like images of Indra in those auspicious groves of Sarasvatī and shāla trees.
The great-souled bull of the Kurus, that king, gratified all the renouncers and sages in that forest, and the foremost among the twice-born, with abundant roots and fruits.

The family priest Dhaumya, of full and brilliant splendour, performed the ancestral and the first-offering sacrificial rites for the Pāṇḍavas dwelling in the great forest, treating the Kurus as a father would.
While they were dwelling there having gone from their kingdom, the ancient sage Mārkaṇḍeya, glowing with intense and full radiance, came as a guest to that hermitage of the illustrious Pāṇḍavas.
That all-knowing, great-souled one of immeasurable might, beholding Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna, and then mentally recalling Rāma, smiled amid the assembly of ascetics.
Dharmarāja, as if troubled, spoke to him: "All these ascetics present feel shame — why does Your Honour seem to smile with joy, looking at me as the ascetics watch?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: I do not rejoice, dear one, nor do I smile; neither elation nor pride comes upon me. But seeing your misfortune today, I call to mind Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, true to his vow.
That king too, bearing his bow, together with Lakṣmaṇa, dwelling in the forest by his father's command, was seen by me long ago, O Pārtha, on the slopes of mount Rishyamuka.
That great-souled one, equal to Sahasranetra, conqueror of Maya and slayer of Namuci, the faultless son of Daśaratha, fulfilled his own dharma by dwelling in the forest at his father's command.
He too, equal in might to Śakra, of great power, unconquerable in battles, gave up his pleasures and roamed through the forests — for one who has the strength should not act unrightously.

And kings such as Nābhāga, Bhagīratha and others, having conquered this earth to its ocean shores, also won the worlds through truth, dear one — for one who has the strength should not act unrighteously.

They call Alarka, O best of men, a righteous one — the king of the Kāśi and Rūsha lands, true to his vow; he renounced his kingdoms and his wealth — for one who has the strength should not act unrighteously.
Honouring the ancient ordinance ordained by the Creator, O best of men, the seven righteous sages shine in heaven, O Pārtha — for one who has the strength should not act unrighteously.

Behold the elephants, O lord of men, great in strength, as large as mountain peaks, bearing tusks — they stand within the Creator's ordinance, O best of men — for one who has the strength should not act unrighteously.
Behold all beings, O lord of men — each one, however mighty, acts according to what the Creator has ordained from its own nature — for one who has the strength should not act unrighteously.

Through truth, through righteousness, through conduct befitting your station, and through modesty, surpassing all beings — your glory and your radiance blaze too, O Pārtha, like that of the fire and the sun.
And as you have vowed, O great-souled one, having endured this hard dwelling in the forest, you shall then, O lord of the earth, wrest from the Kauravas a sovereignty blazing with your own radiance.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, that great sage, in the company of ascetics and friends, took leave of Dhaumya and the sons of Pṛthā together, and then set out towards the northern direction.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the great-souled Pāṇḍavas were dwelling in the Dvaita forest, that great wilderness became filled with brahmanas on all sides.
Constantly resounding from all quarters with the chanting of Vedic hymns, the sacred lake of Dvaita forest became equal to the realm of Brahmā in its holiness.
The resonant sound of Yajus, Ric, Sāman, and prose recitations being chanted on all sides was deeply pleasing to the heart.
The twang of the Pāṇḍavas' bowstrings and the Vedic chanting of the wise ones mingled together, and the Kṣatriya joined with Brahman shone all the more brilliantly.
Then Baka of the Dalbhya lineage addressed Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who was seated at twilight surrounded by sages.
"Behold, O Pārtha, O foremost of the Kurus, the oblation-hour of the ascetic brahmanas in the Dvaita forest, with their sacred fires blazing brightly.
Protected by you and firm in their vows, the descendants of Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, and the Kashyapas practice righteousness in this sacred place.
The illustrious descendants of Agastya and the Ātreyas of highest vows — brahmanas who are the best in all the world — have gathered around you.
"But hear this word of mine, O Pārtha, O son of Kuntī, O Kaurava, with concentrated mind, together with your brothers, as I speak it to you.
The Brahman united with the Kṣatriya, and the Kṣatriya united with the Brahman — when both are roused, they burn enemies like fire and wind burn forests.

A king who is without a brahmana, dear one, cannot long endure; desiring to conquer this world and the next, having learned dharma and artha, freed from delusion — having obtained a twice-born, a king drives away his enemies.
Practicing the highest dharma and dedicated to the protection of his subjects, Bali found no sacred ford in the world other than the twice-born.

The desires of that asura were fulfilled and the prosperity of Vairocana was inexhaustible — having obtained the earth through association with brahmanas; but having acted wickedly toward them, he perished on that account.
This earth with its creatures does not long serve the second varna if without a brahmana; the sea-girdled earth bows to him whom a well-instructed brahmana guides with righteous counsel.
Just as an elephant in battle whose mahout with the goad has let go of the hold — so the strength of the Kṣatriya deprived of brahmanas wanes away.
In the Brahman there is unparalleled wisdom; in the Kṣatriya there is unmatched strength. When these two act together, then the world rejoices.
Just as a great fire aided by wind burns dry grass, so a king together with a brahmana burns his enemies.
The wise man should seek the guidance of brahmanas — for the gaining of what has not been gained, and for the increase of what has already been gained.

For the gaining of the ungained and the growth of the gained, for the proper endowment of worthy tirthas — keep near you a brahmana who is illustrious, learned in the Vedas, wise, and widely versed in scripture.
Your conduct toward brahmanas is always excellent, O Yudhiṣṭhira; because of that your wide-spread fame blazes forth in all the worlds.
Then all those brahmanas honored Baka of the Dalbhya lineage, and as Yudhiṣṭhira was praised, they became even more pleased in their hearts.
Dvaipāyana, Nārada, Jāmadagnya, Pṛthu-shravas, Indradyumna, Bhāluki, Kritachetas, Sahasrapat —
— Karnashravas, Munja, Lavanashva of the Kaśyapa lineage, Harita, Sthūṇākarṇa, Agnivesha, and Śaunaka —
— Ritavak, Suvak, Bṛhadaśva, Ritavasu, Urdhvareta, Vrishamitra, Suhotra, and Hotravāhana —
— these and many other brahmanas of sharpened vows praised Ajātaśatru as sages praise Purandara.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the Pārthas, who had gone to the forest, sat down in the evening together with Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) and engaged in conversation, absorbed in grief and sorrow.
Then Kṛṣṇā — beloved, beautiful, wise, and devoted to her husband — spoke these words to Dharmarāja.
"Surely that sinful, cruel, evil-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra feels no pain at all at what has befallen us.
"That evil-minded, wicked-souled wretch, O king, sent you away to the forest clad in deerskins along with me and all your brothers, and said not a word — and he did not repent.
"Surely the heart of that evil-doer is made of iron — the one who made you, the foremost upholder of dharma, hear such harsh words at that time.
"That evil-souled wicked man, with his band of allies, having brought such suffering upon one accustomed to ease and undeserving of pain, now rejoices.
"When you, O Bhārata, departed for the forest to dwell in deerskins, the eyes of only those four sinners shed no tears.
"Those four were Duryodhana, Karṇa, the evil-souled Śakuni, and that fierce wicked-brother Duḥśāsana.
"But from the eyes of all the other Kurus, O foremost of the Kurus, who were overwhelmed with grief, water fell down in tears.
"Seeing this bed now and remembering what was yours before, O great king, I grieve for you — you who are undeserving of suffering and accustomed to ease.
"Seeing the ivory gem-adorned seat that was yours in the assembly-hall and now seeing this grass mat — this grief overwhelms me.
"I who once saw you in the assembly surrounded by kings — now not seeing that, O king — what peace can there be in my heart?
"I who used to see you anointed with sandalwood paste and radiant as the sun — now seeing you smeared with mud and dust, I am bewildered, O Bhārata.
"I who formerly saw you, O lord of kings, dressed in silk garments, white and richly woven — now I see you wearing bark garments.
"That food, prepared and fulfilling every desire, which was carried from your house in thousands of golden vessels to be given to brahmanas —
"— that food of exceeding excellence which was given to wandering ascetics and to householders alike, O king, O lord — not seeing that now, O king, what peace can there be in my heart?
"Those brothers of yours, O great king — young men wearing bright earrings — your cooks used to feed with the most perfectly prepared and pure food —
"— all of them I now see living in the forest on forest fare, though they are undeserving of such hardship, O lord of men. My mind does not find peace.
"And seeing Bhīmasena here, afflicted and dwelling in the forest, brooding in thought — why does your anger not grow, now that the time has come?
"Seeing Bhīmasena, who is deserving of ease, doing all tasks himself and now afflicted — O steadfast one, why does your anger not grow?
"He who was honored with various conveyances and garments of high and low quality alike — seeing him now gone to the forest, why does your anger not grow?
"This Vṛkodara, who is capable of slaying all the Kurus, endures only awaiting your favor, O lord.
"He who, though having only two arms, is equal to Arjuna of many arms in the speed of his arrow-release — a man like Yama and the Destroyer of Time —
"— by whose weapon-prowess all the kings were made to bow down and waited upon the brahmanas at your sacrifice, O great king —
"— seeing this tiger among men, Arjuna, honored by gods and demons, now brooding in thought — why does your anger not grow?
"Seeing Pārtha gone to the forest, undeserving of sorrow and accustomed to ease — your anger does not grow; by this I am bewildered, O Bhārata.
"He who, with a single chariot, conquered gods, men, and serpents — seeing him gone to the forest, why does your anger not grow?
"He who, surrounded by conveyances of wondrous form and horses and elephants, forcibly seized wealth from kings — that scorcher of foes —
"— he who shoots five hundred arrows in a single swift release — seeing him gone to the forest, why does your anger not grow?
"Seeing Nakula, dark-complexioned, tall, young, supreme among swordsmen in battle, now gone to the forest — why does your anger not grow?
"Seeing the handsome and heroic son of Mādrī, Sahadeva, gone to the forest, O Yudhiṣṭhira — why does your anger not grow?
"Seeing me, born in the lineage of Drupada, the daughter-in-law of the great-souled Pāṇḍu, now gone to the forest — why does your anger not grow?
"Surely you have no anger at all, O foremost of the Bhāratas — for seeing your brothers and me in this state, your mind is not moved to pain.
"It is the established saying that there is no Kṣatriya without anger; yet today I see the opposite of that in you, a Kṣatriya.
"The Kṣatriya who does not display his fiery energy when the time comes — all creatures ever despise him, O Pārtha.
"Therefore you should in no way practice forbearance toward your enemies; it is only through your fiery energy that they can be slain — of this there is no doubt.
"And likewise, the Kṣatriya who does not calm himself when the time for forbearance has come becomes disliked by all creatures and perishes both here and hereafter."
Draupadī said: "On this point they also cite this ancient story — the dialogue of Prahlāda and Bali the son of Vairocana.
"Bali questioned Prahlāda, lord of the asuras, greatly wise, acquainted with the coming and going of dharmas — Prahlāda, lord of the daityas, his father's father.
"'Is forbearance better, dear one, or is fiery energy? This is my doubt, dear one — tell me truly as I ask you.'
"'What is the superior path here, O knower of dharma — tell me that without doubt. I will do all of it according to your instruction.'
"Thus questioned by him, the grandsire, wise and knowing all conclusions, spoke to him in full as he inquired about this doubt.
"Prahlāda said: 'Fiery energy is not always better, nor is forbearance always better — know this, dear one: both of these, without doubt.
"'He who always forbears, dear one, incurs many faults: servants despise him, and indifferent persons likewise.
"'And all creatures never bow to him at any time; therefore perpetual forbearance, dear one, is condemned by the wise.
"'For servants, despising him, go on to great misconduct and the feeble-minded seek to take away his wealth.
"'Conveyances, garments, ornaments, beds and seats, food and drink, and all his equipment —
"'— his officials, mindless, would take as they please, and what has been prescribed to be given they would not give in accordance with the master's command.
"'And they would never honor him with the honors due to a master; for in this world contempt is even more condemned than death.
"'To such a forbearing man, dear one, even servants, sons, subordinates, and those who behave indifferently speak bitter words.
"'They even desire his wives after showing contempt for the forbearing man, and his wives, mindless, behave as they please.
"'And those who are always rising — if they deserve even a small punishment from the lord, the wicked ones transgress and do harm.
"'These and many others are the perpetual faults of those who are always forbearing. Now, O son of Vairocana, know the faults of those who are without forbearance.
"'Whether in the right place or the wrong, constantly overcome by passion, in anger he inflicts various punishments through his own fiery energy.
Enveloped in wrath, he falls into conflict even with his friends, and becomes an object of hatred both from the world and from his own kinsmen.
From contempt, that man gains loss of wealth, reproach, disrespect, grief, hatred, greed, and enemies.
A man who inflicts various punishments on people out of anger quickly falls from his sovereignty, his life, and his own kindred.
He who approaches both those who harm and those who help with sheer force — people shrink from him just as from a serpent that has entered the house.

How can prosperity come to one from whom the world recoils? For when people see any opening, they will surely act against him. Therefore one should neither always unleash fierceness, nor should one always be gentle.
He who is gentle at the right time and harsh at the right time truly attains happiness both in this world and in the next.
Now I shall speak to you at length of the times for forbearance — those occasions that must never be abandoned, as the wise have declared.
If one who has previously done a benefit commits an offense that is not too grave, his transgression should be forgiven in return for that earlier service.
The offenses of those who acted out of ignorance should be forgiven, for wisdom is not easily attained by every person in every situation.
But if those who commit a deliberate wrong then claim it arose from ignorance — those wicked and dishonest men should be punished even for a minor offense.
A single offense by any living being should be forgiven; but if he offends a second time, he deserves to be punished, even if the harm done is small.
If any offense was committed unknowingly, the wise say it should certainly be forgiven — but only after careful investigation.
Gentleness conquers the gentle; gentleness conquers even the harsh. There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by gentleness; thus gentleness is sharper than sharpness.

Having considered place and time and one's own strength and weakness, one should not act at the wrong place or time — place and time must be awaited. Likewise, an offender should be forgiven out of fear of the people's reaction.
These are the enumerated occasions for forbearance. In all other situations where people act contrary to these, it is said to be the time for the display of energy.
Draupadī said: That, I believe, is exactly the time for your energy, O king — with the Dhārtarāṣṭras who are ever greedy and ever harmful.
For there is no occasion for forbearance now toward the Kurus. The time for energy has arrived — you ought to release that energy.
The gentle man is despised; people recoil from the fierce man. He who knows how to use both at the right time — he is a true king of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Know this, O greatly wise one — anger is the destroyer of men, yet anger is also their sustainer. Both existence and non-existence are rooted in anger.
For the man who restrains anger, O lovely one, there is flourishing. But the man who can never endure anger, O auspicious one — for him anger becomes most terribly destructive.
The destruction of creatures in this world is seen to be rooted in anger. How then could one like me release that anger which destroys the world?
An angry man commits sin; an angry man may even slay his elders; an angry man with harsh words insults even his superiors.
When enraged, a man never knows what ought to be said and what ought not to be said. For one who is angry, there is nothing that cannot be done and nothing that cannot be said.
Out of anger one may harm those who should not be harmed, and honor those who deserve to be slain. An angry man may even send himself to the abode of Yama.
Seeing these faults, anger has been conquered by the wise who desire the highest good here and the best in the next world.
How could one like me practice that anger which the steadfast have renounced? Bearing all this in mind, Draupadī, my anger does not grow.
He who does not return anger to one who is angry saves both himself and the other from great danger — he is the healer of both.
If a foolish and powerless man grows angry when afflicted, he ultimately destroys himself before those who are more powerful.
For one bereft of self who abandons himself, the worlds are lost. Therefore, Draupadī, it is prescribed that one who lacks power must restrain his anger.
Likewise, the learned and powerful man who does not become angry when afflicted — having destroyed his tormentor, he rejoices in the next world.
Therefore the wise say that a man — whether powerful or weak — must always be forbearing, even in adversity.
The virtuous here praise the conquest of anger, O Kṛṣṇā. It is the abiding view of the good and the righteous that victory forever belongs to the forbearing.
Truth is better than falsehood, and kindness better than cruelty. How then could one like me release that anger, so full of faults and abandoned by the virtuous — even for the slaying of Suyodhana?
Him whom the learned, far-sighted men call truly energetic — it is certain that anger does not dwell within him.
He who repels anger as it arises by means of wisdom — the learned who see the truth consider him to be truly energetic.
An angry man, O fair-hipped one, does not see his duty as it truly is; an angry man perceives neither duty nor the boundaries of proper conduct.
An angry man slays even those who should not be slain, and wounds even his elders with harsh words. Therefore, when energy is to be exercised, anger should be kept at a great distance.
Skill, intolerance of wrong, courage, and swiftness — these are the qualities of energy. They cannot straightforwardly be attained by one overwhelmed by anger.
Having abandoned anger, a man properly attains energy suited to the occasion, O greatly wise one. Energy wielded by the angry is very hard to bear.
But anger is constantly called energy by the unlearned — that is the quality of rajas, ordained for the destruction of people in the world.
Therefore a man who acts rightly should always abandon anger. It is certain that one who does not deviate from his own duty without anger is better.
If all the transgressions are those of the unintelligent and the witless, how, O blameless one, could there be a transgression by one such as I?
If there were no forbearing men among humans, patient as the earth, there would be no reconciliation among people — for quarrels are rooted in anger.
One who is abused would abuse in return; one who is struck by a senior would strike back. Thus the destruction of beings would spread, and unrighteousness would be proclaimed.
Every man who is reviled would revile in turn; one who is struck would strike back; one who is harmed would cause harm in return.
Fathers would slay sons and sons would slay fathers in return; wives would slay husbands and husbands would slay wives.
In a world thus inflamed with anger, O Kṛṣṇā, there would be no birth. For know, O fair-faced one, that birth is the very root of the continuity of creatures.
In such a state, all creatures would quickly perish, Draupadī. Therefore anger leads to the destruction and non-existence of creatures.
But because patient men, steadfast as the earth, are seen in the world, therefore the birth and existence of creatures continues.
A man must be forbearing in all adversities in this world, O beautiful one. For forbearance is proclaimed to be the very existence and birth of all beings.
He who, though reviled and struck and enraged, forbears against one stronger than himself, and who is always one who has conquered anger — that learned man is the highest of persons.
Even if a man is powerful, eternal worlds are his reward. But the wrathful man of little wisdom perishes both after death and here in this world.
On this very point they cite these verses, eternally belonging to the forbearing — sung by the great-souled Kāśyapa who himself possessed forbearance, O Kṛṣṇā.
Forbearance is dharma; forbearance is sacrifice; forbearance is the Vedas; forbearance is sacred learning. He who knows it thus is worthy of bearing all things.
Forbearance is Brahman; forbearance is truth; forbearance is what has been and what will be; forbearance is austerity; forbearance is purity; and by forbearance the world is upheld.
The forbearing surpass the worlds of those who know Brahman, and the worlds of the ascetics, and even those of the knowers of sacrifice.
Forbearance is the energy of the energetic; forbearance is Brahman for the ascetics; forbearance is truth for the truthful; forbearance is charity; forbearance is renown.

How could one like me abandon such forbearance, O Kṛṣṇā — forbearance in which Brahman, truth, sacrifices, and all the worlds are established? The worlds of sacrificers are enjoyed by sacrificers, and those other worlds likewise by the forbearing.
A wise man must always be forbearing. For when one forbears all things, he attains to Brahman.
This world belongs to the forbearing, and the next world too belongs to the forbearing. Here they attain honor, and in the beyond they attain an auspicious course.
Those men whose anger is always slain by forbearance — they attain the highest worlds. Therefore forbearance is considered supreme.
Thus were sung by Kāśyapa these verses, eternally belonging to the forbearing. Having heard these verses on forbearance, be content, Draupadī — do not be angry.
The grandfather, the son of Śaṃtanu, will honor peace; the preceptor, Vidura the Kṣattā, will counsel peace; and Kṛpa and Saṃjaya will likewise counsel peace.
Somadatta, Yuyutsu, and the son of Droṇa likewise, and our grandfather Vyāsa — all speak of peace always.
Being constantly urged toward peace by these men, it is my belief that the king will return the kingdom — unless greed destroys him.
This dreadful time has come for the destruction of the Bhāratas — this I have always known with certainty, even from before, O passionate one.
Suyodhana does not find forbearance thus, thinking "he does not deserve it." But I think "I am worthy of it" — and therefore forbearance finds me.
This is the conduct of the self-possessed; this is the eternal dharma — forbearance and non-cruelty. I will practice this straightforwardly.
Draupadī said: Homage to Dhātar and Vidhātar, who have created delusion in you! For when your ancestral and patrimonial duty should have been upheld, your mind has turned otherwise.
A man does not attain prosperity here by dharma and non-cruelty, nor by forbearance, nor by straightforwardness, nor ever by compassion.
If this unbearable misfortune has come upon you, O Bhārata — misfortune that neither you nor these your mighty brothers deserve —
— for neither then nor now, O Bhārata, has there ever been anything dearer to you than dharma — even dearer than life itself —
— your kingdom is for the sake of dharma, and your very life is for the sake of dharma — the Brāhmaṇas, the elders, and the gods all know this —
— it is my belief that you would abandon Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the sons of Mādrī, and even me, but that you would not abandon dharma.
"Dharma, when protected, protects the king who guards dharma" — thus have I heard from the noble ones. But I believe dharma does not protect you.
For your mind, O tiger among men, is single-mindedly fixed on dharma forever; it follows you always like a man's own shadow.
You never despised your equals, much less those who were better than you. Having obtained the entire earth, your pride never grew.
With svāhā-offerings, svadhā-offerings, and acts of worship, O Pārtha, you perpetually honored the twice-born, the deities, and the ancestors.
The Brāhmaṇas were always gratified by you with all their desires, O Pārtha; the ascetics, those intent on liberation, and the householders too, O Bhārata.
You give iron vessels to the forest-dwellers; there is nothing in your house that cannot be given to Brāhmaṇas.
That which is offered at the close of the Vaiśvadeva rite morning and evening — having given that to guests and servants, O king, you live on what remains.
Sacrificial rites, animal offerings, optional and occasional ceremonies, domestic fire sacrifices, and the daily performance of sacrificial duties — all these continue.
Even here in this great wilderness, desolate and frequented by bandits, though you have left your kingdom and dwell in exile, your dharma does not decay.
The Aśvamedha, the Rājasūya, the Puṇḍarīka, and the Gosava — you have performed even these great sacrifices with abundant gifts of honor.
O king, with a clouded mind at the calamitous dice defeat, you were vanquished — your kingdom, your wealth, your weapons, your brothers, and even me.
For one who is upright, gentle, generous, modest, and truthful — how did a mind born of addiction to dice come to descend upon you?
Extreme delusion overtakes me and my heart is seared within, witnessing this suffering of yours and such a calamity as this.
On this topic they cite this ancient tale: the world abides under the sway of the Lord, not under the power of one's own self.
The Creator alone indeed apportions pleasure and pain, the pleasant and the unpleasant, for all beings — the Lord who is supreme, who emits the seed from the beginning.
Just as a wooden puppet, O hero among men, when set in motion, moves its limb after limb, so too, O king, does He move these creatures.
Like the sky pervading all beings, O descendant of Bharata, the Lord here ordains both the auspicious and the evil.
Like a bird bound by a string, this creature is controlled and powerless; standing under the sway of the Lord, it is master neither of others nor of itself.
Like a gem threaded on a string, like a bull led by the nose-rope — it follows the Creator's command, for it is constituted of Him alone and wholly surrendered to Him.
This human being is not self-governed for any span of time, like a tree fallen from its bank into the midst of a current.
This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it may go to heaven or even to hell.
Just as the tips of grass come under the sway of the mighty wind, so all beings come under the sway of the Creator, O descendant of Bharata.
Engaging beings in noble actions or again in sin, the Lord pervades and moves through all creatures — yet He is not perceived as such.
This body, known as the field, is merely the instrument of the Creator — through it the all-pervading Lord causes actions of auspicious and inauspicious fruit to be performed.
Behold this power of illusion fashioned by the Lord — He who slays beings by means of other beings, having deluded them with His own māyā.
Things are seen one way by the sages who behold the Veda, yet they turn out otherwise — like the gusts of the wind.
Men indeed think of those various things one way, yet the Lord makes and unmakes them in quite another way.
Just as wood may be split by wood, stone by stone, and iron by iron — all inert and insensate —
— so that blessed God, the Self-Existent, the great Progenitor, slays beings by means of other beings, assuming a disguise, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Joining and separating — this Lord who acts as He wills, the Blessed One, sports with beings as a child with toys.
The Creator does not behave toward creatures as a mother or father would, O king; He acts as if impelled by wrath, like any ordinary person.
Seeing the noble, the virtuous, the modest ground down in livelihood, while the ignoble are prosperous — I am overwhelmed, as it were, with anguish.
Seeing this calamity of yours and the prosperity of Suyodhana, I reproach the Creator, O Pārtha, who looks on unequally.
Having bestowed fortune on the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who transgresses the codes of the noble, who is cruel, greedy, and contemptuous of dharma — what fruit does the Creator enjoy?
If the deed follows its doer and does not go to another, then surely the Lord is stained by that sinful act.
Or if a sinful deed done does not return to its doer, then mere force is the only cause in this world — and I grieve for the powerless.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Yājñasenī, what you have spoken is eloquent, adorned with varied phrases, and smooth — we have heard it; yet you speak in the manner of an atheist.
I do not practice dharma in quest of its fruits, O princess; I give because it is to be given, I sacrifice because it is to be sacrificed.
Whether there be fruit in this or not — whatever a man living as a householder ought to do, O Kṛṣṇā, I do that to the best of my ability.

I practice dharma, O fair-hipped one, not for the sake of its fruit; not transgressing the scriptures, looking to the conduct of the virtuous — it is dharma alone, O Kṛṣṇā, to which my mind is held by its very nature.
He who wishes to milk dharma of its fruit does not attain the fruit of dharma; and he who, after practicing it, doubts it out of atheism, being of sinful mind — he too does not.
Do not excessively doubt dharma out of arrogance or pride; a man who excessively doubts dharma is destined for the state of beasts.
He of weak spirit for whom dharma or the teaching of the seers would be a matter of excessive doubt — he falls away from the undying, undecaying world, as a śūdra falls away from the Veda.
One who is a student of the Veda, devoted to dharma, born of an illustrious family — him should kings who walk in dharma employ among the elders.
He is more wicked than śūdras — especially more so than thieves — that dull-witted transgressor of scripture who excessively doubts dharma.
For you have seen with your own eyes the great ascetic, the seer Mārkaṇḍeya of immeasurable spirit, who has attained long life through dharma.
Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Maitreya, Nārada, Lomaśa, Śuka, and other accomplished seers of pure minds — all have attained perfection through dharma alone.
You see these very ones with your own eyes — endowed with divine yoga, capable of curse and benediction, weightier even than the gods.
These very ones, resplendent as immortals, whose understanding is grounded in direct scriptural knowledge, always declare dharma first as what must be done by me.
Therefore, O auspicious one, you should not revile the Creator or dharma itself with a mind clouded by passion, nor should you doubt them.
He who excessively doubts dharma finds no authority in anything else; puffed up with himself as his own authority, he is contemptuous of the good.
The fool thinks that only this — what is witnessed by the world and bound up with the pleasure of the senses — is all there is, and falls into delusion regarding what lies beyond.
There is no expiation for him who excessively doubts dharma; brooding, that wretch and sinner does not attain the higher worlds.
He who transgresses all authority, reviles the import of the Vedic scriptures, and follows desire and greed — that fool goes to hell.
But he who is always resolute in mind, who resorts to dharma alone without doubting, O auspicious one — he attains eternity in the world beyond.
He who transgresses the authority of the seers, does not protect the duties of dharma, and oversteps all scriptures — that fool finds no welfare across his births.
O Kṛṣṇā, do not excessively doubt the dharma practiced by the disciplined, the ancient teaching proclaimed by the all-knowing, all-seeing seers.
Dharma alone is the raft — there is no other — for those going to heaven, O Draupadī; it is the vessel, like a merchant's ship reaching the far shore of the ocean.
If dharma, when practiced by those who walk in dharma, were to bear no fruit, this blameless world would sink into groundless darkness.
Men would not attain liberation, they would live the life of beasts, they would be joined only with destruction, and they would attain nothing of value.
Austerity, celibacy, sacrifice, study, generosity, and uprightness — if all these were indeed fruitless —
— then neither those here nor those far beyond would practice dharma; this would be utter deceit if all these acts were fruitless.
The seers and the gods, the gandharvas, asuras, and rākṣasas — lords all — for what reason would they practice dharma with devotion?
Knowing the Creator here to be the giver of fruit in the certain highest good, they practice dharma, O Kṛṣṇā — for that is the eternal dharma.
And this dharma is indeed fruitful; dharma is not said to be fruitless — for the fruits of learning and likewise of austerities are visibly seen.
Know this to be so in your own case, O Kṛṣṇā, as it has been heard; you also know how the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born.
This much is sufficient illustration, O bright-smiling one — that there is fruit to actions; the wise man is satisfied even by a small example.
For the ignorant who lack understanding are never satisfied even by much; for them there is no solace born of dharma or of action after death.
The arising of the fruit of actions — both meritorious and sinful — their origin and their dissolution: these are the secret mysteries of the gods, O passionate one.
No one whatsoever knows these things — creatures are bewildered in this matter; these are to be kept hidden by the gods, for the deities have concealed their mysteries.
Slender-limbed, of good vows, their sins burned away by austerity, endowed with serene minds — such brāhmaṇas indeed behold these things.
Dharma should not be doubted because its fruit is not visible, nor should the gods be doubted; one should sacrifice with diligence and give without envy.
"There is fruit to actions" — thus runs this eternal dharma; Brahmā declared it to his sons, and the seer Kaśyapa knows it.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇā, let your doubt vanish like mist; resolve that all this exists, and abandon the disposition of atheism.
Do not revile the Lord, the Creator of all beings; learn from Him, bow to Him — let such a disposition as this not be in you.
By whose grace His devotee, though mortal, attains immortality — O Kṛṣṇā, do not speak ill in any way of that supreme divinity.
Draupadī said: I do not disrespect dharma, nor do I blame it in any way, O Pārtha; how should I disrespect the Lord, the Progenitor of creatures?
Know me to be speaking thus in grief, O descendant of Bharata; and I shall lament yet further — hear that from me with a peaceful mind.
Action must indeed be performed in this world by one who is born, O crusher of foes; for it is only the immobile that live without action — not other beings.
