Janamejaya said: This deed of Pārtha of boundless splendour is most wondrous — what did the great-spirited Dhṛtarāṣṭra say, O brahman, upon hearing it?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that Pārtha had gone to Śakra's world, the king, son of Ambikā, spoke these words to Saṃjaya through the foremost of sages, Dvaipāyana.
'I have heard the complete account of the wise Pārtha's deed — do you too know it accurately as it truly is, O charioteer?'
'My son, heedless, devoted to base pleasures, dull-minded, fixed on evil, utterly foolish of understanding, will bring destruction upon the earth.'
'Even the words of that great-souled one are ever true even in casual speech — even the three worlds would belong to one whose warrior is Dhanaṃjaya.'
'As he releases his feathered arrows and sharp iron shafts whetted on stone, who could stand before Arjuna — not even Death that surpasses old age?'
'My wicked sons have all gone under death's dominion, against whom battle with the formidable Pāṇḍavas now looms.'
'Even thinking constantly, I see no chariot-warrior who could rise up against the wielder of Gāṇḍīva in battle.'
'Even if Droṇa and Karṇa were to face him, or even Bhīṣma in battle, there would be great uncertainty in the world — yet I see no victory for us.'
'Karṇa is compassionate and careless, the teacher is old and venerable, while Pārtha is wrathful, powerful, fierce and of firm valour.'
'There would be a most tumultuous battle, unconquered on all sides — for all are versed in weapons, all are heroes, all have won great glory.'
'Even were they defeated, they would not desire sovereignty over everything — only in the death of them or of Phalguna would there certainly be peace.'
'Yet there is no slayer of Arjuna, no conqueror of him exists — how could his rage be appeased, risen as it is against these base ones?'
'Equal to the lord of the thirty gods, the hero satisfied Agni in the Khāṇḍava forest and conquered all kings at the great Rājasūya sacrifice.'
'A thunderbolt falling on a mountain's peak might leave some remnant, O Saṃjaya — but the arrows and weapons shot by the Diademed one, my son, would leave nothing.'
'Just as the rays of the sun scorch all that moves and is still, so the arrows released from Pārtha's arm will scorch my sons.'
'Or even by the din of the chariot of Savyasācin, the entire Bhārata army appears to me as if shattered in every direction, stricken with terror.'
'As he stands discharging and raining down arrows in battle — Kirīṭī, the aggressor — like Death sent forth by Fate to take all, he would be unstoppable.'
Saṃjaya said: What you have declared here, O king, regarding Duryodhana — all of it is exactly as you say; this is not false, O lord of the earth.
For the Pāṇḍavas, those of immeasurable might, were seized with rage upon seeing Kṛṣṇā — their lawful wife, that glorious lady — dragged into the assembly hall.
Having heard those terrible words spoken by Duḥśāsana and by Karṇa, O great king, it is my conviction that they will not sleep peacefully.
For you have heard, O great king, how the eleven-formed Śiva — the Immovable One — was gratified by Pārtha's bow in battle.
The lord of all the gods himself, the braid-haired Bhagavān, wishing to test him, assumed the guise of a Kirāta mountaineer and fought with Phalguna.
Then those world-guardians revealed themselves to Arjuna — that bull of the Kauravas who had striven with ascetic power — for the purpose of granting him celestial weapons.
No other man on earth is capable of obtaining the direct vision of these divine lords — none other than Phalguna.
O king, that hero whose body, though seized, was not worn down by Maheśvara himself — what man is capable of exhausting him in battle?
This dreadful, tumultuous, hair-raising situation was brought about by those who dragged Draupadī about and provoked the Pāṇḍavas to fury.
Therein, with quivering lips, Bhīma uttered his great vow upon seeing Duryodhana display both his thighs to Draupadī.
"I shall shatter your thighs, O wretch, with my thunderbolt-like mace at the end of thirteen years — you who played that wicked game of dice."
They are all foremost among warriors, all of immeasurable energy, all masters of every weapon, and even the gods find them exceedingly difficult to overcome.
I believe that the Pārthas, blazing with wrath, filled with valor and indignation, will bring your sons to their end in battle.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: What has Karṇa achieved, O charioteer, by speaking those harsh words? Enmity enough already exists from the fact that Kṛṣṇā was brought into the assembly hall.
Will my sons of dull intellect stand firm now — they whose elder brother, their elder and guide, does not abide by proper conduct?
Even my counsel, O charioteer, that dull-witted one does not heed, seeing me bereft of sight, motionless, and as though without consciousness.
And his dull counselors — Karṇa, Śakuni and the rest — those men of confused understanding, only increase his faults further.
Even arrows loosely shot by Pārtha of immeasurable energy would burn down my sons — how much more so those impelled by rage?
Arrows hurled by the strength of Pārtha's arms, discharged from his great bow, and empowered by the mantras of celestial weapons, could lay low even the gods.
He whose counselor, protector, and friend is Janārdana — Hari, the lord of the three worlds — what indeed has he not conquered?
And this too is a most wonderful marvel concerning Arjuna, O Sañjaya — so the tradition tells — that he came to grips with Mahādeva himself, arm to arm.
And what was done long ago in the Khāṇḍava forest before the eyes of all the world by Phalguna, together with Dāmodara, for the sake of helping Agni —
— in every way my son has no hope — not with his ministers, not with his kinsmen — when Pārtha, Bhīma, Vāsudeva, and the Sātvata are enraged.
Janamejaya said: O sage, this lamentation of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra — having already sent the heroic Pāṇḍavas into exile — is entirely futile.
For how could a king neglect his own son of mean understanding — Duryodhana — who was provoking those great chariot warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu?
What was the food of the sons of Pāṇḍu in the forest — please tell me: was it forest-gathered, or was it cultivated grain? Let your honor recount this.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those bulls among men ate forest produce and deer brought down by pure arrows, first offering the food to the brahmanas before eating it themselves.
Those valiant great bowmen dwelling in the forest were followed, O king, by brahmanas both with their sacred fires and without.
Thousands of brahmanas who were graduates of sacred learning, great-souled, and ten thousand likewise who were versed in the knowledge of liberation — all these Yudhiṣṭhira sustained.
He slew black deer, rurupastures, and other fit forest animals with arrows, and duly offered them to the brahmanas in the prescribed manner.
There, no man was seen with a sickly complexion or afflicted by disease, nor thin or weak, nor wretched or fearful.
The foremost of the Kauravas, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, cherished them as beloved sons, as kinsmen, as own-born brothers.
And the glorious Draupadī, having fed all her husbands and all the twice-born first, like a mother, would then herself eat what remained.
The king hunted in the east and Bhīmasena in the south; the twins in the west and north — those bowmen ranging daily in pursuit of deer for meat brought great slaughter.
And so, while they dwelt in the Kāmyaka forest — longing anxiously for Arjuna, bereft of him — five full years passed by, as they studied, recited prayers, and performed oblations.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, heaving a long and hot sigh, summoned Sañjaya the charioteer and spoke to him, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Nakula and Sahadeva — those two sons of the divine Aśvins, those two greatly blessed Pāṇḍavas, of radiance equal to the king of the gods — are fierce and intoxicated in battle.
They are firm-weaponed, of far-striking range, resolute in battle, quick of hand, of firm wrath, ever ready, and swift in action.
When those two — Bhīma and Arjuna — stand at the forefront of battle, striding like lions, as irresistible as the twin Aśvins, I see no remnant of my army left then, O Sañjaya.
For those two, who are peerless on the chariot in battle, those two great chariot warriors who are sons of the gods, burning with indignation, will not forgive that torment inflicted on Draupadī.
Whether the great bowmen of the Vṛṣṇis or the mighty Pāñcālas — protected in battle by Vāsudeva who is true to his word — the Pārthas will burn down my sons' army in combat.
O son of a charioteer, the onslaught of the Vṛṣṇis led by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa cannot be withstood even by mountains in battle.
In the midst of them, the great bowman Bhīma of terrible prowess will range about with his iron mace that slays heroes.
Likewise, the twang of the Gāṇḍīva — like the crack of a thunderbolt — and the force of Bhīma's mace: no lords of men are capable of enduring them.
Then I, who have followed in Duryodhana's wake, will recall — too late — the words of friends that I should have heeded and acted upon before.
Sañjaya said: This is a very great transgression that you have let pass, O king — that through delusion your son was not restrained, even though you had the power to do so.
For upon hearing that the Pāṇḍavas had been defeated at dice, Madhusūdana — the infallible Acyuta — hastened to Kāmyaka to visit the Pārthas.
Likewise the sons of Drupada headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Virāṭa, and Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the Kekayas — all great chariot warriors.
And all that was spoken by them upon seeing the defeated Pārthas — all of it was learned by me through spies, and I have informed you of it.
There, after meeting the Pāṇḍavas, Madhusūdana pledged himself to be Phalguna's charioteer in battle, and Hari said to them: "So be it."
For Kṛṣṇa too was filled with indignation upon seeing the Pārthas reduced to such a condition — wearing black deer-skins as upper garments — and he spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"That prosperity of the Pārthas which existed at Indraprastha during the Rājasūya sacrifice — which I witnessed, unmatched by other kings —
"— where I saw all the rulers of the earth, terror-struck by the might of weapons, along with the Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, Paundras, Oḍras, Colas, Draviḍas, and Andhakas —
"— and those who dwell along the ocean coast, and those who inhabit cities, the Sinhalas, Barbaras, Mlecchas, and those who dwell in the arid lands —
"— and the western kingdoms by the hundreds down to the sea-shore, the Pahlavas, the Daradas, all the Kirātas, the Yavanas, and the Śakas —
"— the Harahunasand Chinas, the Tukhāras, the Saindhavas, the Jagudas, the Ramathas, the Mundas, the kingdoms of women, and the Taṅgaṇas —
"— these and many others, O bull of the Bhāratas, I saw arrive as tributaries at your sacrifice —
"— that prosperity of yours which those fickle and treacherous men have seized — taking their lives in return, I shall recover it for you."

"Together with Rāma, O descendant of Kuru, and with Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins, and with Akrūra, Gada, Sāmba, and Pradyumna, and with Āhuka, and with the hero Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and with the son of Śiśupāla —
"— having slain Duryodhana in battle forthwith, and Karṇa, O Bhārata, and Duḥśāsana and the son of Subala, and whoever else shall oppose us —
"— then you, dwelling in Hāstinapura together with your brothers, having obtained the sovereignty of the Dhārtarāṣṭras, shall govern this earth."
Then the king spoke to him in that assembly of heroes, while all of them were listening — those headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
"I accept your true word, O Janārdana; O mighty-armed one, you shall slay my enemies together with their allies."
"After the completion of thirteen years, make your word true, O Keśava; for this exile in the forest has been pledged by me in the assembly of kings."
Having heard those words of Dharmarāja, the assembly members headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna straightway pacified the enraged Keśava with sweet words suited to the occasion.

And they spoke to the unsullied Pāñcālī while Vāsudeva listened: "Duryodhana shall forfeit his life through your anger, O goddess; we pledge you this truthfully — weep not, O you of lovely complexion."
"Those who laughed at you, O Kṛṣṇa, when they saw you enraged — beasts and birds shall laugh in turn while eating their flesh."
"Vultures and jackals shall drink their blood, dragging away their heads — the heads of those who dragged you along the floor of the assembly hall."
"You shall see, O Pāñcālī, the limbs of those men dragged across the earth and devoured again and again by flesh-eating creatures."
"The earth shall drink the blood of those — their heads severed — who tormented you then, and of those also who looked on in indifference."
Thus spoke those bulls among men in many various words — all of them radiant, all warriors, all bearing the marks of the unvanquished.
Those great chariot warriors, chosen by Dharmarāja, after the completion of thirteen years shall march forth with Vāsudeva at their head.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya, Pradyumna and Sāmba, Yuyudhāna and Bhīma, the sons of Mādrī, the sons of the Kekaya king, the sons of Pāñcāla — together with Dharmarāja.

Who, wishing to preserve his life, would rise to oppose in battle all these heroes of the world, these invincible great-souled ones with their allies and armies — enraged as they are, like maned lions?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: What Vidura told me at the time of the dice game — "If you defeat the Pāṇḍavas, O king, this is certainly the end-time of the Kurus; there will be a great fear, a flood of blood" —

— I believe that will indeed come to pass, O charioteer, just as Kshattar spoke those words to me before. Without doubt this war will happen when the time of the Pāṇḍavas has expired, as was foretold.
Janamejaya said: When the great-souled Pārtha had gone to the realm of Śakra for the purpose of obtaining weapons, what did the Pāṇḍavas headed by Yudhiṣṭhira do?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the great-souled Pārtha had gone to the realm of Śakra for the purpose of obtaining weapons, those bulls among men continued to dwell at Kāmyaka together with Kṛṣṇā.

Then one day, in a secluded and solitary place, in a grassy spot, those best of the Bhāratas sat down in grief together with Kṛṣṇā, lamenting for Dhanañjaya, their throats choked with tears, deeply sorrowful.
Grief overwhelmed them all on account of that separation — afflicted by the loss of Dhanañjaya and by the loss of their kingdom.
Then Bhīma of mighty arms spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira: "At your command, O great king, that bull among men has gone — Arjuna, in whom the vital breath of the sons of Pāṇḍu is established."
If he were lost, the Pāñcālas with their sons, and we ourselves, and Sātyaki and Vāsudeva — all would perish without doubt.
That radiant one goes, ignoring countless hardships, by your command — Arjuna does so; what then is more painful than this?
Relying on whose arms we all consider the foes already defeated in battle and the earth already won.
Because of whose power I did not send all the Dhārtarāṣṭras together with Subala's son to the other world in the midst of the assembly hall, though he was armed with his bow.
We, endowed with the strength of our arms, endure the anger rising within us — anger rooted in your decision — while being protected by Vāsudeva.
For we, together with Kṛṣṇa, having slain the enemies headed by Karṇa, could rule the entire earth conquered by our own arms.
By the fault of your dice-playing we are all overwhelmed — we whose valor is undiminished, O king, who are mightier than the mighty.

You ought to consider the duty of a warrior, great king; for dwelling in the forest is not the dharma of a kṣatriya, great king — the wise know that sovereignty alone is the highest dharma of a kṣatriya.
You who know the warrior's dharma, O king — do not stray from the righteous path. Before the twelve years are up, O king, let us slay the Dhārtarāṣṭras.
Calling back Pārtha from his quest and summoning Janārdana, great king, I will swiftly dispatch the Dhārtarāṣṭras with their arrayed forces to the other world in great battle, O lord of the people.
I shall slay all the Dhārtarāṣṭras together with Subala's son, Duryodhana and Karṇa, and whoever else shall oppose us in battle.
After I have pacified them you can return from the forest. If done this way, no fault will attach to you, O lord of the people.
And having shaken off the sin committed through various sacrifices, O subduer of enemies, O great king, we can go to the highest heaven.
This could indeed be so, O king, if the king were not foolish; but you are one who procrastinates for us, O you who are devoted to dharma.
It is settled that the deceitful, whose intelligence is deceit, must be slain by deceit; for slaying the treacherous by treachery is not called a sin.
So too in matters of dharma it is seen by those who know dharma, O Bhārata — a single day and night, great king, is equal to a full year.
And likewise the Vedic word is heard always, O lord — a year, O great king, becomes complete through difficulty.
If the Vedas are your authority, O unfailing one, reckoning beyond the single day — the time of thirteen years is to be understood as fully elapsed.
The time has come to slay Duryodhana together with his followers, O subduer of foes — lest he make the entire earth under one sole rule first, O king.
While Bhīma was speaking thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-king, addressed him soothingly, smelling the Pāṇḍava's head.
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, you will slay Suyodhana after the thirteenth year is past, together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
And what you say to me — "the time has come, O lord" — I cannot bring myself to speak an untruth; for this is not in me.
Even without resorting to treachery or evil resolve, O son of Kuntī, you shall be the slayer of Suyodhana and his followers, O invincible one.
While king Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-king, was speaking thus to Bhīma, the great and fortunate sage Bṛhadaśva arrived.
Beholding him who had arrived — the righteous one who walks in dharma — the dharma-souled king of righteousness honored him according to the scriptures with the madhuparka offering.
When he was seated at ease, Yudhiṣṭhira, the mighty-armed, sitting near him and beholding him, spoke many words piteously.
By dice-play, O blessed one, my wealth and kingdom have been taken from me — having been summoned and cheated by deceitful gamblers who were skilled at dice.
I, knowing nothing of dice, was cheated by those of evil resolve — and my wife, dearer to me than life itself, was dragged into the assembly hall.
Is there any king more unfortunate than I on this earth — one seen by you before, or even heard of before? It is my belief that there is no man more miserable than I.
Bṛhadaśva said: What you say, great king, that nowhere is there any man more unfortunate than I — hear this, O Pāṇḍava.
I shall tell you of this, if you wish to hear, O sinless one — there was a king more miserable than you, O lord of the earth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king said to him, "Let the blessed one speak" — I wish to hear of the king who has come to such a condition.
Bṛhadaśva said: Listen attentively, O king, together with your brothers, O steadfast one — there was a king more miserable than you, O lord of the earth.
There was a king of the earth among the Niṣadhas known as Vīrasena; his son was named Nala, who was versed in dharma and the goals of life.
That king was defeated by deceit — by Puṣkara, as we have heard — and though undeserving of such hardship, he dwelt in the forest with his wife.
For that king dwelling in the forest, O king, neither horse, nor chariot, nor brother, nor kinsman ever remained with him.
But you are surrounded by heroic brothers equal to the gods, and by foremost twice-born ones who are like Brahmā — therefore you ought not to grieve.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear at length, O best among speakers, the story of the great-souled Nala — please narrate it to me.
Bṛhadaśva said: There was a king named Nala, the powerful son of Vīrasena, endowed with desired virtues, handsome, and skilled in the knowledge of horses.
He stood at the head of human kings as the lord of the gods stands above all — above all others, like the sun in radiance.
Devoted to the Brahmins, learned in the Vedas, heroic, the great lord of the earth among the Niṣadhas, fond of dice, truthful in speech, the great commander of armies.
Desired by the best of women, generous, with controlled senses, a protector, the foremost of archers — like Manu himself in person.
And likewise among the Vidarbhas there was Bhīma of terrible valor, a hero endowed with all virtues, who desired offspring but had none.
He made supreme effort, well-composed in mind, for the sake of offspring; and the brahmarṣi named Damana came to him, O Bhārata.
Bhīma who desired offspring — knowing dharma — gratified that lustrous one together with his queen, O lord of kings, with reverent hospitality.
Pleased with him, the greatly famous Damana granted a boon to him and his wife — a jewel of a daughter and three noble, greatly glorious sons.
Damayantī, Dama, Dānta, and Damana of fine radiance — all endowed with every virtue, formidable as Bhīma, of terrible valor.
But Damayantī, the slender-waisted one, gained fame in the worlds through her beauty, splendor, renown, fortune, and good fortune.
When she came of age, a hundred well-adorned maidservants and companions waited upon her as upon Śacī herself.

There the daughter of Bhīma — adorned with all ornaments, her limbs beyond reproach — shone among her companions like a flash of lightning, exceedingly endowed with beauty, like Śrī herself with wide eyes.
Nowhere among gods, nor among yakṣas, nor among other humans, had such a beautiful woman been seen before or even heard of — the young girl who confounded the mind, beautiful even to the gods.
And Nala, the tiger among men, was unequaled on earth in beauty — like the god of love embodied in form itself.
In her presence they praised Nala out of curiosity, and in the presence of the Niṣādha king they praised Damayantī again and again.
Love arose between the two of them who constantly heard each other's virtues without having seen each other, O son of Kuntī — and that longing of the heart kept growing toward each other.
Unable to bear the love in his heart, Nala then stayed alone in the garden near the inner apartments.
He then saw geese with golden-colored plumage wandering in the garden; of those birds he caught one.
Then that sky-traveler spoke to Nala: "I am not to be killed by you, O king — for I shall do you a favor."
"I shall speak of you in the presence of Damayantī, O king of the Niṣadhas — such that she will never think of any man other than you."
Addressed thus, the lord of the earth then released the goose. And those geese flew up and went from there to Vidarbha.
Having gone to the city of Vidarbha, the winged ones alighted near Damayantī; and she then saw those birds.
Seeing those birds of wondrous form, surrounded by her group of companions, she joyfully and eagerly set about to catch the birds.
Then the geese scattered in all directions through the ladies' garden; and then the maidens each chased after those geese one by one.
But the goose that Damayantī ran after close at hand — that one, adopting a human voice, then spoke to Damayantī:
"Damayantī, there is a king named Nala, lord of the earth among the Niṣadhas, equal to the Aśvins in beauty — no humans are equal to him."
"If you were to become his wife, O fair-complexioned one, your birth would be fruitful and this beauty of yours, O slender-waisted one."
"For we have seen gods, gandharvas, humans, serpents, and rākṣasas — and yet one such as him has never been seen by us before."
"And you are a jewel among women, and Nala is the best among men — the union of the excellent with the excellent would be full of virtue."
Thus addressed by the goose, Damayantī, O lord of the people, said to that goose there: "Say the same to Nala as well."
The bird, having said "So be it" to the daughter of the lord of Vidarbha, O lord of the people, came back again to the Niṣādha country and reported everything to Nala.
Bṛhadaśva said: Damayantī, having heard that word of the goose, O Bhārata, from that time onward became unsettled in mind regarding Nala.
Then Damayantī became absorbed in thought, wretched, pale-faced, thin, constantly sighing at that time.
With upward gaze, absorbed in meditation, she appeared as one deranged — never finding pleasure in bed, seat, or enjoyment at any time.
She slept neither by night nor by day, saying "Alas! Alas!" again and again; and her companions recognized her unsettled state and such condition through signs.
Then the group of Damayantī's companions reported to the lord of Vidarbha that Damayantī was not herself, O lord of men.
Hearing that from Damayantī's group of companions, king Bhīma reflected deeply on that very great matter concerning his own daughter.
The lord of the earth, observing his own daughter who had reached the bloom of youth, saw that the proper course of action for him was Damayantī's svayaṃvara.
He summoned the lords of the earth, O lord of the people: "Let this svayaṃvara be attended, O heroes, O lords" — so said he.
Hearing of Damayantī's svayaṃvara, all the kings then came to Bhīma, those rulers summoned by Bhīma's command.
Making the earth resound with the noise of elephants, horses, and chariots, with their forces well-adorned with varied garlands and ornaments and fine to behold.
At this very time two ancient foremost sages, the great-souled wanderers, departed from here and went to Indra's world.
Nārada and Parvata, both great-souled and of mighty vows, entered the abode of the king of gods, and were received with great honour.
Having worshipped them, the thousand-eyed lord, the all-pervading one, then asked them of their welfare and enquired also about the health of all in every place.
Nārada said: O god, O lord, our welfare extends everywhere; and O Maghavan, O all-powerful one, the kings throughout the entire world are prospering.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having heard Nārada's words, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra asked about those kings who know righteousness and who fight having cast off all attachment to life.
Those who meet their death by weapons at the proper time, without turning their backs in battle — for them this world is imperishable, just as it fulfils all my desires.
Where now are those heroic warriors? I do not see them here. The kings who used to come as beloved guests to my dwelling — where are they?
Thus addressed by Śakra, Nārada replied: Hear me, O blessed lord — I shall tell you why those rulers of the earth are not to be seen here.
The daughter of the king of Vidarbha, renowned as Damayantī, has surpassed all women on earth in beauty.
O Śakra, her svayaṃvara will take place very soon; kings and princes are all going there from every direction.
Desiring her who is a jewel of the world, the rulers of the earth are longing for her especially, O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra.
While this was being told, the guardian deities of the worlds, together with Agni, came — those best among the immortals — to the presence of the king of gods.
Then all of them heard Nārada's important words, and having heard, they said joyfully: Let us also go there.
Then all of them, O great king, along with their retinues and their vehicles, set out toward Vidarbha, where all the earthly kings were headed.
King Nala too, O son of Kuntī, having heard of the assembly of kings, set out with undaunted spirit, devoted to Damayantī.
Then the gods on the way saw Nala standing on the earth — his beauty making him seem like the god of love himself standing there in bodily form.
Seeing him radiant as the sun, those guardians of the worlds stood still, their purposes forgotten, astonished at the perfection of his form.
Then the celestial beings, having stationed their aerial cars in the sky, descended from the heavens and spoke to the king of Niṣadha.
Ho, ho, Naiṣadha, king of kings! You, Nala, are a man of true vows. Do us a service — be our messenger, O best of men.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having promised them "I shall do it," O Bhārata, Nala then stood with palms joined and asked them further.
Who indeed are you? And who is that person whose messenger I am desired to be? And what task must I do there? Tell me everything exactly as it is.
When the king of Niṣadha spoke thus, Maghavan replied: Know us indeed to be immortals who have come on account of Damayantī.
I am Indra; here is Agni; and likewise here is the lord of waters; and this is Yama, the ender of men's bodies, O king.
Therefore announce our arrival to Damayantī: the guardians of the worlds together with Indra are coming, desiring to see her.
Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and Yama — the gods desire to obtain her; let her choose one among these gods as her husband.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Nala said with joined palms: You ought not to send me on a mission that concerns the very same purpose that brings me there.
The gods said: Having previously promised us "I shall do it," why now, O Naiṣadha, will you not do it? Go, Naiṣadha, do not delay.
Bṛhadaśva said: Thus urged by those gods, the king of Niṣadha replied again: How can I dare to enter her well-guarded chambers?
"You shall enter," Śakra said to him again; and he, saying "so be it," went to Damayantī's dwelling.
There he saw the princess of Vidarbha surrounded by her circle of friends, blazing with her bodily beauty and splendour, that excellent-complexioned one.
Her limbs were supremely tender, her waist was slender, her eyes most beautiful — and with her own radiance she seemed to snatch away even the light of the moon.
On seeing her, that lovely-smiling one, desire grew within him; but wishing to keep his promise true, he restrained the longing of his heart.
Then those most excellent women, seeing the king of Niṣadha, rose up startled from their seats, overpowered by his radiance.
Full of delight and wonder, they praised Nala, yet could not bring themselves to address him; they only contemplated him in their minds.
"What beauty! What charm! What composure this great-souled one possesses! Is he a god, or a yakṣa, or a gandharva?"
But all those lovely, modest women, overpowered by his radiance, were unable to say anything at all to him.
Then Damayantī, astonished, smiled slightly and, as one who speaks first with a smile, addressed the hero Nala.
"Who are you, O one whose limbs are altogether faultless, O increaser of the longing in my heart? You have come like an immortal, O hero — I wish to know you, O sinless one."
"How did you come here? And how were you not noticed? My chambers are well-guarded, and the king too is one of fierce commands."
Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, Nala replied to her: Know me to be Nala, O auspicious one, come here as a messenger of the gods.
"The gods desire to obtain you — Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and Yama. O beautiful one, choose one among them as your husband."
"By their divine power alone I entered unseen; as I entered, no one saw me and no one barred my way."
"For this purpose I was sent by those best of gods, O fortunate one. Having heard this, O auspicious one, make up your mind as you wish."
Bṛhadaśva said: She, having paid homage to the gods, said laughingly to Nala: O king, show your affection as you trust — what shall I do for you?
"I myself, and whatever other wealth of mine there is — all of that is yours with confidence; show your desire, O lord."
"That message of the swans burns within me, O king; it is for your sake, O hero, that I have assembled all these kings."
"If you should reject me who am devoted to you, O bestower of honour, I shall resort to poison, fire, water, or a rope — on your account."
Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, Nala replied to her: With the guardians of the worlds present, how can you desire a mortal?
"I am not even equal to the dust of the feet of those great-souled lords, the creators of the worlds. Let your mind dwell on them."
"A mortal who acts contrary to the gods' wishes meets his death. Protect me, O you of faultless limbs, and choose those best among the gods."
Then Damayantī, whose smile was pure, her voice laden with tears, spoke slowly to king Nala.
"There is a means I have devised, O lord of men — a flawless means, O king, by which no blame will fall on you in any way."
"You, O best of men, and the gods with Agni at their head — let all of them come together to the place of my svayaṃvara."
"Then in the presence of the guardians of the worlds I shall choose you, O lord of men, O tiger among men — thus no blame will arise."
Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, king Nala, O lord of people, returned again to the place where the gods had assembled.
The guardians of the worlds together with their lord saw him coming thus; having seen him, they asked him about everything that had transpired.
The gods said: O king, did you see Damayantī of the pure smile? What did she say to us all? Tell us, O lord of the earth, O sinless one.
Nala said: Commanded by you, I entered the dwelling of Damayantī — that very great enclosure surrounded by staff-bearing elders.
"And as I entered there, no man saw me, except that princess — by your divine power alone."
"Her friends too I saw, and they in turn noticed me; on seeing me, O lords of the gods, all of them became astonished."
"And even as I was describing you to her, that lovely-faced one has fixed her resolve upon me alone. She will choose me, O best among gods."
"And the young woman said to me: Let the gods come together, along with you, O best of men, to the place of my svayaṃvara."
"'In their presence I shall choose you, O best of men — thus, O mighty-armed one, no blame will fall upon you,' she said."
"This is all that happened, recounted by me as it truly occurred; you, O lords of the thirty gods, are the final authority in this matter."
Bṛhadaśva said: Then, when an auspicious time had arrived, on a holy lunar day and at a propitious moment, king Bhīma summoned the rulers of the earth for the svayaṃvara.
Hearing that, all the rulers of the earth, tormented by the longing of their hearts, came hastening, eager to win Damayantī.
Those kings entered the great hall, resplendent with its archway and gleaming with golden pillars, like lions entering a mountain cave.
There the rulers of the earth were seated on various thrones, all wearing fragrant garlands, adorned with well-polished jewelled earrings.
That full assembly of kings was like Bhogavatī filled with serpents, or like a mountain cave filled with tigers — those tigers among men.
There could be seen massive arms like iron bars, well-shaped and very smooth, like five-headed serpents.
The beautiful faces of the kings, with fine hair and handsome noses, shone like the constellations in the sky.
Then Damayantī of the auspicious face entered the arena, stealing away with her radiance the eyes and minds of the kings.
The gaze of those great-souled ones fell upon her limbs and remained fixed wherever it landed, unmoving in those who beheld her.
Then, O Bhārata, as the names of the kings were being proclaimed, the daughter of Bhīma saw five men who looked exactly alike.

Surveying them all, standing there indistinguishable in form, the princess of Vidarbha could not in her perplexity recognise king Nala — whichever one among them she looked at, she thought that one to be king Nala.
She, thinking and reasoning with her mind, that spirited woman wondered: How shall I recognise the gods? How shall I know king Nala?
Thus thinking deeply, that princess of Vidarbha, greatly distressed, called to mind the marks of the gods that she had heard of, O Bhārata.
"The marks of the gods that I have heard of from the elders — not a single one of those do I see on any of these five standing here on the ground."
Having deliberated in many ways and considered again and again, she thought it was time to take refuge with the gods themselves.
With speech and with her mind she offered salutation; becoming trembling with joined palms before the gods, she spoke these words.
"Having heard the message of the swans, I have chosen the king of Niṣadha as my husband — by that truth, let the gods point him out to me."
By this truth — that neither in word nor in mind have I ever been unfaithful to him — let the wise gods point him out to me.
By this truth — that the lord of Niṣadha was ordained to be my husband by the gods themselves — let the gods point him out to me.
May the world-guardians together with Īśvara manifest their own true forms, so that I may recognize the glorious king Nala.
Having heard Damayantī's piteous lamentation, her supreme and truthful resolve, and her passionate love for the Niṣadhan,
the gods, O Bhārata, perceiving the purity of her mind, her intelligence, her devotion, and her love, did just as she had asked — they assumed the power to display their own distinctive marks.
She saw all the gods: unsweat­ing, with motionless eyes, their garlands fresh and untouched by dust, standing without touching the earth.
But Nala the Niṣadhan was revealed by contrast: he had a shadow beside him, his garland was wilted, he was covered in dust and sweat, he stood on the ground, and he blinked his eyes.
Having thus distinguished the gods from the glorious Nala, O Bhārata, the daughter of Bhīma chose the Niṣadhan as her husband in accordance with dharma.
With downcast eyes, blushing, she took hold of the hem of her garment; on his shoulder she placed a supremely beautiful garland, and thus the fair-complexioned lady chose him as her lord.
Then suddenly a great cry of "Alas, alas!" burst forth from the assembled kings; and the gods and great sages, filled with wonder and praising King Nala, cried out "Excellent! Excellent!" O Bhārata.
Once Bhīma's daughter had chosen the Niṣadhan, the world-guardians of great majesty, their hearts filled with joy, all granted Nala eight boons.
The lord of Śacī, Indra, delighted, granted to the Niṣadhan the gift of his direct visible presence at sacrifices and the most excellent and auspicious of goals in the afterlife.
Agni granted that he would arise wherever the Niṣadhan desired; and the fire-devourer gave him worlds radiant with Agni's own light.
Yama granted him the finest flavor of food and supreme steadiness in dharma; and the lord of waters granted him the presence of water wherever the Niṣadhan might wish.
All of them together gave him a garland richly laden with the finest fragrance, and also a pair of each gift. Having thus bestowed their boons upon him, those gods departed to the triple heaven.
The assembled kings, having witnessed her wedding, departed each to his own home filled with wonder and delight at Damayantī's choice.
Having won that jewel among women, the glorious king, that lord among men, rejoiced together with her, even as the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra delights with Śacī.
Exceedingly joyful, the king shone like the sun; that hero delighted his subjects, protecting them according to dharma.
The wise king also performed the horse-sacrifice, like Yayāti son of Nahuṣa, and many other rites with abundant sacrificial fees.
And again in charming forests and pleasure-groves, Nala, equal to the immortals, sported together with Damayantī.
Thus that lord of men, while performing sacrifices and taking his pleasures, protected the wealth-filled earth as lord of the earth.
Bṛhadaśva said: Now when the Niṣadhan had been chosen by Bhīma's daughter, the world-guardians of great majesty, as they were departing, saw Dvāpara and Kali approaching together.
Then Indra, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, regarding Kali with Dvāpara as his companion, spoke: "Kali, tell me — where are you going?"
Then Kali answered Indra: "I am going to Damayantī's svayaṃvara to choose her for myself, for my mind is set upon her."
Indra laughed and said to him: "That svayaṃvara is over. King Nala was chosen as her lord in our very presence."
Thus addressed by Indra, Kali was filled with rage; taking leave of all the gods, he then spoke these words:
"She who found her husband among humans in the very midst of the gods — surely it is right that she should receive a great and fitting punishment."
When Kali had spoken thus, the dwellers in heaven replied: "It was with our full consent that Nala was chosen by Damayantī."
"Who indeed would not seek shelter with King Nala, who is endowed with every virtue, who knows all the dharmas fully as they are, and who has always kept his vows?"
"In that tiger among men, that king equal to the world-guardians, truth, steadfastness, generosity, austerity, purity, self-control, and tranquility are all firmly established."
"He would be a fool who desired to curse such a one as Nala, O Kali; he would curse himself and destroy himself by his own hand."
"He would sink into a dreadful, fathomless, and boundless hell from which there is no escape." Having spoken thus to Kali and Dvāpara, the gods departed to heaven.
Then, when the gods had gone, Kali said to Dvāpara: "I cannot contain my anger; I will dwell within Nala, O Dvāpara."
"I will make him fall from his kingdom; he shall not enjoy happiness together with Bhīma's daughter. You too should enter into the dice and render your assistance."
Bṛhadaśva said: Having thus made this pact together with Dvāpara, Kali came to that place where King Nala of Niṣadha dwelt.
Watching constantly for an opportunity, he lived in Niṣadha for a long time; but only in the twelfth year did Kali find his opening.
One day the Niṣadhan, having urinated and touched water, sat for the twilight prayers without having purified his feet; and at that moment Kali entered into him.
Having entered into Nala, he went straightway to Puṣkara and said to him: "Come, let us play at dice with Nala."
"With me by your side you will defeat Nala at the game of dice; win back Niṣadha, O king, by defeating King Nala."
Thus instructed by Kali, Puṣkara approached Nala; and Kali himself, taking the form of a bull among cattle, accompanied Puṣkara.
Having reached the heroic Nala, Puṣkara the destroyer of enemy heroes, his brother, said again and again: "Let us play at dice" — urged on by the bull.
The great-souled king could not endure the challenge; with Vaidarbhī watching, he thought the time had come for staking his wager.
Possessed by Kali, Nala at that time was defeated at dice, losing silver, gold, vehicles, yoked animals, and garments.
Not one among his friends was able to restrain him as he played on, intoxicated with the madness of the dice, his mind utterly gone.
Then all the townspeople together with the ministers, O Bhārata, came to see the king, to restrain the one overcome by affliction.
Then the charioteer came up and reported to Damayantī: "All the townspeople stand at the door with urgent business."
"Let it be reported to the Niṣadhan that all his subjects stand here, unable to tolerate the calamity of the king who has always been a guardian of dharma and welfare."
Then she, Bhīma's daughter, wasted by sorrow, her mind struck by grief, spoke to the Niṣadhan in a voice choked with tears:
"O king, the townspeople stand at the door wishing to see you, accompanied by all the ministers, foremost in their devotion to the king. You should see them" — thus she spoke again and again.
But the king, possessed by Kali, said not a single word to her — that lovely-eyed, slender-waisted woman — as she lamented thus.
Then all those ministers and townspeople, afflicted with grief and ashamed, went home saying: "He is not himself anymore."
And so that gambling match between Puṣkara and Nala went on for many months, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and the glorious Nala continued to lose.
Bṛhadaśva said: Then Damayantī, herself sane though witnessing the glorious king, that lord among men, behaving like a madman with his mind entirely consumed by gambling,
overwhelmed by fear and grief, O king, the daughter of Bhīma then thought deeply about what great action needed to be taken concerning her husband.
Suspecting the evil that was at work, yet wishing to do what was best for him, perceiving Nala stripped of all his wealth, she spoke as follows:
"Bṛhatsenā, go and bring the ministers here under Nala's authority, and find out what property has been taken and what wealth remains."
Then all the ministers, having understood the command of Nala, said: "Perhaps there may yet be some portion for us" — and again they came to him.
When all the subjects had come a second time and Bhīma's daughter had reported it to him, he took no pleasure in it.
Seeing her husband taking no pleasure in what was said, Damayantī, ashamed, went back inside the house.
Having heard how the dice continually turned away from the glorious Nala, and seeing Nala stripped of everything, she again spoke to her nurse:
"Bṛhatsenā, go again; by Nala's authority bring the charioteer Vārṣṇeya here, O auspicious one — a great matter is at hand."
Hearing Damayantī's words, Bṛhatsenā brought Vārṣṇeya there with the help of trusted men of action.
Then Bhīma's daughter, knowing time and place, spoke fitting words to Vārṣṇeya with a soothing and gentle voice, that blameless one:
"You know how the king has always treated you rightly; now that he is in distress, you should render him your help."
"The more the king loses to Puṣkara here, the more his craving for the dice increases."
"Just as Puṣkara's dice obey his will, so too is the reverse seen in Nala's dice."
"He does not properly heed the words of his friends and kinsmen; I believe that nothing of the great-souled Niṣadhan remains."
"When the king, deluded, takes no pleasure even in my word, I take refuge in you, O charioteer — do as I say, for my heart cannot be set at rest with the thought that he might be destroyed."
"Harness Nala's beloved horses, those of great speed; place this pair of children upon the chariot and go to Kuṇḍina."
"Having entrusted the two children and also the chariot and these horses to my kinsmen, you may remain there as you please, or go elsewhere."
Vārṣṇeya, Nala's charioteer, reported all of Damayantī's words in full to the chief ministers of Nala.
Having met with them and decided, and having obtained permission from the ministers, O great king, he went to Vidarbha, having placed the pair upon that chariot.
Having deposited the horses there, and that finest of chariots, and the girl Indrasenā, and the boy Indrasena,
having taken leave of King Bhīma, distressed and grieving for King Nala, wandering about, the charioteer then went to the city of Ayodhyā.
Deeply distressed, he presented himself to King Ṛtuparṇa, O great king, and entered his service as a charioteer.
Bṛhadaśva said: Then, after Vārṣṇeya had departed while the glorious one was still gambling, Puṣkara won away his kingdom and whatever other wealth remained.
Laughing, Puṣkara said to Nala, whose kingdom had been taken: "Let the gambling continue; what stake do you still have to wager, O king?"
"Only Damayantī remains to you; everything else has been won by me. Wager Damayantī — it would be good if you think so."
When Puṣkara had spoken thus to the glorious Nala, his heart seemed to split asunder with rage, yet he said not a word to him.
Then Nala, the greatly famous, looking at Puṣkara, his rage at its peak, stripped the ornaments from all his limbs.
Clad in a single garment, unadorned, increasing the grief of his friends, the king then departed, abandoning his vast splendour.
Damayantī, wearing a single garment, followed him as he went. Together with her, the king of Niṣadha dwelt outside the city for three nights.
But Puṣkara, O great king, proclaimed throughout the city: "Whoever properly attends to Nala, let him be put to death on my order."
By Puṣkara's command and out of their own hostility, the citizens showed no honour to him, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus deserving of honour yet receiving none, the king stayed near the city for three nights, subsisting on water alone.
Tormented by hunger after many days, Nala saw certain birds with wings that gleamed like gold.
The mighty lord of Niṣadha thought to himself: "Today there is food for me; this wealth shall be mine."
Then he spread his lower garment over them; but taking his garment, they all flew up into the sky.
As those birds soared up, they addressed Nala, seeing him standing on the ground, bereft of clothes, wretched, head bowed.
"We are the dice, O foolish one! We came desiring to steal your garment. For we have no joy so long as you depart still clothed."
Watching the dice depart and finding himself naked, the glorious king Puṇyaśloka then spoke to Damayantī.
"Through the wrath of those by whom I was deprived of sovereignty, O blameless one, I find no means of sustenance, afflicted and tormented by hunger.
On whose account the people of Niṣadha showed me no honour — those same ones, having become birds, have now stolen even my garment.
Having fallen into the most extreme adversity, afflicted, my mind undone — I am your husband; hear now this counsel that is for your own good.
These many roads go toward the southern country, to Avanti and, passing beyond, to the Ṛkṣavat mountain.
Here is the great mountain Vindhya, and the Payoṣṇī flowing to the ocean, and yonder are the hermitages of the great sages, adorned with flowers and fruit.
This is the road to Vidarbha; this one goes to the Kosalas; and beyond that lies this region in the south, the southern highway."
Then she, her voice choked with tears, emaciated by sorrow, Damayantī spoke these piteous words to the king of Niṣadha:
"My heart trembles and all my limbs sink down as I think again and again of your intention, O lord of the earth.
Your kingdom taken, your wealth taken, stripped of garments, beset with hunger and exhaustion — how could I abandon you and go, alone in the desolate forest?
For you who are weary, tormented by hunger, seeking that happiness — in this dreadful forest, O great king, I will dispel your fatigue.
There is nothing equal to a wife as a remedy in all sufferings — so say the physicians; this is the truth, I tell you."
Nala said: "It is exactly as you say, Damayantī of slender waist; there is no friend equal to a wife as a remedy for a man in distress.
Nor am I wishing to abandon you; why do you fear, timid one? I would abandon myself, but never you, O blameless one."
Damayantī said: "If you do not wish to abandon me, O great king, then why do you keep pointing out the road to Vidarbha?"
"I understand, O lord of men; you ought not to abandon me. Yet with a mind drawn away you would forsake me, O great lord.
For you keep telling me the road again and again, O best of men; by this you increase my grief, O one of godlike radiance.
And if this is your intention, O king, that we should go, then let us go to Vidarbha together, if you think it right.
The king of Vidarbha will honour you there, O giver of honour; honoured by him, O king, you will dwell happily in our home."
Nala said: "Your father's kingdom is as much mine — there is no doubt of that. Yet I will not go there in any manner while I am in this wretched state.
How, going there in prosperity, would I increase your joy? Ruined at the dice, I would only go to increase your sorrow."
Bṛhadaśva said: Saying this, king Nala consoled Damayantī again and again — that noble woman who was now covered with only half a garment.
The two of them, wrapped in a single garment, wandering here and there, exhausted by hunger and thirst, came to some kind of shelter.
Having reached that hall, the lord of Niṣadha sat down upon the bare ground together with the daughter of Vidarbha.
Naked, dirty, hair dishevelled, caked with dust, exhausted, he fell asleep on the ground together with Damayantī.
Damayantī too, that virtuous and tender woman, the wretched one, was suddenly carried off by sleep after encountering such misery.
But while Damayantī slept, O lord of the people, king Nala, his mind and heart churned by grief, could not sleep as before.
He, contemplating the seizure of his kingdom, the complete desertion of his friends, and that ruin in the forest, gave himself over to brooding.
"What would come of my doing this? What would come of my not doing it? Would death be better for me, or abandonment of this person?
This devoted wife suffers this misery on my account; but freed from me, she might at some point return to her own people.
With me, this incomparable woman will undoubtedly meet suffering; but in abandonment there would be uncertainty — she might even find happiness somewhere."
Having deliberated in many ways and weighed it again and again, the lord of men decided that abandonment was better for Damayantī.
Having thought of his own nakedness and of her single garment, the king resolved on cutting off half of that garment.
"How can I cut the garment without my beloved waking?" Thinking thus, the king of Niṣadha paced about the hall.
As Nala ran about here and there, O descendant of Bharata, he came upon an excellent sword, unsheathed, in a corner of the hall.
Having cut half the garment with it and donned it, the scorcher of foes fled away, out of his senses, abandoning the sleeping daughter of Vidarbha.
Then, his heart drawn back, the lord of Niṣadha returned to that hall and, seeing Damayantī lying there thus, wept.
"She whom neither the wind nor the sun formerly beheld — my beloved — she today lies on the floor in the midst of this hall as if without a protector.
She who is beautiful in her smiles, of lovely limbs, now wrapped in a half-cut garment — how will she be when she awakens, like one who has lost her reason?
How will the virtuous and auspicious daughter of Bhīma, separated from me, wander alone in this dreadful forest haunted by beasts and serpents?"
Going away and then returning to the hall again and again, king Nala was pulled back by Kali and pulled away by affection.
His heart seemed as if split in two in his anguish; like a swing it came and went, returning to the hall again and again.
But then, drawn away by Kali and bewildered, Nala fled, having lamented much in pitiable fashion and abandoned his sleeping wife.
His self destroyed, touched by Kali, the king, calculating this and that, went on into the empty forest, sorrowfully abandoning his wife.
Bṛhadaśva said: After Nala had departed, O king, Damayantī of lovely limbs awoke, her fatigue gone, frightened, in the desolate forest.
Not seeing her husband, overcome with pain and grief, she cried out aloud in fear: "O great king!" calling for the king of Niṣadha.
"Alas, my lord! Alas, great king! Alas, my master — why do you abandon me? I am undone, I am destroyed, I am afraid in this desolate forest!"
"Surely, O great king, you are one who knows righteousness and speaks truth — how then, having spoken such vows, have you gone off abandoning me in my sleep?
How can you abandon your devoted, obedient wife and go — especially when no wrong was done by another, or when wrong was done?
Will you be able to make true, O lord of men, those words you once spoke in the presence of the world-guardians on my behalf?
"This much jest is enough, O bull among men; I am afraid, O invincible one — show yourself, O lord.
I see you, I see you, O king — you stand there, O king of Niṣadha, concealing yourself behind the bushes — why do you not speak to me?
How cruel it is, O lord of kings, that you do not embrace me here in this condition, weeping, and comfort me, O king!
I do not grieve for myself, nor for anything else — it is for you that I grieve, O king, thinking of how you will fare all alone.
How will you be, O king, in the evening — thirsty, hungry, wasted by fatigue — at the roots of trees, not seeing me?"
Then she, afflicted with sharp grief, blazing as it were with anger, ran about this way and that, weeping, sorrowful.
Now the young woman leaps up, now she falls down, distraught; now she cowers in fear; now she cries out and weeps.
She, scorched by fierce grief, sighing again and again, distraught, the devoted wife of Bhīma's line, went outside weeping and spoke:
"By whose curse the king of Niṣadha, afflicted with misery, suffers this pain — let that being suffer pain even greater than this.
The wicked one who has done this to Nala, innocent of heart — may he, meeting a suffering greater than this, live a life bereft of happiness."
Thus lamenting, that wife of the great-souled king searched for her husband in the forest haunted by wild beasts.
The daughter of Bhīma, like one gone mad, lamenting here and there, crying "Ah! Ah! O king!" again and again, ran to and fro.
Her, withering excessively, crying like an osprey, grieving pitifully, lamenting again and again —
— the daughter of Bhīma, who had suddenly come near and was moving about close by, was seized by a great serpent of immense body, hungry.
She, being devoured by the serpent, overwhelmed by grief, did not grieve for herself as much as she grieved for the king of Niṣadha.
"O lord, I am being devoured here in the forest, helpless, by this serpent in the wilderness — why do you not run to me?
How will you be hereafter, O king of Niṣadha, when you remember me — freed from evil, having recovered your understanding, your mind, and your wealth?
For you who are weary, tormented by hunger, exhausted, O king of Niṣadha — who will dispel your fatigue, O tiger among kings, O giver of honour?"
Then a hunter, roaming in the dense forest, suddenly heard her crying out and rushed toward her swiftly.
Seeing her thus seized by the serpent, she of large eyes, the hunter quickly stepped forward, hastening toward her.
The hunter, having cut it apart, struck the serpent's head with his sharp blade, knocking the motionless snake to the ground.
The hunter freed her, washed her with water, and having comforted her and given her food, he then questioned her, O Bhārata.
"Whose are you, O doe-eyed one? How did you come to this forest? And how have you arrived at this great calamity, O lovely lady?"
Damayantī, thus questioned by him, O lord of peoples, narrated to him everything exactly as it had occurred, O Bhārata.
Her — clad in only half a garment, with full hips and breasts, tender-limbed and blameless of form, her face like the full moon —
— with curving-lashed eyes, and sweet of speech — the deer-hunter, beholding her, fell under the sway of desire.
Then the hunter, tormented by desire, began to soothe her with smooth and gentle words; but the proud lady perceived it.
But Damayantī, a devoted wife, perceiving that wicked man, was seized with fierce anger and blazed up as it were with fury.
That vile man of evil mind, eager to violate her, reckoned her as one to be overpowered — like a blazing tongue of flame.
But Damayantī, afflicted with grief, bereft of husband and kingdom, at the right moment — when speech was beyond him — cursed him in her wrath.
"As I have never thought of any man other than Naiṣadha, even in my mind, so let this vile hunter fall dead!"
The very moment the words were spoken by her, that hunter fell to the earth lifeless, like a tree struck by lightning.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having slain the deer-hunter, she of lotus eyes set out into the forest — terrible, desolate, and resounding with swarms of crickets.
It was haunted by lions, tigers, boars, bears, deer, and leopards, thronged with flocks of various birds, and frequented by barbarians and bandits.
It was covered with śāla, bamboo, dhava, aśvattha, tinduka, iṅguda, and kiṃśuka trees, with arjuna and ariṣṭa, with sandalwood and śālmalī.
It was crowded with jambu, mango, lodhra, khadira, śāka, and vetasa, and encircled with kāśmarī, āmalaka, plakṣa, kadamba, and udumbara trees.
It was covered with badarī and bilva, thick with nyagrodha trees, and filled with priyāla, tāla, kharjūra, harītakī, and bibhītaka.
She saw mountains bound with hundreds of various ores, diverse groves resounding with birds, caves of wondrous appearance, rivers, lakes, wells, and various animals and birds.
She beheld many fearsome piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas, marshes and ponds, mountain peaks in every direction, and rivers and seas — all wonderful to behold.
And there the daughter of Vidarbha's king beheld, in herds, buffaloes, boars, jackals, bears, monkeys, and serpents.
Endowed with splendor, renown, steadfastness, and supreme beauty, the princess of Vidarbha wandered alone, then, searching for Nala.
That princess, daughter of Bhīma, entering that dreadful forest, was not afraid of anything there, though worn by her husband's misfortune.
The daughter of Vidarbha, O king, wailed in deep sorrow, her body consumed by grief for her husband, leaning against a flat rock.
Damayantī said: "O lion-chested, mighty-armed lord of the Niṣadha people — where have you gone, O king, leaving me in this deserted forest?"
"O hero, O tiger among men, having performed horse-sacrifices and other rites with full sacrificial fees — how do you now act falsely toward me?"
"That which you spoke, O tiger among men, of great splendor, in my presence — you should make that true, O auspicious one, O bull among kings."
"What was spoken by the geese, those birds, in your presence, O lord of earth, and what they said in my presence — that you should bear in mind."
"The four Vedas in full, with all their supplements and appendices, well studied, O best of men, weigh equally on one side; but Truth alone weighs on the other."
"Therefore you should make truth your deed, O destroyer of foes, O lord of men — do what you, O hero, once declared in my presence."
"Alas, O hero! Was I not truly dear to you, O sinless one? Why do you not speak to me in this dreadful forest?"
"This fierce lord of the forest, with gaping jaws and terrible form, hunger-maddened, threatens me — why do you not protect me?"
"'There is no one dear to me other than you, O fortunate one' — so you said then. Make those words true, O auspicious king."
"O lord of men, O my desired lord, why do you not speak to me — your beloved wife, distraught and wailing?"
"Emaciated, wretched, pale, and soiled, O lord of earth, clad in half a garment, alone, wailing like one without protector —"
"— like a doe separated from her herd, O wide-eyed one — why do you not regard me weeping, O crusher of foes, though you are worthy of honor?"
"O great king, in this great forest, why do you not speak to your devoted wife who calls out to you, left here alone?"
"Endowed with noble lineage and character, beautiful in every limb — I do not see you today, O best of men, on this mountain or in this dreadful forest frequented by lions and tigers."
"Whether lying down, or sitting, or standing, O lord of Niṣadha, or departing, O best of men — you are the one who increases my grief."
"Whom shall I ask, afflicted with sorrow, wasted by grief for your sake — 'Have you seen king Nala anywhere in this forest?'"
"Who today will tell me of Nala — handsome, noble-souled, destroyer of enemy arrays — dwelling in this forest?"
"The king Nala whom you seek, he of lotus-like eyes — whose sweet voice shall I hear today saying, 'Here he is'?"
"This glorious lord of the forest, the tiger with four fangs and great jaws, comes toward me — I shall question him without fear."
"You are the lord of beasts, the master of this forest — know me as Damayantī, the daughter of the king of Vidarbha."
"The wife of Nala, lord of Niṣadha, slayer of enemies — alone, wretched, worn by grief, seeking her husband — comfort her, O king of beasts, if you have seen Nala."
"Or else, O lord of the forest, if you do not tell me of Nala, then devour me, O best of beasts, and free this grieving one from sorrow."
Having heard my lament in the forest, the king of beasts himself goes away toward that clear-watered river flowing to the sea.
"This holy mountain with its many peaks, lofty, gleaming, sky-touching, of varied colors and lovely —"
"— filled with various ores, adorned with diverse gems, rising like a banner of this great forest —"
"— filled with lions, tigers, elephants, boars, bears, and deer, resounding on all sides with many kinds of birds —"
"— adorned with kiṃśuka, aśoka, bakula, and puṃnāga trees, beautified with bird-filled rivers and peaks — this king of mountains I shall now question concerning the king."
"O blessed best of mountains, of divine appearance, famous, a refuge, full of blessings — homage to you, O upholder of the earth!"
"I bow to you in approach — know me as a princess, daughter-in-law of a king, wife of a king, known by the name Damayantī."
"My father is the king, lord of Vidarbha, a great warrior — the lord of the earth named Bhīma, protector of the four social orders."
"The best of kings, he has performed rājasūya and aśvamedha sacrifices with full fees; broad and lovely are his slightly upturned eyes."
"He is devoted to Brāhmaṇas, of virtuous conduct, truthful, free from envy, of good character, well-behaved, of broad glory, learned in dharma, and pure."
"He is the proper guardian of the Vidarbhas, the lord who has conquered all enemies — know me, O blessed one, as his daughter who has come to you."
"Among the Niṣadhas, O great mountain, my father-in-law is the best of kings, of auspicious name — famous as Vīrasena."
"His son is a hero, glorious, of true valor, who duly governs the kingdom that properly passed to him from his father."
"He is called Nala, subduer of foes, renowned as Puṇyaśloka — devoted to Brāhmaṇas, learned in the Vedas, eloquent, doer of righteous deeds, drinker of soma, builder of sacred fires."
"He is a sacrificer, a giver, a warrior, and a righteous ruler — know me, O best of mountains, as his wife who has come here."
"I am bereft of fortune, husbandless, without protector, beset by misfortune, searching for that best of men, my husband."
"With these hundreds of peaks that scrape the sky — have you seen the king, O best of mountains, in this dreadful forest? Has Nala been seen by you?"
"My husband — of the prowess of a lordly elephant, wise, long-armed, intolerant of insult, valiant, truthful, steadfast, of great renown, lord of the Niṣadhas — has he, Nala, been seen by you?"
"Why do you not comfort me with your voice today, O best of mountains, wailing alone in sorrow, as a father would his grieving daughter?"
"O hero, O valiant one, O knower of dharma, O king of steadfast truth — if you are in this forest, O king, reveal yourself by yourself."
"When shall I hear that affectionate, deep voice of the Niṣadha king, resembling the sound of a cloud — that speech of his, like nectar?"
"That auspicious speech of the noble king, simply saying 'O Vaidarbhī,' flowing like a sacred text, rich, the destroyer of my grief?"
Having spoken thus to that best of mountains, the princess Damayantī, daughter of a king, then set off again toward the northern direction.
After traveling for three days and nights, that most excellent of women beheld an incomparable hermit-forest, of divine woodland appearance.
It was adorned by ascetics equal to Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Atri — disciplined, controlled in diet, possessed of self-restraint and purity.
Among them were those who subsisted on water, those who lived on air, and those who ate only leaves — masters of their senses, greatly blessed, desirous of seeing the path to heaven.
She beheld a lovely hermitage-grove, inhabited by ascetics, sages clad in bark garments and hides, with restrained senses.
Seeing the hermitage frequented by various animals, thronged with troops of monkeys, and accompanied by ascetics —
— she of beautiful brows, lovely hair, shapely hips, fine breasts, and beautiful teeth-adorned face, radiant, of noble bearing, moving with a graceful, lofty gait —
— she, the beloved wife of Vīrasena's son, a gem of womanhood, greatly blessed, the spirited Damayantī, entered that hermitage.
She greeted the elders in austerity and stood with bowed reverence; all the ascetics there welcomed her, saying, "Welcome."
The wealth-in-austerity ascetics honored her duly, then said, "Be seated" and "Tell us — what may we do for you?"

The lovely-hipped one asked them: "O sinless ones, O greatly blessed ones, is all well with you here — in your austerities, sacred fires, in dharma, among the animals and birds, and in the practice of your own dharma?"
Told by them that all was well, O fortunate one, the renowned and perfectly-limbed one was addressed: "Tell us — who are you, and what do you wish to do?"
"On seeing your supreme beauty and supreme radiance here, wonder has arisen in us — take courage, do not grieve."
Are you the great deity of this forest, or of this mountain, or of this river? O auspicious one, O blameless one, tell us the truth.
She said to those sages: I am not the deity of this forest, O brahmins, nor of this mountain, nor of this river — I am no deity at all.
Know me as a mortal woman, all of you who are rich in austerity. I shall tell you at length — listen to me fully.
In Vidarbha there is a great king named Bhīma, blazing in glory. Know me as his daughter, O best of the twice-born.
The wise lord of Niṣadha, famed Nala of great renown, a hero victorious in battle, a learned man — he is my husband, the lord of his people.
Devoted to the worship of the gods, affectionate toward the twice-born, the protector of the Niṣadha lineage — he is greatly fortunate and blazing in splendor.
Truthful in speech, knowing dharma, wise, true to his vows, a crusher of enemies, devoted to brahmins and to the gods, glorious, a conqueror of enemy cities.
Nala, best of kings, resplendent as the king of gods — he is my husband, wide-eyed, with a face like the full moon, a slayer of foes.
A performer of the foremost sacrifices, master of the Vedas and their auxiliaries, a slayer of rivals in battle, shining like the sun and moon together.
That king, devoted to truth and dharma, was challenged by certain wicked and base men skilled in deceit, and defeated in gambling by those crooked ones — he lost his kingdom and his wealth.
Know me as the wife of that bull among kings — Damayantī, famous by name, longing to behold her husband.
I have been searching through forests and mountains, through lakes and rivers, through pleasant marshes and forests everywhere —
— seeking my husband Nala, skilled in battle, great-souled, versed in arms; I wander here in grief.
Has king Nala, lord of the Niṣādas, perhaps come to this holy hermitage of your lordships?
For his sake, O brahmins, I have entered this exceedingly terrible forest — frightful, dreadful, haunted by tigers and wild beasts.
If within some days and nights I do not find King Nala, I shall join myself to what is best — I shall release myself from this body.
What is the purpose of my life without that bull among men? How shall I go on, I who am afflicted today by grief for my husband?
While the daughter of Bhīma, Damayantī, lamented thus alone in the forest, those truthful ascetics then spoke to her.
"Auspicious will be your outcome, O auspicious one, O fortunate one — we see this through our austerities. You will swiftly behold the Niṣāda king."
"You will see Nala, lord of the Niṣādas, slayer of enemies, O daughter of Bhīma, best among those who uphold dharma — your fever of grief will be gone."
"Freed from all sins, endowed with every jewel, ruling that same foremost of cities, the subduer of enemies —
— striking fear into his foes, dispelling grief for his friends — you shall see your husband, O auspicious one, that king of auspicious lineage."
Having spoken thus to the beloved queen of Nala, daughter of a king, those ascetics vanished then — along with their sacred fires and hermitage.
Damayantī of flawless limbs, daughter-in-law of King Vīrasena, was filled with wonder at witnessing that great marvel.
"Was this a dream I saw? What has happened here? Where have all those ascetics gone? Where is that hermitage?"
"Where is that lovely river of holy waters frequented by many birds? And where are those charming trees adorned with fruits and flowers?"
Having reflected long, the daughter of Bhīma, Damayantī of bright smile, overcome with grief for her husband, became wretched, her face pale.
Moving on to another place, her voice choked with tears, her eyes brimming with weeping, she lamented upon seeing an ashoka tree.
She approached that finest of trees, the ashoka, then in bloom, bending with new shoots, lovely, resonant with birds.
"Ah, how this tree shines glorious in the depths of this forest, radiant with its many garlands of blossoms, like the glorious king of the Dravidians!"
"Free me quickly from grief, O ashoka, O fair to behold — have you seen the king who is himself freed from grief, fear, and affliction?"
"Have you seen Nala, the subduer of enemies, the beloved husband of Damayantī, the lord of the Niṣādas — my beloved?"
"Clad in half a single garment, with a body and skin delicate as a child's, that hero tormented by misfortune who has come to this forest?"
"Do that whereby I may go without grief — O ashoka tree, be true to your name, cause the destruction of my sorrow!"
Having thus circumambulated that ashoka tree three times in her distress, that most excellent woman, daughter of Bhīma, went on to a still more fearsome place.
She saw many trees and many rivers, many lovely mountains and many beasts and birds.
She saw ravines and mountain slopes and streams of wondrous appearance — all this the daughter of Bhīma beheld as she searched for her husband.
Having traveled a great distance, Damayantī of bright smile then saw a great caravan teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots.
It was crossing a lovely river with clear and auspicious waters — cool, broad, lake-like, bordered by cane reeds.
The river rang with the cries of cranes and curlews, cooed over by ruddy geese, filled with turtles, crocodiles, and fish, adorned with sandbars and islands.
The glorious wife of Nala, that woman of shapely hips, upon seeing the great caravan, approached it and entered among the people.
She looked like a madwoman, afflicted by grief, covered only by half a garment, gaunt, discolored, dirty, her hair matted with dust.
On seeing her there, some of the people fled in fear, others stood lost in thought, and some cried out.
Some laughed at her, others showed disdain; some felt pity for her; and others asked her questions, O Bhārata.
"Who are you? Whose are you, O auspicious one? What do you seek in this forest? We are troubled at the sight of you — are you perhaps a mortal woman?"
"Tell us truly — are you the deity of this forest, or of this mountain, or of one of the directions? O auspicious one, we take refuge in you."
"Are you a yakshini, or a rakshasi, or perhaps a most excellent woman? In any case, grant us well-being and protect us, O blameless one."
"Arrange things so that this entire caravan may depart from here safely and quickly, O auspicious one — we take refuge in you."
Thus addressed by the caravan, the virtuous Damayantī, daughter of a king, afflicted by grief over her husband's misfortune, then replied to the caravan leader, the caravan, and all who were there.
"Young, old, and children, and leaders of the caravan — know me as a mortal woman, daughter of a lord of men, daughter-in-law of a king, wife of a king, longing to behold my husband."
"My father is the king of Vidarbha; my husband is the king of Niṣadha — Nala by name, greatly fortunate. I search for that unconquered one."
"If you know the king, quickly tell me of my beloved — Nala, tiger among kings, slayer of troops of enemies."
The lord of the great caravan, the caravan leader named Shuchi, spoke to her of flawless limbs: "Hear my words, O auspicious one."
"I am the leader and guide of this caravan, O bright-smiling one. I see no man by the name of Nala, O glorious one."
"I see elephants, rhinoceroses, buffaloes, tigers, bears, and deer in this harsh forest uninhabited by humans; even so, may Maṇibhadra, king of yakshas, be gracious to us now."
She then said to all the merchants and to that caravan leader: "Where is this caravan going? Please tell me that."
The caravan leader said: "This caravan will soon go to the realm of Subāhu, the truth-speaking king of Cedi, for the purpose of profit, O daughter of a lord of men."
Bṛhadaśva said: She of flawless limbs, having heard those words of the caravan leader, then set out with him, longing to behold her husband.
Then after many days, in the great and dreadful forest, they came upon a large lake, auspicious on all sides, fragrant with lotuses.
The merchants saw it was lovely, abounding in fodder and fuel, richly supplied with roots and fruits, thronged with flocks of various birds.
Seeing it with its clear and pleasant waters, charming and comfortable, they — their draft animals thoroughly weary — set their minds to making camp.
With the caravan leader's approval, they entered that excellent forest grove; the great caravan settled in at the approach of evening.
Then at midnight, in the stillness and silence, while the caravan lay exhausted and asleep, a herd of elephants came to drink from a mountain stream turbid with the flow of their rut.
Blocking the path, the herd suddenly trampled the sleeping, thrashing caravan where it lay upon the ground near the lotus lake.

The caravan folk, crying out in lamentation and seeking refuge, fled into the forest thickets, blind with sleep and overwhelmed by the great fear; some men were killed by tusks, some by trunks, some by feet.
Crowded with oxen, donkeys, camels, and horses, thick with foot soldiers, that mass of people fled in terror, striking against one another.
Uttering terrible cries they fell to the earth, dashed against trees and broken, fallen on uneven ground — so the entire prosperous company of that caravan was destroyed.
When the next day came, the survivors emerged from the forest thickets, lamenting the slaughter — a brother, a father, a son, a companion, O lord of men.

There Damayantī of Vidarbha grieved: "What evil deed have I done, that even this ocean of people that came to me in the deserted forest has been slain by the elephant herd — on account of my wretched fate?"
"Surely I am destined to suffer grief for a long time without doubt — one does not die before one's appointed time; this is what the teaching of the elders says."
"That I today, wretched as I am, was not trampled by the elephant herd — nothing that happens to men here is not wrought by fate."
"Not even in childhood did I do any wrong by act, thought, or word that could have brought this suffering upon me."
"I think the world-guardians who assembled at my svayamvara, the gods whom I rejected there for Nala's sake — surely by their power I have come to this separation."
Having lamented thus and more, that most excellent woman, wholly given over to grief and sorrow, went on with the survivors — brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, O tiger among kings.
Traveling on after a long time, she reached at evening a great city — the foremost of cities of the truth-speaking king of Cedi, Subāhu — and entered it, covered in half a garment.
The city's inhabitants saw her walking — pale, thin, wretched, her hair loose and ungroomed — looking like a madwoman.
Seeing her entering the city of the Cedi king, the village boys and children followed after her out of curiosity.
Surrounded by them, she came near the royal palace; the queen mother, standing on the palace terrace, saw her encircled by the crowd.
She, O king, having turned away that crowd and brought Damayantī up to the excellent palace terrace, asked her in wonder:
"Even afflicted as you are by unhappiness, you bear a supreme beauty; you shine like lightning among clouds. Tell me, who are you and whose are you?"
For your form is not merely human — even without ornaments you are not alarmed, unaccompanied, before men, O one who has the splendour of an immortal.
