Hearing those words, the daughter of Bhīma spoke in reply: Know me as a human woman, wholly devoted to following my husband.
I am a skilled sairandhrī attendant, a free woman living by choice, subsisting on fruits and roots alone, sheltering wherever evening finds me.
My husband is of virtues beyond counting, and he was ever faithful to me; I too followed that hero like his own shadow, never departing.
By fate an excessive addiction to gaming came upon him; defeated at dice, he went alone into the forest.
Comforting that hero, clad in a single garment, distraught and seeming maddened, I followed my husband into the forest.
Then that hero, overcome with hunger in the forest for some other reason, deeply troubled in mind, even cast away that one garment.
Following him — naked, having shed his single garment, maddened, bereft of his senses — I spent many nights without sleep.
Then, after a long while, he abandoned me as I lay sleeping — cutting off half the garment, he forsook me, blameless though I was.
Searching for that husband, burning with grief through days and nights, I cannot find my beloved — he who is like an immortal, the lord of my life and wealth.
Seeing her weeping, her eyes filled with tears, lamenting greatly — the queen mother, herself deeply distressed, spoke to the anguished daughter of Bhīma.
Dwell with me, O auspicious one — my heart goes out to you; O fortunate lady, my men will search for your husband.
Or perhaps he himself will come, wandering here and there; staying here, dear one, you will meet your husband.
Hearing the queen mother's words, Damayantī replied: I am willing to stay with you, O mother of heroes, but only on certain conditions.
I will never eat leavings, nor wash the feet of others, nor will I converse with any man under any circumstance.
Should any man importune me, let him be punished by you; but to seek my husband I should be permitted to meet with brahmin men.
If these conditions can be observed here, I will stay without doubt; otherwise, to remain anywhere holds no place in my heart.
With a gladdened heart the queen mother spoke to her: All this I will grant — how fortunate is your vow of such a kind!
Having spoken thus to the daughter of Bhīma, O lord of the people, the queen mother then addressed her daughter named Sunandā, O Bhārata.
Know this sairandhrī, O Sunandā, as one whose form is divine; rejoice freely with her, your heart at ease.
Bṛhadaśva said: After abandoning Damayantī, O lord of the people, king Nala beheld a great forest fire blazing in the deep woods.
There in the midst of the fire he heard the voice of some creature crying out loudly, again and again: "Run here, Nala! O Puṇyaśloka!"
Saying "Fear not!" Nala entered into the midst of the fire and saw the king of serpents lying there, coiled in a ring.
That serpent, joining his palms in supplication and trembling, then spoke to Nala: Know me, O king, as the serpent Karkoṭaka, O lord.
I deceived a sinless brahmin seer of great ascetic power; enraged by that, he cursed me, O lord of men.
Because of his curse I cannot move a single step from this spot; I will point out the path of good to you — you should rescue me.
I will become your ally — there is no serpent equal to me; I will make myself light — quickly take me up and go.
Having said this, the lord of serpents shrank to the size of a thumb; taking him up, Nala proceeded toward a region free of the forest fire.
Having reached an open place, free from the dark-pathed fire, as Nala was about to release him, the serpent Karkoṭaka spoke again.
Go counting your own steps, O Naiṣadha — a certain number; there, O great king, I will bestow on you the highest good.
Then, as Nala began to count, the serpent bit him at the tenth step; the form of the bitten man quickly vanished.
Nala stood astonished to behold himself transformed; the lord of the earth saw that the serpent now bore his own natural form.
Then the serpent Karkoṭaka, consoling Nala, said: I have concealed your appearance so that people may not recognise you.
He for whose sake you have been transformed and suffered great grief — that one, through my venom now lodged within you, will dwell in torment.
So long as he does not release you, the venom pervading your limbs will persist in him, O great king — he shall abide in suffering.
By him who wronged you without cause, O lord of men — undeservedly, out of jealousy and anger — you were deceived; this protection I have now rendered you.
You shall have no fear, O tiger among men, from fanged creatures, from enemies, or from those learned in sacred lore — by my grace, O lord of men.
By reason of my venom, O king, no affliction shall come to you; and in battles, O lord of kings, you shall always win victory.

Go from here, O king, presenting yourself as a charioteer saying "I am Bāhuka," to the court of Ṛtuparṇa — for he knows the science of dice — into the lovely city of Ayodhyā, this very day, O lord of Niṣadha.
That glorious king, born in the Ikṣvāku line, will give you the secret of dice in exchange for the secret of horses, and will become your friend.

When you have mastered the lore of dice you will be joined with good fortune; then you will be reunited with your wife — do not give your mind to grief — and with your kingdom and your children. I speak the truth to you.
And when you wish to behold your true form, O lord of men, you must remember me then and put on this garment.
Clothed in this garment you will recover your own form — so saying, he then bestowed upon him a divine pair of garments.
Having thus instructed Nala and given him the garments, O Kaurava, the king of serpents then vanished from that very spot, O king.
Bṛhadaśva said: When the serpent had vanished, Naiṣadha Nala set forth and entered the city of Ṛtuparṇa on the tenth day.
He presented himself to the king, saying "I am Bāhuka"; in the driving of horses on this earth there is none my equal.
In matters of difficulty and in the arts, I am also worth consulting; in the preparation of food I have skill that surpasses others.
Whatever crafts exist in this world and whatever else is hard to accomplish, I will strive to do it all — employ me, Ṛtuparṇa.
Ṛtuparṇa said: Stay, Bāhuka, good fortune to you; you shall do all of this — in the matter of swift driving my thoughts are especially fixed.
You therefore apply your skill so that my horses may be swift; you are superintendent of horses — your wages are a hundred of hundreds.
These two, Vārṣṇeya and Jīvala, shall constantly attend upon you; you shall find enjoyment in their company — stay with me, Bāhuka.
Bṛhadaśva said: Thus addressed by him, Nala dwelt there, honoured, in the city of Ṛtuparṇa, together with Vārṣṇeya and Jīvala.
Dwelling there, the king, brooding constantly on the daughter of Vidarbha, would sing this one verse aloud each and every evening.
Where now does she lie — weary, afflicted by hunger and thirst, that suffering woman — remembering that foolish one? Whom does she approach today for shelter?
Hearing the king speak thus in the night, Jīvala said: For whom do you grieve constantly? I wish to hear, Bāhuka.
King Nala replied to him: There was a woman dearly beloved of some fool of poor understanding; he was deeply devoted to her.
That fool was separated from her on some account; parted from her, that feeble-spirited one wanders, tormented by unhappiness.
Burning with grief day and night without rest, he sings this one verse in the night watches, remembering her.
Wandering over the whole earth, he has settled somewhere upon obtaining something — undeservedly, remembering again and again that same sorrow.
That woman who had followed that man even into the hardship of the forest — abandoned by that man of little merit — if she still lives, it is a hard thing.
Alone, inexperienced, unfit for such ways, overcome with hunger and thirst — if she still lives, it is a hard thing.
In the great and dreadful forest frequented always by beasts of prey, abandoned by that feeble-minded man of little merit — O dear one.
Thus it was that king Naiṣadha, ceaselessly remembering Damayantī, lived incognito in the residence of that king.
Bṛhadaśva said: After Nala, with his kingdom lost, had gone into servitude along with his wife, Bhīma sent forth brahmin men, longing for news of Nala.
Bhīma instructed them and gave them abundant wealth, saying: Seek out both Nala and my daughter Damayantī.
When this task is accomplished and the lord of Niṣadha is found — to him among you who brings them both, I will give a thousand cattle, and I will also grant a village the size of a city.
And if Damayantī or Nala cannot be brought here, even for merely finding where they are I will give ten hundred cattle as wealth.
Thus instructed, those brahmin men went out joyfully in all directions, searching cities and kingdoms for Naiṣadha together with his wife.
Then a brahmin named Sudeva, searching the lovely city of Cedi, saw the daughter of Vidarbha standing in the royal palace at the auspicious recitation of the king, together with Sunandā.
Though her peerless beauty shone but dimly, she was like the radiance of the sun shrouded in a net of smoke.
Closely observing her — wide-eyed, exceedingly soiled, emaciated — he concluded by reasoned inference that this was the daughter of Bhīma.
Sudeva said: This woman is exactly as I saw her before; I have achieved my purpose today in beholding this one who is like Śrī, beloved of all the world.
Her face is like the full moon, she is dark of complexion, her breasts beautifully rounded; by her radiance, O goddess, she renders all directions free of darkness.
Her eyes are lovely as lotus petals; she is like Rati, the beloved of Manmatha; beloved of all the world, she shines like the radiance of the full moon.
She seems like a lotus stalk snatched from that lake of Vidarbha by the fault of fate, her limbs smeared heavily with the mud of filth.
She is like a full-moon night when the moon is swallowed by Rāhu; overwhelmed with grief for her husband, wretched, she is like a river with dried-up streams.
She is like a lotus pond whose leaf-lotuses are ruined, whose birds have been frightened away, and which has been crushed by an elephant's trunk — agitated and distressed.
She is tender, her limbs finely formed, fit to dwell in a jewel-laden palace — yet she is like a lotus stalk just torn from the water, scorched as if by heat.
Endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, worthy of adornment yet unadorned, she is like a fresh crescent moon in the sky covered by dark clouds.
Deprived of the beloved pleasures of love, deprived of her kinsmen, wretched — she sustains her body in longing for the sight of her husband.
A husband is indeed the supreme ornament of a woman, beyond all other ornaments. Separated from him, even one who is beautiful does not shine.
Nala performs a deed most difficult to bear — deprived of her, he still sustains his own body and does not sink under grief.
Seeing her, with dark-tipped hair and eyes as wide as lotus petals, she who deserves happiness yet is plunged in sorrow — even my own heart is pained.
When shall this auspicious and chaste woman reach the far shore of her sorrow through reunion with her husband, even as Rohiṇī is reunited with the moon?
Surely, upon winning her back, the king of Niṣadha will rejoice, like a king fallen from his kingdom who has recovered his realm.
The lord of Niṣadha deserves the daughter of Vidarbha, who matches him in character, age, and lineage — and she, dark-eyed one, deserves him in return.
It is fitting that I comfort the wife of that immeasurable hero endowed with valor and steadfastness — she who longs to behold her husband.
I shall now comfort her — she whose face resembles the full moon, who has never before known such sorrow, who is afflicted with grief and absorbed in brooding.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having thus deliberated by various reasons and identifying marks, the brahmin Sudeva then approached the daughter of Bhīma and spoke.
I am Sudeva, O daughter of Vidarbha, the beloved friend of your brother; by the command of King Bhīma I have come here to search for you.
Your father the king is well, O queen, and your mother and brothers; your two children are there in good health and long-lived; but all your kinsmen, on your account, live as if bereft of vitality.
Recognizing Sudeva, Damayantī, O Yudhiṣṭhira, then inquired after all her own dear friends and kinsmen one by one.
The daughter of Vidarbha, emaciated by sorrow, wept bitterly, O king, upon suddenly seeing Sudeva, the best of brahmins and beloved friend of her brother.
Then Sunandā, seeing her weeping and wasted with grief, and speaking privately with Sudeva, O descendant of Bharata —
— sent word to the queen-mother: "The handmaid is weeping greatly upon meeting a brahmin; if you think fit, go know who she is."
Then the mother of the king of Cedi came forth from the inner apartments to the place where that young woman was together with the brahmin.
The queen-mother then summoned Sudeva and questioned him, O lord of people: "Whose wife is this woman, or whose daughter, O spirited one?"
"How did this lovely-eyed one come to be lost from her kinsmen or her husband? And how did you, O brahmin, come to know her, and how did she fall into this condition?"
"All this I wish to know from you without remainder; tell me truly, for one who is asking, of her who has the beauty of a goddess."
Thus addressed by her, O king, Sudeva the best of twice-born, having seated himself at ease, described Damayantī's story exactly as it was.
Sudeva said: The king of Vidarbha, Bhīma, is righteous-souled and of terrible prowess. This auspicious woman is his daughter, renowned as Damayantī.
The king of Niṣadha, Nala by name, son of Vīrasena — this auspicious woman is the wife of that wise and celebrated lord.
That lord of the earth was defeated at dice by his brother, stripped of his kingdom; he departed together with Damayantī and was not found anywhere thereafter.
We wander this earth in search of Damayantī; and this young woman has been found in the dwelling of your son.

No mortal woman here equals her in beauty. Between her brows she bears a congenital mole, a mark of excellence — on that dark-complexioned one it resembles a lotus; I spied it though it was concealed.
Covered by grime, it is like the moon veiled by a thin cloud. This mark was fashioned by the Creator as a sign for the sake of her glory.
As the crescent of the tarnished moon does not shine forth fully, yet her beauty does not perish; though her body is covered with grime and unadorned, it shines plainly like gold.
By this form and by this very mole I recognized her, this goddess — as a fire is identified by its heat even when covered.
Bṛhadaśva said: Hearing that speech of Sudeva, O lord of people, Sunandā cleansed away the grime that concealed the mole.
With the grime wiped away, the mole of Damayantī shone forth — like the night-maker revealed in a cloudless sky.
Seeing the mole, Sunandā and the queen-mother, O descendant of Bharata, wept and embraced her and stood still for a moment; then, shedding tears softly, the queen-mother spoke thus:
"You are the daughter of my sister, identified by this mole — both I and your mother are daughters of that high-souled king of the Daśārṇas, of Sudāman, O lovely-faced one."
"She was given to King Bhīma, the mighty-armed, while I went to another; and you I saw as a child born in the house of your father in the Daśārṇa land."
"As your father's house is to you, so too is this house, O spirited one; as my sovereignty is mine, Damayantī, so too is it yours."
With a joyful heart, Damayantī, O lord of people, bowed to her mother's sister and spoke these words:
"Even while being unrecognized, I have lived here happily, well provided with all desires and always protected by you."
"The dwelling will be even happier than this — of that there is no doubt. But O mother's sister, you must give leave to me who have long been separated from my home."
"My two little children are there, living without their father, afflicted with grief and without me as well — how must they be?"
"If you wish to do anything dear to me, I desire to go to Vidarbha; appoint a conveyance for me quickly."
"So be it," said the mother's sister joyfully to her, O king; and then, with the consent of her son, she escorted her under a great guard —
— the queen-mother dispatched her in a splendid chariot drawn by men, O best of the Bharata line, furnished with food, drink, and all necessities.
Then the auspicious one reached Vidarbha before long; all her kinsmen received and honored her with great joy.
Seeing all her kinsmen in good health, and her two children, and her mother and father, and all her circle of friends —
— the glorious and auspicious Damayantī worshipped the gods and the brahmins with the highest rites, O lord of people.
The king, overjoyed at the mere sight of his daughter, satisfied Sudeva with a thousand cows and also with a village and riches.
After spending the night rested in her father's house, that spirited woman, O king, spoke these words to her mother:
Damayantī said: If you wish me to live, mother — I speak truly — then strive for the bringing back of that hero among men, Nala.
Bṛhadaśva said: Thus addressed by Damayantī, that queen, deeply grieved and choked with tears, O king, spoke not a single word in reply.
Seeing her in that condition, the entire inner chamber was then thrown into great lamentation and wept bitterly.
Then the queen spoke to Bhīma, O great king: "Your daughter Damayantī grieves for her husband."
"And she herself has spoken to me, setting aside her shame, O king: 'Let your servants make effort to find the celebrated Nala.'"
Urged by her, the king dispatched obedient brahmins in all directions: "Seek and find Nala."
Then by the command of the lord of Vidarbha, those best of brahmins, having come before Damayantī, said "we set out" and addressed her thus:
The daughter of Bhīma then spoke these words to them: "Proclaim this speech in all kingdoms, in public assemblies here and there, again and again:"
"Where have you gone, O gambler, cutting off half my garment, abandoning in the forest your beloved and devoted one who lay asleep, O beloved?"
"As commanded by you, she waits there for you, that young woman, burning greatly with longing, wrapped in half a garment."
"For her who weeps ceaselessly with that grief, O lord of the earth, show grace, O hero, and give a word in reply."
"This and something else is to be said — that he may show compassion to me; for fire fanned by wind burns the forest."
"A wife must always be maintained and protected by her husband — why have both these duties been abandoned by you, who are righteous and good?"
"You are renowned, wise, well-born, and always compassionate; now you are transformed to mercilessness — I think it is because of the destruction of my fortune."
"Therefore show compassion to me, O great archer, O bull among men; non-cruelty is the highest virtue — this very teaching I heard from you."
"If, while you speak thus, any man responds to you, that man is to be fully identified — who he is and where he dwells."
"Whatever answer a man gives upon hearing your words, bring back that speech and report it to me swiftly, O best of twice-born."
"And act with diligence so that he may not know you are wandering by Bhīma's command and that you will be returning."
"Whether he be prosperous, or whether he be without wealth, or whether he desire riches — his intentions are to be discerned."
Thus instructed, those brahmins set out in all directions, O king, to search for Nala who was then afflicted with adversity.
Those twice-born ones searched cities with their kingdoms, villages, cow-herding settlements, and hermitages, O king, but did not find Nala.
And all those brahmins, O lord of people, proclaimed that message here and there, everywhere, exactly as Damayantī had directed.
Bṛhadaśva said: Then, after a long time, a brahmin named Parṇāda returned to the city and spoke these words to the daughter of Bhīma:
"Searching day and night for the lord of Niṣadha, O Damayantī, I went to the city of Ayodhyā and presented myself before Bhāṅgasvari (Ṛtuparṇa)."
"And I caused that greatly blessed Ṛtuparṇa to hear your message in a great assembly, exactly as it was spoken, O fair-complexioned one."
"Hearing that, Ṛtuparṇa, the lord of men, said nothing; nor did any member of his court speak, even as I proclaimed it repeatedly."
"But when I was dismissed by the king, someone spoke to me in a private place — a servant of Ṛtuparṇa named Bāhuka."
"He is the charioteer of that lord of men, misshapen in form and with short arms — Bāhuka is his name; he is supremely skilled in swift driving and also a fine preparer of food."
"He sighed deeply many times and wept again and again; having inquired after your welfare, he then spoke these words:"

"'Women of good family, even when fallen into adversity, protect themselves by their own virtue; those who are true and have won heaven — of that there is no doubt — never become angry, even when abandoned by their husbands.'"
"'She who was abandoned by one placed in adversity, by one confused, by one fallen from happiness — in that she ought not to be angry with him.'"
"'At one who was struggling to sustain his very life, whose garments were stolen by birds, who was burning with anguish — the dark-complexioned one ought not to be angry.'"
"'Whether honored or dishonored, upon seeing her husband who has come to such a pass — fallen from his kingdom, bereft of prosperity — the dark-complexioned one ought not to be angry.'"
"Having heard his words, I have come here in haste; having heard, O noble lady, you must weigh this evidence and also inform the king."
Hearing this, O lord of the people, Damayantī — her eyes filled with tears — went privately to her mother and addressed her thus.
"This matter must not be known to Bhīma in any way, mother. In your presence I shall send for Sudeva, that best of brahmins."
"You must take care that king Bhīma does not come to know my intention, if you wish me well."
"And as Sudeva quickly brought me back to my kinsmen by that same auspicious mission, so let Sudeva depart at once — do not delay, mother — to bring Nala here from the city of Ayodhyā."
Then, after he had rested, the beautiful Vaidarbhī honored Parṇāda, that best of brahmins, with great wealth.

"When Nala arrives here, O brahmin, I shall give you wealth again, for you have done me great service such as no other would do — that I shall be reunited swiftly with my husband, O foremost of the twice-born."
Thus addressed, he honored her with most auspicious blessings and departed to his home, that high-minded one, his purpose fulfilled.
Then Damayantī, O Yudhiṣṭhira, had that brahmin Sudeva summoned and, filled with grief and sorrow, spoke in her mother's presence.
"Go, Sudeva, to the city of Ayodhyā and speak to king Ṛtuparṇa these words: 'Wishing to take another husband, the daughter of Bhīma, Damayantī, will hold a svayaṃvara once more.'"
"Kings and princes are all going there, and the time has been reckoned such that it shall take place tomorrow at sunrise."
"If you think this worthy of consideration, go quickly, O subduer of enemies — at sunrise tomorrow she will choose a second husband, for that hero Nala is not known to be alive or dead."
Exactly as she had instructed, Sudeva the brahmin went and spoke those words to king Ṛtuparṇa, O great king.
Bṛhadaśva said: Hearing the words of Sudeva, king Ṛtuparṇa, lord of men, soothing him with gentle speech, addressed Bāhuka.
"I wish to go to Vidarbha for Damayantī's svayaṃvara — in a single day, if you think it possible, O Bāhuka, who knows the truth about horses."
Hearing these words of the king, O Kaunteya, Nala's heart was torn with grief, and that high-minded one fell into deep reflection.
"Could this be Damayantī, bewildered by grief, doing this? Or could this be a great stratagem devised for my sake?"
"Alas, is the noble Vaidarbhī, that wretched woman, seeking to do something cruel, she who was abandoned by me — petty, sinful, of perverted judgment?"

"The nature of women in the world is fickle, and my offense against her was severe — she might do this, being helpless, her affection gone, distressed by grief over me, that slender-waisted one, in despair."

"Yet she would never do this, especially as she has children. Whatever is true and right in this matter, I shall go and ascertain for certain. I shall fulfill Ṛtuparṇa's desire as well as my own purpose."
Having resolved thus in his mind, Bāhuka, though downcast in heart, folded his hands and spoke these words to Ṛtuparṇa, lord of men.
"I promise you truly, O lord of men, O tiger among men, O king — you shall reach the city of Vidarbha in a single day."
Then, O king, Bāhuka went to the stables and, by the command of king Bhāṅgasvari, examined the horses.
Though repeatedly urged by Ṛtuparṇa, Bāhuka selected lean horses that were capable and fit for the road.
They were endowed with vigor and strength, of good breed and character, free from inferior marks, broad-nostriled and large-jawed, pure in ten whorls, born in Sindhu, swift as the wind.
Seeing them, the king spoke with some irritation: "What is this? Is it your intention to deceive us with what you propose to do?"
"How shall these horses of mine, feeble in strength and vitality, carry me? The road is great, to be traveled by horses — how can it be done with such as these?"
Bāhuka said: "These horses will go to Vidarbha — there is no doubt in this. But if you think otherwise, O king, tell me which ones I should harness for you."
Ṛtuparṇa said: "You alone know the truth about horses and are skilled in this, Bāhuka. Those which you judge capable, harness them quickly."
Bṛhadaśva said: Then that skilled man harnessed four excellent horses of good breed and character, possessed of speed, to the chariot.
Then the king mounted the harnessed chariot in great haste, but those best of horses sank to their knees on the ground.
Then Nala, best of men, the splendid king, O lord of the people, pacified those horses endowed with vigor and strength.
And taking up the reins, Nala desired to set out, seating the charioteer Vārṣṇeya and adopting the highest speed.
Those best of horses, urged on properly by Bāhuka, leaped up as if into the sky, as if bewildering the chariot's passenger.
Seeing those horses moving with the speed of the wind in that fashion, the wise lord of Ayodhyā was filled with the greatest amazement.
Hearing that thunder of the chariot and witnessing that mastery of the horses, Vārṣṇeya began to reflect on Bāhuka's knowledge of horses.
"Can this be Mātali, the charioteer of the king of the gods? For such great marks are seen in the hero Bāhuka."
"Or could this be Śālihotra, who knows the true lineage of horses, having taken on a supremely beautiful human form?"
"Or could this be king Nala, the conqueror of enemy cities — is this the king arrived here?" Thus he reflected.
"Or else Bāhuka possesses the very knowledge that Nala knew, for I perceive the knowledge of Bāhuka and Nala to be equal."
"And even the age of this man I judge to be the same as Nala's — yet this is not Nala the great hero; still, he must be one who knows the same art."
"For great-souled ones roam this earth in disguise, driven by the ordinance of fate and disfigured by means spoken of in the scriptures."
"Yet my judgment wavers regarding the deformity of the body — that he is diminished in measure from his standard form is my conviction."
"Age and stature are the same, but there is a difference in appearance; ultimately I think Bāhuka to be Nala, endowed with all virtues."
Thus deliberating again and again, Vārṣṇeya, the charioteer of the glorious Nala, reflected in his heart, O great king.
But Ṛtuparṇa, O lord of kings, reflecting on Bāhuka's knowledge of horses, rejoiced, the king together with his charioteer Vārṣṇeya.
Observing that strength, valor, and energy, that mastery of the horses, and that supreme effort, he attained the highest joy.
Bṛhadaśva said: He swiftly crossed rivers, mountains, forests, and lakes — like one moving through the sky, as if flying through the air.
As the chariot moved on in this way, king Bhāṅgasvari, conqueror of enemy cities, saw his upper garment had fallen off.
Then, as the cloth had fallen, the high-minded king said hastily to Nala: "I shall retrieve it."
"Hold back these swift horses, O one of great intelligence, while Vārṣṇeya fetches this cloth for me."
Nala replied to him: "Your cloth has fallen far away — we have gone past it by a yojana. It is not possible to retrieve it again."
When Nala had said this, O king, king Bhāṅgasvari then noticed a vibhītaka tree laden with fruit standing in the forest.
Seeing it, the king addressed Bāhuka in haste: "Look, charioteer, I too have supreme power in counting."
"No one knows everything; there is no one who is omniscient. Knowledge does not reach its fullness in one place in any person anywhere."
"On this tree, Bāhuka — the leaves and fruits, and those that have fallen here — one more than a hundred, one leaf more than that, and one fruit — [tell me the count], Bāhuka."
"There are five crores of leaves on both of its two branches — cut these two branches of it with all their sub-branches; from these two there are two thousand fruits and ninety-five."
Then Bāhuka leaped down from the chariot and said to the king: "You are boasting of something beyond my sight, O king, O afflicteor of enemies."
"But if you have counted it, O king, it is not beyond sight — I shall count the vibhītaka before your eyes, O great king."
"I do not know whether it is so or not — I shall count the fruits of this before your watching eyes, O lord of men. Let Vārṣṇeya hold the reins of the horses for a moment."
The king said to the charioteer: "This is no time to delay." But Bāhuka, exerting his utmost effort, addressed him.
"Wait a moment — or if you are in haste, this road leads safely onward; go with Vārṣṇeya as your charioteer."
Ṛtuparṇa said, pacifying him, O joy of the Kurus: "You alone are the driver — there is no other on earth, Bāhuka."
"It is for your sake I wish to go to Vidarbha, O expert in horses — I have taken refuge in you; you ought not to create an obstacle."
"I shall fulfill your desire in whatever you tell me, Bāhuka, if you show me the sun while traveling to Vidarbha today."
Then Bāhuka said to him: "After counting this vibhītaka I shall go to Vidarbha — do this at my word."
The king said as if unwillingly: "Count then." He quickly descended from the chariot and felled that tree.
Then, filled with wonder, after counting — there were exactly as many fruits as had been said — he spoke these words to the king.
"This is truly extraordinary, O king — I have witnessed your power. I wish to hear of that knowledge by which this is known, O king."
Then the king, eager to proceed on his way, said to him: "Know me to be one who knows the heart of dice and is expert in calculation."
Then Bāhuka said to him: "Give me this knowledge, and receive from me in return the heart of horses, O bull among men."
Then king Ṛtuparṇa, out of the importance of his purpose and out of desire for knowledge of horses, said to Bāhuka: "So be it."
"Take as you wish this supreme heart of dice; let my horse-knowledge remain deposited with you, Bāhuka." Having spoken thus, Ṛtuparṇa gave the knowledge to Nala.
From the body of that knower of the heart of dice, Kali emerged, constantly vomiting from his mouth the sharp poison of Karkoṭaka.
From that afflicted Kali went forth the fire of a curse. By him the king had been tormented for a long time, without self-mastery.
Then Kali, freed from the poison, assumed his own form. The enraged lord of Niṣadha, Nala, desired to curse him.
Kali, trembling with fear and with folded hands, said to him: "Restrain your anger, O king — I shall give you the highest fame."
"Formerly the mother of Indrasena, enraged, cursed me when she was abandoned by you — from that time I was greatly tormented."
"I dwelt within you, O unconquered lord of kings, in the greatest misery, burning day and night with the poison of the serpent king."
"And those men in the world who shall celebrate you without ceasing — fear arising from me shall never come to them."
Thus addressed, king Nala restrained his anger. Then Kali, frightened, quickly entered into the vibhītaka tree; and Kali was not seen by others, as he conversed thus with the Niṣadhan.
Then the king of Niṣadha, destroyer of enemy heroes, fever gone, O king — when Kali had wholly vanished — counted the fruits.

Filled with supreme joy and blazing with surpassing splendour, the radiant king mounted his chariot and set off with swift horses; the vibhītaka tree, once inauspicious, was now redeemed of its connection with Kali.
With a heart overflowing with delight, Nala urged on the excellent horses again and again as they sprang forward like flying birds.
The great-souled king set forth toward Vidarbha; and as Nala passed on, Kali too went home.
Then, O lord of earth, king Nala became free of fever, O king — released by Kali, though still deprived of his own form alone.
Bṛhadaśva said: Then, toward evening, the people reported to king Bhīma the arrival of Ṛtuparṇa, a man of true valour, in Vidarbha.
At Bhīma's word, the king entered the city of Kuṇḍina, making all ten directions resound with the thunder of his chariot.
Then Nala's horses there heard that chariot-roar; and having heard it, they rejoiced just as they used to in Nala's presence of old.
And Damayantī too heard that chariot-sound of Nala — deep as the roar of a cloud at the coming of the rains.
The daughter of Bhīma deemed the chariot-roar exactly like the sound when Nala had held the reins of Nala's own horses of old; and so too did those very horses.
The peacocks on the terraces, the elephants in their stalls, and the horses there all heard the chariot-roar of the king.
Hearing that chariot-roar, the elephants and peacocks likewise cried out with uplifted heads, O king, as if beholding the rise of storm-clouds.
Damayantī said: As that chariot-roar fills the earth as it were, it gladdens my heart — this must be Nala, lord of the land.
If I do not today behold Nala of moon-like face, that hero of numberless virtues, I shall surely perish — there is no doubt.
If I do not enter today between the arms of that hero, so pleasant to the touch, I shall surely perish — there is no doubt.
If the Niṣadhan, whose voice is like thunder, golden in lustre, does not come to me today, I shall surely perish — there is no doubt.
If the lord of kings, bold as a lion, matchless as a rutting elephant, does not come to me, I shall surely perish — there is no doubt.
I do not recall any falsehood from him, nor any unkindness, nor even a stale word spoken carelessly by that great soul.
Master of himself, forbearing, heroic, gentle, self-controlled, with conquered senses, and in private never bowing to the base — my Niṣadhan was docile as a child.
As I, devoted entirely to him, recall his virtues day and night, this heart of mine, bereft of my beloved, is riven by grief.
Bṛhadaśva said: Thus lamenting, she, like one who had lost her senses, O Bhārata, ascended the great palace longing to behold the one of blessed renown.
Then in the middle courtyard she saw the chariot with Ṛtuparṇa, the guardian of the earth, standing in it together with Vārṣṇeya and Bāhuka.
Then Vārṣṇeya and Bāhuka alighted from that finest of chariots, unyoked those horses, and stationed the chariot.
Alighting from the body of the chariot, Ṛtuparṇa, lord of men, presented himself, O great king, before Bhīma of terrible prowess.
Bhīma received him with the highest honour; but the secret purpose concerning his daughter, for which he had come so suddenly and unexpectedly, Bhīma could not fathom.
"What is your business? Welcome" — so asked by the king, O Bhārata, that lord of men did not reveal that he had come on account of his daughter.
King Ṛtuparṇa too, wise and of true valour, saw neither king nor prince present there, nor any sign of a svayaṃvara assembly, nor any gathering of brahmins.
Then the king, lord of Kosala, reflecting in his mind, said to him: "I have come to pay my respects to you."
King Bhīma too, smiling inwardly, pondered the reason for his journey of more than a hundred yojanas.
Passing over many villages, he had not found things as expected; the stated purpose of his coming seemed trivial indeed.
Thus reasoning, that lord of men honoured him and dismissed him, saying again and again: "Rest — you must be weary."
Honoured and cheerful of heart, delighted by the delighted king, escorted by royal attendants, he entered the appointed dwelling.
After Ṛtuparṇa the king had departed, O king, along with Vārṣṇeya, Bāhuka led the chariot to the carriage-stable.
Having unyoked those horses and tended to them according to the rules, he himself comforted them and then sat down in the body of the chariot.
But Damayantī, stricken with grief, having seen the king Bhāṅgasvari, the charioteer's son Vārṣṇeya, and Bāhuka in such a guise —
— the daughter of Vidarbha pondered: "Whose was this great chariot-sound, so like Nala's? Yet I do not see the Niṣadhan."
"Perhaps Vārṣṇeya learned that very skill from him — and therefore his chariot-roar has become as great as Nala's."
"Or could Ṛtuparṇa himself drive as king Nala does — and hence this chariot-roar is marked as like the Niṣadhan's?"
Having thus deliberated, Damayantī, O lord of the people, O king, sent a female messenger to search out the Niṣadhan.
Damayantī said: Go, Keśinī, find out who this charioteer is — disfigured, short-armed Bāhuka, seated in the body of the chariot.
Approach him, dear one, and enquire after his well-being; then, composed, question this man gently and learn the truth about him, O blameless one.
I have a great suspicion about this: he may be king Nala — for so too does my mind feel satisfied and my heart find peace.
At the end of the conversation you must tell him the words of Parṇāda exactly, O fair-hipped one, and then discern his reply, O blameless one.
Bṛhadaśva said: The messenger, thus composed, went and spoke to Bāhuka; and the auspicious Damayantī, standing on the terrace, watched on.
Keśinī said: Welcome to you, O lord among men; I convey your well-being from Damayantī — hear her words well, O bull among men.
When did you set out, and for what purpose have you come here? Tell me truthfully — the daughter of Vidarbha wishes to hear.
Bāhuka said: The illustrious king of Kosala heard that a second svayaṃvara of Damayantī was to take place tomorrow, O fair lady.
Hearing that, the king set out with horses swift as the wind that can cover a hundred yojanas, and I am his charioteer.
Keśinī said: And this third person of yours — where does he come from, and to whom does he belong? And whose man are you, and how did this service come to be placed in you?
Bāhuka said: He is a charioteer of the blessed Nala, celebrated as Vārṣṇeya; when Nala fled, O dear one, he attached himself to Bhāṅgasvari.
I myself am skilled with horses and well-established as a cook; Ṛtuparṇa himself took me on for the driving of chariots and for cooking.
Keśinī said: Does Vārṣṇeya know where king Nala has gone? Has he perhaps told you anything about it, Bāhuka?
Bāhuka said: Having left his two children here, after that evil act of Nala's, he went wherever he wished; he does not know where the Niṣadhan is.
Nor does any other man know Nala, O renowned lady; the king wanders in this world concealed, deprived of his own form.
Only Nala himself knows Nala — and the one who is closest to him next; for those outward marks never truly reveal Nala at any time.
Keśinī said: That brahmin who went first to Ayodhyā at that time, reciting again and again these words of a woman —
"Where have you gone, O gambler, cutting off half my garment and setting out, abandoning your beloved who lay sleeping in the forest, devoted to you, O dear one?" —
"She, as you instructed, abides there waiting for you, burning day and night, covered only by half a garment" —
"Show grace, O hero, O king, to her who weeps constantly in that pain — give her an answer" —
Speak that dear story of hers, O great-minded one; that very word the blameless daughter of Vidarbha wishes to hear from you.
The response you gave upon hearing that then — the daughter of Vidarbha wishes to hear that again from you.
Bṛhadaśva said: Thus addressed by Keśinī, O joy of the Kurus, Nala's heart was afflicted and his eyes filled with tears.
Suppressing his own grief, burning within, the lord of the earth spoke again with a voice choked with tears.
Even when fallen into adversity, noble women guard themselves by themselves; true women of such virtue win heaven — there is no doubt.
Separated from their husbands, true women never grow angry at any time; they sustain their lives here clad in the armour of good conduct.
The dark-complexioned one ought not to be angry with one who was struggling to preserve his life, from whom birds had stolen his garment, and who was burning with anguish.
Whether honoured or dishonoured, seeing a husband come in such a state — fallen from his kingdom, destitute of fortune, hungry, overwhelmed by calamity —
Speaking these words thus, Nala, deeply tormented, could not hold back his tears and wept aloud, O Bhārata.
Then Keśinī went and reported to Damayantī all that had been said, and also that emotional change she had seen in him.
Bṛhadaśva said: But Damayantī, hearing that, deeply absorbed in grief, suspecting that he might indeed be Nala, said this to Keśinī.
Go again, Keśinī, and test Bāhuka; stand near him speaking to him, and observe his behaviour.
And whenever he performs some action there, O fair lady, carefully mark his movements as he goes about.
Do not give him fire when he is obstructed either, O fair lady; and do not give water immediately when he asks — take your time properly.
Having observed all this, report his conduct to me; and whatever else you may see, that too you must tell me.
Thus addressed by Damayantī, Keśinī went quickly and, having observed the marks of the horse-knower, returned.
She reported to Damayantī everything exactly as it happened — the sign she had seen in Bāhuka that was both divine and human.
Keśinī said: His manner of service is immaculate — never before have I seen or heard of a man like that, O Damayantī.
Approaching a low passage, he does not stoop anywhere; yet seeing it, he rises naturally as it suits him — even in a narrow space a very large opening is created for him.
For Ṛtuparṇa's meal, food was sent in many portions by the king, and a large quantity of animal meat as well.
A water-pot was prepared there for washing it; he merely glanced at that pot and it became full straightaway.
Then, having washed his hands and approached the hearth, Bāhuka took up a handful of grass, swung it around, and placed it upon the fire.
Thereupon the fire-carrier blazed up suddenly in that place; marvelling at that most wondrous sight, I came here astonished.
And another great wonder was observed by me there, O fair one: that even on touching the fire he is not burnt at all.
Water rises up to him willingly and swiftly by his mere wish; and yet another exceedingly great wonder have I witnessed.
That taking up flowers and crushing them gently in both his hands — those flowers crushed thus in his palms —
became all the more fragrant and bloomed afresh. Having seen these things that are near to miracles, I came running here.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having heard this account of the deeds of the illustrious Nala, Damayantī concluded that Nala had been found, indicated by those acts and movements.
Suspecting that her husband Nala was concealed in the form of Bāhuka, she again spoke to Keśinī, weeping, in a gentle voice.
"Go again, O fair one, and while Bāhuka is unaware, take the cooked meat that has been prepared by him from the kitchen and bring it here."
She went, and while Bāhuka was occupied, drew away that meat, still piping hot; then swiftly, the ever-obliging Keśinī at that very moment gave it to Damayantī, O joy of the Kurus.
She who had long been accustomed to the cooking of Nala tasted that meat and, recognising Nala in the cook, cried out in great grief.
And overcome with extreme anguish, she washed her face, then sent the pair of children together with Keśinī, O Bhārata.
Recognising Indrasenā together with her brother, Bāhuka the king rushed forward and, embracing them, drew them into his lap.
But Bāhuka, approaching his two children who were like the children of gods, his heart overwhelmed with deep grief, wept aloud.
The king of Niṣadha, having shown his agitation more than once, then quickly let go of his children and said this to Keśinī:
"This pair, O good woman, is very similar to my own children; that is why on merely seeing them I immediately shed tears."
"People seeing you come here so many times might suspect some fault. We too are but guests in this land — go, O good woman, I salute you."
Bṛhadaśva said: Having observed all the emotions of the wise and illustrious Nala, Keśinī came quickly and reported everything to Damayantī.
Then Damayantī, afflicted with sorrow and agitated by her suspicion that it was Nala, sent Keśinī once more to her mother.
"Bāhuka has been tested by me many times on suspicion that he is Nala; I have one single doubt about his form — I wish to know it myself."
"Either let him be brought in to me, mother, or you should give me leave to go; whether it be known or unknown, let my father arrange it."
Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, that queen spoke to Bhīma, and the king assented to his daughter's intention.
Permitted thus by her father and mother, O bull of the Bhāratas, she brought Nala in to the place where her own quarters were.
But seeing Nala arrived in that form, Damayantī of excellent complexion was then seized by sharp grief.
Then Damayantī, clad in ochre garments, matted-haired and begrimed with dirt, O great king, spoke these words to Bāhuka:
"Have you ever seen, Bāhuka, a man who knows the law, one who abandoned a sleeping woman in the forest and went away?"
"Who but Nala of celebrated fame could abandon in a lonely place, exhausted and stupefied with fatigue, a beloved wife who had committed no offence?"
"What wrong was done to him by me, that lord of the earth, who went away leaving me in the forest, carried off by sleep?"
"How could he have abandoned me, who was devoted to him, who desired him above all, who was then a mother — me, whom of old I chose setting aside the gods themselves?"
"Where has that truth gone — the promise he swore: 'I will provide for you' — made when he took my hand in the fire, when he trusted the words of the swans?"
As Damayantī spoke all this, O subduer of enemies, tears born of grief flowed copiously and unhappily from both her eyes.
Seeing those tears flowing from her dark-pupilled, red-cornered eyes, Nala, distressed with grief, spoke thus:
"My kingdom was destroyed — yet that was not done by me of my own will; it was done by Kali, O timid one, and so too was my abandoning of you."
"And by you, O best upholder of dharma, was Kali then struck with a curse — by you who were in the forest, wretched and mourning me who had been exiled."
"Scorched by your curse, Kali dwelt within my body burning; burnt by your curse constantly, he was like one fixed in fire."
"And he was conquered by my resolution and by ascetic endurance as well; and with this ending of sorrow, O fair one, there must now be happiness for us two."
"That wretch has released me and gone; then I came here, O broad-hipped one, for your sake — I have no other purpose here."
"How could a woman ever forsake a husband devoted and faithful to her and choose another, as you, O timid one, are alleged to have done?"
"Messengers roam the whole earth by order of a king: it is said that Bhīma's daughter is about to choose a second husband."
"As one acting wantonly according to her own desire, as if suited to herself — having heard this very thing, Rituparna, son of Bhangasvara, arrived hastily."
But Damayantī, hearing that lamentation of Nala, trembling and frightened, spoke with joined palms.
Damayantī said: You must not, O noble one, suspect me of wrongdoing; for it was I who chose you setting aside the gods themselves, O lord of Niṣadha.
For the purpose of finding you, brahmins went in all directions, singing my words in verse throughout the ten quarters.
Then a learned brahmin named Parnada, O king, came upon you in the abode of Rituparna in Kosala.
When the message was duly conveyed by him and the reply likewise received, this stratagem was devised by me for bringing you back, O lord of Niṣadha.
"For there is no other in the world, O lord of the earth, O lord of men, capable of covering a hundred yojanas in a single day with horses — none but you."
"And so, O ruler of the earth, I clasp your feet in the same way as I have never committed any wrong even in my mind."
"This wind that moves in this world, witness to all beings and ever present — let it take my life if I am guilty of any sin."
"Likewise the fierce-rayed sun that always moves beyond this world — let it take my life if I am guilty of any sin."
"The moon that moves within all beings as their inner witness — let it take my life if I am guilty of any sin."
"These three gods indeed uphold the entire triple world; let them declare what is true, and today let them forsake me if I have sinned."
When she had spoken thus, the wind then spoke from the sky: "She has not committed any sin, Nala — I speak the truth to you."
"O king, the great treasure-house of her virtue has been well guarded by Damayantī; we have been her witnesses and protectors for three full years."
"And this unequalled stratagem was devised by her for your sake; for there is no other man here who could travel a hundred yojanas in a single day but you."
"Bhīma's daughter is worthy of you, and you are worthy of Bhīma's daughter, O lord of the earth; you must entertain no doubt here — come together with your wife."
As the wind spoke thus, a shower of flowers fell; the divine kettledrums resounded, and an auspicious breeze blew.
Seeing that most wondrous event, O Bhārata, Nala the king, that subduer of enemies, then cast away his suspicion regarding Damayantī.
Then the lord of the earth put on that spotless garment; calling the king of the serpents to mind, he then regained his own form.
Seeing her husband in his own form, the blameless daughter of Bhīma then cried out loudly, embracing the illustrious Nala.
King Nala too embraced Bhīma's daughter, radiant as before; and he greeted his own children duly as well.
Then, burying her lovely face upon his chest, overwhelmed by that accumulated grief, she of beautiful eyes sighed deeply.
Just so, her limbs still begrimed with dirt, the pure-smiled one stood clinging to that tiger among men for a long time, her eyes flooded with tears.
Then Damayantī's mother joyfully told Bhīma everything that had occurred concerning Damayantī and Nala, O king.
Then the great king said: "Tomorrow I shall see Nala, who has bathed and purified himself, dwelling happily together with Damayantī."
Then those two, together through the night, narrating all the former tale of their wandering in the forest, passed the night joyfully, O king.
And he, meeting again with his wife in that fourth year, all his wishes fully accomplished, attained supreme joy.
And Damayantī too, having regained her husband, was greatly refreshed — like the earth receiving rain when the crops are half-grown.
She thus reunited, her weariness dispelled, her fever stilled, her spirit swelling with joy — Bhīma's daughter shone in her fulfilled desire like the night risen with the cool-rayed moon.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having passed that night there, King Nala, well adorned and accompanied by the princess of Vidarbha, presented himself at dawn before the lord of the earth.
Then Nala, with due reverence, saluted his father-in-law; and after him, the fair Damayantī bowed to her father.
Bhīma received him with great joy as if he were a son; having honoured him fittingly, the lord consoled Damayantī, devoted to her husband, there together with Nala.
King Nala received that honourable gift according to due rite and duly reported to him his own service rendered.
Then in the city arose a very great sound of jubilation from the people, delighted to see Nala returned in such a manner.
The city was adorned and made beautiful with garlands of banners and flags; the royal roads were sprinkled, swept, and richly strewn with flowers.
At the doorway of every townsman, garlands of flowers were arranged; and all the shrines of the gods were worshipped and adorned.
Rituparna too heard that Nala, who had been disguised as Bāhuka, was united with Damayantī, and the lord of men rejoiced.
King Nala, summoning him, begged pardon of the king; and that king too begged his pardon with reasons approved by reason.
That lord of the earth, duly honoured, filled with wonder, congratulated the lord of Niṣadha saying: "By good fortune you are reunited with your own wife."
"Have I not done you any wrong, O lord of Niṣadha, O ruler of Niṣadha, while you dwelt unknown in my house?"
"Whether done deliberately or unknowingly, whatever improper things were done by me — those you must forgive."
Nala said: You have not committed even the slightest offence against me, O king; and even if you had, I would not be angry — for I must forgive you.
For you are my old friend and my kinsman, O lord of men; and from this day forward you should show me even greater affection.
I have dwelt happily in your house, provided with every comfort; indeed, O king, I was never so well cared for even in my own home.
This science of horses that belongs to you still remains with me; I wish to render it back to you now, if you so agree, O king.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having spoken thus, the king of Niṣadha imparted the science to Ṛtuparṇa, and he received it in accordance with the rite prescribed.
Then, having obtained the secret lore of horses, the king Bhāṅgasvari took another charioteer and departed for his own city.
After Ṛtuparṇa had departed, King Nala, O lord of the people, remained in the city of Kuṇḍina for not too long a time.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having stayed a month, O son of Kuntī, the king of Niṣadha took leave of Bhīma and set out toward Niṣadha with a small retinue.
He went with a single splendid chariot, sixteen elephants, fifty horses, and six hundred foot-soldiers.
That great-minded lord of the earth, trembling with eagerness, as if shaking the very ground, entered swiftly and with intense resolve.
Then Nala, son of Vīrasena, confronted Puṣkara and said: Let us play again — I have earned great wealth.
Damayantī and whatever other wealth I have acquired — this is my stake. Your kingdom, O Puṣkara, is the wager on your side.
Let the dice game resume — such is my firm resolve. With a single throw, and let it be well for you; we shall wager even our lives.
Having won and seized another's wealth — whether a kingdom or goods — the counter-stake must be given; for the property of another is said to be the highest wealth at stake.
If you do not wish to play at dice, then let the dice of battle commence; let there be a duel by chariot, and whichever of us wins, O king — let that be the end of it.
This kingdom that is the heritage of our lineage must be recovered by whatever means — that is the teaching of the elders.
Let one of the two decisions be made today, O Puṣkara — either bend the bow in the game of dice or bend it in battle.
Thus addressed by the king of Niṣadha, Puṣkara laughed as if certain of his own victory, and replied to the lord of the earth.

By good fortune you have earned wealth to serve as the counter-stake, O king of Niṣadha; by good fortune the evil done to Damayantī has come to an end; and by good fortune you still live, O king, together with your wife, O crusher of foes.
With this wealth, once won, the princess of Vidarbha, adorned in full, will surely attend upon me as an apsarā attends upon Indra in heaven.
For I have always remembered you and awaited you, O king of Niṣadha; and I take no pleasure in gambling with those who are not my friends.
But having won today the blameless Damayantī of noble form, I shall consider my purpose fulfilled — for she is ever in my heart.
Hearing those many incoherent and boastful words of his, Nala, filled with fury, desired to cut off his head with his sword.
But smiling, his eyes red with anger, the king then said to him: Why do you boast before the wager? Speak after you have won.

Then the game of dice began between Puṣkara and Nala; with a single throw — and let it be well for you — Puṣkara was defeated by Nala, along with all his treasury of gems, even though his very life had been wagered.
Having won, the king laughed and declared: This entire kingdom is mine, undisturbed and free of thorns.
The princess of Vidarbha cannot even be looked upon by you, O vile king; you and your retinue, O fool, have now come to servitude before her.
It was not by your deed that I was defeated before — that deed was done by Kali, though you, O fool, do not understand this. I will not lay upon you the fault that was done by another.
Live in happiness — I release your life; and my affection for you, O hero, remains undimmed, of that there is no doubt.
My brotherly love toward you will never perish, O Puṣkara; for you are truly my brother. Live a hundred years.
Having thus comforted his brother, the valiant Nala embraced him again and again and sent him off to his own city.
Thus consoled by the king of Niṣadha, Puṣkara saluted that king of holy renown with joined palms and replied.
May your fame be imperishable; live happily for ten thousand years — you who grant me both my life and my dwelling, O king.
Thus honoured by the king, Puṣkara stayed a month, then departed joyfully for his own city, surrounded by his kinsmen.
With a great army, O king, and with well-disciplined attendants, he departed blazing in his person like the sun, O bull among men.
Having sent off Puṣkara, now wealthy and in good health, the glorious king entered his greatly adorned city; and having entered, the lord of Niṣadha comforted his townspeople.
Bṛhadaśva said: When the city had become peaceful and joyful, and a great festival was under way, the king, with a great army, brought Damayantī home.
And Damayantī's father, the immeasurable-spirited Bhīma of formidable valour, who destroys the heroes of his enemies, honoured her and sent her forth.
When the princess of Vidarbha arrived with her children, King Nala dwelt in joy like the king of the gods in Nandana.
And thus having risen to eminence among the kings of Jambūdvīpa, the great-famed Nala dwelt again in his own kingdom, having recovered it.
He performed various sacrifices with proper rites and with generous fees. In the same way, you too, O king of kings, will soon be spoken of together with your friends.
Such great sorrow was suffered by Nala, conqueror of enemy cities — through gambling, O best of men, O bull of the Bharata line — together with his wife.
Entirely alone, O lord of the earth, Nala endured enormous and terrible suffering, and yet he attained prosperity once more.
But you, O Pāṇḍava, are together with your brothers and with Kṛṣṇā, dwelling happily in this great forest, meditating only on righteousness.
You are constantly attended by greatly blessed brahmins who are versed in the Vedas and their ancillaries, O king — what cause for lamentation is there?
And this story is said to destroy the power of Kali; a man of your sort, O lord of the people, is able to find consolation upon hearing it.
Reflecting always on the impermanence of human fortune — its rise and its fall — be consoled and do not grieve.
Those who will recount this great story of Nala, and those who will hear it repeatedly — ill-fortune will not befall them; wealth will come to them and they will attain blessedness.

Having heard this ancient and ever-excellent story, one will obtain sons, grandsons, and cattle, and will attain pre-eminence among men; he will be free from disease and full of joy — of this there is no doubt.
The fear you have that someone may challenge you again, calling you ignorant of dice — that fear I will destroy for you, O king.
I know the complete secret lore of the Vedas and of dice, O you of true valour; receive it, O son of Kuntī — I speak to you with goodwill.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, with a joyful heart, said to Bṛhadaśva: Venerable sir, I wish to know the secret of dice in its true nature.
Then he imparted the secret lore of dice to the great-souled Pāṇḍava; and having given it, the great ascetic went to the horse-shrine to perform his ablutions.
After Bṛhadaśva had departed, Pārtha heard that the wise Savyasācin was engaged in fierce austerities, living on air alone.
He heard this from ascetic brahmins arriving from various places, and from those who had gathered from the best of sacred fords and mountains — he who was firm in his vows.
So Pārtha of the mighty arms had undertaken an austerity hard to attain — "such a fierce ascetic as this has never been seen before" — thus it was said.
Dhanaṃjaya Pārtha was thus an ascetic, firm in his vows, a sage moving alone, glorious, like Dharma himself embodied.
Hearing of him thus engaged in austerity in the great forest, O king, the son of Kuntī lamented for his beloved brother Jaya.
With his heart burning, Yudhiṣṭhira, seeking refuge, questioned the brahmins of various kinds of knowledge in the great forest.
Janamejaya said: Blessed one, when Pārtha, my great-grandfather, had gone from Kāmyaka, what did the Pāṇḍavas do without that left-handed archer?
For he was their great bowman, their refuge, the conqueror of armies — he appears to me as Viṣṇu is among the Ādityas.
Separated from him who was equal in valour to Indra and who never turned back in battle, how did those heroic forefathers of mine fare in the forest?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin had departed from Kāmyaka, O dear one, those descendants of Kuru became wholly absorbed in grief and sorrow.
Like gems with their strings snapped, like birds with their wings cut, all the Pāṇḍavas became joyless in heart.
And that forest, deprived of him whose deeds were without blemish, became like the forest of Caitraratha bereft of Kubera.
Without that tiger among men, O Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt in Kāmyaka unable to find any delight.
Striving for the sake of the brahmins, those great warriors slew many kinds of sacrificially pure deer with clean arrows, O best of the Bharata line.
For those tigers among men, those tamers of foes, ever going forth and gathering forest food, they regularly offered it to the brahmins.
Thus those bulls among men dwelt there full of yearning, all joyless in heart, O king, now that Dhanaṃjaya had gone.
Then Pāñcālī, remembering the hero, the middle husband, the best of the Pāṇḍavas who was away, spoke these words.
He who, though two-armed Arjuna, is Arjuna's equal with his many arms — without that best of Pāṇḍavas, the forest does not appear beautiful to me; everywhere I look I see this earth as if empty.
This wonderful forest with its flowering trees — without the left-handed archer it is not as charming to me.
Without him — dark as a rain cloud, with the gait of a lordly elephant, with lotus eyes — Kāmyaka does not shine bright for me.
He whose bow resounds like the crash of a thunderbolt — remembering the left-handed archer, O king, I find no peace.
Hearing her lamenting thus, Bhīmasena, the slayer of enemy heroes, O great king, spoke these words to Draupadī.
What you say, O gracious slender-waisted one, brings joy to the mind; it gladdens my heart like the drinking of nectar.
He whose two arms are long, even, full, like iron bars, hardened with the calluses of the bowstring, rounded, bearing sword and weapon and mace —
Adorned with golden armlets and diadems, like two five-headed serpents — without that tiger among men, this forest is as if its sun has vanished.
Relying upon him of the mighty arms, the Pāñcālas and the Kurus alike do not fear even the arrayed armies of the gods.
Relying upon the arms of that great-souled one, we all consider our enemies defeated in battle and the earth already won.
Without that hero Phalguna I find no peace of mind in Kāmyaka; wherever I look, this earth seems to me empty and void.
Nakula said: He who journeyed to the northern region and, conquering in battle mighty foes — the leading Gandharvas by the hundreds — obtained horses, that son of Vāsava —
O king, the glorious one swift as the wind — in his love he gladly gave those tittiri-spotted steeds to his brother at the great Rājasūya sacrifice —
Without him, the terrible-bowed younger brother of Bhīma, I have no desire to dwell in the Kāmyaka forest, which now seems to me no heaven at all.
Sahadeva said: He who, having conquered great warriors in battle, formerly brought home both riches and maidens for the king at the great Rājasūya sacrifice —
He of immeasurable splendour who, single-handedly defeating the assembled Yādavas in battle, carried off Subhadrā with Vāsudeva's approval —
Seeing the seat of that Jiṣṇu empty in our encampment, my heart, O great king, cannot find peace at any time.
O crusher of foes, I have a mind to leave this forest; for without that hero, this forest holds no delight for us.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yearning for Dhanañjaya, those great warriors the Pāṇḍavas of great fortune, together with Draupadī, dwelt in that forest.
Then they beheld there the great-souled divine seer Nārada, blazing with the splendour of Brahmā, brilliant as a kindled fire.
The glorious foremost of the Kurus, surrounded by those brothers, shone with surpassing radiant energy, even as Śatakratu surrounded by the gods.
And just as the Sāvitrī does not abandon the Vedas, so the chaste Yājñasenī never abandoned the Pārthas from righteousness, even as the sun-bright Śrī does not desert Mount Meru.
Receiving that worship, the blessed seer Nārada comforted the son of Dharma with words fitly spoken, O sinless one.
And he spoke to the great-souled Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira: "Speak, O foremost of the upholders of righteousness — what purpose do you have, and what shall I give you?"
Then the king, son of Dharma, having bowed together with his brothers, spoke with joined palms to Nārada, who is comparable to the gods.
"When you are pleased, O greatly fortunate one, worshipped by all the worlds, I consider my purpose accomplished by your grace, O one of excellent vows.
Yet if I, together with my brothers, am worthy of your favour, O sinless one, O best of sages, please be pleased to resolve the doubt that dwells in my heart.
He who circumambulates the earth, devoted to holy places of pilgrimage — what is the full fruit of that? O Brahman, please tell it to me in its entirety."
Nārada said: "Listen attentively, O king, O Bhārata — all this was heard by Bhīṣma himself from the presence of Pulastya; hear it as he received it.
Long ago on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, Bhīṣma, best of the upholders of righteousness, having undertaken the ancestral vow, dwelt there at that time like a sage.
In an auspicious place, O great king, a holy site frequented by divine sages — at the gate of the Gaṅgā, that mighty one of great energy, frequented by gods and gandharvas.
He of supreme brilliance satisfied the ancestors and the gods, and pleased the sages with actions prescribed by sacred ordinance.
Then after some time, while engaged in reciting prayers, that great ascetic beheld the seer Pulastya, best among sages, wondrous in appearance.
Seeing him who was fierce in austerity and blazing as it were with splendour, he was filled with incomparable joy and overcome with the greatest wonder.
Bhīṣma, best of the upholders of righteousness, when he had appeared before him, O great king, O Bhārata, honoured him with actions prescribed by sacred ordinance.
With pure body and composed mind, he took the honorific offering with his head bowed and announced his name to that best of brahmin seers.
"I am Bhīṣma — blessings to you; I am your servant, O one of excellent vows; by the very sight of you I am freed from all sins."
Having spoken thus, O great king, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, best of the upholders of righteousness, controlled his speech, folded his hands, and fell silent.
Seeing him, that best of the Kuru lineage, Bhīṣma, thus disciplined and emaciated by recitation and scriptural study, the sage became filled with affection.
Pulastya said: "By this humility of yours, O knower of righteousness, and by your self-restraint and truthfulness, O greatly fortunate one, I am entirely pleased with you.
Because of this righteousness of yours, rooted in devotion to your father, O sinless one, you behold me, my son; and my affection too is yours.
O Bhīṣma, I am one whose sight does not go in vain — tell me, what shall I do for you? Whatever you shall say, O best of the Kurus, that I shall give you, O sinless one."
Bhīṣma said: "When you are pleased, O greatly fortunate one worshipped by all the worlds, I count it accomplished — that I have beheld the lord.
Yet if I am worthy of your favour, O best of the upholders of righteousness, I shall state the doubt that lodges in my heart — and please be pleased to resolve it for me.
O blessed one, I have a certain question about righteousness concerning sacred pilgrimages; I desire to hear it explained by you one by one.
He who circumambulates the earth, O sage among brahmins, O treasury of austerity — what is the fruit of that? Tell me this, O man of immeasurable might."
Pulastya said: "Well then, I shall tell you what is the highest resort of the sages — with mind focused, my dear, hear what the fruit is in holy places of pilgrimage.
He whose hands and feet and mind are well controlled, and who possesses learning, austerity, and fame — he enjoys the fruit of a pilgrimage to holy places.
He who has withdrawn from accepting gifts, who is contented, disciplined, pure, and free from ego — he enjoys the fruit of a pilgrimage to holy places.
He who is free from deceit, free from worldly undertakings, light in eating, master of his senses, and released from all faults — he enjoys the fruit of a pilgrimage to holy places.
He who is free from anger, O king of kings, whose nature is truthfulness, whose vows are firm, and who regards all beings as equal to himself — he enjoys the fruit of a pilgrimage to holy places.
The sages have declared sacrifices in the Vedas in proper order, with their fruit exactly as it is, both in the hereafter and in this world, in every respect.
Those sacrifices cannot be performed by one who is poor, O lord of the earth; sacrifices require many instruments and a vast array of various materials.
These are accessible to kings or to wealthy men somewhere; but not to those deficient in means and equipment, who are isolated and unsupported.
O lord of men, O best of warriors, learn then of that practice which even the poor can accomplish and which equals the merit of sacrifices in its holy fruit.
This is the supreme secret of the sages, O best of the Bhāratas — the holy act of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites excels even sacrifices.
Not fasting for three nights, not visiting holy places, not giving gold and cows — through these omissions one is born poor.
Having performed sacrifices like the Agniṣṭoma with generous sacrificial fees, one does not obtain that fruit which comes from visiting holy places of pilgrimage.
In the world of men, the holy place of the god of gods, famous throughout the three worlds, known as Puṣkara — a fortunate man should enter it.
Ten thousand crores of holy places are present at Puṣkara, O lord of the earth, at the three twilight junctions of day, O joy of the Kurus.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the Marut hosts, as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases, are always present there, O lord.
Where the gods, the Daityas, and the brahmin sages as well, endowed with divine yoga and possessed of great merit, performed austerities, O great king.
Even for the wise man who desires Puṣkara only in mind, all sins are purified, and he is honoured on the back of heaven.
At that holy place, O greatly fortunate one, the Grandfather himself ever dwelt, supremely pleased, revered by gods and Dānavas alike.
At Puṣkara, O greatly fortunate one, the gods together with the leading sages attained perfection, endowed as they were with great merit.
He who bathes there while devoted to honouring ancestors and gods — the wise declare it ten times the equal of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Even if one feeds a single brahmin while dwelling in the Puṣkara forest, by that act, O Bhīṣma, he rejoices both in the hereafter and in this world.
Or whoever sustains himself on vegetables, roots, and fruits — if he, faithful and free from envy, gives even that to a brahmin, by that very act the wise man attains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Whether a brahmin, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O best of kings — those who bathe at the holy place of that great soul do not go to a degraded birth.
But he who comes to Puṣkara especially on the full moon of Kārttika — his fruit there grows without limit, O bull of the Bhāratas.
He who remembers Puṣkara morning and evening with joined palms — it is as though he has touched all holy places, O Bhārata; and that man attains the imperishable worlds in the abode of Brahmā.
Whatever sin has accumulated since birth — whether of a woman or a man — all of it perishes completely for one who has merely bathed at Puṣkara.
Just as Madhusūdana is declared the first among all the gods, so too, O king, Puṣkara is declared the first among all holy places.
He who dwells at Puṣkara for twelve years with discipline and purity obtains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
But he who tends the Agnihotra fire for a full hundred years — to reside at Puṣkara for even a single Kārttikī night is equal to that.
It is difficult to go to Puṣkara; difficult to perform austerity at Puṣkara; difficult to give charity at Puṣkara; and to reside there is very difficult indeed.
Having dwelt there for twelve nights with discipline and regulated eating, one should proceed, circumambulating as one goes, and enter the path of Jambū.
Having entered the path of Jambū, frequented by gods, sages, and ancestors, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having dwelt there for five nights, enduring until the sixth period, a man does not reach misfortune and attains the highest perfection.
Having turned back from the path of Jambū, one should proceed to the hermitage of Taṇḍulika; he does not reach misfortune and is honoured in the celestial world.
Having reached the lake of Agastya, devoted to honouring ancestors and gods, and fasting for three nights, O king, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Living on vegetables or fruits alone, one attains the state of Kumāra; having reached the hermitage of Kaṇva, graced with prosperity and worshipped by the world —
For that is the holy and primordial forest of righteousness, O bull of the Bhāratas, where one who has merely entered is freed from all sins.
Having worshipped the ancestors and the gods with discipline and regulated eating, one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice rich in all desired things.
Having circumambulated it, one should then go to Yayātipātana; there one truly obtains the fruit of the Hayamedha sacrifice.
From there one should go to Mahākāla with discipline and regulated eating; having touched the Koṭi holy place, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
From there, O knower of righteousness, one should go to the holy site of Umā's lord named Bhadravata, famous throughout the three worlds.
Having come there and worshipped Īśāna, one obtains the fruit of a gift of a thousand cows; and by the grace of Mahādeva, one attains the rank of chief of Gaṇas.
Then reaching the Narmadā, the river famous throughout the three worlds, having satisfied the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Reaching the southern Sindhu as a celibate student with mastered senses, one obtains the merit of an Agniṣṭoma and ascends to a celestial chariot.
Reaching the Carmaṇvatī river, self-controlled and abstemious, with the blessing of Rantideva one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to Arbuda, the son of the Himālayas, where, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a cleft in the earth once existed in ancient times.
There stands the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds; by spending a single night there one obtains the merit of gifting a thousand cows.
By bathing at the Pinga tirtha, O tiger among men, a celibate who has conquered his senses obtains the merit of gifting a hundred tawny cows.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to Prabhāsa, renowned throughout the world, where Agni himself, the mouth of the gods and charioteer of the wind, is ever present, O hero.
By bathing at that excellent tirtha, pure and with a composed mind, a man obtains the combined fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.

Then, going to the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows and is honored in the heavenly world, blazing perpetually with radiance like fire, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Dwelling there for three nights and gratifying the ancestors and the gods, one shines like the moon and obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then one should go to the tirtha called Varadana, O best of the Bhāratas, where a boon was granted to Viṣṇu by Durvasa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
By bathing at Varadana a man obtains the merit of a thousand cows. Then one should go to Dvāravatī, self-controlled and abstemious; by bathing at Piṇḍāraka a man obtains abundant gold.
At that tirtha, O greatly fortunate one, marks bearing the signs of the lotus are visible even today — that is wondrous, O slayer of foes.
Lotuses marked with the trident are seen there, O joy of the Kurus; the presence of Mahādeva is there indeed, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Reaching the confluence of the ocean and the Sindhu river, O Bhārata, and bathing at the tirtha of the lord of waters with a composed mind —
— and having gratified the ancestors, the gods, and the sages, O bull of the Bhāratas, one attains the world of Varuṇa, blazing with one's own splendor.
By worshipping the god Shankukarneshvara, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise declare one obtains tenfold the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Having circumambulated it, one should proceed, O bull of the Bhāratas, O best among the excellent Kurus, to the tirtha renowned throughout the three worlds, known by the name Drimi, which liberates one from all sins.
Where Brahmā and the other gods worship Maheśvara — there, by bathing and worshipping Rudra surrounded by his divine hosts, a man destroys the sins committed from birth.
And here Drimi, O best of men, is praised by all the gods; by bathing there, O tiger among men, one obtains the fruit of the Hayamedha sacrifice.
Where the all-powerful Viṣṇu, of great wisdom, O king, having conquered and slain those who were thorns to the gods, performed purification in ancient times —
— then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the celebrated Vashodhara; by the mere act of going there one obtains the fruit of the Hayamedha sacrifice.
Having bathed there, O best among the excellent Kurus, with a purified soul, and having gratified the gods and the ancestors, a man is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
