And here there is a supremely holy tirtha of the Vasus, O bull of the Bhāratas; by bathing and drinking the waters there, one becomes honored among the Vasus.
Known as Sindhuttama, the destroyer of all sins — by bathing there, O best of men, one obtains abundant gold.
Reaching Brahmatunga, pure and with composed mind, a meritorious and stainless man attains the world of Brahmā.
At the tirtha of Śakra's maidens, frequented by the Siddhas — by bathing there a man swiftly attains the world of Śakra.
And there also is the tirtha of Reṇukā, frequented by the gods; by bathing there a brahmin becomes as spotless as the moon.
Then, going to Pañcanada, self-controlled and abstemious, one obtains in succession the five sacrifices that have been enumerated.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the excellent abode of Bhīma; by bathing there at the womb-shaped place, O best of the Bhāratas —
— a man becomes as if a son of the goddess, with a form adorned with glowing earrings, O king, and obtains the great merit of a hundred thousand cows.
Reaching Girimunjha, renowned throughout the three worlds, and bowing to the Grandfather Brahmā, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the excellent and pure tirtha where even today fish of gold and silver are seen.
By bathing there, O best of men, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; with a soul purified of all sins, one attains the highest state.
Then one should go to Malada, renowned throughout the three worlds, and at the western twilight touch its waters according to the prescribed rites.
One should offer oblation to the seven-flamed fire according to one's ability, O king of men; the wise declare this to be an inexhaustible gift to the ancestors.
The oblation to the seven-flamed fire is superior to the gift of a hundred thousand cows, to a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, and to a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then, returning, O king of kings, one should enter Vastraapada; having approached Mahādeva there, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Reaching Manimanta, a celibate with a composed mind, having spent a single night there, O king, obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the world-renowned Devikā, where the origin of the brahmins is said to have occurred, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And there is the abode of the trident-bearing one, renowned throughout the three worlds; bathing in the Devikā and duly worshipping Maheśvara —
— and offering oblation there according to one's ability, O bull of the Bhāratas, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
There is the tirtha of Rudra called Kamakhya, frequented by divine sages; by bathing there a man swiftly attains perfection, O Bhārata.
Going to Yajanam and Yajanam and likewise to Brahmavaluka, and touching the water at Pushpanyasa, one need not grieve at death thereafter.
Half a yojana wide and five yojanas long — such is the extent of the holy Devikā, frequented by divine sages.

Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to Dirghasatra in proper order, where Brahmā and the other gods, the Siddhas and the great sages, perform the long Dirghasatra sacrifice with ritual gifts, observing their vows.
By the mere act of going to Dirghasatra, O king of kings, O slayer of foes, a man obtains the combined fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then one should go to Vinashana, self-controlled and abstemious, where the Sarasvatī disappears into the desert surface, but reappears at Chamasa, at Shivodbheda, and at Nagodbheda.
By bathing at Camasodbheda one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; by bathing at Shivodbheda a man obtains the merit of a thousand cows.

By bathing at Nagodbheda a man attains the world of the serpents; and reaching the tirtha called Shashayanu, which is difficult to attain, O king of kings, where the lotus ponds are covered in the form of hares, O Bhārata —
— on the Sarasvatī, O great king, they bathe every year throughout the year, O best of the Bhāratas, always on the Kartika full-moon day.
By bathing there, O tiger among men, one shines forever like the moon, and obtains the merit of a thousand cows, O bull of the Bhāratas.

Reaching Kumarakoti, self-controlled, O joy of the Kurus, one should perform the ablution there, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods; one obtains the fruit of the cow-sacrifice and also elevates one's lineage.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to Rudrakoti with a composed mind, where, O great king, a crore of sages once assembled, filled with joy, longing for the vision of the god.
"I first, I first shall see him of the bull-banner" — thus the sages set out, O king, O Bhārata.
Then even the Lord of Yoga, O master of the earth, assuming his yoga form, in order to remove the anger of those sages of cultivated souls —
— created a crore of Rudras who stood before the sages, so that each one thought separately: "I have seen him before the others."
Mahādeva, pleased with those sages of fierce splendor, by their supreme devotion, O king, granted them a boon: "From this day forward, your dharma shall ever increase."
By bathing there, O tiger among men, at Rudrakoti, a pure man obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and elevates his lineage as well.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the Sangama, renowned throughout the world, supremely holy on the Sarasvatī, where Janārdana is worshipped.
Where Brahmā and the other gods, sages, Siddhas and Cāraṇas come, O king of kings, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
By bathing there, O tiger among men, one obtains abundant gold; with a soul purified of all sins, one goes to the world of Brahmā.
Where the sacrificial sessions of the sages were completed, O lord of men — reaching Satravashana, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows.
Pulastya said: Then one should go, O king of kings, to the celebrated Kurukṣetra; all living beings who go there are freed from their sins.
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra, I dwell at Kurukṣetra" — even one who constantly says this is freed from sins.
One should dwell there for a month on the Sarasvatī, O hero, O Yudhiṣṭhira, where Brahmā and the other gods, sages, Siddhas and Cāraṇas —
— Gandharvas, Apsaras, Yakṣas and serpents, O lord of the earth, visit the supremely holy Brahmakshetra, O Bhārata.
Even for one who merely desires Kurukṣetra in mind, O Yudhiṣṭhira, sins are utterly destroyed and one goes to the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, going to Kurukṣetra with faith, O chief of the Kurus, a man obtains the combined fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then, by duly saluting Machacruka, O king, the mighty Yakṣa who is the gatekeeper, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the incomparable abode of Viṣṇu called Satatam, O king of kings, where Hari is ever present.
By bathing there and worshipping Hari, the origin of the three worlds, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then one should go to Pariplavama, the tirtha renowned throughout the three worlds; a man obtains the combined fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
Reaching the tirtha of the earth, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows. Then, going to Shalukinim, O lord of men, a devotee of tirthas, by bathing at Dashasvamedha obtains that same fruit.
Reaching Sarpadarvi, the excellent tirtha of the serpents, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and attains the world of the serpents.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to Tarantuka the gatekeeper; by spending a single night there one obtains the merit of a thousand cows.

Then, going to Pañcanada, self-controlled and abstemious, by touching the waters of Koṭitīrtha one obtains the fruit of the Hayamedha sacrifice; reaching the tirtha of the Aśvins, one is born with great beauty.

Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the excellent Varaha tirtha, where Viṣṇu formerly stood in the form of the boar; by bathing there, O tiger among men, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then from Jayanti, O king of kings, one should enter the Somatirtha; by bathing there a man obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By bathing at Ekahansa a man obtains the merit of a thousand cows; reaching Kritashauca, a devotee of tirthas, O chief of the Kurus, obtains the Pundarika sacrifice and becomes purified.
Then at the place called Munjavata of the wise Mahādeva, by spending a single night there one obtains the lordship of the Ganas.
And there too, O great king, dwells a Yakshi renowned throughout the world; by approaching her, O king of kings, one attains the holy worlds.
That renowned gateway of Kurukṣetra, O bull among Bhāratas — the pilgrim, collected in mind, having circumambulated it clockwise,

having bathed at the measure of Puṣkara and having worshipped the ancestors and the gods — that which was brought by the great-souled Rāma, son of Jamadagni — O king, such a person becomes fulfilled and obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Then the tirtha-pilgrim should go to the lakes of Rāma, O lord of men; where Rāma, O king of kings, with his blazing splendour and swiftness, having extirpated the kshatriya class by his valour, established five lakes.
Having filled them with blood — thus we have heard — all the fathers were gratified, and likewise the grandfathers. Then those pleased fathers spoke to Rāma, O lord of the earth.

"Rāma, Rāma, O greatly fortunate one, O Bhārgava, we are pleased with you — by this devotion to ancestors and by your valour, O lord. Choose a boon, may you prosper; what do you desire, O greatly resplendent one?"
Thus addressed, O king of kings, Rāma, the foremost of warriors, spoke words with folded hands to the fathers standing in the sky:
"If you are pleased with me, if I am worthy of your grace, then by the favour of the ancestors I wish for increase of my austerities again.
And from the sin by which, overcome with wrath, I exterminated the kshatriya class — may I be freed from that sin by your splendour; and may these lakes become sacred tirthas renowned on earth."
Having heard these auspicious words of Rāma, the fathers then replied to Rāma, supremely delighted and filled with joy:
"May your austerities increase further, especially through your devotion to the ancestors; and as for what was done by you in anger — the extermination of the kshatriyas —
from that sin you are freed, and those brought low by your deeds — and these lakes shall undoubtedly attain the status of sacred tirthas."

Whoever, having bathed in these lakes, will gratify his ancestors — the fathers, well-pleased with him, will grant what is difficult to obtain on earth: the desired wish of his heart and the eternal heavenly world.
Having thus bestowed the boons upon Rāma, O king, the fathers then, taking leave of the Bhārgava, pleased, vanished on the spot.

Thus the lakes of Rāma are holy, belonging to the great-souled Bhārgava. A celibate of pure vow, having bathed in the lakes of Rāma and having worshipped Rāma, O king of kings, would obtain much gold.
Reaching Vamshamulaka, O foremost of the Kurus, the tirtha-pilgrim, having bathed at Vamshamulaka, would lift up his own lineage, O king.

Reaching the tirtha called Kayashodhana, O best of Bhāratas, the body of one who has bathed at that tirtha is without doubt purified; and with a purified body he goes to the excellent, unsurpassable worlds.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the tirtha renowned in all three worlds, where the worlds were formerly lifted up by Viṣṇu the mighty.

Reaching Lokoddhara, the tirtha renowned in all three worlds, having bathed at that best of tirthas, O king, one lifts up one's own kindred; and reaching Shritirtha, one obtains the highest prosperity.
Reaching the tirtha of Kapila, a celibate with collected mind, having bathed there and having worshipped the gods and ancestors, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand kapila cows.

Reaching the tirtha of the Sun, having bathed with a disciplined mind, having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, devoted to fasting, one obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun.
Reaching Gavambhavana, the tirtha-pilgrim, performing the ritual bath there in proper order, would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.
Reaching Shankhini there, O foremost of the Kurus, a man having bathed at the tirtha of the goddess obtains excellent beauty.

Then one should go, O king of kings, to the gatekeeper Arantuka — the tirtha of that great-souled king of yakshas on the Sarasvatī; having bathed there, O king, a man would obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to Brahmāvarta, O lord of men; a man having bathed at Brahmāvarta would attain the world of Brahmā.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the unsurpassable Sutirthaka, where the ancestors are always present together with the gods.
There one devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods should perform the ritual bath; one obtains the Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of the ancestors.
Then, O knower of dharma, reaching Ambuvasya in proper order, and bathing at the tirthas of Kosheshvara, O best of Bhāratas, one is freed from all diseases and is honoured in the world of Brahmā.
And Matritirtha is there likewise, where, O Bhārata, for one who has bathed, O king, his progeny multiplies and he enjoys boundless prosperity.
Then one should go to Shitavana, disciplined and with regulated diet; the tirtha there, O great king, is great and difficult to find elsewhere.
It purifies even one guilty of using a stick merely by seeing it, O lord of men; and having sprinkled one's hair at that place, one becomes purified, O Bhārata.
That tirtha there, O great king, is known as the remover of dog's hair; where, O tiger among men, learned brahmins devoted to tirthas —
— at this tirtha for the removal of dog's hair, O best of Bhāratas, the best of twice-born remove dog's hair through pranayama practices.

With purified souls, O king of kings, they proceed to the highest state; and the Dashasvamedha fruit too — at that tirtha, O lord of the earth, having bathed there, O tiger among men, one proceeds to the highest state.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to Manusham, renowned in the world; where, O king, black deer tormented by a hunter, having plunged into that lake, attained human form.
A man having bathed at that tirtha, a celibate with conquered senses, with a soul purified of all sins, is honoured in the heavenly world.
To the east of Manusham, at the distance of a krosa, O lord of the earth, is the famous river called Apaga, frequented by the siddhas.
Whatever man offers a meal of shyamaka grain there, dedicating it to the gods and ancestors — his religious merit is great; when one brahmin is fed, a crore of brahmins count as fed.
Having bathed there and having worshipped the gods and ancestors, and having stayed one night, one would obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the supreme abode of Brahmā, known on earth as Brahmodumbara, O Bhārata.
There, for one who has bathed in the pools of the seven sages, O bull among Kurus, and also at Kedara, O king of kings, through the greatness of Kapishtala —
— having approached Brahmā, pure and with controlled mind, one with a soul purified of all sins attains the world of Brahmā.
Reaching the Kedara of Kapishtala, which is very difficult to reach, one whose sin is burned away by austerity obtains invisibility.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to Saraka, renowned in the world; approaching Vṛṣadhvaja on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one obtains all desires and goes to the heavenly world.
Thirty million tirthas are in Saraka, O joy of the Kurus; Rudrakoti also at the well, and in the lakes, O lord of the earth; and Ilaspada too is there as a tirtha, O best of Bhāratas.
Having bathed there and having worshipped the ancestors and gods, O Bhārata, one does not come to ill fate and obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice.
A man having bathed at Kimdana and at Kimjapya, O lord of the earth, obtains immeasurable fruit of gift-giving and of recitation, O Bhārata.
And touching the waters at Kalashya, a man who is faithful and has conquered his senses obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
To the east of Saraka is the tirtha of the great-souled Nārada, O foremost of the best of Kurus, known as Anajanma.
A man having bathed at that tirtha and having given up his life, O Bhārata, with the permission of Nārada, attains worlds difficult to reach.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight one should enter Pundarika; a man having bathed there, O king, would obtain the fruit of the Pundarika sacrifice.
Then one should go to Trivishthapa, renowned in all three worlds; there is the holy river Vaitaraṇī, the remover of sins.
Having bathed there and having worshipped Shulapani, the bearer of the bull-banner, with a soul purified of all sins, one would proceed to the highest state.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Phalakirvana; where the gods, O king, ever resorting to Phalakirvana, perform great austerities for many thousands of years.
A man having bathed in the Drishadavati and having gratified the gods obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and the Atirātra, O Bhārata.
And having bathed at the tirtha of all the gods, O best of Bhāratas, a man, O king of kings, obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
A man having bathed at Panikhata and having gratified the gods obtains the Rājasūya sacrifice and goes to the world of the sages.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent tirtha of Mishraka; there the tirthas have been mixed together, O king of kings, by the great soul —
— by Vyāsa for the sake of the twice-born, thus we have heard, O tiger among kings; whoever bathes at Mishraka, he bathes in all the tirthas.
Then one should go to the forest of Vyāsa, disciplined and with regulated diet; a man having bathed in Manojava would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.

And going to Madhuvati, the tirtha of the goddess, a man who is pure, having bathed there and worshipped the gods and ancestors with controlled mind and purity, with the permission of the goddess, would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.
Whoever, at the confluence of the Kauśikī and the Drishadavati, O Bhārata, bathes with regulated diet, is freed from all sins.
Then there is a place named Vyasasthali, where by the wise Vyāsa, tormented by grief for his son, a resolve to abandon his body was made —
— but then restored by the gods, O king of kings. Approaching that place of his, one would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.
Reaching the well of Kimdatta and having offered a flat sesame-cake, one would attain the highest perfection, freed from debts, O foremost of Kurus.
And Ahas and Sudina — two tirthas very difficult to reach; having bathed in both of them, O tiger among men, one would attain the world of the Sun.

Then one should go to Mrigadhuma, renowned in all three worlds; having bathed in the lake of the Gaṅgā there and having worshipped Shulapani, the great god Mahādeva, a man would obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha.
A man having bathed at Devatirtha would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows; then one should go to Vamanaka, renowned in all three worlds.
Having bathed there at the footprint of Viṣṇu and having worshipped Vāmana, with a soul purified of all sins, one would attain the world of Viṣṇu.

A man having bathed at Kulampuna purifies his own lineage; going to the lake of Pavana, the excellent tirtha of the Maruts, having bathed there, O tiger among men, one is honoured in the world of Vāyu.
Having bathed in the lake of the immortals among the immortals, O lord of men, by the power of the immortals one is honoured in the heavenly world.
At the Shalisurpa of Shalihotra, O king of kings, having bathed according to rule, O foremost among the best of men, one would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows.
And Shrikunja on the Sarasvatī is a tirtha, O best of Bhāratas; a man having bathed there, O king, would obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma.

Then reaching Naimishakunja, O foremost of the Kurus, the sages of Naimiṣa, O king of kings, those whose wealth is austerity, with tirtha-pilgrimage as their purpose, went to Kurukṣetra in ancient times.
Then a grove on the Sarasvatī was made, O best of Bhāratas, so that it might be a great and pleasing resort for the sages.
A man having bathed in that grove would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows; a man having bathed at Kanyatirtha would obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma.

Then one should go, O tiger among men, to the supreme abode of Brahmā; there even a man of lower birth, having bathed, attains brahminhood; and a brahmin of pure soul would proceed to the highest state.
Then one should go, O foremost of men, to the unsurpassable tirtha of Soma; a man having bathed there, O king, would attain the world of Soma.
Then one should go to the tirtha of the seven Sarasvatas, O lord of men; where Maṅkaṇaka, the perfected great sage, renowned in the world —
— in ancient times, O king, Maṅkaṇaka — thus we have heard — was wounded in the hand by the tip of a blade of kusha grass, O king, and vegetable juice flowed from it.
He, that great ascetic brahmin-sage, seeing the vegetable juice, overcome with joy, began to dance, it is said, with eyes wide open in wonder.
Then, as he danced, O hero, whatever was immovable and whatever was moving — both were bewildered by his blazing energy as he danced.

The gods headed by Brahmā and the sages rich in austerities petitioned Mahādeva, O king, on behalf of the sage, O lord of men: 'This one should not dance thus; O god, it is fitting that you act accordingly.'
Then, approaching the one who was dancing, his mind filled with joy, the god, desiring the welfare of the gods, spoke to the sage.
'Ah, O great sage, O knower of dharma, why do you dance? What is your occasion for rejoicing today, O best among sages?'
The sage said: 'Do you not see, O god, the drop of Śākara's essence that has flowed from my hand? Having seen it I have danced, filled with great joy.'
Pulastya said: Laughing, the god spoke to the sage who was deluded by passion: 'I, O brahmin, am not amazed — look at me.'
Having spoken thus, O best of men, by the wise Mahādeva, with the tip of his finger, O lord of kings, his own thumb was struck, O sinless one.
Then ashes, white as snow, emerged from the wound, O king. Seeing this, the sage, ashamed, O king, fell at his feet.
'I regard no other god as greater than Rudra. You are the refuge of the world of gods and demons, O bearer of the trident.'
'This universe, the three worlds with their moving and unmoving beings, was created by you; at the end of the age, O blessed lord, all enter into you alone.'
'You cannot be fully known even by the gods — how then by me? All the gods, with Brahmā at their head, are seen in you, O sinless one.'
'You are the all, the maker and the cause of all worlds; by your grace all gods here rejoice, fearless. Having thus praised Mahādeva, the sage bowed low.
The sage said: 'By your grace, O Mahādeva, my austerity shall not be diminished.'
Pulastya said: Then the god, his heart delighted, spoke these words to the brahmin-sage: 'O brahmin, may your austerity increase a thousandfold by my grace.'
'And here in this hermitage I shall dwell together with you, O great sage. Those who bathe at the Saptasārasvata and worship me —'
'— nothing shall be unattainable for them in this world or the next, and they shall go to the world of Sārasvata — there is no doubt.'
Then one should go to Auśanasa, celebrated in the three worlds, where the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages rich in austerity —
— and the blessed Kārttikeya, at the three junctions of the day, O Bhārata, made his presence there, desiring to please Bhārgava.
The tīrtha Kapālamocana releases one from all sins; bathing there, O tiger among men, one is freed from all sins.
Then one should go to Agnitīrtha; having bathed there, O bull among men, one attains the world of Agni and also redeems one's family.
There too is the tīrtha of Viśvāmitra, O best of the Bhāratas; having bathed there, O great king, one is reborn into brahminhood.
Reaching Brahmayoni, pure and with a collected mind, and bathing there, O tiger among men, one attains the world of Brahmā and purifies one's family to the seventh generation — there is no doubt.

Then one should go, O lord of kings, to the tīrtha celebrated in the three worlds, known as Pṛthūdaka, O king, belonging to Kārttikeya; one should perform ablutions there, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods.
Whatever inauspicious act has been done out of ignorance or knowledge, by a woman or a man, with human understanding —
— all of that perishes for one who has merely bathed there, O Bhārata, and one also gains the fruit of the Aśvamedha and goes to the heavenly world.
They say Kurukṣetra is holy; holier than Kurukṣetra is Sarasvatī; holier than Sarasvatī are the tīrthas; and holiest among the tīrthas is Pṛthūdaka.
One who, at the best of all tīrthas, gives up his body at Pṛthūdaka, devoted to silent prayer, will not grieve at tomorrow's death.
It is declared by Sanatkumāra and by the great-souled Vyāsa, and is fixed in the Veda, O king — one should go to Pṛthūdaka.
There is no tīrtha more holy than Pṛthūdaka, O best of men; this is pure, sacred, and purifying — there is no doubt.
Even those who have committed sins go to heaven after bathing there, O best of men at Pṛthūdaka — so the wise declare.
And there too is the tīrtha Madhusrava, O best of the Bhāratas; a man who bathes there, O king, obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then one should go in order, O best of men, to the tīrtha of the goddess — the confluence of Sarasvatī and Aruṇā, celebrated throughout the world.
Fasting for three nights and bathing, one is freed from the sin of killing a brahmin, and a man gains the merit of Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.

And one purifies one's family to the seventh generation, O bull of the Bhāratas. There too is the tīrtha Avatīrṇa, O chief of the Kuru lineage, formerly created by Darbhiṇa out of compassion for the brahmins.
A twice-born, whether through vow and sacred thread ceremony or through fasting, accompanied by rites and mantras, shall become a true brahmin — there is no doubt.
Even one destitute of rites and mantras, having bathed there, O bull among men, shall become a brahmin who has fulfilled his vows — this has been seen in ancient tradition.
The four oceans were also brought together there by Darbhiṇa; one who has bathed in them, O tiger among men, shall not attain an evil end, and he gains the merit of four thousand cows.
Then one should go, O lord of kings, to the tīrtha Śatasāhasraka; and there too is Sāhasraka — two tīrthas celebrated throughout the world.
For a man who bathes in both obtains the merit of a thousand cows, and any gift or fast done there becomes a thousandfold in merit.

Then one should go, O lord of kings, to the excellent tīrtha of Reṇukā; one should perform ablutions there, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods; with a soul purified of all sins, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Touching the waters of Vimocana, with anger conquered and senses mastered, one is freed from all the faults incurred by accepting gifts.
Then, going to Pañcavaṭa as a celibate with senses mastered, endowed with great merit, one is honoured in the world of the righteous.
There the lord of yoga, Sthāṇu himself, whose banner is the bull — having worshipped that lord of gods, one attains perfection by going there alone.
The tīrtha of Varuṇa at Aujasa blazes with its own splendour; there Guha was consecrated as the commander-in-chief of the gods by the gods headed by Brahmā and by the sages rich in austerities.
To the east of Aujasa is Kurutīrtha, O chief of the Kurus; a man who bathes at Kurutīrtha, a celibate with senses mastered and soul purified of all sins, attains the world of the Kurus.
Then one should go to Svargadvāra with discipline and regulated diet; one attains the heavenly world and also goes to the world of Brahmā.
Then one who frequents tīrthas should go to Anaraka, O lord of men; a man who bathes there, O king, shall not attain an evil end.
There Brahmā himself is ever attended, O lord of the earth, O best of men, by the gods led by Nārāyaṇa.
And the presence of Rudra's consort is there, O lord of kings, O chief of the Kurus; having approached that goddess, one shall not attain an evil end.
And there too, O great king, by approaching Viśveśvara, the husband of Umā, the great god, one is freed from all sins.
And by approaching Nārāyaṇa of the lotus-navel, the subduer of enemies, one shines forth, O great king, and attains the world of Viṣṇu.
But one who has bathed at the tīrtha of all the gods, O bull among men, having abandoned all sorrows, shines forever like the moon.
Then a frequenter of tīrthas should go to Svastipura, O lord of men; reaching this purifying tīrtha and satisfying the ancestors and gods, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And there too is a pool of the Gaṅgā and a well, O bull of the Bhāratas; three crores of tīrthas are in that well, O lord of the earth; a man who bathes there, O king, attains the heavenly world.
A man who bathes in the Āpagā river and worships Maheśvara attains a place among the hosts of Gaṇa and also redeems his own family.
Then one should go to Sthāṇuvaṭa, celebrated in the three worlds; having bathed there and stayed the night, one would attain the world of Rudra.
One should go to Badarīpācana, then to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; a man should eat the jujube fruit there, having fasted for three nights.
One who properly eats the jujube fruit for twelve full years, as well as one who fasts for three nights, shall be equal in merit, O lord of men.
Reaching Indramārga, a frequenter of tīrthas, O lord of men, is honoured in the world of Śakra by fasting for a day and a night.
Staying for one night, a man who has remained there for a single night, disciplined and truthful in speech, is honoured in the world of Brahmā.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the tīrtha celebrated in the three worlds, where is the hermitage of Āditya, that great-souled mass of radiance.
A man who bathes at that tīrtha and worships Vibhāvasu goes to the world of Āditya and also redeems his family.
A man who bathes at Somatīrtha, a frequenter of tīrthas, O chief of the Kurus, attains the world of Soma — there is no doubt.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the most holy tīrtha of the great-souled Dadhīca, O king — purifying and celebrated throughout the world.

Where, O king, that Sārasvata, that Āṅgirasa, that treasury of austerity dwells — a man who bathes at that tīrtha obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and also attains the state of Sārasvata — there is no doubt.
Then one should go to Kanyāśrama, disciplined and celibate, fasting for three nights, O king, devoted to fasting; one obtains a hundred divine maidens and goes to the world of Brahmā.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the tīrtha Saṃnihitī, where the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages rich in austerity, endowed with great merit, come together month after month.
Touching the waters of Saṃnihitī when the sun is seized by Rāhu, one has the eternal merit of a hundred Aśvamedha sacrifices performed.
Whatever tīrthas there are on earth and those that move through the sky, rivers large and small, lakes and all springs —
— wells and embankments, and all the holy sanctuaries — they all come to Saṃnihitī month after month — there is no doubt.

Whatever evil deed has been done by a woman or a man — all of that perishes for one who has merely bathed there, there is no doubt, and one goes to the world of Brahmā in a vehicle the colour of a lotus.
Having paid reverence to the Yakṣa, the doorkeeper Arantuka, and having touched the form of Koṭi, one obtains much gold.

And there too is the pool of the Gaṅgā, a tīrtha, O best of the Bhāratas; one who has bathed there, O knower of dharma, as a celibate with a collected mind, obtains the eternal merit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Naimiṣa is holy on earth, and Puṣkara in the sky, but Kurukṣetra is distinguished among all three worlds.
Even the dust of Kurukṣetra, stirred up by the wind, leads even one of evil deeds to the highest state.
Those who dwell in Kurukṣetra, to the south of Sarasvatī and to the north of Dṛṣadvatī, dwell in heaven.
'I will go to Kurukṣetra,' 'I dwell at Kurukṣetra' — even uttering one such word, one is freed from all sins.
Kurukṣetra, the altar of Brahmā, holy, frequented by brahmin-sages — those who dwell there, O king, are not to be pitied in any way.
What lies between Tarantuka and Arantuka, and the lakes of Rāma and Macakruka — this Kurukṣetra-Samantapañcaka is called the northern altar of the Grandfather.

Pulastya said: Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the ancient tīrtha Dharmatīrtha; a man who bathes there, O king, virtuous in conduct and with a collected mind, purifies his family to the seventh generation, O king — there is no doubt.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the most excellent Kārāpatana; there one attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and proceeds to the world of sages.
Then, O king, a person should proceed to the Saugandhika forest, where Brahmā and the other gods dwell, and where the sages rich in austerities reside.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras, and great serpents inhabit that forest — merely by entering it one is freed from all sins.
For there flows that best of rivers, the supreme stream among all rivers — the goddess Sarasvatī, O king, issuing from the Plakṣa tree, supremely holy.
There one should perform the ablution in the water that issues from the anthill; having honoured the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
That holy ford there, called Īśānādhyuṣita and exceedingly rare, lies within the distance of six throws of a śamyā stick from the anthill — this is certain.
By bathing there, O tiger among men, one obtains the merit of a thousand tawny cows and of the Vājimedhā rite — this has been seen in ancient tradition.
Having visited Sugandhā, Śatakumbhā, and Pañcayajñā, O Bhārata, the best of men is honoured in the heavenly world.

Having reached that same ford known as Triśūlakhāta, O Bhārata, one should perform the ablution there, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods; upon leaving the body that person attains lordship among Gaṇas — of this there is no doubt.
Then, O best of kings, one should go to the exceedingly rare abode of the goddess known as Śākaṃbarī, renowned throughout the three worlds.
For a divine thousand years, O faithful one, she maintained herself on vegetables alone, subsisting on them month by month, O lord of men.
Sages rich in austerities came there out of devotion to the goddess, and she offered them hospitality with vegetables, O Bhārata; from that act her name Śākambharī became established.
Having reached Śākaṃbarī, a celibate student, composed and intent, should stay three nights, eating only vegetables with restraint and purity.
Whatever merit accrues from properly subsisting on vegetables for twelve years — that very merit becomes his through the grace of the goddess, O Bhārata.
Then one should go to Suvarṇākṣa, renowned in all three worlds, where Viṣṇu formerly propitiated Rudra in order to win his favour.
He obtained very many boons, exceedingly rare even among the gods; and the destroyer of Tripura, being fully pleased, spoke to him, O Bhārata.
"Even more dear to us than ourselves shall you be in the world, O Kṛṣṇa, and the entire universe shall face toward you — of this there is no doubt."
Having gone there and worshipped the bearer of the bull-banner, O best of kings, one obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and also attains lordship among the Gaṇas.
Then a person who has fasted three nights should go to Dhūmāvatī; he obtains whatever desires he has sought in his mind — of this there is no doubt.

By the southern side of the goddess is the holy ford Rathāvarta, O lord of men; one who is faithful and has his senses under control should ascend there, O knower of dharma; through the grace of Mahādeva he attains the supreme destination.

After circumambulating it in the clockwise direction, one should go, O bull of the Bhāratas, O greatly wise one, to the ford called Dhārā, which destroys all sins; having bathed there, O tiger among men, the lord of men grieves no more.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go, having paid homage to the great mountain, to Gaṅgādvāra, which is equal to the very gate of heaven — of this there is no doubt.
One should perform ablution there at Koṭitīrtha with a concentrated mind; one attains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and also lifts up one's lineage.
By duly offering libations to gods and ancestors at Saptagaṅgā, Trigaṅgā, and Śakrāvarta, one is honoured in the worlds of the meritorious.
Then a person who has fasted three nights and bathed at Kanakhala obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and proceeds to the heavenly world.
A pilgrim, O lord of men, should also go to Kapilāvaṭa; by spending a single night there, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows.
O best of kings, the ford of the great-souled serpent-king Kapila, O best among the Kurus, is renowned in all the worlds.
One should perform ablution at that Nāgatīrtha, O lord of men; a person thereby obtains the merit of a thousand tawny cows.
Then one should go to Lalitikā, the most excellent ford of Śaṃtanu; having bathed there, O king, a person does not reach an evil fate.
A person who bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā — at those two meeting-points — obtains the merit of ten Aśvamedha sacrifices and also lifts up his lineage.
Then, O best of kings, one should go to Sugandhā, renowned throughout the worlds; with soul purified of all sins, one is honoured in the world of Brahmā.
A pilgrim, O lord of men, should then go to Rudrāvarta; having bathed there, O king, a person is honoured in the heavenly world.
One who bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī, O best of men, obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and proceeds to the heavenly world.
Having gone to Bhadrakarṇeśvara and worshipped the god according to proper rite, one does not reach an evil fate and proceeds to the heavenly world.
A pilgrim should then go to Kubjāmraka in due sequence; one obtains the merit of a thousand cows and proceeds to the heavenly world.
A pilgrim, O lord of men, should go to Arundhatīvaṭa; by touching the ocean-ford after fasting three nights, a person obtains the merit of a thousand cows and also lifts up his lineage.
A celibate student, composed in mind, should then go to Brahmāvarta; he obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and proceeds to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the source of the Yamunā and touched its waters, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha and is honoured in the heavenly world.
Having reached the ford Darvīsaṃkramaṇa, renowned throughout the three worlds, one obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and proceeds to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the source of the Sindhu, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, by staying there five nights one gains much gold.
Then, having reached the Vedī, which is most difficult of access, a person obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and attains the destination taught by Uśanas.
Having reached the Ṛṣikulyā and also the Vāsiṣṭha ford, O Bhārata, by crossing beyond the Vāsiṣṭha, all the castes become twice-born.
A person who bathes in the Ṛṣikulyā attains the world of the sages; if he stays there a month subsisting on vegetables, O lord of men, he reaches the world of the sages.
Having reached Bhṛgutuṅga, one obtains the fruit of the Vājimedhā; and by going to Vīrapramokṣa, one is freed from all sins.
Having reached the ford at the junction of Kṛttikā and Maghā, O Bhārata, a person of meritorious deeds obtains the combined fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
Then, having reached Saṃdhyā and touched the incomparable ford of knowledge, Vidyātīrtha, one becomes accomplished in all branches of learning.
One who stays the night at Mahāśrama, which releases one from all sins, and eats but once a day or fasts completely, inhabits auspicious worlds.
By fasting at the sixth part of the day and staying a month at Mahālaya, one whose soul is purified of all sins gains much gold.
Then, having gone to Vetasikā, frequented by the Grandfather Brahmā himself, one obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and attains the destination taught by Uśanas.
Then, having reached the ford of Sundarikā, frequented by Siddhas, one becomes endowed with beauty — this has been seen in ancient tradition.
Then a celibate student with senses subdued, having gone to the Brāhmaṇī river, attains the world of Brahmā riding in a lotus-hued vehicle.
Then one should go to the holy Naimiṣa, frequented by Siddhas, where Brahmā eternally dwells, surrounded by hosts of gods.
For one who merely longs for Naimiṣa, half his sin is destroyed; a person who has but entered it is freed from all sins.
A wise person devoted to holy fords should stay a month at Naimiṣa; whatever holy fords exist on earth are all contained in Naimiṣa, O Bhārata.

One who performs ablution there with self-control and regulated diet obtains the fruit of the Gavāmayana sacrifice, O Bhārata, and purifies his lineage even to the seventh generation, O best of the Bhāratas.
One who abandons his life at Naimiṣa while fully devoted to fasting rejoices having attained the heavenly world — so say the wise ones; Naimiṣa is ever holy and pure, O best of kings.
A person who has fasted three nights, having reached Gaṅgodbheda, obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and is born merged with Brahmā.
Having reached the Sarasvatī and offered libations to ancestors and gods, one rejoices in the worlds of Sarasvatī — of this there is no doubt.
Then a celibate student, composed in mind, should go to the Bāhudā; a person thereby obtains the fruit of the Devasatra sacrifice.
Then one should go to the holy Cīravatī, thronged with the most meritorious souls; devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya.
Having reached Vimalāśoka, one shines like the moon; by staying there a single night one is honoured in the heavenly world.
Then one should go to Gopratāra, the most excellent ford of the Sarayū, where Rāma ascended to heaven together with his servants, forces, and mounts.
He departed to heaven having left his body, through the power of that ford and by the grace of Rāma and by his own determination, O Bhārata.
A person who bathes at that ford, Gopratāra, O lord of men, with his soul purified of all sins, is honoured in the heavenly world.
A person who bathes at the ford of Rāma on the Gomatī, O joy of the Kurus, obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha and purifies his lineage.

There exists there a ford worth a hundred thousand, O best of the Bhāratas; by touching it with self-discipline and regulated diet, one obtains the holy merit of a thousand cows, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then, O best of kings, one should go to the incomparable abode of the Lord; having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and worshipped Guha, O king, a person obtains the merit of a thousand cows and becomes radiant.
Then, having gone to Vārāṇasī and worshipped the bearer of the bull-banner, a person who bathes in the Kapilāhrada obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having reached the rare ford of Mārkaṇḍeya, O best of kings, at the world-renowned confluence of the Gomatī and the Gaṅgā, one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma and also lifts up one's lineage.
Then a celibate student with senses subdued, having reached Gayā, obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha by the very act of going there, O Bhārata.
There is the famous Akṣayavaṭa, renowned in all three worlds; whatever is offered there to the ancestors becomes imperishable, O lord.
Having touched the waters of the great river and offered libations to ancestors and gods, one attains imperishable worlds and also lifts up one's lineage.
Then one should go to Brahmasaras, beautified by the Dharmaraṇya forest; one obtains the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice even by the dawn of the very same night.
In that lake, O best of kings, stands the sacrificial post of Brahmā; by circumambulating that post clockwise, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Then, O best of kings, one should go to Dhenukā, renowned throughout the world; having stayed one night, O king, one should offer a cow of sesame — with soul purified of all sins one certainly reaches the world of Soma.
There is a sign there, O great king, and even today it is beyond doubt: a tawny cow roams the mountain with her calf, and the footprints of that cow with calf are visible even today, O Bhārata.
By touching those footprints, O best of kings, O best of lords, whatever inauspicious deeds one may have done are destroyed, O Bhārata.
Then one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the wise God; having approached the bearer of the bull-banner there, one should bathe with ashes.
For a brahmin this equals the observance of a twelve-year vow; for persons of the other castes all sins are destroyed.
Then one should go to the Udyanta mountain, resounding with songs; there the foot-print of the Sāvitrī is seen, O bull of the Bhāratas.
There a brahmin of firm vows should worship the twilight; by that act his worship of twilight becomes equal to twelve years of observance.
There too is the famous Yonidvara, O bull of the Bhāratas; by visiting that place a man is freed from the sin of mixing castes.
The man who dwells at Gaya through both the dark and bright fortnights purifies his family to the seventh generation, O king — of this there is no doubt.
Many sons should be desired so that even one may go to Gaya, perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or release a dark-coloured bull there.
Then, O king, the pilgrim should go to the Phalgu river; the lord of men attains the merit of the Aśvamedha and reaches great spiritual perfection.

Then, O lord of kings, one should go with a composed mind to Dharmaprishtha, where Dharma himself eternally abides, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira; by visiting that place one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the excellent tirtha of Brahmā; there, O lord of kings, after worshipping Brahmā of immeasurable splendour, a man attains the combined fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then the pilgrim, O lord of men, should go to Rājagṛha; by bathing in its hot springs he rejoices like Kakṣīvat of old.
There a pure man should partake of the daily offering of the Yakshini; by the grace of the Yakshini he is freed from the sin of foeticide.
Going then to Maninnaga, one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows; the man who partakes of the daily offering of Maninaga gains that reward.
Even if bitten by a venomous serpent, the poison does not spread through him; by spending a single night there he is freed from all sins.
Then, O king, one should go to the forest of the brahmin-sage Gautama; by bathing in Ahalyā's lake one attains the highest state and, visiting it, O king, one finds the most exalted prosperity.
There is a well famous in all three worlds, O knower of dharma; by bathing there one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
There is the well of the royal sage Janaka, worshipped by the gods; by bathing there one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Then one should go to Vinashana, which removes all sins; one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya and goes to the world of Soma.
Reaching the Gandaki, whose waters arise from all sacred tirthas, one obtains the Vājapeya merit and goes to the world of the Sun.
Then, O knower of dharma, entering the forest hermitage of Adhivamshya, one rejoices among the Guhyakas, O great king — of this there is no doubt.
Reaching the river Kampana, frequented by the Siddhas, one obtains the Pundarika merit and goes to the world of the Sun.
Then reaching the Viśālā, a river famous in all three worlds, one obtains the Agniṣṭoma merit and goes to the heavenly world.
Then reaching the Maheshvari stream, O lord of men, one obtains the Aśvamedha merit and uplifts one's family.
A pure man reaching the divine Pushkarini pond does not attain an evil state and gains the Vājapeya merit.
A celibate student of focused mind should go to Maheshvarapada; by bathing at Maheshvarapada one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

There, O bull of the Bhāratas, a crore of tirthas are renowned; O lord of kings, they were being carried off by a wicked demon in the form of a tortoise but were recovered, O king, by the all-powerful Viṣṇu.
One who bathes there in that crore of tirthas, O Yudhiṣṭhira, obtains the Pundarika merit and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then one should go, O lord of kings, to the abode of Nārāyaṇa; Hari of marvellous deeds forever dwells there, O Bhārata — that place is known as Shalagrama.
By visiting Viṣṇu, the imperishable lord of the three worlds and granter of boons, one obtains the Aśvamedha merit and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
There is a well that frees one from all sins, O knower of dharma; the four oceans are ever present in that well; by bathing there, O lord of kings, one does not attain an evil state.
By visiting Mahādeva and the imperishable boon-granting Viṣṇu, one shines like the moon freed from its debts, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
A pure man of focused mind bathing at Jatismara attains the state of remembering past births — of this there is no doubt.
Going to Vateshvarapura and worshipping Keśava, one obtains all desired wishes through fasting — of this there is no doubt.
Then going to Vāmana, which removes all sins, and saluting the god Hari, one does not attain an evil state.
Going to the hermitage of Bharata, which removes all sins, and frequenting the Kauśikī river there — destroyer of great sins — a man obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the excellent Campakaaranya forest; by spending a single night there one obtains the merit of gifting a thousand cows.
Then reaching Jyeshthila, a tirtha held in the highest esteem, by fasting for a single night one obtains the Agniṣṭoma merit.
By beholding there Viśveśvara of great radiance together with the Goddess, one attains the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa, O bull among men.
Reaching Kanyasamvedya with self-restraint and regulated diet, one attains the worlds of Manu the Progenitor, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Those who give drink and food at Kanya, O Bhārata — that gift is imperishable, so declare the sages of firm vows.
Reaching the Nishchira, famous in all three worlds, one obtains the Aśvamedha merit and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Those men who make gifts at the confluence of the Nishchira go to the world of Brahmā, O tiger among men — of this there is no doubt.
There is the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, famous in all three worlds; one who bathes there obtains the Vājapeya merit.
Reaching Devakuta, frequented by hosts of brahmin-sages, one obtains the Aśvamedha merit and uplifts one's family.
Then, O lord of kings, one should go to the lake of the sage Kauśika, where Viśvāmitra surnamed Kauśika attained the highest perfection.
One who resides there for a month on the Kauśikī river, O hero, O bull of the Bhāratas, attains in that month whatever merit belongs to the Aśvamedha.
One who dwells in the great lake, the foremost of all tirthas, does not attain an evil state and finds abundant gold.
By going to Kumar who dwells in the hermitage of heroes, a man obtains the Aśvamedha merit — of this there is no doubt.
Reaching Agnidhara, famous in all three worlds, one obtains the Agniṣṭoma merit and does not return from heaven.
Going to Pitamahasara, established by the king of mountains, one who bathes there obtains the Agniṣṭoma fruit.
Flowing from Pitāmaha's lake is the world-purifying Kumaradhara stream, famous in all three worlds right there.
One who bathes there perceives himself as having attained his purpose; by fasting at the sixth part of the day one is freed from the sin of killing a brahmin.
A devout man should ascend the peak of the great goddess Gaurī, famous in all three worlds, and enter into the breast-shaped pools there.
One who bathes there, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods, obtains the Hayamedha merit and goes to the world of Indra.
A celibate student of focused mind reaching Tamraruna obtains the Aśvamedha merit and goes to the world of Indra.
Reaching the well on the Nandini river, worshipped by the thirty gods, one attains whatever merit belongs to the Naramedha sacrifice, O scion of the Kurus.
A wise man who fasts for three nights and bathes at the confluence of the Kalika, where the Kauśikī and Aruṇā rivers meet, is freed from all sins.
Reaching the tirtha of Urvaśī and then the hermitage of Soma, a wise man who bathes at the hermitage of Kumbhakarṇa is honoured upon this earth.
A celibate student of regulated vows who bathes at the holy Kokamukha attains the power of remembering past births — this has been seen from ancient times.
A twice-born man who visits Nandā even once becomes purified in soul; his soul cleansed of all sins, he goes to the world of Indra.
Reaching Rishabhadviipa, the resort of Kraunchanisudan, and bathing in the Sarasvatī, one shines seated in a celestial chariot.
One should bathe at the tirtha of Uddālaka frequented by sages, O great king; by bathing there one is freed from all sins.
Reaching the holy Dharmatirtha frequented by brahmin-sages, a man obtains the Vājapeya merit — of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, reaching Campā and performing water-rites on the Bhāgīrathī, and then visiting Dandarka, one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
Then one should go to the holy Lavedika, frequented by the pious; one obtains the Vājapeya merit and is honoured while seated in a celestial chariot.
Pulastya said: Then reaching the excellent tirtha of Samvedya at the twilight hour, a learned man who bathes there becomes purified — of this there is no doubt.
By the grace of Rāma was this tirtha created of old, O king; reaching the Lohitya, one finds abundant gold.
A man who fasts for three nights and reaches the Karatoya, in accordance with the Vedic rites of the Pitāmaha, obtains the Aśvamedha merit.
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, O lord of kings, the wise declare one attains ten times the merit of the Aśvamedha.
One who reaches the further island of the Gaṅgā and bathes there, O Bhārata, fasting for three nights, O king, attains all desires.
Going then to the Vaitaraṇī, the river that removes sins, and reaching the tirtha of Viraja, one shines like the moon.
One is born in a holy family, removes all sin, and having obtained the merit of a thousand cows, that man purifies his family.
A pure man dwelling at the confluence of the Shona and the Jyotirathya, having satisfied ancestors and gods, obtains the Agniṣṭoma merit.
At the source of the Shona and the Narmadā, O delight of the Kurus, bathing at Vamshagulma, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Reaching the tirtha of Rishabha in Koshala, O lord of men, a man who fasts for three nights obtains the Vājapeya merit.
Reaching Kalatirtha in Koshala and bathing there, one obtains the merit of eleven bulls — of this there is no doubt.
A man who fasts for three nights and bathes in the Pushpavati gains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows and uplifts his family.
Then bathing at the tirtha of Badarika with a focused mind, one attains long life and goes to the heavenly world.
Then reaching Mahendra, frequented by Jāmadagnya (Parashurama), a man who bathes at the tirtha of Rāma obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
There too is the Kedara of Mataṅga, O delight of the Kurus; a man who bathes there, O king, obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
Reaching Shriparvata and bathing on the riverbank there, one obtains the Aśvamedha merit and goes to the heavenly world.
On Shriparvata the great and radiant Mahādeva dwelt with the Goddess in great delight, and Brahmā dwelt there surrounded by the thirty gods.
A pure man of focused mind who bathes there in the divine lake obtains the Aśvamedha merit and attains the highest perfection.
Having gone to Mount Ṛṣabha in the Pāṇḍya country, worshipped by the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and rejoices on the back of heaven.
Then one should go to the Kāverī river, attended by hosts of Apsarases; bathing there, O king, a man obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
Then on the seashore one should touch the waters at the Kanyā-tīrtha; having touched the waters there, O lord of kings, one is freed from all sins.
Then having reached Gokarṇa, renowned in the three worlds, situated amid the ocean, O lord of kings, saluted by all the worlds—
—where gods headed by Brahmā, sages rich in austerities, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Kiṃnaras, and great serpents—
—Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, men, Nāgas, rivers, oceans, and mountains all worship the Lord of Umā—

—there, having duly worshipped Īśāna with a three-night fast, a man obtains the merit of ten Aśvamedha sacrifices and attains membership in Gaṇeśa's host; having dwelt there for twelve nights, a man becomes purified in soul.
Right there too is the abode of Gāyatrī, renowned in the three worlds; dwelling there for three nights one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
There is even a visible proof for Brāhmaṇas, O lord of men: he who recites the Gāyatrī — even one born of a mixed union — or sings a hymn or a song there, to him it becomes fully effective, O king.
Having reached the difficult-to-find well of the sage Saṃvarta, one becomes endowed with beauty and is born fortunate.
Then having reached the Veṇṇā river, one should satisfy the ancestors and gods; a man thereby obtains a celestial chariot adorned with peacocks and swans.
Then having reached the Godāvarī, ever frequented by Siddhas, one attains the merit of the Gavāmayana sacrifice and reaches the world of Vāsuki.
Bathing at the confluence of the Veṇṇā one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; bathing at the confluence of the Varadā one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
Having reached Brahmasthāna, a man who has dwelt there for three nights obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows and goes to the world of heaven.
Having reached Kuśaplavana, a celibate with concentrated mind, having dwelt and bathed there for three nights, obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then at the beautiful Devahrada, born from the waters of the Kṛṣṇa-Veṇṇā, and also at the Jātimātra lake, and at the Kanyāśrama, O king—
—where the king of gods went to heaven having offered a hundred sacrifices, one obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices merely by going there, O Bhārata.
Bathing in the Sarvadevahrada one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows; bathing in the Jātimātra lake a man becomes one who remembers his former births.
Then having reached the greatly holy Payoṣṇī, best of rivers, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods, one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
Having reached the Daṇḍaka forest, O great king, and touching the sacred waters, one who merely bathes there obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows, O Bhārata.
Having gone to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and of the great-souled Śuka, a man does not attain an evil state and he purifies his lineage.
Then one should go to Śūrpāraka, frequented by the son of Jamadagni; a man bathing at the Rāma-tīrtha there obtains abundant gold.
Bathing at the Sapta-Godāvarī, disciplined and with regulated food, one attains great merit and goes to the world of the gods.
Then one should go to Devapatha, disciplined with regulated food; a human being obtains the merit of a Devasatra sacrifice.
Having reached the Tuṅgaka forest, a celibate with controlled senses — there the sage Sārasvata taught the Vedas in former times.
There the Vedas that had been lost — the son of the sage Aṅgiras — sitting upon the upper garments of the great sages, O Bhārata—
—through the Oṃkāra properly and correctly uttered, whatever each sage had formerly studied came back present to him.
There sages and gods — Varuṇa, Agni, Prajāpati, Lord Hari-Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva as well—
—and the blessed Grandfather of great splendour, together with the gods, appointed the great-resplendent Bhṛgu for the purpose of performing the sacrificial rites.
Then the blessed one duly performed for all those sages once more the sacred fire-installation, through the rites prescribed by the scriptures.
There indeed the gods, duly satisfied with their shares of clarified butter, went to the three worlds, and the sages departed in happiness.
All sin of one who has entered that forest Tuṅgaka, O best of kings, is destroyed — whether of a woman or a man.
A wise man who dwells there for a month, disciplined and with regulated food, goes to the world of Brahmā, O king, and the man purifies his lineage.
Having reached Medhāvika and satisfying the ancestors and gods, one attains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and gains memory and intelligence.
Then having gone to Mount Kālaṃjara, renowned in the world, bathing there in the Devahrada, one obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
One should discipline oneself there on Mount Kālaṃjara, O king; a man would be honoured in the world of heaven — there is no doubt about this.
Then on Citrakūṭa, best of excellent mountains, O lord of peoples, having reached the Mandākinī river that removes sins—
—one who performs ablutions there, devoted to the worship of ancestors and gods, obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the highest state.
Then one should go, O lord of kings, to the unequalled abode of the Lord, where the god Mahāsena is ever present, O king.
A man, O best of men, succeeds there merely by going; bathing at Koṭi-tīrtha, a man obtains the merit of a gift of a thousand cows.
Having circumambulated in the rightward direction, a man should go to the Jyeṣṭhāsthāna; having visited Mahādeva there, he shines like the moon.
There is a renowned well there, O great king, O bull of the Bhāratas; four oceans dwell there, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having touched the sacred waters there, O lord of kings, and having performed the circumambulation, a man of controlled soul, purified, goes to the highest state.
Then one should go, O best of Kurus, to the great city of Śṛṅgavera, where Rāma son of Daśaratha once crossed the river, O great king.
A celibate man with concentrated mind, bathing in the Gaṅgā there, becomes free of sin and obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having visited and duly worshipped Mahādeva, O lord of men, and having circumambulated, one attains membership in the host of Gaṇa.
Then one should go, O lord of kings, to Prayāga, praised by the sages, where gods headed by Brahmā, the directions with their lords—
—guardians of the worlds, Sādhyas, Nairṛtas, the ancestors, the great sages headed by Sanatkumāra—
—and the Brahmā-sages headed by Aṅgiras, other sages, and Nāgas, Suparṇas, Siddhas, and those who move in circles—
—rivers, oceans, Gandharvas, and Apsarases dwell, and the blessed Lord Hari abides there, honored by Prajāpati.
There are three fire-altars there, in the midst of which the Jāhnavī, departing from Prayāga, is regarded as the foremost of all tīrthas.
There the daughter of the Sun, renowned in the three worlds, Yamunā, meets with the Gaṅgā, she who purifies the worlds.
The confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is regarded as the lap of the earth; Prayāga the sages know as the front part of that lap, its innermost core.
Prayāga along with Pratiṣṭhāna, Kambala and Aśvatara, the tīrtha of Bhogavatī — these are declared the sacrificial altar of Prajāpati.

There the Vedas and sacrifices in embodied form, O Yudhiṣṭhira, attend upon Prajāpati; the sages of great vows also attend there; the gods and those who move in circles worship with sacred rites, O king.
There is nothing more holy than that in the three worlds, O Bhārata; Prayāga surpasses all other tīrthas, O lord.
By merely hearing of that tīrtha, even by the chanting of its name, or even by taking hold of its clay, a man is freed from sin.
One who performs ablutions at the confluence there, firm in vow, obtains the holy fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
For this is the sacrificial ground honoured even by the gods; whatever is given there, even if small, becomes great, O Bhārata.
Neither by the word of the Veda, dear one, nor by the word of the world either, should your mind be turned away from dying at Prayāga.
Ten thousand tīrthas and sixty crore more — their proximity here at Prayāga alone is celebrated, O joy of the Kurus.
The merit that resides in the four Vedas and the merit that resides in those who speak the truth — all that a bather obtains at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
There is the excellent tīrtha of Vāsuki named Bhogavatī; one who performs ablutions there obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
There is the tīrtha of Haṃsaprapatana, renowned in the three worlds, and also the Daśāśvamedhika on the Gaṅgā, O joy of the Kurus.
Wherever the Gaṅgā flows, O great king, that region is a forest of austerities; it should be known as a holy field of the Siddhas, situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
This truth one should whisper in the ear of twice-born persons, the virtuous, one's own sons, one's friends, and one's devoted pupils.
This is righteous, this is holy, this is auspicious, this is joyful, this leads to heaven, this is delightful, this is the highest purifier.
This is the secret of the great sages, the remover of all sin; having studied it, among twice-born men one attains purity.
Whoever constantly hears this merit of the tīrthas, always pure, remembers many former births and rejoices on the back of heaven.
The tīrthas that can be reached as well as those that have been named as unreachable — one should go to them all in mind, with a view to visiting all tīrthas.
These tīrthas have been resorted to by the Vasus, Sādhyas, Ādityas, Maruts, Aśvins, sages equal to gods, and those who seek merit.
Thus you too, O Kauravya, O one of excellent vows, should visit the tīrthas according to this rule, in a disciplined manner; merit grows through merit.
Through causes cultivated in former lives, through faith, and through the guidance of the Vedas, those tīrthas are reached by the virtuous who follow the example of the learned.
One without vows, one who has not disciplined himself, the impure, a thief — they do not truly bathe at tīrthas, O Kauravya, nor does a man of crooked conduct.
But by you, of proper conduct, always seeing the aims of righteousness, your ancestors have been ferried across, dear one, and all your great-grandfathers as well.
The gods headed by the Grandfather, together with the host of sages, O king, are ever pleased, O knower of righteousness, by your righteousness.
You shall attain the worlds of the Vasus, O one like Vāsava, and great fame, O Bhīṣma, you shall obtain upon earth that is eternal.
Nārada said: Having thus spoken and having taken leave, the blessed sage Pulastya, pleased and with a joyful mind, vanished there on the spot.
And Bhīṣma, O tiger among Kurus, who beheld the true import of the scriptures, following the words of Pulastya, traversed the earth.
One who shall traverse the earth according to this rule shall, after death, enjoy the foremost fruit of a hundred Aśvamedha sacrifices.
And beyond this, O Pārtha, you shall attain supreme merit eightfold; since you are the guide of the sages, therefore shall the fruit be eightfold for you.
These sacred tirthas, O Bhārata, are overrun by bands of rakshasas — there is no passage for any other, O joy of the Kuru line, save for you.
Whoever rises at dawn and recites this account of the divine sages, which comprises the essence of all the tirthas, shall be freed from all sins.
The foremost of sages are ever present there — Vālmīki and Kaśyapa, Atreya and Kaundinyа, Viśvāmitra and Gautama,
And Asita Devala, and Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava, and Bharadvāja, and Vasiṣṭha, and the sage Uddālaka as well,
And Śaunaka together with his son, and Vyāsa the foremost among those who recite prayers, and Durvasa the best of sages, and Gālava of great austerities —
All these greatest of sages, rich in austerities, await you. With them, O great king, do traverse these sacred tirthas.
And this divine sage named Lomaśa, of boundless radiance, shall join you — travel together with him as well.
And together with me, O knower of dharma, traverse these tirthas; you shall attain great renown, even as did King Mahābhiṣa.
As the righteous Yayāti shone, as King Purūravas shone, so you, O tiger among the Kurus, shine by your own dharma.
As King Bhagīratha shone, as the celebrated Rāma shone, so you outshine all kings, like the sun with its rays.
As Manu, as Ikṣvāku, as Pūru of great glory, as Vainya of mighty splendor — so are you too renowned.
And as the slayer of Vṛtra once burned away all his foes, so shall you, having destroyed your enemies, protect your subjects.
Having won the earth through your own dharma, O lotus-eyed one, you shall win renown through righteousness as did Kārtavīrya Arjuna.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus comforted the king, the blessed sage Nārada, taking leave of the great-souled one, vanished on the spot.
And the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, reflecting on that very matter, reported to the sages the holy purpose of going on a pilgrimage to the tirthas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having learned the opinion of his brothers and of the wise Nārada, King Yudhiṣṭhira addressed Dhaumya, who was equal to the Grandfather.
That tiger among men, Jiṣṇu, of true valor, the mighty-armed one of immeasurable soul — it is I who have sent him away for the sake of obtaining weapons.
For he is a hero, devoted and capable, O wealth of austerities, highly skilled in weaponry — a lord like Vāsudeva himself.
For I know these two, O brahmin — both Kṛṣṇas, slayers of foes, the valiant pair; and so does the mighty Vyāsa: three-epoch lords, the lotus-eyed ones, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya.
Nārada too knows it thus; he always proclaimed it to me; and I too know them — those two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Thinking 'He is capable,' I have dispatched Arjuna. He is the son of the gods, no less than Indra in power; he was sent away to meet the lord of the gods and receive weapons from Indra.

Bhīṣma and Droṇa, both atiratha warriors, Kṛpa and the son of Droṇa, the unconquerable — arrayed in battle by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all mighty; all are learned in the Vedas, all heroes, all skilled in arms.
And he who is ever eager to fight with Pārtha, that greatly powerful one — Karṇa, the son of a charioteer, a great warrior, knower of divine weapons.

He, swift as a horse and mighty as the wind, whose arrows blaze like fire, whose bowstring sounds like a thunderclap — the dust of battle his smoke, the heat of his weapons like fire, fanned by the wind of the Dhārtarāṣṭra forces.
Unleashed as if by Time itself, like the fire at the end of an age, he will burn the tinder of my army — of this there is no doubt.
But him — that great cloud of divine weapons, fanned by the wind of Kṛṣṇa, bearing its flock of white-horse cranes, blazing with the Gāṇḍīva as its lightning —
This Arjuna-cloud, surging forward with unceasing streams of arrows, will quench the blazing fire of Karṇa in battle.
That conqueror of enemy cities, Bībhatsu, shall in truth receive directly from Śakra all the divine weapons.
He alone is equal to all of them — such is my conviction; there is no surpassing him, no counter-action by enemies against his action in battle.
We shall all see that Pāṇḍava, Dhanañjaya, once he has taken up his weapons; for Bībhatsu does not falter when he takes up a burden.
But without that hero, O best among the two-footed, we shall not stay unmindful in this forest of Kāmyaka together with Kṛṣṇa.
Please describe to us another forest, good and delightful, abounding in food and fruit, pure, frequented by those of meritorious deeds.
There, dwelling for some time, we shall await the hero Arjuna of true valor, as those who long for rain await the rain-cloud.
Describe to us various hermitages heard of among the twice-born, as well as lakes and rivers and delightful mountains —
Tell us, O brahmin; for without Arjuna we have no liking for this forest of Kāmyaka — we go to another direction.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Seeing all the Pāṇḍavas anxious and downcast in heart, Dhaumya, equal to Bṛhaspati, then spoke to comfort them.
Listen, O bull of the Bhāratas, O king, as I describe the holy hermitages approved by the brahmins, the directions, the tirthas, and the mountains.
First, O king, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe to you the eastern direction, lovely and frequented by hosts of royal sages, as I recall it.
In that direction, beloved of divine sages, lies what is called Naimiṣa, O Bhārata, where the supremely holy tirthas of the gods are found, each distinct.
Where flows the holy and lovely Gomatī, frequented by divine sages; where is the sacrificial ground of the gods and the shamitra altar of Vivasvat.
In that direction is the excellent and holy mountain Gaya, honored by royal sages; and the auspicious lake Brahmasaras frequented by the thirty divine sages.
On account of which, O tiger among men, the ancients declare: Many sons should be desired, if even one might go to Gaya.

There too, O sinless one, is the great river and the Gayashira, where that banyan tree is celebrated by the brahmins as conferring inexhaustible merit, O lord — where food offered to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
There too is the holy-watered Phalguna, a great river; and the Kauśikī, abounding in roots and fruits, O bull of the Bhāratas — where Viśvāmitra, rich in austerities, attained brahminhood.
Where the holy river Gaṅgā flows, on whose banks Bhagīratha, dear one, performed many sacrifices with abundant fees.
And among the Pāñcālas, O Kauravya, they speak of Utpalavata, where Viśvāmitra Kauśika sacrificed together with Śakra; where the venerable son of Jamadagni sang the genealogical hymns.
Beholding that superhuman glory of Viśvāmitra, Kauśika drank soma at Kanyakubja together with Indra, and then departed from the kshatriya estate, declaring 'I am a brahmin.'
The confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, O hero, holy and sanctified, pure and supremely purifying, beloved of the sages, is famed throughout the worlds.
Where the soul of all beings, the Grandfather himself, first performed sacrifice — it is therefore renowned as Prayāga, O best of the Bhāratas.
And there is the great and excellent hermitage of Agastya, O lord of kings — Hiraṇyabindu, as it is called, on Mount Kalanjara, O king.
Surpassing all other mountains, O king, is the holy and auspicious lord of mountains called Mahendra, O Kauravya — belonging to the great-souled son of Bhṛgu.
Where the Grandfather himself first performed sacrifice, O son of Kuntī; where the holy Bhāgīrathī was present as a participant, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Where that spot is known as the holy Brahmasala, O lord of the people, thronged with those whose sins have been washed away — and meritorious is even the sight of it.
Sacred and auspicious, renowned in the world from ancient times, and also Kedara, and the great and excellent hermitage of Mataṅga —
Mount Kundoda, lovely, abounding in roots, fruits, and water, where the Naiṣadha king, when thirsty, found water and comfort.
Where lies the lovely divine forest adorned with ascetics, and the river Bahuda, and the Nandā at the mountain summit —
The tirthas, rivers, mountains, and holy sanctuaries in the eastern direction, O great king, have been described by me to you.
Now hear from me the holy tirthas in the other three directions — the rivers and mountains and holy sanctuaries as well.
Dhaumya said: Now hear of the holy tirthas in the southern direction, O Bhārata, described in detail as best as I recall, O Bhārata.
In that direction is found the holy river Godāvarī, abounding in gardens, rich in water, frequented by ascetics, auspicious.
Both the Venna and the Bhīmarathī — two rivers that dispel fear of sin, filled with deer and birds, adorned with the dwellings of ascetics.
And there the river of the royal sage Nṛga, O bull of the Bhāratas — the Payoṣṇī, with lovely tirthas, rich in water, frequented by twice-born sages.
And here the great yogi Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerities sang the genealogical song of Nṛga, the lord of the earth.
We have heard that at the sacrifice of Nṛga as the sacrificer, Indra was intoxicated with soma and the twice-born with their sacrificial fees — witnessed directly.
The holy and auspicious forest of Mathara, abounding in roots and fruits, and the sacrificial post, O best of the Bhāratas, on the mountain by the stream of Varuṇa.
And on the northern bank of the Praveni, the holy hermitage of Kanva; and the forests of the ascetics, described as I have heard.
The sacred altar at Śūrpāraka, dear one, of the great-souled Jamadagni; and the lovely Pashanatirtha, and Purashchandra, O Bhārata.
The tirtha of Aśoka among mortals, O son of Kuntī, the hermitage of Bahula; the tirtha of Agastya among the Pāṇḍyas, and the tirtha of Varuṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Kumaris are said to be holy, among the Pāṇḍyas also, O bull among men. Now I shall describe the Tamraparni, O son of Kuntī — hear of her.
Where the gods performed great austerities at the hermitage, seeking the highest — known as Gokarṇa throughout the three worlds, O Bhārata.
That lake is cool-watered, rich in water, holy, dear one, and auspicious — supremely difficult of access for men who have not disciplined their souls.
There too, on Mount Devasabha, is the holy hermitage of a disciple of Agastya, the son of Trinasoma and Agni, abounding in ripe fruits and roots.
There too is the Vaidūrya Mountain, glorious, made of jewels, auspicious; and the hermitage of Agastya himself, abounding in roots, fruits, and water.
I shall also speak of the holy sanctuaries in Surastra, O lord of men — the hermitages, rivers, mountains, and lakes.
The brahmins there also speak of the Camasonmajjana; and Prabhāsa, the tirtha of the thirty gods on the ocean, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
There is Piṇḍāraka by name, an auspicious place frequented by ascetics; and Ujjayanta, the great peaked mountain that quickly grants success.
There an ancient verse celebrated by the foremost of divine sages, Nārada, is heard — listen to it, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
'On the holy mountain among the Surāṣṭras, frequented by deer and birds, Taptanga performed austerities on Ujjayanta and is glorified on the summit of heaven.'
Holy is Dvāravatī there, where dwells the Madhusūdana — that one is the primeval God himself, for he is the eternal Dharma.
Those brahmins who know the Vedas and those people who know the inner self declare that the great-souled Kṛṣṇa is the eternal Dharma.
Govinda is declared to be the highest of all purifying things; he is the most meritorious of all meritorious things and the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
The lotus-eyed one, the eternal god of gods, Hari of incomprehensible nature — that very Madhusūdana dwells there in the three worlds.
Dhaumya said: In the western direction, in the land of Avanti, I shall describe to you the sacred and holy shrines that exist there.
O Bhārata, there is the sacred river Narmadā, adorned with groves of priyangu and mango trees, garlanded with forests of reeds, flowing with its current toward the east.
There is renowned a sacred abode where Kubera, the lord of wealth who rides men, was born as the son of the sage Viśravas.
