There is a holy and auspicious mountain called Vaidūrya-shikhara, where trees with green foliage bear divine flowers and fruits.
On the peak of that mountain, O king, there is a lake of the wise one, covered with blooming lotuses, frequented by gods and gandharvas.
O great king, many wonders are seen on that holy mountain, which resembles heaven, is divine, and is ever frequented by divine sages.
O conqueror of enemy cities, there too is the Viśvāmitra river with its sacred fords, the holy river of the royal sage, and the far bank is sacred.
On the bank of that river, in the midst of the righteous, Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, fell; but he regained the worlds and the eternal dharmas.
There, dear one, is a sacred lake, and the Maināka mountain; and, O hero, there is the mountain called Asita, rich in roots and fruits.

There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is the sacred hermitage of Kakshena, and also the renowned hermitage of Cyavana, known everywhere, O Pāṇḍava; and there, O lord, people attain perfection with but little austerity.
O great king, the Jambū road is the hermitage of sages of purified soul, the best of peaceful places, thronged with flocks of deer and birds.

Beyond that, O king, are the most sacred regions always filled with ascetics — Ketumala, Medhya, the Gaṅgā forest, O lord of the earth, and the renowned Saindhava forest, holy and frequented by twice-born sages.
O Bhārata, there is the sacred lake of the Grandsire called Puṣkara, the beloved hermitage of the perfected Vaikhanasa sages.
Even here, O best of the Kurus, Prajāpati sang a praise-song for Puṣkara — a verse glorifying the meritorious, O best among the virtuous.
For the wise person who desires Puṣkara even in mind alone, sins are destroyed and he rejoices on the ridge of heaven.
Dhaumya said: O tiger among kings, I shall now describe to you the sacred things and holy shrines that exist in the northern direction.
O Pāṇḍava, there the Sarasvatī flows with sacred waters, full of lakes, garlanded with forests, and the Yamunā flows toward the ocean with great speed.
There is the most sacred, auspicious ford called Plakṣāvaraṇa, where twice-born sages who have worshipped at Sārasvata tirthas go for the final purificatory bath.
O sinless one, O Bhārata, the divine and auspicious Agni-shiras is also described as sacred — there Sahadeva worshipped by the throwing of the shami stick.
Regarding this very place, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there circulates in this world a verse sung by Indra, being sung by the twice-born.
The fires kindled by Sahadeva along the Yamunā numbered a hundred times a hundred thousand, each with a thousand hundredfold sacrificial gifts.
There too, King Bharata, the great wheel-turning emperor of great fame, performed twenty-seven and eight horse sacrifices.
O dear one, I have heard of one who was a wish-fulfiller for the twice-born; his utterly holy and renowned hermitage called Saraka is famous.
O Pārtha, the river Sarasvatī is ever honoured by the virtuous; O great king, there the Vālakhilya sages formerly performed their desired sacrifices.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the most sacred Dṛṣadvatī is renowned there; and there, O lord of men, two figures of differing colour are most holy.
Both are knowers of the Vedas, known through the Vedas, masters of knowledge and Veda — both ever worshipping with sacred rites, O best of Bhāratas.
Long ago the gods together with Indra and Varuṇa repeatedly gathered and performed austerities at the Viśākha sacrificial post — therefore that place is the most sacred.
The great, greatly fortunate sage Jamadagni of great fame, who overcomes all, worshipped in the sacred and lovely Palashaka forests.
There all the foremost rivers, bringing their own waters, surrounded and attended upon that best of sages in person.
Moreover, O great king, O hero, Viśvāvasu himself sang this verse there upon witnessing the might of that great-souled one.
When the great-souled Jamadagni was performing the sacrifice, all the rivers came there and satisfied the gods with sweet water.
That best of peaked mountains, adorned with gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas and apsaras, is the dwelling of kiratas and kinnaras.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there the Gaṅgā burst through with great force at Gaṅgādvāra; O king, that sacred place is renowned, frequented by hosts of brahmin sages.
O descendant of Kuru, Sanatkumāra is associated with the sacred Kankahala; and there is the mountain named Pūru, where Purūravas was born.
O king, the hermitage where Bhṛgu performed austerities attended by hosts of great sages is renowned — the great mountain called Bhṛgu-tunga.
O bull among men, whatever has existed, will exist, and exists now — Nārāyaṇa is the lord, Viṣṇu the eternal, the highest of beings.
Along the sacred and vast Badarī of that supremely glorious one, there is known a sacred hermitage, renowned in all three worlds.
O king, along the vast Badarī, one tributary of the Gaṅgā carries warm water and another carries cold water; one has golden sands.
There, sages and gods of great fortune and great power, having reached that place, constantly bow in reverence to the divine and all-pervading Nārāyaṇa.
O Pārtha, wherever the divine Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, abides — there is the entire universe, all the sacred fords and holy shrines.
That is the sacred, that is the supreme Brahman, that is the ford, that is the forest of austerity; there all divine sages and perfected ones and those whose wealth is austerity dwell.
Where the primeval god, the great yogi Madhusūdana dwells — that is the most sacred even among sacred things; let there be no doubt in you about that.
O king, O lord of the earth, O best of men, these sacred fords and holy shrines upon the earth have now been described.
These have been frequented by the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Aśvins, and by great-souled sages who are equal to Brahmā.
O Kaunteya, wandering to these places together with the foremost brahmins and your greatly blessed brothers, you will cast off your longing and grief.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O joy of the Kurus, while Dhaumya was thus conversing, the sage Lomaśa of very great splendor arrived there.
The eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, the king, along with his companions and those brahmins, stood up for that greatly blessed one, as the immortals stand for Śakra in heaven.
The Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira, having duly honoured him, asked the reason for his coming and the purpose of his wandering.
Asked by the son of Pāṇḍu, the great-minded one, filled with affection, spoke in a gentle voice, as if gladdening the Pāṇḍavas.
I was wandering through all the worlds at will, O Kaunteya; having gone to the abode of Śakra, I saw the lord of the gods there.
And I saw your heroic brother, the ambidextrous Arjuna, seated on half of Śakra's throne; seeing Pārtha thus arrived there, O tiger among men, great was my wonder.
The lord of gods spoke to me there: 'Go to the sons of Pāṇḍu.' So I have come quickly, wishing to see you together with your brothers.
By the command of Puruhuta and the great-souled Pārtha, O dear Pāṇḍava-joy, I shall tell you something greatly pleasing.
O king, hear this together with your brothers and Kṛṣṇa — that which the mighty-armed Arjuna, bull among Pāṇḍavas, was asked by you for the sake of weapons.
That weapon has been obtained by Pārtha from Rudra — the incomparable and great weapon called Brahmā-shiras, which came to Rudra through austerity.
That fearsome weapon born from amrita has been obtained by the ambidextrous Arjuna — along with its mantras, its withdrawal formula, its expiation rite and auspicious ceremony.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O joy of the Kurus, Pārtha of boundless valour has also learned the thunderbolt and other weapons — the rod and others — from Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Indra, all divine weapons.
And from the son of Viśvāvasu he has properly and duly acquired singing, dancing, chanting of samans, and instrumental music.
Thus Kaunteya Bībhatsu, having mastered weapons and acquired the Gandharva-veda, dwells happily — he who is the younger brother of your younger brother.
The purpose for which the best of gods spoke this message to me — that too I shall tell you, O Yudhiṣṭhira; hear me attentively.
'You will certainly go to the world of men; there, O best of twice-born, speak to Yudhiṣṭhira on my behalf' — thus said he.
Your brother Arjuna, having mastered weapons, will come to you soon, having accomplished a great task for the gods — one which even the celestials could not achieve.
But you — engage yourself along with your brothers in austerity; for there is nothing higher than austerity, and through austerity one obtains great things.
And I know Karṇa truly, O bull of the Bhāratas — in battle against Pārtha, he is not worth a sixteenth part.
And whatever fear of him lies in your heart, O subduer of foes — that too I shall remove when the ambidextrous Arjuna arrives here.
And whatever is in your mind, O hero, regarding this pilgrimage to the sacred fords — all of that Lomaśa will certainly tell you without doubt.
And whatever fruit connected with austerity is found at the sacred fords, O Bhārata — whatever this great sage says, that is to be trusted without any doubt.
Lomaśa said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, hear also what was said by Dhanañjaya: 'You should unite my brother Yudhiṣṭhira with righteous prosperity.'
For you know the highest dharmas and austerities, O wealth of austerity, and you know the eternal dharma of prosperous kings.
Let you, who know what is highest and purifying for men, unite this Pāṇḍava with the merit of the sacred fords.
'That king should visit the sacred fords and donate cows — this should be done with one's whole soul' — thus Vijaya spoke to me.
Protected by you, he should wander to all the sacred fords; and he must be guarded from rakshasas in difficult and dangerous places.
As Dadhīca protected the lord of the gods, and as Aṅgiras protected the sun, so protect this son of Kuntī from the rakshasas, O best of twice-born.
For many flesh-eating rakshasas, mountain-like in size, would not be able to approach the sons of Kuntī when they are under your protection.
Therefore I, by the command of Indra and the commission of Arjuna, protecting you from dangers, will wander together with you.
O joy of the Kurus, I have previously visited the sacred fords twice; this will be my third visit, and I shall see those same fords together with you.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O great king, this pilgrimage to sacred fords, which was undertaken by royal sages beginning with Manu who had accumulated merit, dispels fear.
Neither the dishonest, nor the undisciplined self, nor the ignorant, nor the sinful, nor the crooked-minded man, O Kauravya, bathes in the sacred tirthas.
But you, whose mind is ever set on dharma, who are learned in righteousness and true to your vows, shall be freed from all sins and become even greater.
Just as King Bhagīratha and kings like Gaya, and just as Yayāti, O son of Kuntī, so too shall you, O Pāṇḍava.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In my joy I cannot find words to reply. Who is greater than the one whom the king of gods himself remembers? What name surpasses that?
Who is greater than he who has your company, whose brother is Dhanañjaya, and whom Vāsava himself remembers?
And as for what you, reverend sir, have told me regarding the visitation of tirthas — this resolve was already made by me earlier, upon the counsel of Dhaumya.
Therefore, when you think it right, O brahmin, for the journey to visit the tirthas, I shall go then and there — this is my firm and highest resolve.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To that Pāṇḍava who had resolved to set out, Lomaśa said: Travel light, O great king; traveling light, you shall go freely.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Let the brahmins who live by begging and the ascetics turn back, and likewise those citizens who have followed out of devotion to the king.
Let them go to the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra; he shall give in due time to each person the appropriate support.
And if that lord of men does not give the fitting livelihood, then for our sake and your welfare, the king of Pāñcāla shall provide for you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thereupon most of the citizens, weighed down with heavy burdens, and the brahmins and devoted ascetics went toward Nāgapura.
The king, son of Ambikā, received all of them with love, as befitting the Dharma-king, and satisfied them with gifts of wealth according to proper rites.
Then the king, son of Kuntī, greatly pleased, dwelt for three nights at Kāmyaka with a reduced company of brahmins and with Lomaśa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O king, the brahmins dwelling in the forest approached the son of Kuntī as he was about to depart and spoke these words to him.
O king, you are going to the holy tirthas together with your brothers, accompanied by the divine sage, the great-souled Lomaśa.
You should take us along as well, O great king, O Pāṇḍava; for without you, O Kaurava, we are unable to reach those tirthas.
The tirthas are beset by wild beasts, are difficult and treacherous, and impassable for men of small number, O lord of men.
You and your brothers are heroes, the foremost bearers of the bow; protected always by you brave ones, we too would journey there.
By your grace we shall attain the auspicious fruit of the tirthas and of our vows, O protector of the earth, O lord of men.
Protected by your valor, purified by immersion in the tirthas, we would become cleansed of sins through the sight of the holy places, O king.
And you, O Bhārata, shall also attain the worlds of King Kārtavīrya, of the royal sage Aṣṭaka, and of Lomapada —
— and of the heroic universal sovereign Bharata, O king; you will surely attain worlds difficult to reach, by bathing at the tirthas.

The tirthas beginning with Prabhāsa, the mountains beginning with Mahendra, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and the sacred trees beginning with the Plaksha — we wish to see all these together with you, O protector of the earth.
If you have any affection for brahmins, O lord of the people, heed our words quickly, and you shall attain the highest good.
For the tirthas, O mighty-armed one, are always thronged with rakshasas that obstruct austerities; you must protect us from them.
The tirthas spoken of by Dhaumya and by the wise Nārada, and those spoken of by the divine sage Lomaśa of great austerity —
— visit all of those duly, O lord of men; purified of sins, with us, protected by Lomaśa and purified by the visit to tirthas and by the sight of great souls.
Thus honored by them, his eyes filled with tears of joy, surrounded by his brothers — the heroes led by Bhīmasena — the bull of the Pāṇḍavas said to all those sages: "So be it."
Having taken leave of Lomaśa and of Dhaumya the family priest, that foremost of Pāṇḍavas, self-controlled, together with his brothers and with the flawless-limbed Draupadī, set his mind on departure.
Then the greatly blessed Vyāsa, and likewise Nārada and Parvata, those wise ones, came to Kāmyaka to see the Pāṇḍava.
King Yudhiṣṭhira paid homage to them according to the proper rites; and those greatly blessed ones, duly honored, then spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, Bhīma — maintain purity of mind; with the mind made clean and pure, go to the tirthas."
For the brahmins declare bodily discipline to be the human vow, while the twice-born call purity of mind and intellect the divine vow.
An undefiled mind is indeed sufficient for heroes, O lord of men; abiding in a spirit of friendliness, go pure to the tirthas.
You who are pure in mind, observing the vow of bodily discipline, and embracing the divine vow, shall obtain the fruit as prescribed.
Having pledged "So be it," the Pāṇḍavas together with Kṛṣṇa were blessed with benedictions by all the sages both divine and human.
Grasping the feet of Lomaśa, of Dvaipāyana, of Nārada, O king of kings, and of the divine sage Parvata —
— the heroes, together with Dhaumya and other forest dwellers, then set out when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa had passed, under the Puṣya asterism.
Taking up their hard bows, clad in bark garments and deer skins, with matted locks, wearing impenetrable armor, they then traversed the tirthas.
With servants headed by Indrasena, with fourteen chariots, those engaged in kitchen duties, and other attendants —
— armed with weapons, swords girded at their sides, bearing quivers and arrows, facing east, those heroes the Pāṇḍavas set forth, O Janamejaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I do not consider myself to be without virtue, O best of divine sages; yet I am tormented by sorrow as no other king on earth is.
And I see others devoid of virtue and not devoted to dharma — yet they, O Lomaśa, prosper in this world; by what standard does this happen?
Lomaśa said: You must not grieve over this at all, O king, O Pārtha — that those who delight in adharma flourish through unrighteousness.
A man may prosper through unrighteousness, then see good fortune, then conquer his enemies — but he is destroyed root and all.
For I have seen the Daityas and Dānavas, O lord of the earth, thriving through unrighteousness and then coming to ruin again.
Long ago, even in the age of the gods, I witnessed everything, O lord: the gods embraced dharma, while the asuras abandoned dharma.
The gods entered the sacred tirthas; the asuras, O Bhārata, did not enter them. Those who practiced adharma were first overtaken by arrogance.
From arrogance came pride; from pride, anger arose; from anger came shamelessness; then disgrace; and thus their conduct perished.

From those who had lost shame, shed modesty, fallen in conduct, and broken their vows — forbearance, Lakṣmī, and dharma soon departed; Lakṣmī went to the gods and ill-fortune came to the asuras, O king.
Those Daityas and Dānavas, thus overcome by ill-fortune and their minds shattered by arrogance, were then also entered by Kali.
Those Dānavas, overcome by ill-fortune and Kali, overwhelmed by arrogance, devoid of ritual acts and bereft of understanding, O son of Kuntī —
— conquered by pride, soon met with destruction; the Daityas, stripped of glory, were utterly annihilated.
But the gods, virtuous by nature, resorted to the oceans, rivers, lakes, and sacred dwelling places.
Through austerities, sacrifices, charity, and receiving blessings, O Pāṇḍava, they cast off all sins and attained the highest good.
Thus the gods, endowed with charity and full of ritual acts in every way, went to the tirthas, and thereby attained the highest prosperity.
Likewise, O king of kings, you too, bathing at the tirthas together with your brothers, shall regain that Lakṣmī; this is the eternal path.
Just as King Nṛga, and Śibi the son of Uśīnaras, Bhagīratha, Vasumanas, Gaya, Pūru, Purūravas —
— always practicing austerity, by the touch of the sacred waters, purified by visiting the tirthas and by the sight of great souls —
— they obtained sacred fame and wealth, O lord of men; likewise, you too, O king of kings, shall attain abundant glory.
And as Ikṣvāku wandered with his sons, kinsmen, and relatives; as Mucukunda, Māndhātā, and the king Marutta —
— won sacred fame just as the gods did through the power of austerity, and the divine sages entirely; so too shall you obtain the same.
But the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, controlled by arrogance and delusion, shall soon be destroyed just like the Daityas — there is no doubt.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those heroes, thus united, dwelling here and there in succession, O protector of the earth, arrived at the Naimiṣa forest.
Then at the holy tirthas of the Gomatī, O king, the Pāṇḍavas performed their ritual baths and gave away cows and wealth, O Bhārata.
There, satisfying the gods, ancestors, and brahmins again and again, the Kauravas visited the Kanya-tirtha, the Aśva-tirtha, and the Gava-tirtha.
At Valakoti, at Vrishaprastha mountain, and at Bahuda, O protector of the earth, all the Pāṇḍavas performed their ablutions.
At Prayāga, the divine sacrificial ground of the gods, O lord of the earth, they dwelt, immersing their limbs, and undertook the highest austerities.
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, those great souls true to their vows, freed from sin, gave wealth to the brahmins.
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu, O king, O Bhārata, went together with brahmins to the altar of Prajāpati frequented by ascetics.
There those heroes dwelt and undertook the highest austerities, constantly satisfying the twice-born with forest offerings.
Then they went to the holy mountain honored by the righteous royal sage Gaya of incomparable splendor who had performed meritorious deeds.
There is the lake called Gayaśiras, the holy great river, the tirtha beloved of the sages — that supremely holy lake of Brahmā.
It is where the blessed Agastya went to meet Vaivasvata, and where eternal Dharma himself, O king, abode.
It is the source of all rivers, O lord of men, where Mahādeva who bears the Pināka bow is ever present.
There the heroic Pāṇḍavas passed the four-month rainy season rites with a great sacrifice in the manner of the sages, where the great imperishable banyan tree stands.
Brahmins rich in austerity came there in hundreds, and they performed the four-month sacrifice at that time according to the ancient seer-prescribed rites.
There brahmins ever devoted to learning and austerity, masters of the Vedas, seated in the assembly, told sacred stories of great souls.
There, O king, Shamatha — who had bathed at the completion of his studies and vows and was observing the vow of celibacy from childhood — told of Gaya, son of Amurtarayas.
The son of Amūrtarayas was Gaya, that best of royal sages; hear from me, O Bhārata, of his meritorious deeds.
His sacrifice here was one of abundant food and rich fees; at it, O king, there were mountains of food by the hundreds and thousands.
There were streams of clarified butter and rivers of curds by the hundreds, and flows of condiments of great worth by the thousands.
Day after day all this was given to those who asked; and beyond that, O king, the brahmins partook of food excellently prepared.
At the time of the sacrificial fees, the chanting of the Veda rose up to heaven; nothing whatsoever could be distinguished through the noise of the Veda, O Bhārata.
As that meritorious king moved about, the earth, the directions, the sky, and the heavens were filled with the sound — and that too was a great wonder.
There men of radiant glory, satisfied with auspicious food and drink, sang songs in every region, O bull of the Bhāratas.
"Who are the living beings today that desire to eat at Gaya's sacrifice, where twenty-five mountains remain as the leftover of the feast?"
Neither did the people before nor will those after accomplish what Gaya, the royal sage of boundless splendour, did at his sacrifice.
How indeed could the gods, fully satisfied with the oblations offered by Gaya, ever again accept whatever may be given by others?
Many such wonders as these occurred at the sacrifice of that great-souled one near his lake, O joy of the Kurus.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, son of Kuntī, he of abundant largesse, set out and, reaching the hermitage of Agastya, took up residence at Durjayā.
There the king, best among speakers, asked Lomaśa: "For what reason was Vātāpi here quelled by Agastya?"
"What power had that daitya, the destroyer of men? And why did the wrath of the great-souled Agastya arise?"
Lomaśa said: There was a daitya named Ilvala, O joy of the Kurus, and in the city of Maṇimatī of old, Vātāpi was his younger brother.
That son of Diti said to a brahmin possessed of austerities: "May the reverend one grant me a single son equal to Indra."
The brahmin did not grant him a son equal to Vāsava; thereupon that asura became exceedingly wrathful toward that brahmin.
Whomever he called out to by name, even one who had gone to the abode of Vivasvat's son, would appear again alive, having reassumed a body.
Then, turning the asura Vātāpi into a goat and having it well prepared, he fed it to that brahmin and then called out to him again.
Tearing through the side of that brahmin, the great asura Vātāpi came out laughing, O king, O lord of the people.
In this way, O king, the daitya Ilvala, of wicked mind, repeatedly fed the brahmins and then slew them.
And the venerable Agastya too, at precisely that time, saw his ancestors hanging head downward in a pit.
He asked those hanging ones: "What is your condition here?" — inquiring for the sake of lineage; and they, expounders of the Veda, spoke to him.
They told him: "We are your own ancestors; we have descended into this pit and hang here, desiring offspring."
"If you were to beget upon us a noble descendant of Agastya, we would be released from this hell, and you yourself would attain the goal by having a son."
That splendid one, devoted to truth and righteousness, said to them: "I shall fulfil your wish, O ancestors; let the fever of your minds depart."
Then the venerable sage, reflecting on begetting a lineage, found no woman suitable for his own procreation.
He collected the choicest limb of each creature, and with limbs to match from each he fashioned a supreme woman.
The sage of great austerity gave that woman, fashioned for his own purpose, to the king of Vidarbha who was anguished in his longing for a son.
She was born there, the blessed one, radiant as a streak of lightning; shining with her form, she grew up, she of beautiful face.
And seeing her the moment she was born, the lord of the earth of Vidarbha, with great joy, announced her to the twice-born, O Bhārata.
All the brahmins rejoiced at her, O lord of the earth; and those twice-born ones gave her the name Lopāmudrā.
She grew up, O great king, bearing a supreme beauty — swiftly like a lotus in water, like the auspicious flame of fire.
When she had come to youth, O king of kings, a hundred maidens well adorned and a hundred maidservants waited upon that lovely one, obedient to her will.
Surrounded by a hundred maidservants and seated among a hundred maidens, the radiant girl shone like Rohiṇī in the sky, O lord.
Though she was come to youth and endowed with good character and conduct, no man chose her out of fear of that great-souled one.
But that true-natured maiden, surpassing even the apsarases in beauty, pleased her father and likewise her kinsmen with her conduct.
Seeing the maiden of Vidarbha thus endowed with every virtue, her father thought in his mind: "To whom shall I give my daughter?"
Lomaśa said: When Agastya concluded that she was fit for householder life, he went and spoke to the lord of the earth of Vidarbha.
"O king, my mind tends toward settled household life for the sake of offspring; I ask this of you, O protector of the earth — give me Lopāmudrā."
Addressed thus by the sage, the lord of the earth was bewildered — unable to refuse yet unwilling to give.
Then the lord of the earth went to his wife and said: "This great and powerful sage, if angered, would burn us with the fire of his curse."
Seeing the lord of the earth thus distressed together with his wife, Lopāmudrā approached at the right moment and spoke these words.
"O protector of the earth, you should not suffer distress on my account; give me to Agastya — save yourself through me, O father."
At his daughter's word, the king then gave Lopāmudrā to the great-souled Agastya according to proper rite, O lord of the people.
Having received his wife, Agastya addressed Lopāmudrā: "Set aside these precious garments and ornaments."
Then she of lovely thighs and long eyes put off those beautiful, precious, fine garments.
And then the long-eyed one took up bark garments, bast-cloth, and deer-skins, and became one who followed the same vow and practice as he.
Then the venerable sage, best of seers, came to Gaṅgādvāra and undertook severe austerities together with his devoted wife.
She then served her husband with love and great respect; and Agastya, the lord, cherished supreme affection toward his wife.
Then after a long time, O lord of the people, the venerable sage saw Lopāmudrā radiant with austerity and bathed in her season.
Pleased by her devoted service, her purity, her self-restraint, her grace, and her beauty, he summoned her for conjugal union.
Then she, the passionate one, joining her palms as if embarrassed, spoke these words to the venerable one with affectionate longing.
"Without doubt a husband obtains a wife for the sake of progeny; the love that I have for you, O sage, you should reciprocate."
"As I had a bed in a palace in my father's house, O brahmin — on such a bed you should come to me here."
"I desire to approach you freely — you adorned with a garland and decorated with ornaments — I myself adorned with divine jewels."
Agastya said: "O Lopāmudrā, O fair-waisted one, I do not have wealth of the kind befitting your father's house, O auspicious one."
Lopāmudrā said: "You are capable, O lord, of gathering through your austerities in an instant all the wealth that exists in the living world."
Agastya said: "It is exactly as you say; but it would consume my austerities. Tell me how I may act so that my austerities are not destroyed."
Lopāmudrā said: "Very little of this season remains for me, O wealth of austerities; and I have no wish to approach you in any other manner whatsoever."
"Nor do I wish to infringe upon your dharma, O wealth of austerities; but this desire of mine you should fulfil."
Agastya said: "If this desire of yours is settled in your mind, O blessed one, then very well — I shall go and seek wealth; stay here, dear one, and let your desire abide."
Lomaśa said: Then Agastya went, O Kauravya, to seek wealth — to king Śrutarvan, who surpassed other kings in knowledge of the Veda.
And the king, knowing that the jar-born one had come, went to the frontier of his realm with his ministers and received him with full honour.
The lord of the earth, having brought the guest offering duly, stood with folded hands, composed, and asked the purpose of his arrival.
Agastya said: "Know that I have come desiring wealth, O lord of the earth; share with me what you can without harming others."
Lomaśa said: Then the king laid out for him his income and expenditure in full, saying: "Take from this, O learned one, whatever wealth you think fit."
Then, seeing income and expenditure equal, the even-minded brahmin concluded that taking from it would in every way cause suffering to living beings.
Taking Śrutarvan along, he then went to Vadhryaśva; and Vadhryaśva received those two at the frontier of his realm in due form.
Vadhryaśva presented them with the guest offering and water for their feet; then, having asked leave, he inquired about their purpose at the start.
Agastya said: "Know that we two have come here desiring wealth, O lord of the earth; share with us what you can without harming others."
Lomaśa said: Then the king laid out his income and expenditure in full before those two; knowing this, they took whatever there was in surplus.
Then, seeing income and expenditure equal, the even-minded brahmin concluded that taking from it would in every way cause suffering to living beings.
Then Agastya, Śrutarvan, and king Vadhryaśva went to Trasadasyu, son of Purukutsa, who was of great wealth.
And Trasadasyu received all of them in due form, O great king, coming to the frontier of his realm with his retinue.
Having honoured them duly, that best of kings of the Ikṣvāku line put them at ease and then asked their purpose at the start.
Agastya said: "Know that we have come here desiring wealth, O lord of the earth; share with us what you can without harming others."
Lomaśa said: Then the king laid out his income and expenditure in full before them, saying: "Knowing this, take whatever is in surplus here."
Then, seeing income and expenditure equal, the even-minded brahmin concluded that taking from it would in every way cause suffering to living beings.
Then all those kings came together and, looking at one another, spoke these words to that great sage, O great king.
O brahmin, this demon Ilvala is truly wealthy on earth. Approaching him together, today we shall all beg wealth from him.
That plan to beg from Ilvala was pleasing to all of them. Then, O king, they together approached Ilvala.
Lomaśa said: Knowing that the kings accompanied by the great sage had arrived, Ilvala, together with his ministers, honored them at the border of his realm.
Then that foremost of demons, O Kaurava, performed hospitality for them — indeed with his brother Vātāpi, who had been cooked and prepared.
Then all the royal sages became dejected and lost heart upon seeing the great demon Vātāpi, who had been transformed into a ram and cooked.
Then Agastya, foremost of sages, spoke to those royal sages: "You must not be despondent. I myself shall consume the great demon."
The great sage then took his seat at the head-place and sat down. Ilvala, lord of the Daityas, served him, as if smiling.
Agastya alone then ate Vātāpi in his entirety. When the sage had finished eating, Ilvala called out to his brother.
Then a wind emerged from the great-souled Agastya, and Ilvala became distressed upon seeing the great demon had been digested.
With folded hands, together with his ministers, he spoke these words: "For what purpose have you come? Speak — what may I do for you?"
Then Agastya replied to Ilvala with a smile: "O demon, we all know you to be a lord, a master of wealth."
"These kings here are not overly wealthy, and my own need for wealth is great. Give us a share according to your capacity, without injuring others."
Then Ilvala, bowing to the sage, spoke these words: "If you know what I intend to give, then I will give you that wealth."
Agastya said: "Ten thousand cows for each of the kings, O demon, and that same amount in gold — that is what you intend to give, O great demon."

"And for me, twice that amount, plus a golden chariot and two horses swift as thought — that is what you intend to give, O great demon. Let the chariot be examined at once; it will be evident this one is golden."
Lomaśa said: When examined, that chariot proved to be made of gold, O son of Kuntī. Then the demon, distressed, gave even more than the specified wealth.

The two horses named Vivaja and Suvaja, yoked to that chariot, swiftly carried all those riches toward Agastya's hermitage, along with all the kings and Agastya himself, as if in the blink of an eye, O Bhārata.
Dismissed by Agastya, the royal sages departed. And the sage did everything that Lopāmudrā had desired.
Lopāmudrā said: "You have done all that I desired, O blessed one. Now beget for me a single offspring endowed with great valor."
Agastya said: "I am pleased, O auspicious and beautiful one, with your conduct. But regarding offspring, I shall offer you a consideration — listen to it."
"Do you wish for a thousand sons, or a hundred equal to ten, or ten equal to a hundred, or one who shall be equal to a thousand?"
Lopāmudrā said: "Let me have one son equal to a thousand, O you whose wealth is asceticism. For one learned and virtuous person is better than many who are not."
Lomaśa said: Having agreed with the words "So be it," the sage united with her in due season — she who was of equal virtue, full of faith and devotion.
Then, having planted the embryo, he went back into the forest. In the forest that embryo grew for seven autumns.

And when the seventh year had passed, that great poet was born just as Pracyavana was — blazing with power, named Dridhasyu, O Bhārata, of great renown, chanting the Vedas with their supplements and Upaniṣads even at birth.

That son of the sage became a radiant, great sage. Even as a child, full of brilliance, he would bring loads of firewood to his father's dwelling — hence he came to be called Idhmavaha, the firewood-carrier.
Seeing him thus engaged and fit, the sage rejoiced greatly. And his ancestors, O king, obtained the desired worlds.
The hermitage of Agastya is renowned, adorned with flowers of every season. Thus was Vātāpi, the descendant of Prahlāda, destroyed by Agastya.
This is his hermitage, O king, delightful and endowed with virtues. This is the sacred Bhāgīrathī — bathe in it to your heart's content.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "I wish to hear more at length of the deeds of that wise great sage Agastya, O best of twice-born men."
Lomaśa said: "Listen, O king, to a divine, wondrous, superhuman tale — O great king, the power of the immeasurable-souled Agastya."
In the Kṛta age there were terrible demons, frenzied for battle, known as the Kāleyas — groups of the most dreadful kind.
Taking refuge with Vṛtra, wielding all manner of weapons, they charged from all sides against the gods led by great Indra.
Then the thirty gods, making effort for the slaying of Vṛtra, placing Purandara foremost, approached Brahmā.
The Lord of the highest heaven spoke to all of them as they stood with folded hands: "O gods, I know all that you wish to accomplish."
"I shall tell you the means by which you will slay Vṛtra. There is a great sage known as Dadhīca, of noble intellect."
"Go to him together, all of you, and beg a boon. That righteous-souled one, with his innermost heart delighted, will give it to you."
"He should be told by all of you together, you who desire victory: 'Give us your bones for the welfare of the three worlds.' He will surrender his body and bestow his own bones."
"From his bones, let a most terrible, firm thunderbolt be fashioned — mighty, enemy-slaying, sharp, six-edged, and with a fearsome sound."
"With that thunderbolt the Performer-of-a-hundred-sacrifices shall indeed slay Vṛtra. All of this has been told to you — therefore act quickly."
Thus instructed, the gods took leave of the Grandfather, placed Nārāyaṇa at their head, and went to Dadhīca's hermitage.

On the far bank of the Sarasvatī, covered with diverse trees and creepers, it rang with the melodious sounds of bees as if with the chanting of Sama singers, mingled with the calls of male cuckoos and resounding with the cries of jivamjivaka birds.
Buffalo, boar, sambar deer, and yaks wandered here and there without fear of tigers.
It resounded on all sides with female elephants and bull elephants with faces streaming with ichor, who had waded into the lake and were at play.
It echoed with lions and tigers roaring mighty roars, and with others hidden and dwelling in caves and ravines.
Beautiful and most pleasing, adorned in all its various open spaces, resembling the heavenly realm — to that hermitage of Dadhīca they came.
There they saw Dadhīca, blazing with the radiance of the sun, shining in his form just as the Grandfather shines with his glory.
The gods, O king, saluted his feet and bowed down, and all of them begged the boon just as the Supreme Lord had instructed.
Then Dadhīca, supremely pleased, spoke thus to those best of gods: "I shall do today, O gods, what is beneficial to you — and I shall also abandon my own body."
Having spoken thus, that best of two-footed beings, master of himself, suddenly released his vital breaths. Then those gods took his bones — his very marrow — according to instruction.
The gods, with joyful countenances and eager for victory, went to Tvaṣṭṛ and stated their purpose. Tvaṣṭṛ, hearing their words, was himself joyful of countenance and with great and careful effort —

— fashioned the thunderbolt, exceedingly fierce in form. Having fashioned it, he joyfully spoke to Śakra: "With this finest of thunderbolts, O god, reduce to ashes today the fierce enemy of the gods."
"Then, your enemy and his hosts destroyed, rule happily and completely the triple heaven, O dweller in heaven." Thus instructed by Tvaṣṭṛ, Purandara joyfully and reverently accepted the thunderbolt.
Lomaśa said: Then the bearer of the thunderbolt, protected by the mighty gods, encountered Vṛtra, who stood filling both heaven and earth.
He was guarded on all sides by the great-bodied Kāleyas, with weapons upraised, looking like mountains with their peaks.
Then a great battle arose between the gods and the demons, a moment terrifying to all the worlds, O foremost of the Bhāratas.
There arose an exceedingly tumultuous sound as swords raised and clashing in the arms of heroes fell upon bodies.
With heads falling down from mid-air to the great earth, it looked, O lord of the earth, like palm fruits falling from their stalks.
The Kāleyas, clad in golden armor and armed with iron clubs, charged against the thirty gods like mountains scorched by a forest fire.
The thirty gods could not withstand the onslaught of those swift ones charging together; broken, they fled in fear.
Seeing them fleeing in fear, and as Vṛtra waxed ever greater, the thousand-eyed Purandara was overcome by a great stupor.
Seeing Śakra overcome by stupor, the eternal Viṣṇu poured his own energy into Śakra, augmenting his strength.
Seeing Śakra replenished by Viṣṇu, the hosts of gods then infused their own respective energies into him, and likewise the pure brahmin-sages.
Replenished thus by Viṣṇu together with the gods and the greatly blessed sages, Śakra became powerful again.
Knowing the lord of the thirty gods to be restored in strength, Vṛtra roared tremendous roars. At his roar, the earth and the directions, the sky, heaven, and mountains — all of it trembled.
Then great Indra, exceedingly tormented, upon hearing that mighty roar of terrible form, plunged into fear and swiftly hurled the great thunderbolt for his slaying, O king.
Struck by Śakra's thunderbolt, that great demon, wearing his golden garland, fell — just as the great mountain Mandara fell before, released from Viṣṇu's hand.

When that foremost of demons was slain, Śakra, overcome by fear, fled to enter a lake. Out of fear he did not acknowledge the thunderbolt discharged from his own hand, nor did he acknowledge Vṛtra as slain.
All the gods, delighted and joyful, together with the great sages praising Indra, quickly gathered and slew all the demons who were anguished at the slaying of Vṛtra.
Being slaughtered by the thirty gods at that time, they fled in fear and entered the ocean itself — plunging into the immeasurable sea, teeming with fish and filled with gems.
There, together, they took counsel, intent on the destruction of the three worlds. Some among them, knowing the determination of minds, enumerated those various strategies.
Then, in due course of time and circumstance, a terrible resolve arose in those deliberating: "Those who are endowed with learning and austerity — their destruction must be accomplished first."

"For all the worlds are sustained by austerity; therefore hasten to destroy austerity. Whoever there are on this earth — the ascetics who know dharma and the sciences — let their slaughter be accomplished quickly. When they are destroyed, the world is destroyed."
Thus all of them, their minds bent on destruction, supremely delighted in the annihilation of the world, took refuge in the stronghold of the great-waved ocean, the jewel-filled abode of Varuṇa.
Lomaśa said: Taking refuge in the ocean, the treasury of Varuṇa's waters, the Kāleyas set about the destruction of the three worlds.
At night they would emerge in fury and continually devour the sages who dwelt in hermitages and in holy sanctuaries.
At Vasiṣṭha's hermitage, eight thousand eight hundred brahmins were devoured by those evil-souled ones, and nine more ascetics besides.
Going to Cyavana's hermitage, holy and frequented by twice-born ones, a hundred sages who lived on fruits and roots were devoured.
Thus they would act at night and enter the ocean by day. At Bharadvāja's hermitage too, twenty disciplined celibate students who lived on air and water were struck down.

Thus, in this manner, the demons would range through all those hermitages at night, intoxicated with the power of their arms — those Kāleyas, driven by fate, slaughtering multitudes of twice-born men.
And men, O best of men, did not perceive those demons acting thus against the ascetics engaged in their austerities.
At dawn the sages were seen lying on the ground, their bodies emaciated by regulated diet, lifeless, their vital breath departed from their frames.
The earth was strewn and heaped with their flesh-wasted, bloodless, marrow-drained, jointless bodies, like piles of conch shells scattered about.
The ground was covered with overturned water pots, broken ladles, and scattered sacred fire-vessels strewn all around.
The world, tormented by fear of the Kāleyas, was without Vedic recitation or the vaṣaṭ-call, deprived of sacrifice and festive rites, and utterly devoid of all enthusiasm.
And so, being thus destroyed, O lord of men, humans — intent only on self-preservation and overcome by fear — fled in all directions out of terror.
Some entered into caves; others took shelter near waterfalls; and yet others, consumed by dread of death, gave up their very lives out of fear.
Some great archers there, O hero, proud and valiant warriors, making every effort in their search, set about hunting down the demons.
Yet they could not find those demons who had taken refuge in the ocean; they suffered great fatigue and in the end met with destruction.
When the world had fallen into this state of desolation, stripped of sacrifice and festive rites, the gods too fell into the greatest distress, O lord of men.
The gods assembled together and, prompted by fear, took counsel, placing Nārāyaṇa — the invincible lord of Vaikuṇṭha — at their head.

Then all the assembled gods spoke to Madhusūdana: "You are the creator, protector, and sustainer of the universe, O lord. All this world — both what moves and what does not move — has been created by you."
"When the earth was lost and sunk beneath the ocean, O lotus-eyed one, you assumed the form of a boar and lifted her up for the sake of the world."
"The primordial demon Hiraṇyakaśipu, of mighty valor, was slain by you, O best of beings, after you took the form of the man-lion."
"And Bali, that great demon invincible to all creatures, was cast out from the three worlds by you after you assumed the form of a dwarf."
"And the demon renowned as Jambha, a great wielder of the bow who cruelly disturbed the sacrifices, was likewise struck down by you alone."
"Such deeds as these are innumerable; no count of them is possible. You are the refuge of us who are seized with fear, O Madhusūdana."
"Therefore, O God, lord of gods, we bring this matter before you for the sake of the world. Protect the worlds, the gods, and Indra from this great danger."
The gods said: "From the offerings made here all four kinds of creatures sustain themselves; those creatures, thus nourished, in turn nourish the celestial beings with oblations of havis and kavya."
"The worlds thus sustain one another in mutual dependence; by your grace they dwell free from anxiety, protected by you alone."
"Now this great danger has come upon the worlds, and we do not know by whom these brahmins are being slain in the night."
"When the brahmins are destroyed, the earth will perish; and when the earth perishes, the celestial realm of the three heavens will also perish."
"By your grace, O mighty-armed lord of the world, all the worlds, protected by you, need not come to destruction."
Viṣṇu said: "O gods, I know fully the cause of the destruction of creatures. I shall tell you too — hear me with your anxieties laid aside."
"The horde known as the Kāleyas is exceedingly terrible; sheltering behind Vṛtra, they have afflicted the entire world."
"Seeing Vṛtra slain by the wise thousand-eyed Indra, and wishing to preserve their own lives, they entered the abode of Varuṇa — the ocean."
"Having entered that terrible ocean teeming with crocodiles and sea-monsters, they come out at night and slay the sages here in order to destroy the worlds."

"But they cannot be brought to destruction, for they take refuge in the ocean. Your counsel must now be directed toward the drying up of the ocean — for who other than Agastya is capable of draining the sea?"
Having heard these words thus spoken by Viṣṇu, the gods took leave of Brahmā, the supreme lord, and set out for the hermitage of Agastya.
There they beheld the great-souled son of Varuṇa, blazing with radiance, attended upon by sages as the Grandsire himself is attended upon by the gods.
Approaching that great-souled and steadfast son of Mitra and Varuṇa — that mass of ascetic power dwelling in his hermitage — they praised him with their own hymns of devotion.
The gods said: "You were formerly the refuge of the worlds when they were tormented by Nahuṣa, and you cast down that thorn of the worlds from his lordship over the gods, for the good of all."
"The great mountain Vindhya, which in anger suddenly began to grow — blocking the path of the sun — no longer grows, not transgressing your word."
"When the world was enveloped in darkness and creatures were oppressed by death, they attained the highest peace by finding you as their lord."
"O blessed one, you are always the refuge of us who are seized with fear. Therefore, afflicted as we are, we beg a boon of you — for you are indeed a giver of boons."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Why did the Vindhya mountain suddenly grow, seized with rage? I wish to hear this in full, O great sage."
Lomaśa said: "The sun used to go around in a clockwise direction — at rising and at setting — the great golden mountain Meru, that king of mountains."
"Seeing this, the Vindhya mountain then spoke to the sun: 'Just as Meru is constantly circumambulated by you in a clockwise manner, do the same for me, O maker of light.'"
"Thus addressed, the sun then replied to the lord of mountains: 'I do not circumambulate Meru of my own will, O mountain — this is the path prescribed for me by the one who created this world.'"
"Thus addressed, the mountain then suddenly began to swell up in anger, O chastiser of foes, wishing to block the path of the sun and moon."
"Then all the gods together — along with Indra — came and tried by every means to restrain that great king of mountains; but he heeded not their words at all."
"Then the gods together went to the sage dwelling in his hermitage — to Agastya, the greatest bearer of dharma among the righteous, blazing with most wondrous power — and told him their purpose."
The gods said: "This Vindhya, king of mountains, overcome by anger, is blocking the path of the sun and moon and likewise the course of the constellations."
"No one else is capable of restraining him, O best of twice-born men, save you alone, O greatly blessed one. Therefore restrain him."
Lomaśa said: "Hearing those words of the gods, the brahmin went to the mountain; approaching Vindhya, together with his wife he addressed him as he stood before him."
"'I desire passage granted by you, O best of mountains — I am going to the southern region for some purpose.'"
"'Until my return, wait for me; when I have come back, O lord of mountains, then grow as you please.'"
"Having made this agreement with Vindhya, O crusher of foes, Agastya, the son of Varuṇa, has not returned from the southern land even to this day."
"All this has now been told to you — how the Vindhya does not grow, by the power of Agastya — which you asked me about."
"Now hear from me as I tell how the Kāleyas were slain by all the gods, O king, after a boon was obtained from Agastya."
"Hearing the words of the gods, Agastya, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, said: 'Why have you come to me? What boon do you seek from me?' Thus addressed by him, the gods then spoke to the sage."
"'We wish this to be done by you, O great sage, O great-souled one: drink up the great ocean; then we shall slay those enemies of the gods known as the Kāleyas, together with all their followers.'"
"Hearing the words of the gods, the sage replied, 'So be it' — 'I shall fulfil your wish and bring great happiness to the worlds.'"
Having spoken thus, that sage of excellent vows then went to the ocean, the lord of rivers, accompanied by sages perfected through austerity and by the gods.
Humans, serpents, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kiṃpuruṣas likewise followed that great-souled one, eager to witness that wonder.
They then all drew near together to the ocean with its terrifying roar, which seemed to dance with its waves and to leap about like the wind.
Seeming to laugh with its surging foam, stumbling into its caverns, teeming with all manner of sea-monsters, and filled with countless flocks of birds of every kind.
The gods together with Agastya, along with gandharvas and great serpents, and the greatly blessed sages, approached the vast deep.
Lomaśa said: "Having arrived at the ocean, the blessed sage, son of Varuṇa, spoke to the assembled gods and sages who had gathered together."
"'For the welfare of the world, I shall now drink up this abode of Varuṇa. Let that which needs to be done by you all be arranged swiftly.'"
Having said just these words, the steadfast son of Mitra and Varuṇa, filled with fierce resolve, drank up the ocean before the eyes of the entire world.
Seeing the ocean being drunk up, the gods together with Vāsava were struck with supreme wonder, and they honored him with hymns of praise.
"'You are our savior, the ordainer of the worlds, the nourisher of the worlds; by your grace, the world together with the gods will not come to utter destruction.'"
Worshipped by the gods on all sides while gandharva music resounded everywhere, and showered with divine flowers, the great-souled one rendered the mighty ocean waterless.
Seeing the mighty ocean rendered waterless, all the gods were supremely joyful; taking up their divine and excellent weapons, those undaunted beings slew those demons.

Struck down by those great-souled gods of mighty power who charged forth with battle-cries, the demons could not at that time withstand the onslaught of those swift and great-souled dwellers of heaven.
Those terrible-roaring demons, being slain by the gods, fought a most tumultuous battle for a brief while, O descendant of Bharata.
Already scorched in former times by the austerities of the self-perfected sages, and now exerting their utmost strength, they were annihilated by the gods.
Those slain demons, adorned with golden necklaces and wearing ear-rings and armlets, lay in great splendor like kiṃśuka trees in full bloom.
Then some of the surviving Kāleyas, O best of men, split open the earth goddess and took refuge in the depths of Pātāla.
Seeing the demons slain, the gods praised the foremost of sages with various words and also spoke these words to him.
"'By your grace, O greatly blessed one, the worlds have attained great happiness; and by your power the Kāleyas of cruel valor have been slain.'"
"'Fill the ocean again, O mighty-armed nourisher of the worlds; release back into it the water that you have drunk.'"
Thus addressed, the blessed foremost of sages replied: 'That water has indeed been digested by me. Some other means must be devised by you, striving with effort for the purpose of filling the ocean.'
Having heard this word of the great sage of perfected soul, all the gods together were filled with amazement and became downcast.
Taking leave of one another and bowing to that foremost of sages, O great king, all creatures departed the way they had come.
The gods, together with Viṣṇu, went to the Grandsire and, having deliberated again and again about the filling of the ocean, all spoke with joined palms concerning the replenishment of the sea.
Lomaśa said: "To those assembled gods, Brahmā, the Grandsire of the worlds, spoke: 'Go, O gods, all of you, as you desire and as you wish.'"
"'In the fullness of great time the ocean will return to its natural state, making the kinsmen of the great king Bhagīratha the cause thereof.'"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "How are his kinsmen the cause, O brahmin? What is that cause, O sage? And how was the ocean filled through the exertions of Bhagīratha?"
O ascetic wealth, O brahmin, I wish to hear in full detail, as narrated by you, the excellent conduct of kings.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the great-souled king of righteousness, that foremost of brahmins proceeded to narrate the greatness of the noble-souled Sagara.
Lomaśa said: Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus was a king named Sagara, endowed with beauty, virtue, and strength, yet childless and of great valour.
Having destroyed the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas, O Bhārata, and having brought other kings under his sway, he ruled his own kingdom.
He had two wives proud of their beauty and youth — the Vaidarbhī and the Śaibyā, O best of the Bhāratas, O bull among the Bhāratas.
That king, desiring sons, performed great austerities together with his two wives, O lord of kings, repairing to Mount Kailāsa.
While he was performing great austerities accompanied by the discipline of yoga, he approached the great-souled three-eyed one, the destroyer of Tripura.
Shankara, Bhava, Īśāna, the trident-bearer, the wielder of the Pināka bow, Tryambaka, Śiva, the fierce lord, the many-formed, the husband of Umā.
Upon seeing that granter of boons, the king, together with his wives, prostrated himself — that mighty-armed one — and besought him for sons.
Hara, greatly pleased, spoke to that best of kings along with his wife: 'In this very moment, O king, you have chosen me here for a boon.
Sixty thousand heroic sons, proud in battle, shall be born from one of your wives, O best of men.
Yet all of them together shall meet their destruction, O king; one heroic perpetuator of the lineage shall be born from the other wife.' Having said this to him, Rudra vanished on the spot.
And King Sagara too returned to his own dwelling with his two wives, O dear one, his mind exceedingly joyful at that time.
Then, O best of men, those two lotus-eyed wives of his — both the Vaidarbhī and the Śaibyā — became pregnant.
In the course of time the Vaidarbhī gave birth to a gourd of a womb, and Śaibyā gave birth to a son, a prince of divine appearance.
The king resolved to cast away that gourd, but then from the sky he heard a voice of deep resonance.
'O king, do not commit this rash act; you must not abandon your sons. Extract the seeds from within the gourd and preserve them with care.
Place them each in vessels filled with clarified butter and kept warm; then, O king, you shall obtain sixty thousand sons.
The birth of sons has been ordained for you by Mahādeva, O lord of men, through this graduated process — let your mind not think otherwise than this.'
Lomaśa said: Hearing this from the sky, that best of kings, O bull among the Bhāratas, did exactly as had been said, with faith.
Sixty thousand sons of that royal sage of incomparable energy were born, O king, by the grace of Rudra.
They were terrible, cruel in their deeds, roaming through the skies, and by reason of their great numbers they scorned all the worlds together with the gods.
They harassed the thirty gods as well as gandharvas and rakshasas, and all beings — those heroes distinguished in battle.
The worlds, being tormented by those dull-witted Sagaras, took refuge with Brahmā, all the gods going together.
The greatly blessed grandfather of all the worlds spoke to them: 'Go, all you thirty gods, along with the worlds, as you came.'
'Within no very long time, O gods, there shall be a great and utterly terrible destruction of the Sagaras by their own deeds.'
Thus addressed, the gods and worlds, O lord of men, took leave of the Grandfather and dispersed as they had come.
Then, after much time had elapsed, O bull among the Bhāratas, the mighty King Sagara was initiated for the horse sacrifice, and his sacrificial horse roamed the earth well-guarded by his sons.
Reaching the ocean — waterless and terrible to behold — while being carefully guarded, it disappeared right there.

Then those Sagaras, O dear one, thinking the best of horses had been stolen, came and reported to their father that the horse had been taken and was unseen; told by him they all searched for the steed in all directions.
Then those Sagaras, by their father's command, searched for that horse in all directions, O great king, and all over the surface of the earth.
Then all those Sagaras, meeting together, could find neither the horse nor the horse-thief.

Coming before their father with folded hands they reported: 'The entire earth with its oceans, forests, and islands, with its rivers, streams, and gorges, with its mountains, woodlands, and all its regions, O king —
— has been searched by us, O king, by your command, O earth-lord; yet we find neither the horse nor the horse-thief.'
Hearing their words, that king, overcome with rage, spoke then to all of them — those who were subject to fate — O king.
'Go and do not return; search again for the sacrificial steed. Without that horse you must not come back, O my sons.'
Accepting that command, the sons of Sagara proceeded once again to search the entire earth.
Then those heroes saw the earth torn asunder; approaching that cavity, the sons of Sagara began digging it with mattocks and spades, and dug out the ocean at that time.
That abode of Varuṇa, being dug by the Sagaras together, suffered extreme distress as it was split on all sides.
Asuras, serpents, rakshasas, and various other creatures raised cries of anguish as they were slain by the Sagaras.
Creatures with severed heads, dismembered, with broken knees, bones, and skulls were seen by the hundreds and thousands.
As they dug in this way through the ocean, the abode of the makaras, a very great time passed, yet the horse was not seen.
Then in the northeastern region of the ocean, O lord of the earth, the enraged sons of Sagara, having rent open the underworld, saw the horse roaming there on the ground.
And they saw the great-souled Kapila, that unsurpassed mass of energy, blazing with austerity like fire with its flames.
Lomaśa said: Seeing that horse, O king, their hair bristling with excitement, disregarding the great-souled Kapila, driven by fate, they rushed forward in fury, eager to seize the horse.
Then Kapila, that best of sages, became enraged, O great king — that best of sages whom they call Vāsudeva.
He, of surpassing energy, opened his eyes and releasing his fiery power upon them, burned those dull-witted Sagaras.
Seeing them reduced to ashes, Nārada of very great austerity came to Sagara and reported this to him.

Hearing that terrible word issued from the mouth of the sage, the king became dejected for a moment, then contemplated the words of the Immovable One; consoling himself, he then reflected only on the horse.
Summoning Aṃśumat, the son of Asamañjas, his grandson, O tiger among the Bhāratas, he spoke these words.
'Sixty thousand sons of mine of immeasurable energy have met their death on my account, having encountered the fiery power of Kapila.
And your father too, O dear blameless one, was abandoned by me while I was protecting righteousness and seeking the welfare of the townspeople.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For what reason did King Sagara, that tiger among kings, abandon his own son, that hero so hard to abandon? Tell me this, O wealth of austerity.
Lomaśa said: There was a son of Sagara known as Asamañjas, whom Śaibyā bore — he would seize the children of the townspeople who were crying, and fling the helpless little ones into the river.
Then the townspeople came together, overwhelmed with fear and grief, and all of them besought Sagara, standing with folded hands.
'You are our protector, O great king, from fears such as enemy armies; from this terrible fear of Asamañjas you must therefore protect us.'
Hearing that terrible word of the townspeople, that best of kings became dejected for a moment and then spoke thus to his ministers.
'My son Asamañjas is to be expelled from the city today. If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, let this be done swiftly.'
Thus addressed by that lord of men, those ministers, O lord of men, swiftly did exactly as had been said and as the king had commanded.
All this has been narrated to you — how the son was exiled by the great-souled Sagara who desired the welfare of the townspeople.
What was said to Aṃśumat, that great archer, by Sagara — all that I shall now tell you as it is recounted; hear it from me.
Sagara said: I am tormented, my child, by the abandonment of your father, and by the death of my sons, and likewise by the non-recovery of the horse.
Therefore, from the hellish state in which I am, scorched by grief and deluded by this obstacle to the sacrifice — rescue me, O grandson, by bringing back the horse.
Lomaśa said: Thus addressed by the great-souled Sagara, Aṃśumat departed with a sorrowful heart toward the place where the earth had been split open.
He entered the ocean by that very same path and saw there the great-souled Kapila and that horse.
Seeing that ancient best of sages, that mass of radiance, he bowed his head to the ground in prostration and reported his purpose to him.
Then the greatly radiant Kapila became pleased with Aṃśumat, and that righteous-souled one spoke to him saying 'I am a granter of boons,' O Bhārata.
He chose the horse as the first boon, for the sake of the sacrifice; the second boon he chose was water — desiring purification for the ancestral spirits.
The greatly radiant Kapila, foremost of sages, spoke to him: 'I grant you whatever you seek, blessings be upon you, O blameless one.'
'Forbearance, righteousness, and truth are established in you. Sagara is fulfilled through you, and your father too has sons through you.

'By your very power shall the Sagaras ascend to heaven; and your grandson shall bring down the triple-pathed one from the celestial realm, having pleased Maheśvara, for the purpose of purifying the Sagaras.'
'Take the sacrificial horse — blessings upon you, O bull among men; let the sacrifice of the great-souled Sagara be completed, O dear one.'
Thus addressed by the great-souled Kapila, Aṃśumat came back with the horse to the sacrificial enclosure of the great-souled king.
He then saluted the feet of the great-souled Sagara, was smelled on the head by him, and reported everything to him.
He described to him the destruction of the Sagaras as he had seen and heard it, and told him of the horse that had come to the sacrificial enclosure.
Hearing this, King Sagara set aside the grief born of his sons' fate, honored Aṃśumat, and completed that sacrifice.
With his sacrifice completed, Sagara, honored by all the gods, declared the ocean — the abode of Varuṇa — to be his son.
That lotus-eyed one, having ruled the kingdom for a very long time, placed the burden upon his grandson and departed to the three heavens.
And Aṃśumat, righteous-souled, ruled the earth girt by the ocean, O great king, just as his grandfather had done.
His son was born — named Dilīpa, a knower of righteousness; having entrusted the kingdom to him, Aṃśumat too passed away.
Then Dilīpa, upon hearing of the great destruction of his ancestors, was tormented by grief and pondered on their fate.
The king made an immense effort to bring down the Gaṅgā, but try as he might with all his strength, he could not cause her to descend.
His son was born — glorious, devoted to righteousness, known as Bhagīratha, truthful in speech and free from envy.
Having consecrated him in the kingdom, Dilīpa retired to the forest; and that king, O bull of the Bhāratas, in time attained the perfection of austerity and departed from the forest to heaven.
Lomaśa said: That king, a great archer, a wheel-turner of empire, a mighty chariot-warrior, became the delight of the hearts and eyes of all the worlds.
The mighty-armed one heard of the terrible destruction of his ancestors by the great-souled Kapila and of their failure to attain heaven.
He, the lord of men, entrusted the kingdom to his ministers with a heart torn by sorrow, and went to the slopes of the Himālayas to perform austerities.
Wishing to propitiate the Gaṅgā and having burned away his sins through austerity, he, best of men, beheld Himavat, the greatest of mountains.
It was adorned with peaks of many varied forms rich in minerals, and embraced on all sides by clouds that clung to the winds.
It was beautified by river-thickets and water-bearing slopes, and frequented by lions and tigers lurking in caves and ravines.
It rang with the varied calls of vividly coloured birds — with the songs of the bhṛṅgarāja, the haṃsa, the dātyūha, and the water-hen.
It resounded with peacocks, lotus-birds, cuckoos, jīvajīvaka birds, dark-eyed cakor partridges, and also the birds called putrapriya.
Its lovely water-places were crowded with lotus-groves, and it was adorned by the sweet cries of sārasa cranes.
Its rocky surfaces were frequented by kiṃnaras and apsarases, and its trees were rubbed on all sides by the tusk-tips of the elephants of the quarters.
It was roamed by vidyādharas, teeming with gems of every kind, and haunted by venomous serpents with flaming tongues.
He approached Himavat — golden in some places, silver-white in others, resembling heaps of collyrium in yet others.
There that best of men embraced fierce austerity, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water for a thousand years.
When a thousand years had passed, the divine great river Gaṅgā revealed herself to him in embodied form.
The Gaṅgā said: What do you desire from me, great king, and what shall I give you? Speak, best of men — I will fulfil your word.

Lomaśa said: Thus addressed, the king replied to the daughter of Himavat then: 'O boon-giving great river, my grandsires, while searching for the horse, were carried off to the abode of Vaivasvata by Kapila.'
'Those sixty thousand great-souled sons of Sagara, encountering the fire of Kapila, perished in an instant.'
'For those thus destroyed, there is no dwelling in heaven so long as you do not sprinkle their bodies with your waters.'
'O most blessed one, convey my ancestors, the sons of Sagara, to heaven — for their sake I implore you, O great river.'
Hearing the king's words, the Gaṅgā, worshipped by all worlds, was greatly pleased and spoke these words to Bhagīratha.
'I will fulfil your word, great king — there is no doubt of this. But my current as I fall, discharged from the sky, is hard to bear.'
'No one in the three worlds is able to hold me, O king, except the best of the immortals, the blue-throated Maheśvara.'

'Propitiate him, O mighty-armed one, Hara the boon-giver, through austerity; that god will bear me on his head as I descend, and will fulfil your wish out of desire for the welfare of your ancestors.'
Hearing these words, O king, great king Bhagīratha went to Mount Kailāsa and pleased Śaṃkara.
Then, having met with him after some time had passed, that best of men received from him the boon of bearing the Gaṅgā, O king, with the aim of securing heaven for his ancestors.
Lomaśa said: Hearing the words of Bhagīratha and for the benefit of the gods as well, the Blessed Lord replied to the king: 'So be it.'
'I will bear the auspicious divine holy river of the gods as she falls from the sky — for your sake, best of kings, O mighty-armed one.'
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one approached Himavat, surrounded by terrible attendants brandishing various weapons.
Then, having stationed himself there, he said to Bhagīratha, best of men: 'O mighty-armed one, pray to the daughter of the mountain-king — I shall bear the best of rivers as she falls from heaven.'
Hearing the words spoken by Śarva, the king, purified and bowing in reverence, meditated upon the Gaṅgā.
Then the lovely, pure-watered river, thought upon by the king and seeing Īśāna standing ready, suddenly fell from the sky.
Seeing her fall, the gods together with the great sages, along with gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas, came together to witness the sight.
Then the Gaṅgā, daughter of Himavat, fell from the sky with her great eddies swirling wildly, teeming with fish and crocodiles.
Hara received her, O king — the Gaṅgā, girdled by the sky — as she fell upon his forehead, like a garland of pearls.
She spread out, O king, flowing in three streams to the ocean, her waters thick with masses of foam, like rows of swans.

Somewhere she wound in sweeping curves, somewhere she leapt and stumbled, wrapped in her own veil of foam she moved like an ecstatic woman; somewhere she roared with the great sound of rushing waters.
Performing many such displays as she fell from the sky and reached the surface of the earth, she then spoke to Bhagīratha.
'Show me the way, great king — where shall I go? It is for your sake, O lord of the earth, that I have descended to the earth.'
Hearing these words, King Bhagīratha set out toward where the bodies of those great-souled sons of Sagara lay, so that they might be purified, O best of men, by the sacred waters.
Having borne the Gaṅgā, Hara, worshipped by all worlds, departed to Kailāsa, best of mountains, together with the gods.
Reaching the ocean together with the Gaṅgā, the king filled with her rushing current the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa.
The king adopted the Gaṅgā as a daughter, and there, his heart's desire fulfilled, he performed the water-offering for his ancestors.
I have told you everything — how the Gaṅgā, flowing through three paths, was brought down to earth for the filling of the ocean.
And how the ocean was drunk by that great-souled one for a purpose, and how Vātāpi, that slayer of brahmins, was brought to destruction by Agastya, O great king — this is what you asked me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the son of Kuntī journeyed onward, O bull of the Bhāratas, and came in succession to the rivers Nandā and Aparanandā, which dispel the fear of sin.
Approaching the salubrious mountain Hemakūṭa, the king beheld very many inconceivable and wondrous phenomena.
There, where sounds became clouds and thousands of stones rained down, people with despondent minds could not climb it.
The wind always blew there, rain always fell there, and morning and evening the blessed fire-carrier was to be seen.
Having observed these many wondrous phenomena, the Pāṇḍava then questioned Lomaśa again about those marvels.
Lomaśa said: As I have heard it of old, O destroyer of foes, hear it from me now with focused mind, O king.
On this Ṛṣabhakūṭa there lived an ascetic named Ṛṣabha, who lived for many hundreds of years — a man of austerity and exceedingly wrathful.
Once, when addressed by others, he declared in anger to the mountain: 'Whoever speaks here shall rain down stones.'
Summoning the wind, that ascetic declared: 'Let there be no noise!' — and indeed, whoever speaks is blocked by a cloud.
Thus, O king, these phenomena were set in motion by that great seer — some out of anger, others as prohibitions.
It is heard, O king, that long ago, men who were seers of the gods suddenly followed after the gods who had come to Nandā.
Not wishing to be seen, the gods led by Śakra made this region impassable, in the form of a mountain barrier.
From that time onward, O son of Kuntī, men were never able to even see this mountain, let alone climb it.
This great mountain cannot be seen or climbed by one who has not heated himself with austerity, O son of Kuntī — therefore keep your speech restrained.
Here all the gods have always conducted supreme sacrifices, and the marks of those sacrifices are visible even today, O Bhārata.
This grass resembles kuśa, this ground appears as if strewn with sacred grass, and these many trees stand like sacrificial posts, O lord of the people.
Gods and sages still dwell here even today, O Bhārata, and their fire-bearer is to be seen at evening and at morning.
For those who bathe here, O son of Kuntī, sin is immediately destroyed. Therefore, O best of the Kurus, perform ablution together with your brothers.
Then, with limbs purified by bathing in the Nandā, you will proceed to the Kauśikī, where Viśvāmitra performed his fierce and unsurpassed austerity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having bathed there, the king with his retinue set off toward the Kauśikī — the holy, lovely river with auspicious waters.
Lomaśa said: This is the holy river of the gods, the Kauśikī, O bull of the Bhāratas, and here shines forth the lovely hermitage of Viśvāmitra.
Here too is the hermitage known as holy, that of the great-souled Kāśyapa, whose son was the ascetic Ṛśyaśṛṅga, master of his senses.
He who by the power of his austerity caused Vāsava to send rain, and out of fear of whom the mighty slayer of Vṛtra rained during a drought.
That radiant, mighty son of Kāśyapa was born of a doe, and in the kingdom of Lomapāda he performed a great wonder.
When the crops had been restored, the king Lomapāda gave him Śāntā as his daughter, just as Savitṛ gave Sāvitrī.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the son of Kāśyapa, born of a doe through a union contrary to nature, and how did he come to be endowed with austerity?
And why, when drought had set in, did the mighty Śakra, slayer of Vṛtra, rain out of fear of that wise boy?
And what manner of woman was Śāntā, the king's daughter, strict in her vow, who captivated the heart of that one who had been as a deer?
And Lomapāda, the royal sage heard of as righteous — how was it that in his kingdom Pākaśāsana did not rain?
All this, O blessed one, you should tell me in full and as it truly happened — I am eager to hear of the deeds of Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
Lomaśa said: Of Vibhāṇḍaka the brahmin-seer, whose self was refined by austerity, whose virility was infallible, who was righteous and of splendour equal to Prajāpati —
— hear how was born his son Ṛśyaśṛṅga of great valour, greatly radiant, a boy esteemed by the elders, born in a great lake.
Having approached the great lake, Kāśyapa stood fixed in ascetic practice; long-wearied was that sage, esteemed among the divine seers.
His seed fell upon beholding the apsarā Urvaśī while he touched the waters, O king, and a doe drank it then.
Thirsty, she drank it together with the water and became with child, O king — by the infallibility of fate and the inevitability of what was divinely ordained.
From that doe was born his great son, the sage Ṛśyaśṛṅga, ever devoted to austerity; he grew up in the forest itself.
On the head of that great-souled one there was the horn of a deer, O king; hence he became known by the name Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
No other person had ever been seen by him apart from his father; therefore his mind was always fixed in celibacy, O king.
At this very time, the lord of the Aṅgas who was known as Lomapāda, a friend of Daśaratha, ruled.
By him a false promise had been made to brāhmaṇas — so the tradition goes; and that lord of the earth was then abandoned by the brāhmaṇas.
And on account of the wrong done to the royal priest, the thousand-eyed Indra did not send rain by chance; thereafter the people were greatly afflicted.
That lord of the earth consulted the brāhmaṇas — the wise, endowed with austerity — who were capable of inducing the great Indra to send rain.
"How may the rain-cloud pour forth? Let a means be found." Thus prompted by him, the wise ones declared their own views.
Then one foremost among sages said to that king: "The brāhmaṇas are angered with you, O king of kings; make atonement."
"Bring Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the son of the sage, O king — he who is forest-born, unacquainted with women, and devoted to uprightness."
"If that great ascetic should descend into your kingdom, O king, the rain-cloud will pour forth immediately — of this I have no doubt."
Hearing this counsel, O king, and having made atonement for himself, he went and returned; when the twice-born were appeased, the people, seeing the king had returned, welcomed him with joy.
Then the lord of the Aṅgas, summoning his ministers skilled in counsel, applied himself with effort to the settled plan for bringing Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
He, together with those ministers — fully versed in scripture, skilled in affairs, and thoroughly grounded in statecraft — devised a means.
Then that lord of the earth summoned the foremost of courtesans — women expert in every art — and the king spoke to them thus:
"Bring Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the son of the sage, by stratagem — enticing him, winning his trust, and drawing him into my kingdom, O lovely ones."
