Those women, fearing the king and fearing the curse, declared the task impossible, pale-faced and dispirited.
Then one aged woman among them said this to the king: "I will endeavour, great king, to bring that treasure-house of austerity."
"You must grant the desires I have in mind; then I shall be able to entice Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the son of the sage."
That king agreed to her entire intention, and gave her abundant wealth and various jewels.
Then, O lord of the earth, endowed with beauty and youth, she took some women with her and went straightway into the forest.
Lomaśa said: She fashioned a floating hermitage for the accomplishment of the king's purpose — both by the king's command and by her own wit, O Bhārata.
It was adorned with artificial trees bearing various flowers and fruits, furnished with various shrubs and creepers that yielded sweet and desirable fruits.
She made that floating hermitage exceedingly delightful and exceedingly charming — lovely and wondrous to behold.
Then, having moored that vessel not far from the hermitage of Kāśyapa, she had men spy out the movements of that sage.
Then the courtesan, having settled upon the plan and watching for an opportunity when Kāśyapa was away, sent her daughter — deemed wise — forward.
She, skilled in her craft, went there near where the perpetual ascetic dwelt, approached that hermitage, and beheld the son of the sage.
The courtesan said: "Are the ascetics well, O sage? Is your supply of roots and fruits abundant? Do you take pleasure in this hermitage? I have come just now to see you."
"Do the austerities of the ascetics increase? Is your father of undiminished splendour? Does he take pleasure in you, O brāhmaṇa? Is Vedic recitation performed, O Ṛśyaśṛṅga?"
Ṛśyaśṛṅga said: "You shine like a brilliant light, prosperous; I consider you worthy of reverence. I will gladly offer you water for your feet, as is proper, and also fruits and roots."
"Sit at your ease on this silken mat covered with a black antelope skin for comfort. Where is your hermitage, and what is your name? And what vow do you practise, O brāhmaṇa, for you are like a god?"

The courtesan said: "My hermitage is lovely, O son of Kāśyapa, beyond this hill at a distance of three leagues. There it is our custom not to receive reverence, nor do we accept water for washing of feet."
Ṛśyaśṛṅga said: "I will give you ripe fruits — marking-nut fruits and emblic myrobalans, parūṣaka berries and inguda fruits of the desert. Eat your fill of the priyāla nuts."
Lomaśa said: Rejecting all those offerings, she gave him precious delicacies instead. Those things, full of exquisite flavour, exceedingly beautiful in form, truly pleased the taste of Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
She gave him fragrant garlands, bright and variegated garments, and excellent drinks; then she rejoiced, sported, and laughed.
She played with a ball at his side, like a fruit-laden creeper swaying — pressing her limbs against his limbs, she embraced Ṛśyaśṛṅga repeatedly.
Bending down and breaking off the fully-flowering sarja, aśoka, and tilaka trees, as though overcome with intoxication and feigning bashfulness, she enticed the son of the great sage.
Then, having observed Ṛśyaśṛṅga stirred and having pressed his body again and again, she slowly departed, taking as pretext the maintenance of the sacred fire.
After she departed, Ṛśyaśṛṅga became overwhelmed by passion and bewildered; emptied of all feeling save longing for her, sighing and appearing distressed.
Then, after a moment, Vibhāṇḍaka Kāśyapa appeared — tawny-yellow-eyed, his body covered with hair to the tips of his nails, devoted to Vedic recitation and absorbed in the practice of vows.
Approaching, he saw his son sitting alone, in meditation, with an agitated mind, sighing repeatedly with upward gaze; Vibhāṇḍaka addressed his son in a gentle tone.

"The kindling sticks are not being arranged — what is this, my son? Have you performed the agnihotra oblation today? Have the ladle and pouring-spoon been well cleaned? Has the ritual cow with her calf been tended today?"
"You are not as you were before, my son — you are lost in thought and bewildered, exceedingly dejected here today. What is this? I ask you: who has come here today?"
Ṛśyaśṛṅga said: "A matted-haired celibate student came here — neither short nor overly tall, mindful, golden in complexion, with eyes long as lotus petals, shining like the son of the gods."
"Perfectly formed and radiant as the sun, with eyes clearer and whiter than even the cakora bird's — dark, lustrous, fragrant matted locks, braided with golden cords and very long."
"On the neck, something serving as a necklace shines like lightning in the sky; and two rounded forms below the neck, hairless and most charming to the heart."
"Slender in the middle at the navel-region, yet the hips of extraordinary measure; and his girdle, shining through the bark garment, seemed to me like a girdle of gold."
"And another wondrous thing — a jingling at the feet was radiant, and likewise on the hands, making a sweet sound, bound there — like rosaries worn as armlets."
"And as he moved about, those things jingled like maddened swans on a lake. His bark garments were wondrous to behold — mine are not so beautiful as those."
"And the face was wondrous to behold — the words spoken seemed to gladden the heart; and the voice like that of a male cuckoo — hearing it my inner self was moved and troubled."
"As a forest in the month of Mādhava wafts its scent in the middle when stirred by the breeze, so he breathed forth a fragrance of supreme purity when caressed by the wind, O father."
"And the matted locks, well-bound and parted, divided in two, gleamed evenly upon the forehead; and the ears were adorned with rings beautiful as painted wheels."
"And a round, variegated fruit — he struck it with his right hand; touching the ground again and again, it bounded up in a wondrous manner, high into the air."
"And striking it still, he turned about like a tree shaken by the wind; beholding him, who seemed to me like the son of the immortals, a great delight and joy arose in me, O father."
"He embraced my body, took hold of my matted locks, and bowed his face; pressing his mouth to my mouth, he made a sound — that produced in me the greatest delight."
"He thought nothing of the water for his feet, nor of these fruits I had brought; saying 'Such is my vow,' he gave me other fruits, fresh ones."
"Those fruits I ate — these here are not equal to those in flavour; nor is the skin of these like those, nor do these have the essence that those had."
"And waters of surpassing flavour that noble-formed one gave me to drink; having drunk them, a great joy arose in me — the very earth seemed to sway."
"And these variegated fragrant garlands, unstrung from their silk threads, which he scattered here as he went to his own hermitage — he who blazes with austerity."
"After he departed, I was made bewildered; my body seems to burn. I desire to go quickly to his side, and to have him ever moving here."
"I will go to his very side, O father — what is that vow he practises? I desire to practise it together with him, even as he performs that fierce austerity."
Vibhāṇḍaka said: "These are demons roaming about, my son, in that wondrous form — of incomparable appearance, exceedingly terrible; they ever contrive obstacles to austerity."
"Those beings of beautiful form, O son, entice sages in the forests by various stratagems, and cause them to fall from the worlds of blessedness — they of fierce and evil deeds."

"A self-controlled sage seeking the worlds of the righteous should never associate with them in any way; those of evil conduct make sport of obstructing the austerities of ascetics — and they steal the heat of austerity."
"These pleasures practised by the wicked, O son, are sweet but should not be tasted; and these garlands, bright and fragrant — they are not at all considered suitable for sages."
Lomaśa said: Having restrained his son by saying "these are demons," Vibhāṇḍaka went off on a hunt; when he had not obtained game within three days, he then returned to the hermitage.
When Kāśyapa went again to gather fruits according to the rites of the forest-student, then again that courtesan went to entice the sage Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
The very moment he saw her, Ṛśyaśṛṅga was overjoyed; agitated in appearance, he ran toward her at once and spoke: "Let us go to your hermitage before my father comes."
Then, O king, having lured the sole son of Kāśyapa on board by stratagem, they set sail, and enticing him with various means, they came to the presence of the lord of the Aṅgas.
Having anchored the exceedingly bright vessel in view of the hermitage and taken it from the bank, the king likewise made a wondrous forest called the "Royal Hermitage."
When the king had settled the only son of Vibhāṇḍaka in the inner palace, he suddenly saw rain pour down, and the world filling with water.
That Lomapāda, his wish fulfilled, gave his daughter Śāntā to Ṛśyaśṛṅga; he also made amends for the wrong done, and had cattle drag ploughs along the roads.
For the approaching Vibhāṇḍaka, that king deployed abundant cattle and valiant herdsmen — eager for his son — so that when the great sage Vibhāṇḍaka should question you, they would answer:
"He is to be told by you with folded hands: 'These cattle and this ploughing are your son's. What is pleasing to you, let it be done, great sage — we are all your servants, bound to your word.'"
Then that sage of fierce wrath approached his own hermitage, carrying roots and fruits; searching but not finding his son there, he was greatly enraged.
Then, bursting with fury and suspecting the king's contrivance, he marched toward Campā intent on burning that king of the Aṅgas and his kingdom.
Weary and hungry, Kāśyapa came to those prosperous cow-herding settlements; honoured duly by those cowherds as though he were a king, he spent that night there.
Having received exceptional honour from them, he asked: 'Whose celebrated ones are you, O gentle ones?' Then all of them approached and said: 'This wealth has been appointed for your son.'
Honoured in every region, listening to those sweet words, with his passion now largely appeased and his heart gladdened, he approached the lord of Aṅga who stood before him.
Duly honoured by that bull among men, he saw his son radiant as a god in heaven like Indra; and there too he saw his daughter-in-law Shanta, rising up like a flash of lightning.
Having seen the villages, the settlements, his son, and Shanta, his great anger was pacified; Vibhāṇḍaka bestowed his highest blessing on that lord of the earth, O king of kings.
There the great seer, having entrusted his son of solar and fiery brilliance, spoke: 'When a son is born, you should return to the forest, having done all that is pleasing to this king.'
Rishyashringa did as his father instructed and went to where his father had been; and Shanta attended upon him faithfully, as Rohiṇī in the sky attends upon the moon in harmony.
As the blessed Arundhatī served Vasiṣṭha, or as Lopāmudrā served Agastya, or as Damayantī was to Nala, or as Śacī to the wielder of the thunderbolt—
And as Nadayani Indrasenā was ever devoted to Mudgala, O descendant of Ajamīḍha — so Shanta, filled with love, waited upon Rishyashringa dwelling in the forest, O king.

This holy hermitage of his, renowned for its sanctity, shines forth, adorning the great lake. Having bathed here, with all duties fulfilled and purified, go on, O king, to visit the other sacred tirthas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the Pāṇḍava departed from the Kauśikī, O Janamejaya, and visited all the sacred shrines in due order.
Reaching the ocean at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, O king, he bathed together with hundreds of rivers at the meeting of five streams.
Then along the seashore that lord of the earth, the hero, accompanied by his brothers, proceeded toward the Kaliṅgas, O Bhārata.
Lomaśa said: These are the Kaliṅgas, O son of Kuntī, where the river Vaitaraṇī flows — where even Dharma himself sought refuge with the gods and performed sacrifice.
This northern bank, adorned with mountains, consecrated for sacrifice, enriched by sages, is always frequented by the twice-born.
Those who have attained heaven by the straight Devayana path — here too other sages in former times performed sacrifices with great rites.
Right here, O king of kings, Rudra seized the sacrificial animal at the sacrifice; Rudra said, O lord of men: 'This is my share.'
When the animal was taken, the gods then said to him, O bull of the Bhāratas: 'Do not seize what belongs to another; do not transgress all the laws of dharma.'
Then with words of auspicious form they praised Rudra, and having propitiated him with offerings they then honoured him.
Then he released the animal and departed by the Devayana path. Hear now the lineage of Rudra that is associated with this place, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Out of fear of Rudra, the gods forever resolved that the choicest, freshest share — the best of all portions — would always belong to him.
Whoever sings this hymn here and touches the waters — the Devayana path and his eyes shall become illumined for him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all the Pāṇḍavas, and Draupadī of great fortune, descended into the Vaitaraṇī and made offerings to the ancestors.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Having touched the waters of this river, O blessed one, O treasure of austerity, I feel as though I have passed beyond the human realm — behold, O Lomaśa.
By your grace, O one of good vows, I behold all the worlds; this is the sound of the great-souled Vaikhanasa sages engaged in recitation.
Lomaśa said: Three hundred thousand yojanas distant is the place where you hear that sound, O Yudhiṣṭhira — be silent, O lord of the people.
This, O king, is the delightful forest of Svayambhu that shines forth, where the mighty Viśvakarman performed his sacrifice, O son of Kuntī.
At that sacrifice, the entire earth — with its mountains and forests — was given by Svayambhu as the sacrificial fee to the great-souled Kaśyapa.
And no sooner was the earth given than it sank down, O son of Kuntī; and it spoke in anger to that lord of the worlds, its master.
'O blessed one, you ought not give me to any mortal; this gift of yours is in vain — I shall sink into the nether world.'
Seeing her despondent, the blessed sage Kaśyapa then began to appease the earth, O lord of the people.
Then the earth, appeased by his austerity, O Pāṇḍava, rose up again from the waters and stood shining in the form of an altar.
This is that altar shining here, O king, marked by its distinctive form; ascend it, O great king, and you shall become mighty.
And I shall perform a benedictory rite for you, so that you may ascend it today; for once touched by a mortal, this altar sinks into the ocean, O descendant of Ajamīḍha.

Speaking these true words, O Pāṇḍava: 'You are Agni, you are Mitra, you are the womb, you are the divine waters, you are the seed of Viṣṇu, you are the navel of immortality' — swiftly ascend this altar.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the great-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, the benediction performed, proceeded to the ocean; and having done all that Lomaśa commanded, he reached Mahendra and spent the night there.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spent that one night there, the lord of the earth offered the highest honour to the ascetics together with his brothers.
And Lomaśa introduced to him all those ascetics there — the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, the Vasishthyas, and the Kashyapas.
Meeting them, that royal seer paid his respects with joined palms and then asked Akṛtavraṇa, the heroic companion of Rāma.
'When will the blessed Rāma show himself to the ascetics? On that very occasion I wish to behold the descendant of Bhṛgu.'
Akṛtavraṇa said: Your coming is already known to Rāma, who knows all souls; and Rāma's affection for you is such that he will show himself to you soon.
The ascetics see Rāma on the fourteenth and the eighth lunar days; when this night has passed, the fourteenth will arrive.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have accompanied that hero, the son of Jamadagni, of great might, and are an eyewitness to all his past deeds.
Let you therefore tell us how Rāma conquered all the kshatriyas in battle, and by what means and for what reason.
Akṛtavraṇa said: In Kanyakubja there was a great and exceedingly mighty king, renowned in the world as Gādhi; he went to live in the forest.
While he lived in the forest, a daughter was born to him who was like an apsara; the Bhārgava Richika sought her in marriage, O Bhārata.
Then the king said to that brahmin of rigorous vows: 'There is something customary in our family, established by our ancestors—'
'Know this as the bride-price, O best of twice-born: a thousand swift white horses, each with one black ear.'
'And do not say, O blessed Bhārgava, that the price should be waived — my daughter is to be given to a great soul such as you.'
Richika said: I will give you a thousand swift white horses, each with one black ear; let your daughter be my wife and your son-in-law be me.
Akṛtavraṇa said: Having agreed to this, O king, he addressed Varuṇa: 'For the bride-price, let a thousand swift white horses, each with one black ear, be given to me.'
Varuṇa gave him a thousand horses at that time; that place is known as Ashvatirtha, where those horses emerged.
At Kanyakubja on the Gaṅgā, Gādhi then gave his daughter Satyavatī to him; and upon receiving the thousand horses and seeing them, the gods dwellers in heaven rejoiced.
Having won her as his wife by righteous means, Richika, the best of twice-born, sported with that slender-waisted one to his heart's content and delight.
After the marriage was performed, O king, the foremost of the Bhṛgus came to look upon his son together with his wife, and upon seeing him was filled with joy.
The husband and wife, honouring that teacher who was worshipped even by the host of gods, stood attending him on either side with joined palms.
Then the blessed Bhṛgu, delighted, said to his daughter-in-law: 'Choose a boon, O fortunate one, for I am here to grant what you desire.'
She then propitiated that teacher for the sake of children — both for herself and for her mother; and he granted his grace to both.
Bhṛgu said: 'At the proper season, you and your mother, having bathed with the rite of pumsavana for a male child, must each embrace a different tree — you the udumbara, and the ashvattha.'
But the two of them, O king, exchanged the trees in their embrace; and when Bhṛgu came by, he discerned the exchange.
Then the greatly splendid Bhṛgu said to his daughter-in-law Satyavatī: 'Your son will be a brahmin who follows the conduct of a kshatriya.'
'And your mother's great son will be a kshatriya who follows brahminical conduct — of great valour and treading the path of the righteous.'
Then she repeatedly propitiated her father-in-law, saying: 'Let not my son be such — let my grandson be so instead, if you will.'
'So be it,' said he; she was thus granted her wish, O Pāṇḍava; and in time she gave birth to her son Jamadagni, the delight of the Bhṛgus, endowed with brilliance and radiance.
Growing up, that splendid one, of great brilliance, surpassed many sages through his study of the Vedas, O descendant of the Pāṇḍavas.
The entire science of archery, along with the fourfold knowledge of weapons, became manifest to him, O bull of the Bhāratas, whose radiance was like the sun.
Akṛtavraṇa said: Jamadagni, of great austerity, devoted to Vedic study, performed tapas and thereby brought the gods under his control by his discipline.
Approaching king Prasenajit, O king, lord of men, he sought Reṇukā in marriage; and the king gave her to him.
Having thus obtained Reṇukā as his wife, the delight of the Bhṛgus lived in the hermitage and performed austerities together with her, who was devoted and compliant.
Four sons were born to her, Rāma being the fifth; Rāma, the last-born, was the youngest of them all.
One day, all the sons having gone out to gather fruits, Reṇukā, steadfast in her vows, went to bathe.
And Reṇukā, as she was going along, happened by chance to see a king named Chitraratha, the lord of Martikavata, O king.
Seeing him sporting in the water with his wife, garlanded with lotuses, in the full flush of his prosperity, Reṇukā was filled with longing for him.
On account of that transgression in her mind, she came back trembling and distraught, her clothes still wet from the water, and entered the hermitage; her husband perceived it in her.
Seeing her fallen from her steadfastness and stripped of her brahminical radiance, the greatly splendid and valiant one censured her with words of reproach.
Then the eldest son of Jamadagni named Rumanvan arrived, and Suṣeṇa, and Vasu, and Viśvāvasu as well.
The blessed one urged them each in turn to kill their mother; but they, overcome with confusion, said nothing, standing senseless.
Then in anger he cursed them; cursed, they lost their consciousness and quickly became like inert beings, taking on the nature of animals and birds.
Then Rāma, the slayer of enemy heroes, came to the hermitage afterward; and Jamadagni, greatly wrathful and of great austerity, said to him—
'Kill this sinful mother, and let not grief afflict you, my son.' Then taking up the axe, Rāma struck off his mother's head.
Then, O great king, the anger of the great-souled Jamadagni suddenly departed; and, now pleased, he spoke these words.
This difficult deed has been done by you at my word, dear son. Now choose as many boons as your heart desires, O knower of dharma.
He chose the revival of his mother, her forgetting of the killing, the freedom of his brothers from that sin's taint, and the restoration of their natural dispositions.
Invincibility in battle and a long life — all these boons the great ascetic Jamadagni granted, O Bhārata.
Then one day, when his sons had gone out, the heroic king of the river-land, Kārtavīrya, came to that hermitage, O lord.
The sage's wife duly honored the king when he arrived at the hermitage, but intoxicated with the pride of battle, he did not acknowledge that hospitality.
Forcibly overpowering the hermitage, he then seized the calf of the sacrificial cow by force even as she lowed in distress, and he broke the great trees.
When Rāma returned, his father himself told him what had happened; and seeing the cow bellowing in grief, anger entered Rāma.
Seized by wrath, he charged at Kārtavīrya; and in battle the Bhārgava, slayer of enemy heroes, displayed his valor.
Taking up his splendid bow, O king, he cut off Kārtavīrya's arms — a thousand of them, like iron clubs — with sharp broad-headed arrows.
Then the sons of Arjuna Kārtavīrya, enraged at what Rāma had done, attacked Jamadagni in his hermitage when Rāma was absent.
They killed that mighty ascetic who would not fight, crying out again and again "Rāma! Rāma!" as if helpless and without a protector.
The sons of Kārtavīrya, O Yudhiṣṭhira, after slaying Jamadagni with their arrows, departed the way they had come, O subduer of foes.
After they had departed and Jamadagni lay thus fallen, the son of the Bhṛgu clan, with fuel-sticks in hand, returned to the hermitage.
Seeing his father the hero had fallen thus under the power of death — he who deserved no such fate — he lamented in deep grief.
Rāma said: Through my fault you have been killed, dear father, by those petty fools, the sons of Kārtavīrya, in the forest like a deer by arrows.
How is such a death fitting for one who knows dharma and walks the righteous path, O father — one who has never wronged any living being?
What sin have those men not committed, by whom you — established in austerity, an old man who would not fight — were slain with hundreds of sharp arrows?
What shall those shameless ones say to their counselors and friends, having slain a single man who knew dharma and would not fight?
Akṛtavraṇa said: Having lamented thus in grief in many various ways, O king, that great ascetic performed all the funeral rites for his father.
Rāma, the conqueror of enemy citadels, burned his father on the funeral pyre and vowed to exterminate the entire Kṣatriya order, O Bhārata.
In fierce anger, that exceedingly mighty hero, taking up his weapon, single-handedly slew the sons of Kārtavīrya, like Death himself.
And those Kṣatriyas who were their followers — Rāma, best among warriors, crushed them all, O bull among Kṣatriyas.
Having cleared the earth of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times, the lord made five lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka.
With those lakes of blood he propitiated his ancestors; the upholder of the Bhṛgu clan saw Richika in person, and Richika restrained Rāma.
Then the illustrious son of Jamadagni, through a great sacrifice, propitiated the lord of the gods, and gave the earth to the officiating priests.
He also gave to the great-souled Kaśyapa a golden sacrificial altar, ten fathoms in length and nine in height, O lord of the people.
With Kaśyapa's consent those Brahmins then divided it into pieces; hence, O king, they became renowned as the Khandavayanas.
Having given the earth to that great-souled Kaśyapa, Rāma of immeasurable valor dwells on this chief of mountains, Mahendra.
Thus arose his enmity with the Kṣatriyas who dwell in the world, and the earth was conquered by Rāma of immeasurable splendor.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then at the appointed time on the fourteenth day, the great-souled Rāma appeared before those Brahmins and the king of dharma together with his brothers.
That lord, best of kings, honored him together with his brothers; and the foremost of kings paid the highest homage to the twice-born.
After honoring the son of Jamadagni and being honored by him in return, the invincible one spent that night on Mahendra and then departed facing south.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Traveling onward, the great and mighty king visited the sacred and lovely tirthas of the ocean here and there, all beautified by Brahmins, O Bhārata.

Having bathed and performed the prescribed rites there, the son of Pāṇḍu — heir of kings, accompanied by his brothers — went to the most sacred and celebrated river flowing to the sea, O descendant of Parīkṣit.
Having bathed there also, that great and mighty one propitiated the ancestors and gods, distributed wealth to the foremost among the twice-born, and went on to the Godāvarī flowing to the sea.
Then that pure one, O king, in the Dravida country, reaching the ocean sacred to the world, visited the pure and holy tirtha of Agastya and then the hero visited the tirthas of Nari.
There, hearing of the deed of Arjuna — the foremost archer — that was unendurable for enemies, and honored by hosts of great sages, the son of Pāṇḍu was filled with great joy.
Having bathed at those tirthas, his body purified, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and his younger brothers, and extolling the valor of Arjuna, the lord of earth's kings rejoiced upon the earth.
Then, having given thousands of cows at those tirthas of the finest ocean, delighted together with his brothers, he celebrated the gifting of cows in honor of Arjuna.
He, his desires fully fulfilled, visiting in order those sacred tirthas of the ocean and many other holy places, O king, came to Śūrpāraka, most holy of all.

There, passing through a certain region of the ocean, he reached a forest renowned throughout the earth, where gods had formerly performed austerities and the most virtuous of kings had performed sacrifices.
There that long-armed, meritorious king saw the altar of the foremost archer, the son of Richika, surrounded by hosts of ascetics and worthy of worship.
Then that lord of the earth made offerings to the Vasus, the Marut-hosts, the Aśvins, Vivasvat, Āditya, the lord of wealth, Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitar, and the Vibhu.
To Bhaga, the moon, the sun, the lord of waters, the host of Sādhyas, Dhātar, the ancestors, the great-souled Rudra together with his hosts, O king —
To Sarasvatī, the host of Siddhas, Pūṣan, and all other immortals — the king saw their sacred and beautiful shrines.
Having observed various fasts there, and given gems and great wealth at all the tirthas, his body immersed in the sacred waters, he returned again to Śūrpāraka.
Departing from that tirtha of the ocean with his brothers and the twice-born, accompanied by great men, he reached the tirtha of Prabhāsa, celebrated throughout the earth.
There, bathed and with wide red eyes, he propitiated the hosts of gods and the ancestors together with his brothers, and so too did Kṛṣṇa; and the Brahmins as well with Lomaśa.
For twelve days, subsisting only on water and air, performing the ritual bath each night and day, kindling fires on all sides, he practiced austerities — the foremost of those who uphold dharma.
Hearing of him performing this fierce austerity, both Rāma and Janārdana — the foremost of all the Vṛṣṇis — came with their armies to Yudhiṣṭhira, the Ajamīḍha.
The Vṛṣṇis, seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu lying on the ground, their bodies smeared with dirt, and seeing Draupadī who deserved no such fate, cried out in deep grief and anguish.
Then, approaching Rāma and Janārdana, Pradyumna and Sāmba, the grandson of Śini, and the other Vṛṣṇis, that undaunted one honored them all as prescribed by dharma.
And they in turn honored all the Pārthas; honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu, they took their seats surrounding Yudhiṣṭhira as the host of gods surrounds Indra, O king.

With great confidence he told them all that had been done to them by their enemies, the forest exile, and Pārtha's journey to Indra's realm for weapons — he told all this to Kṛṣṇa, son of the king of immortals.
Hearing his words and with confidence, yet seeing them all exceedingly emaciated, those great and mighty Dāśārhas shed tears welling from their eyes, born of grief and pain.
Janamejaya said: When the Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas had come together at the tirtha of Prabhāsa, what did they do? And what conversations took place there, O storehouse of austerities?
For all of them were great-souled, all were versed in every branch of learning — the Vṛṣṇis and the Pāṇḍavas alike, and they were friends to one another.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having reached the sacred tirtha of Prabhāsa on the great ocean, the Vṛṣṇis surrounded and attended upon the heroic Pāṇḍavas.
Then Rāma, wearing a forest garland, bearing the plough, radiant as cow's milk, jasmine, the moon, a lotus stalk, or silver, spoke to the lotus-eyed one.

"It seems, O Kṛṣṇa, that dharma practiced does not bring prosperity to a being, nor does adharma bring defeat — for where the great-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, wearing matted locks, dwelling in the forest, wearing bark, suffers so.
While Duryodhana rules the earth and the earth does not open to swallow him — one might think, if of little understanding, that adharma practiced is weightier than dharma.
With Duryodhana prospering and Yudhiṣṭhira in misery, stripped of his kingdom, doubt has arisen among men — what indeed is to be done now? — whispering among themselves.
For this king born of dharma, devoted to dharma, firm in truth, a generous giver — how could Pārtha be displaced from his kingdom and happiness, and one who has strayed from dharma prosper?
How can Bhīṣma, Kṛpa the brahmin, Droṇa, and the king — the elders of the clan — having exiled the Pārthas, enjoy happiness? Shame on those evil-minded leaders of the Bhāratas!
What will that chief of earth's kings — that sinner — say when he meets his ancestors in the next world: 'I have dealt well with my sons' — he who deposed innocent sons from the kingdom?
He cannot see even now with his understanding: 'What have I done, born thus blind among kings upon earth?' — having exiled the son of Kuntī even from the kingdom.

Surely the son of Vichitraveerya together with his sons sees, alas, those who were flourishing on the earth of the ancestral realm, golden as the horizon at sunrise, reduced to misery — having perpetrated this cruelty.
With high broad shoulders and wide red eyes — he, without asking or heeding these men who were armed, fearlessly sent Yudhiṣṭhira with his brothers, weapon-bearing, to the forest.
He who would slay well-arrayed enemy armies unarmed, that long-armed one — at the mere sound of Vṛkodara's roar the armies void their bowels and urine.

That swift one, emaciated by hunger and thirst and travel, arming himself with weapons and arrows of every kind, remembering this most dreadful forest exile — he will leave none remaining: this is my certain conviction.
For none on earth among men can equal him in valor and strength; his body hardened by cold, heat, wind, and sun — he will leave none of his enemies remaining on the battlefield.

Vṛkodara, who alone with his chariot and retinue conquered the eastern kings in battle and returned in triumph — that foremost of charioteers, that swift hero — now suffers in the forest wearing bark garments.
He who conquered at Dantakura the godlike kings and the assembled southern monarchs — look now at that Sahadeva, clad as an ascetic, in the garb of a forest dweller.

He who, that heroic lover of battle, single-handedly with his chariot conquered kings of the western quarter — now that one wanders in the forest, living on roots and fruits, matted-haired, his body smeared with dirt.

She who sprang from the altar floor of the great sacrifice of that foremost of chariot-warriors, the king — how does she, faithful and deserving of happiness, endure this most painful forest dwelling now?
Sons of the foremost of the three — the wind god, the lord of gods Indra, and the Aśvins — sons of these gods, deserving of happiness, how do they wander in the forest with so little joy?
When the son of Dharma together with his wife, brothers, and followers has been thus vanquished and expelled, and Duryodhana prospers — how does the earth with its mountains not sink?
Sātyaki said: Now is not the time for lamentation, O Rāma. Let us all take that very action that is called for — while time has not yet passed — even if Yudhiṣṭhira says nothing.
Those who have protectors in this world do not undertake action by themselves; in their affairs their protectors act — as Śaibya and others were to Yayāti, O Rāma.
Those heroic men whose protectors thus undertake their affairs in the world according to their own judgment — they have true protectors and do not fall into distress as if they had none.

Why do Rāma and Janārdana, along with Pradyumna and Sāmba, who have reached the lords of the three worlds—why do they dwell in the forest together with their kinsmen, though they have found such protectors?

Let the army of the Dāśārhas march out today, well-armed with many weapons and fine armour. Let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra go to the abode of Yama, overwhelmed by the might of the Vṛṣṇis, together with all his kinsmen.

You alone in your wrath could wrap up even this whole earth; let the bearer of the Śārṅga bow stand firm. Slay that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with all his followers, just as the lord of the gods, great Indra, slew Vṛtra.
He who is my brother, my friend, and my teacher—Pārtha, who is regarded as Janārdana's very self—for his sake the foremost deed, impossible to accomplish, is being undertaken.

I shall repel his showers of weapons with my finest missiles in battle, overwhelming them all; yet from his body, with his best arrows that blaze like serpent-venom and fire, I have been utterly shattered, O Rāma.
With my sharpened sword in battle I shall forcibly cut off his head from his body, and then I shall slay all his followers, Duryodhana, and all the Kurus.

Let the people of this earth watch me here, O son of Rohiṇī, weapons in hand, rejoicing in battle as I single-handedly strike down the foremost Kuru warriors in due season, like the fire of death consuming a great heap of dry grass.
Kṛpa, Droṇa, Vikarṇa, and Karṇa are not able to withstand the sharp arrows released by Pradyumna. I know well the valour of your son—this son of Kṛṣṇa is formidable when he stands on the battlefield.
May Sāmba, forcibly seizing Duḥśāsana along with his charioteer and chariot in his two arms, punish him. For nothing in battle is unbearable for the son of Jāmbavatī, that fierce warrior.

By this young hero the army of the demon Śambara was swiftly routed—he of the rounded thighs and exceptionally long, full arms. By him in battle was Aśvacakra slain. What man in battle could enter the gap between Sāmba's arms and survive?
Just as a man who enters the jaws of Death at the appointed time does not come out again, so who, having entered the gap between his arms in battle, could return alive?
And Vāsudeva will burn Droṇa and Bhīṣma, those two great chariot-warriors, Somadatta surrounded by his sons, and all the armies, with his net of blazing arrows.

What in all the worlds, even among the gods, is unbearable for Kṛṣṇa, who has taken up his weapon, whose hands hold the finest arrows, who wields the discus as his weapon, and who is incomparable in battle?
Then let Aniruddha too, sword and shield in hand, strew this earth with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—senseless, their heads severed, slain—as an altar at a sacrifice is strewn with sacred grass.
Bāhuka, Bhānu, and Nītha bearing clubs and fire-brands, the young hero Niśaṭha who is fierce in battle, the war-eager Sāraṇa and Cārudeṣṇa—let them all spread the deeds befitting their noble lineage.
The assembled army of Kṣatriya heroes, with the foremost warriors of the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Andhakas, shall win wide fame in the world by slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle.
Then let Abhimanyu rule the earth while the great-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, foremost among upholders of dharma, fulfils the vow in exile as declared at the dice-game by that best of Kurus.
With enemies conquered by the arrows we release, Dharmarāja shall then enjoy the earth, rid of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the slain son of the sūta. This is indeed our most glorious duty.

Vāsudeva said: Without doubt, O Mādhava, this is true; we accept your words, O you of undaunted spirit. But the bull of the Kurus does not wish the earth that is yet unconquered by his own two arms, under any circumstances.
For Yudhiṣṭhira would never abandon his own dharma out of desire, fear, or greed—nor would Bhīma and Arjuna, those two great chariot-warriors, nor the twins, nor indeed Kṛṣṇā, daughter of Drupada.
For both Vṛkodara and Dhanaṃjaya are peerless in battle on this earth. Why should he not rule the entire earth, he who is accompanied by the two sons of Mādrī?

But when the great-souled lord of the Pāñcālas, together with the king of the Kekayas, the king of the Cedis, and ourselves, shall fight, advancing against the foe—then indeed Suyodhana shall quit the world of the living.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What you say, O Mādhava, is not surprising; but truth is what I must guard above all, not a kingdom. Kṛṣṇa alone knows me truly, and I know Kṛṣṇa truly.
When this foremost of men shall know the right time for valour, O Mādhava, then in battle you, O foremost of Śini's line, and Keśava shall conquer Suyodhana.
Let the Dāśārha heroes depart today. I am steadfast with these lords, lords of the world of men. O you of immeasurable greatness, be not negligent in dharma; I shall see you again, united and happy.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having taken leave of one another and exchanged salutations, having embraced the elders and all the children, the foremost heroes of the Yadus departed for their own homes; and the king too continued visiting the sacred tīrthas.

Having bid farewell to Kṛṣṇa, the Dharmarāja then came to the Payoṣṇī, that holy river with its excellent fords, honoured by the king of Vidarbha, its waters mingled with the sacred soma pressed by his son; and there he dwelt.
Lomaśa said: It is heard, O king, that here the smasher of citadels, Indra, was satisfied with soma by the sacrificer Nṛga, and being satisfied he became intoxicated with delight.
Here indeed, together with Indra and the gods and the lords of creatures, great sacrifices of many kinds were performed with abundant sacrificial fees.
And here King Āmūrtarayas satisfied the lord who bears the thunderbolt with soma at seven horse-sacrifices.
In his seven sacrifices, all that was appointed for the rite—whether of forest origin or of the earth—was made entirely of gold.
In those very sacrifices of his, seven celebrated rites took place; and on each single sacrificial post seven carved wooden rings were placed above.
In those sacrifices of his, the gods together with Indra themselves raised up the gleaming golden sacrificial posts, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
In those foremost sacrifices of Gaya, the lord of the earth, Indra became intoxicated with soma and the twice-born became intoxicated with the sacrificial fees.
As the grains of sand in the world, as the stars in the sky, as the streams of falling rain—none of these can be counted by anyone—
just so was that wealth which Gaya distributed to the participants at those seven sacrifices beyond all counting, O great king.
What has been enumerated here might indeed be counted; but the sacrificial fees of that generous giver cannot be counted.
With golden cows fashioned by Viśvakarman he satisfied the brāhmaṇas gathered from all directions.
The earth had but few sacred shrines left unadorned by the great-souled sacrificer Gaya here and there, O lord of the people.
By that deed he attained the worlds of Indra, O Bhārata; whoever bathes in the Payoṣṇī will attain the same world as Gaya.
Therefore, O king of kings, O sinless protector of the earth, you along with your brothers should bathe here and you shall be cleansed of all sin.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having bathed in the Payoṣṇī with his brothers, that best of men, the radiant and sinless one, proceeded along with his brothers to Mount Vaidūrya and the great river Narmadā.
There the venerable sage Lomaśa described to him all the charming sacred fords here and there, O lord of the people.
As was proper and as inclination led, he journeyed with his brothers, repeatedly giving wealth by the thousands to brāhmaṇas.
Lomaśa said: One attains the same world as the gods and also as kings, O son of Kuntī, by seeing Mount Vaidūrya and descending into the Narmadā.
This is the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, O best of men; by reaching this place, O son of Kuntī, one is freed from all sins.
This is the place of Śaryāti's sacrifice that shines forth, my dear; here Kauśika directly drank soma together with the Aśvins.
The great Bhārgava, mighty in austerity, also became angry with great Indra; the powerful Cyavana paralyzed Vāsava, and he also won Sukanyā as his wife, as if she were a princess.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was the blessed chastiser of Pāka paralyzed by him? And why did that Bhārgava of great austerity become angry?
And how did he make the two Nāsatyas drinkers of soma, O brahman? Let the venerable one tell me all of this exactly as it happened.
Lomaśa said: The son of the great seer Bhṛgu was Cyavana, a Bhārgava; full of great splendour, he performed austerity near a lake.
Standing motionless like a post, full of great energy, O Pāṇḍava, he stood for very many ages in one place, O lord of the people.
The sage became an anthill, covered over with creepers; in the course of a great length of time, O king, he was filled with ants.
Thus covered over, the wise one looked in every way like a lump of clay; yet he performed austerity, O king, enclosed within the anthill.
Then, after a long time, a king named Śaryāti came to this delightful, excellent lake for recreation.
He had four thousand women as his retinue, and one fair daughter named Sukanyā, O Bhārata.
She, surrounded by her companions and adorned with all ornaments, while wandering about came upon the anthill of the Bhārgava.
That fair-toothed one sported there with her companions, gazing at the charming forest trees and gathering flowers.
Drunk with beauty, youth, desire, and pride, she broke off the supremely flowering branches of the forest trees.
The wise Bhārgava saw her, alone without her companions, clad in a single garment, adorned with jewels, moving like a flash of lightning.
Watching her in the solitude, he of supreme radiance was pleased; the brahmarṣi with emaciated throat, endowed with the power of austerity, spoke to that lovely one—but she did not hear him.
Then Sukanyā, seeing the eyes of the Bhārgava shining in the anthill, overcome by curiosity and a confusion of mind, took a thorn—

saying "What indeed is this?" she pierced his eyes. He became furious when his eyes were pierced by her, filled with supreme wrath; thereupon he caused the army of Śaryāti to be obstructed in their excretion and urination.
Then, with excretion and urination blocked, the army suffering from the obstruction—seeing them in such a state, the king asked them about it.

"Who today has done wrong here to the great-souled Bhārgava, who is ever devoted to austerity, who is old, and who is especially irascible? Tell me the truth at once, whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly."
All the soldiers said to him: "We do not know of any wrong done by us; by all means and as you please, may Your Highness find that out."
Then that guardian of the earth, with gentle and also severe questioning, himself asked his circle of friends; but they too did not know.
Then, seeing the army afflicted with the obstruction and the suffering, and her father in distress, Sukanyā said this:
"While I was roaming here I saw in the anthill a blazing being, recognised by me like a firefly; that one was pierced by me from close by."
Hearing this, Śaryāti swiftly ran to the anthill; there he saw the Bhārgava, great in austerity and great in age.
Then with folded hands the lord of the earth besought him for his army's sake: "What was done to you by a young girl in ignorance—that you ought to forgive."
Then Cyavana the Bhārgava spoke to that guardian of the earth, saying of her who was endowed with beauty and nobility, overcome by the force of greed and delusion:
"Upon receiving her, your daughter, for myself, O king, I will forgive—O guardian of the earth, I tell you this truthfully."
Comprehending the words of the seer, Śaryāti, without deliberation, gave his daughter to that great-souled Cyavana.
And having received that maiden, Cyavana became pleased; the king, having obtained his grace, departed again with his army.
Sukanyā too, having obtained that austere man as her husband, blameless one, constantly attended upon him with devotion, austerity, and self-discipline.
That fair-faced one, devoted to the sacred fires and to guests, free from envy, quickly pleased Cyavana.
Lomaśa said: Then, after some time had passed, O king, the two Aśvins among the gods saw Sukanyā as she had bathed, her garments loose and open.
Seeing her of beautiful limbs, like the daughter of a king of the gods, the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, approached her swiftly and said this:
"Whose are you, O fair-thighed one, and what are you doing in the forest? We two wish to know about you, O auspicious one—tell us about yourself, O beautiful one."
Then Sukanyā, modestly dressed, addressed those two foremost of gods: "Know me to be the daughter of Śaryāti and the wife of Cyavana."
The two Aśvins then laughed and spoke to her again: "How is it, fair one, that your father gave you in marriage to one who had already passed his prime?"
"You shine in the midst of this forest like a flash of lightning in the clouds. We see none equal to you even among the celestials, O passionate one."
"Adorned with all ornaments and clad in the finest garments, you would shine splendidly, O blameless-limbed one — not thus smeared with mud and filth."
"Why, being what you are, do you attend upon a husband shriveled by old age, O fair one — one excluded from the pleasures of love?"

"One incapable of protection or sustenance, O bright-smiling one — it would be well to abandon Cyavana and choose one of us as a husband, O you who are like the offspring of gods. Do not let your youth go to waste."
Thus addressed, Sukanyā said to those two gods: "I am devoted to Cyavana as my husband — do not think otherwise of me."
The two then spoke to her again: "We are the foremost physicians of the gods. We shall make your husband young and handsome."
"Then choose one among us three — your husband included — and convey this offer to him, O fair-faced one."
At their word, O king, she approached the son of Bhṛgu and reported to that descendant of Bhṛgu what the two had said.
Hearing that, Cyavana said to his wife: "Let it be done." Permitted by her husband, she then said: "Let it be done."
The Aśvins, hearing her words of consent, said to that princess: "Let your husband enter the waters."
Then Cyavana quickly entered the waters, seeking a new form. The two Aśvins also, O king, entered that lake, O lord.
After a moment, all three emerged from that lake bearing divine forms — all young, wearing polished earrings, all alike in appearance, gladdening the heart.
All three together said: "Choose one of us, O beautiful one, as the husband you desire, O auspicious and fair-complexioned one. Whomever your heart inclines to, him choose, O most lovely one."
She observed all three standing there with identical forms, and the blessed one, resolving in her mind and understanding, chose her own husband.
Cyavana, having regained his wife and the youth and form he had desired, was delighted, and that great-spirited one spoke these words to the two Nāsatyas:
"As I, though old, have been made by you endowed with beauty and youth, and have regained this my wife —"
"— therefore, with affection, I shall make you both drinkers of soma, even before the eyes of the king of gods. This I declare to you in truth."
Hearing that, those two, with gladdened hearts, departed to heaven. Cyavana and Sukanyā also sported together like two celestials.
Lomaśa said: Then, having heard that Cyavana had been restored to his prime, Śaryāti was overjoyed and came with his army to the hermitage of Bhṛgu's descendant.
Seeing Cyavana and Sukanyā, who looked like two children of the gods, king Śaryāti rejoiced as if he had gained the entire earth.
Honored by that seer, the lord of the earth sat down with his wife and the great-minded one engaged in auspicious conversation.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, consoling him, O king, said: "I shall perform a sacrifice for you, O king — make ready the materials."
Then Śaryāti, lord of the earth, most greatly delighted, O great king, honored that word of Cyavana.
On an auspicious day fit for sacrifice, Śaryāti had an excellent sacrificial hall constructed, filled with every desired abundance.
There the descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana, officiated at the sacrifice for that king. And there were wonders there — hear them from me.
Cyavana then took the soma portion for the two divine Aśvins, but Indra tried to stop that cup being taken for them.
Indra said: "Both these Nāsatyas are not worthy of soma — such is my opinion. Being physicians to the sons of gods by their function, they are not entitled to it."
Cyavana said: "Do not despise those two great souls, superior in beauty and worth, O Maghavan, who made me ageless as if among the immortals."
"Apart from you and the other gods — how could they not deserve the soma feast? Know the Aśvins too as gods, O Indra, O destroyer of citadels."
Indra said: "They are healers, doers of tasks, who assume forms at will and roam the mortal world — how can they be worthy of soma here?"
Lomaśa said: When Vāsava kept repeating this same argument, the descendant of Bhṛgu, disregarding Śakra, took the cup.
Then the god who had slain Bala, seeing him about to take that excellent soma for the Aśvins, spoke these words:
"If you yourself take the soma for those two, I will hurl at you my thunderbolt, fearsome and unequalled in form."
Thus addressed, the descendant of Bhṛgu, smiling, looked at Indra and took, according to the proper rite, the excellent soma cup for the Aśvins.
Then the lord of Śacī hurled his fearsome thunderbolt at him, but the descendant of Bhṛgu paralyzed his arm as it was about to strike.
Having paralyzed him, Cyavana, of surpassing splendor, poured oblations into the fire with mantras, intent on performing a rite and ready to harm the god.

Then from the power of that seer's austerities there arose from the rite a mighty being named Mada — a great asura of immense valor and vast body, whose form could not be described by gods or demons alike.
His mouth was terrifying and immense, with sharp-tipped teeth; one of his jaws rested on the earth and the other reached up to the sky.
His four long fangs each measured a hundred times a hundred leagues, while his other teeth were ten leagues each, shaped like ramparts and appearing like the tips of spears.
His two arms, like mountains, stretched ten thousand leagues each; his eyes resembled the sun and moon; his face was like that of Death himself.
He licked his mouth with a tongue flickering like lightning, his jaws gaping wide, his glance terrible, as if swallowing the entire world by force.
Enraged and about to devour him, he charged at the performer of a hundred sacrifices with his mighty and fearsome form, making all the worlds resound with his roar.
Lomaśa said: Seeing Mada of the dreadful mouth, coming to devour him with jaws agape like Death himself, the god of a hundred sacrifices —
— his arm already paralyzed with fear, repeatedly licking the corners of his mouth, the king of the gods then spoke to Cyavana, oppressed by fear:
"The Aśvins shall be worthy of soma from this day forward, O descendant of Bhṛgu. This word I speak to you truly, O brahmin."
"Let your undertaking not be in vain — this shall be the highest rule henceforth. I know, O seer among brahmins, that you will not act falsely."
"Just as the Aśvins have this day been made worthy of soma by you, O descendant of Bhṛgu, may your power shine even more brightly."
"And may the fame of Sukanyā's father spread through the world — it is for this that I arranged this manifestation of your power. Therefore be gracious to me; let this be as you wish."
When Śakra had spoken thus to the great-souled Cyavana, his anger quickly departed and he released the destroyer of citadels.
And the mighty one divided Mada, O king, distributing him repeatedly — as previously created — among wine, women, dice, and the hunt.
Having thus dispersed Mada, and having satisfied Śakra with the soma, and having officiated at that king's sacrifice with the Aśvins included among the gods —
— having made his power known throughout all the worlds, that best of speakers then sported in the forest with the devoted Sukanyā.
This lake of his, O king, resounds with the chanting of twice-born men and shines with glory. Here you should satisfy the ancestors and the gods together with your brothers.
Having seen this, O lord of the earth, O Bhārata, and reaching the Saindhava forest with its sandy shallows, behold the streams. O great king, touch the water at all the lotus pools.
The Ārcīka mountain is indeed the abode of the wise, ever fruitful, ever flowing, the supreme station of the Maruts. These hundreds of sacred shrines here belong to the thirty gods, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
This is the sacred ford of the Moon, worshipped by seers — the Vaikhānasa sages and likewise the Vālakhilyas attend upon it.
The three sacred peaks and the three springs — circumambulate all of them and touch the waters as you wish.
Here, O son of Kuntī, O lord of men, Śaṃtanu, Śunaka, and both Nara and Nārāyaṇa have attained the eternal abode.
Here the gods who dwell eternally, and the ancestors, practised austerities on the Ārcīka mountain along with the great seers — worship them here, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Here the sages partook of the ritual rice-cakes, O lord of peoples. The Yamunā with its inexhaustible stream is here, and Kṛṣṇa is engaged in austerities in this place.
The twins, Bhīmasena, Kṛṣṇā — all of us will go there, O crusher of enemies, lean and deeply practised in austerities.
This is the sacred spring of Indra, O lord of men, where Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Varuṇa came in ancient times.
Here they dwelt, O king — forbearing and supremely righteous; this finest of mountains is auspicious for those of friendly and upright mind.
This is that Yamunā, O king, attended upon by hosts of royal sages, adorned with many sacrifices, O king — holy, dispelling the fear of sin.
Here king Māndhātā, the great archer, himself performed sacrifice; and Sahadeva, O son of Kuntī, and Somaka, the foremost of the generous, also did so.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Māndhātā, that tiger among kings, is renowned throughout the three worlds — how was he born, O great brahmin? That best of kings, the son of Yuvanāśva, of boundless splendor — how did he attain this supreme eminence?"
"The three worlds were subject to him like those of the great-souled Viṣṇu — I wish to hear the deeds of that wise one."
"And how did the name Māndhātā come to him who equals Śakra in splendor, and whose valor was unmatched? For you are skilled in narrating."
Lomaśa said: "Listen attentively, O king, to how the name Māndhātā of that great-souled king is sung throughout the worlds."
"Yuvanāśva, lord of the earth, sprung from the lineage of Ikṣvāku, O guardian of the earth, performed sacrifices with abundant gifts."
"Having performed a thousand horse sacrifices, that best of those who uphold dharma, and also other foremost and various sacrifices with ample gifts —"
"— yet that great-souled royal seer, firm in his vows, remained without a son; he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and took to living in the forest."
"Uniting himself with his own self by the rule prescribed in scripture, his heart parched with thirst, he entered the hermitage of Bhṛgu."
"That very night, O lord of kings, the great-souled son of Bhṛgu, the great seer, performed a rite for the sake of a son for Saudyumni."

"A great jar filled with water consecrated by mantras stood there, O lord of kings, having been prepared beforehand with concentrated intent — by drinking from it, the wife of him would give birth to a son equal to Śakra."
"Having placed that jar on the altar, the great seers fell asleep, wearied from their vigil through the night; and Saudyumni, passing them by —"
"— the king, parched of throat, sorely tormented by thirst, craving water, entered that hermitage exhausted and begged for water."
"As he, exhausted, cried out with his parched throat, no one then heard him — like the cry of a bird."
Then seeing that water-filled pot, the king rushed toward it swiftly, drank the water, and set it down.
Having drunk the cool water, that wise king — tormented by thirst — attained relief and became greatly content at that moment.
Then those seers, together with the lord of the gods, awoke and all of them saw that the pot was empty of water.
Assembled together they asked, "Whose deed is this?" Yuvanāśva, speaking truth, admitted, "It was I."
"This was not right," said the blessed Bhārgava to him then. "Those waters were stored for the purpose of a son, charged with the power of austerity."
"By me here was sacred power infused through terrible austerity, for the sake of your son, O royal sage of great strength and valor."
"One who would be mighty in strength and valor, endowed with the power of asceticism, who could by his prowess send even Indra to the abode of Yama."
"By this rite, O king, was this prepared by me — the drinking of the water by you, O king, was indeed an improper act done today."
"But now it is not possible for us to undo this otherwise — surely this was wrought by fate, that you acted in this way."

"Those waters which you drank when thirsty, O great king, consecrated with sacred rites and mantras, charged with the power of my exalted austerity — from those waters you yourself shall beget a son of such prowess."
"We shall perform for you in that matter a most wondrous sacrificial rite, so that you, the valiant one, shall beget a son equal to Indra."
Then, when a full hundred years had elapsed, a son burst forth from the left side of that great-souled king, like a second sun.
The one of great radiance came forth, and death did not enter Yuvanāśva the lord of men — that seemed a marvel indeed.
Then Indra of great splendor came desiring to see him, and placed his index finger into the infant's mouth.
"This one shall suckle me" — thus declared the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the gods together with Indra gave the child the name Māndhātṛ.
That infant, having tasted the finger given by Indra, grew, O lord of the earth, thirteen kiṣkus in a single day.
The Vedas along with the Dhanurveda, and the divine weapons, approached him as master, O great king, coming to him in all ways merely by his thought.
The bow named Ājagava, the arrows sprung from horns, and an impenetrable armor — all these immediately came to attend upon him.
He was consecrated by bountiful Indra himself, O Bhārata, and by righteousness he conquered the three worlds with strides like Viṣṇu.
The unstoppable wheel of that great soul set in motion, and jewels of their own accord came to attend upon the royal sage.
This earth full of wealth was his, O lord of the earth, and by him were performed many and varied sacrifices with abundant ritual fees.
Having built altars and having attained abundant merit, that one of immeasurable radiance, O king, won a half-share of Indra's throne.
In a single day this steadfastly righteous wise one conquered, by mere command, the earth with all its jewel-bearing oceans and cities.
By his sacrificial fire-altars, O great king, of those rites with lavish gifts, the four-cornered earth was filled — there was nothing left uncovered.
By that great-souled one, they say, O great king, ten thousand lotus-thousands of cows were given to the brahmins.
By that great-souled one, during a twelve-year drought, rain was caused to fall for the growth of crops, before the very eyes of the thunderbolt-bearer.
By him the great lord of Gāndhāra, born of the Soma lineage, who roared like a great cloud, was overcome and slain with arrows.
The four kinds of subjects were conquered by him, O king, that great-souled one; by his self-austerity were the worlds also established in his splendor.
Here is that divine sacrificial ground, the site of that one radiant as the sun — behold it in the most sacred region, in the midst of Kurukṣetra.
All this has now been told to you — the great deeds of Māndhātṛ and his wondrous birth, O lord of the earth, which you asked me about.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what valor was that king Somaka, O best of speakers? I wish to hear in truth his deeds and his power.
Lomaśa said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, there was a righteous king named Somaka. He had a hundred wives of equal standing, O king.
That lord of the earth, though striving with great effort among them, could not obtain even a single son even over a great span of time.
Once, for that aged one striving with effort, a son named Jantu was born among that assembly of a hundred women.
All the mothers constantly surrounded that newborn and sat attending him, setting aside their pleasures, O lord of the people.
Then once an ant bit Jantu on the buttock, and the child, bitten, cried out, O king, in that pain.
Then all those mothers, deeply distressed, cried out together, surrounding Jantu, and there arose a tumultuous noise.
That distressed cry was suddenly heard by the lord of the earth, seated in the midst of his council of ministers along with his priests.
The king then sent someone asking "What is this?" and the chamberlain reported to him what had occurred regarding his son.
Rising in haste, Somaka the subduer of enemies entered the inner apartments together with his ministers and consoled his son.
Having consoled the son, the king departed from the inner apartments, O king, and sat down together with his officiating priests and ministers.
Somaka said: Shame on having only one son here! Sonlessness would be better. From the perpetual anxiety of all beings, having only one son is pure grief.
"This hundred of wives, O brahmin, was taken by me after careful selection, O lord, desiring sons, yet there is no offspring from them."
"Somehow one son, this Jantu, has been born to me despite my striving among all of them — what greater sorrow is there than this?"
"My age has passed together with my wives, O best of twice-born ones; the lives of all these women depend upon this one son of mine here."
"Is there any appropriate action, whether great or small, whether difficult or not, by which I might have a hundred sons?"
The priest said: There is indeed such an action by which you could have a hundred sons. If you are able to do it, then I shall tell you, Somaka.
Somaka said: Whether it is to be done or not to be done, if by it a hundred sons could be had — know that it is as good as done. Let the revered one tell me.
The priest said: Sacrifice with Jantu, O king, in a rite spread out by me. Then a glorious hundred sons will be yours before long.
When the omentum is being offered and the mothers smell the smoke, they will then bear sons of very great valor for you.
"And Jantu himself will again be born as your son in that very womb, and a golden mark will appear on his right side."
Somaka said: O brahmin, whatever must be done and in whatever manner — do it just so. Desiring sons, I shall do all that you say.
Lomaśa said: Then he caused Somaka to sacrifice with Jantu as the offering. But the mothers by force tried to pull away their son, overcome with compassion.
Crying out "Alas, we are slain!" filled with intense grief, the mothers pulled him back by the right hand, but the sacrificial priest too pulled by taking hold of the left hand.
Like distressed osprey-birds — having pulled away that son, he slew him according to the rite and offered his omentum into the fire.
When the omentum was being offered, the mothers smelled the aroma and swooned suddenly to the ground in anguish, O delight of the Kurus; and all those royal women then conceived.
Then, within ten months, O lord of the people, a full hundred sons were born among all those wives of Somaka, O Bhārata.
Jantu was born again as the eldest, in his own mother, O Bhārata. He was dear to all of them in a way that no other natural sons were.
And that golden mark was there on his right side. Among that hundred sons he was preeminent, endowed with virtues.
Then that teacher of Somaka departed to the highest world. And when time had passed, Somaka too departed to the beyond.
And then he saw him being tormented in a terrible hell. He asked him: "For what reason are you being cooked in hell, O twice-born one?"
That teacher, being tortured greatly by fire, said to him: "You were caused to sacrifice by me, O king — this is the fruit of that action."
Hearing this, that royal sage said to the king of dharma: "I shall enter here — let my officiating priest be freed. For my sake this blessed one is being burned in the fire of hell."
Dharma said: No one else ever experiences the fruit of the doer's act, O king. These rewards are seen as yours, O best of the generous.
Somaka said: I do not desire the meritorious worlds without this speaker of sacred wisdom. I wish to dwell with him in the abode of the gods.
"Or in hell, O king of dharma, I am indeed equal to him in this deed. Let the fruit of merit and demerit be equal for us both, O god."
Dharma said: If such is your desire, O king, then enjoy his fruit together with him for equal time; thereafter you shall attain a good destination along with him.
Lomaśa said: That lotus-eyed king did all this accordingly, and once again won his own auspicious worlds earned by his deeds — together with that brahmin teacher, he who was dear to his guru.
This is that holy hermitage, this one that shines before us. A patient man who dwells here for six nights attains a good passage.
In this place too, O king of kings, we shall dwell free from fever for six nights with controlled minds. Make yourself ready, O foremost of the Kurus.
Lomaśa said: In this place, O king, Prajāpati himself formerly performed a satra called Iṣṭīkṛta, lasting a thousand years.
And Ambarīṣa, son of Nābhāga, performed sacrifices along the Yamunā; through sacrifices and through austerity he attained the highest perfection.
This region of the Nāhuṣa sacrifices is the most sacred, O king — here he sacrificed and gave away ten padmas to those assembled at the rite.
Behold here this sacrificial ground of Yayāti, the universal sovereign, O son of Kuntī, the one of immeasurable energy who rivaled Indra.
Behold the earth covered over with fires of various forms, as if sinking, overwhelmed by the sacrificial acts of Yayāti.
Here is the śamī tree with a single leaf; that is the finest śaraka reed. Behold these lakes of Rāma; behold the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
This, O lord of the earth, is the retreat of the son of Ṛcīka, the one of immeasurable energy, who wanders the earth through his yogic powers, at Raupyā.
Here, O delight of the Kurus, hear from me the lineage recitation — what the piśācī adorned with mortars spoke.
"Having eaten curds at Yugaṃdhara and having dwelt at the place of Acyuta, and likewise having bathed at Bhūtilaya, you wish to dwell there with your sons."
"Having dwelt here one night, if you will stay a second — what happened during the day shall happen differently for you at night."
Here, O best of the Bhāratas, we shall spend the night today — for this, O son of Kuntī, is the gateway to Kurukṣetra, O Bhārata.
Here indeed, O king, King Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, performed sacrifices with many jewel-rich rites, at which even Indra was gladdened.
This is called Plakṣāvaraṇa, the sacred ford of the Yamunā; the wise declare this to be the gateway to the vault of heaven.
Here, O dear one, the great sages who have performed Sārasvata sacrifices, bearing the sacrificial post and the mortar, proceed to the final ablution bath.
Here indeed King Bharata released the consecrated horse — the dark-spotted steed — having won the earth by righteousness more than once.
Here too, O tiger among men, Marutta performed the highest sacrifice session, presided over by Saṃvarta, foremost among divine sages.
By touching the sacred waters here, O king of kings, one beholds all the worlds; and by duly touching them, O Bhārata, one is purified of all evil deeds.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There, having bathed along with his brothers and being praised by the great sages, the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas spoke these words to Lomaśa.
"I behold all the worlds by the power of austerity, O you whose valor is truth; standing here I see the foremost of Pāṇḍavas, the white-horsed Arjuna."
Lomaśa said: Even so, O mighty-armed one, the great sages see this; behold this holy Sarasvatī, adorned with Ekaśaraṇa.
Bathing here, O best of men, one becomes cleansed of sin; here the divine sages, the sages, O son of Kuntī, and the royal sages as well, have worshipped with Sārasvata sacrifices.
This is the altar of Prajāpati, extending five yojanas on all sides — this is the sacred field of Kuru the great soul, devoted to sacrifice.
Lomaśa said: Here, O Bhārata, mortals go to heaven by performing austerities; men desiring death, O king, come here by the thousands.
For such was the blessing pronounced long ago by Dakṣa when he sacrificed — those who die here are truly men who have conquered heaven.
This is the holy, divine Sarasvatī, the river of plentiful waters; and this, O lord of the people, is called Vinaśana, the disappearance of the Sarasvatī.
This is the gateway to the realm of the Niṣādas, out of hatred for whom the Sarasvatī entered the earth — for the river said, "May the Niṣādas not know me."
This is Camasodbheda, where the Sarasvatī becomes visible again, where the divine, holy rivers flowing to the sea converged upon her.
This is the great sacred ford of the Sindhu where Lopāmudrā, O subduer of foes, met and chose Agastya as her husband.
This is the sacred ford called Prabhāsa, O you who shine like the sun — the beloved holy shrine of Indra, pure and destroying sin.
Here is seen the excellent sacred ford named Viṣṇupada; and this is the lovely river Vipāśā, supremely purifying.
Here indeed the blessed sage Vasiṣṭha, overcome by grief for his son, bound himself and fell, but rose again unbound — hence the river Vipāśā, "the freed from bonds."
This is the entirely holy region of Kāśmīra, O subduer of foes, inhabited by great sages — behold it together with your brothers.
Here took place the dialogue of all the northern sages, and of Nahuṣa, and of Agni, and of Kāśyapa as well, O Bhārata.
This, O great king, is the gateway that leads to Mānasa lake; the land in the middle of this mountain was established by the glorious Rāma.
This is the renowned Vāṭikaṣaṇḍa grove — of true valor — the gateway which one who has not surpassed the Videhas and the northerners does not approach.
This is the place called Ujjānaka, where the peaceful Yavakrī dwelt, and where the blessed sage Vasiṣṭha resided together with Arundhatī.
And this is the lake Kuśavān where the lotus blossoms; and here too is the hermitage where the wrathless Rukmiṇī was pacified.
The confluence of the Samādhī rivers you have heard of, O son of Pāṇḍu — you shall behold it, O great king, and also the great mountain Bhṛgutuṅga.
And the rivers Jalā and Upajalā near the Yamunā — it was here that Uśīnara, having sacrificed, surpassed even Vāsava in merit.
To test that king at his divine assembly, both Vāsava and Agni, O lord of the people, came to King Uśīnara, O Bhārata.
Desiring to examine the great-souled Uśīnara, those two boon-givers — Indra taking the form of a hawk and Agni the form of a pigeon — came to his sacrifice.
The pigeon, seeking refuge out of fear of the hawk, came to the king's thigh and pressed itself there, O king, tormented by fear and seeking shelter.
The hawk said: All rulers of the earth proclaim you alone to be righteous of soul, O king — why then do you wish to perform an act contrary to dharma?
The eating of this prey is ordained for me, O king, as I am tormented by hunger — do not deprive me of it; by clinging to one form of dharma you have abandoned dharma altogether.
The king said: This bird, terrified in form, seeking protection, frightened of you, O great twice-born, has come to me clinging to life.
For one who has thus come here seeking refuge — not granting protection to this pigeon would be the greatest adharma; what do you see in this, O hawk?
This pigeon, trembling and distressed, is seen to be seeking life by coming to me, O hawk — to abandon him is blameworthy.
The hawk said: All beings arise from food, O lord of the earth; through food they grow, and by it creatures live.
One may live for a long time even after relinquishing what is hard to abandon; but giving up food, one cannot sustain life for long.
Today, deprived of my prey, O lord of the people, my life-breath will leave this body and travel the path of no return.
If I die, O righteous one, my wife and children will perish; by protecting this pigeon you will destroy many lives.
A dharma that obstructs another dharma is no dharma — that is pseudo-dharma; but dharma that does not conflict with another dharma — that, O you of true valor, is true dharma.
When duties conflict, O lord of the earth, one should weigh what is greater and what is lesser, and practice whichever dharma causes no obstruction to others.
Having determined what is weightier and what is lighter in deciding between dharma and adharma, follow whichever is the greater, O king — thus make your determination of dharma.

The king said: You speak with much that is auspicious and good, O best of birds — are you Suparṇa, king of birds? You are certainly a knower of dharma, without doubt; for you speak much that is varied and full of dharma.
I perceive that there is nothing unknown to you; yet how do you consider it right to abandon one who is seeking refuge?
Your purpose in this undertaking is to obtain food, O bird, and that may be accomplished otherwise — and indeed greater food may be obtained by you.
A bull, or a boar, or a deer, or even a buffalo — let whichever you desire be prepared for you today, or whatever else you may wish for.
The hawk said: I do not eat boar, nor bull, nor various kinds of deer, O great king — what use is such food to me?
But the prey ordained for me by fate, O bull among kṣatriyas — release it to me, O lord of the earth; give me this very pigeon.
Hawks eat pigeons — this is the eternal order of things; O king, knowing this path, do not climb a plantain trunk expecting fruit.

The king said: O hawk, O honored by flocks of birds, rule the prosperous kingdom of the Śibis, or take whatever you desire — I will give you everything, but not this bird, O hawk, who has come seeking refuge.
Whatever act would make you relinquish this one, tell me, O best of birds — I will do it; for I will not give up this little pigeon.
The hawk said: O Uśīnara, O lord of men, if you have such love for this pigeon — then cut flesh from your own body and weigh it against the pigeon in the balance.
When your flesh equals the pigeon's weight in the balance, O king, then give that to me — that will be my satisfaction.
The king said: I consider it a favor, O hawk, that you solicit me thus; therefore I will give you today my own flesh weighed in the balance.
Lomaśa said: Then the king, a supreme knower of dharma, cut flesh from his body and placed it on the scale against the pigeon, O son of Kuntī, O illustrious one.
But the pigeon, when weighed in the balance, outweighed the flesh; so King Uśīnara cut more flesh and added it again.
When no more flesh could be found equal in weight to the pigeon, then that one, his flesh cut away, climbed upon the scale himself.
The hawk said: I am Indra, O knower of dharma, and this pigeon is Agni, the carrier of oblations — we two came to your sacrificial arena wishing to examine you in dharma.
The flesh that has been cut from your limbs, O lord of the people — this your radiant fame will pervade all the worlds.
For as long as men in this world shall tell of you, O king, so long shall your fame and your worlds endure — eternal.
Lomaśa said: Behold, O son of Pāṇḍu, the abode of that great-souled king — see it together with me; it is holy and releases one from sin.
Here the gods and the eternal sages are ever seen, O king, by virtuous brāhmaṇas of great souls.

Lomaśa said: He who is celebrated on earth as a knower of sacred lore and of foremost intellect — Auddālaki Śvetaketu — behold his holy hermitage, O lord of men, adorned with ever-fruitful trees grown from the earth.
Here Śvetaketu directly beheld Sarasvatī in human bodily form; "I shall master sacred speech" — so saying to Sarasvatī, Śvetaketu addressed her.
At that time, the two foremost knowers of Brahman — maternal uncle and nephew — were present: Aṣṭāvakra the son of Kahoḍa, and Auddālaki Śvetaketu, O king.
Those two brāhmaṇas, uncle and nephew, entered the sacrificial arena of the king of Videha, that lord of the earth, and in debate subdued the immeasurable Bandin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What was the power of that brāhmaṇa who thus subdued Bandin? How did Aṣṭāvakra come to be as he was? Tell me all of this truly, O Lomaśa.
Lomaśa said: There was one devoted disciple of Uddālaka, named Kahoḍa, O king, who served his teacher obediently and studied for a long time.
Yet the brāhmaṇa students surpassed him in learning; and knowing this slight, his teacher at once gave him both sacred knowledge and his own beautiful daughter Sujātā as wife.

A child like fire formed in her womb; while still in the womb that child then spoke to its father who was studying: "All night long you study — but, Father, this does not seem to me to be going rightly."
Reproached thus in the midst of his students, the great sage cursed that child in his womb in anger: "Because you speak while still in the belly, therefore you shall be crooked in eight places."
