When the fourth month had fully passed and the first day was gone, a creature in the form of a boar approached near me.
It was striking the earth with its snout, scratching with its hooves as well, sweeping the ground with its belly, and turning about again and again.
Behind it came another great creature in the form of a Kirāta hunter, arrived bearing bow, arrows, and sword, followed by a host of women.
Then I took up my bow and the two inexhaustible quivers and struck that hair-raising creature with an arrow.
Simultaneously that Kirāta, drawing his bow with great force, struck back even more powerfully, making my mind tremble.
He then spoke to me, O king: 'This creature is my prior possession — abandoning the dharma of the hunt, why have you struck it?'
'With my sharp arrows I shall destroy your pride — stand firm!' That great-bodied, towering figure then charged at me.
Then, like a mountain, he overwhelmed me with great arrows; and I in turn covered him with a mighty shower of shafts.
Then I pierced him with blazing-tipped, feathered, and consecrated arrows, striking him as if with thunderbolts striking a mass of rocks.
His form multiplied a hundredfold, then a thousandfold; and all those bodies of his I struck with my arrows.
Again those bodies became one, O Bhārata, O great king, and again I shattered that single form.
He took a form tiny-bodied with enormous head, then enormous-bodied with a tiny head; then, made one again, O king, he came at me in battle.
When I could no longer overcome him in battle with arrows, I then invoked the wind-weapon, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Yet I could not slay him — it was as if a wonder had occurred. When that weapon too was repelled, great amazement overcame me.
And again, O great king, I then covered that being in battle with an even greater multitude of weapons.
Invoking the Sthūṇākarṇa, the iron-net, the arrow-rain, the arrow-tempest, the mountain-weapon, and the stone-shower, I advanced — yet he swallowed all those weapons of mine, laughing, O sinless one.
When all those were spent, I invoked the Brahmā-weapon; thereupon blazing arrows gathered around him from all sides, yet as I pressed him with that great weapon, he only grew in power.
Then the world was scorched by the radiance born from me; in an instant the quarters of the sky and the firmament blazed with light on all sides.
Even that weapon the great-radiant one shattered in an instant; and when the Brahmā-weapon was destroyed, O king, great fear entered into me.
Then, taking up my bow with those two inexhaustible quivers, I struck the being at once with rapid blows — yet it devoured those weapons too.
When all weapons were spent and all arms devoured, between me and that being hand-to-hand combat ensued.
We grappled with fists and struck each other with open palms; but that being hurled me down, and I lay motionless on the ground.
Then that being, laughing, vanished on the spot together with the women, O great king, even as I watched — a sight beyond compare.
Having done all this, the blessed lord then assumed another form of his own — a divine form, O great king, clad in a wondrous garment.
Abandoning the guise of the Kirāta, the blessed lord, master of the thirty gods, assumed his own divine form and stood there — the great lord Maheśvara.
Then the blessed lord appeared in person — he whose banner bears the bull, companion of Umā, tawny-eyed, of many forms, bearer of the Pināka bow.
He approached me as I stood there facing him on the battlefield, and the trident-bearing lord said: 'I am pleased with you,' O scorcher of foes.
Then the blessed lord, taking up that bow along with the two quivers of inexhaustible arrows, gave them back to me and said: 'Choose a boon.'
'I am pleased with you, son of Kuntī; tell me, what shall I do for you? Whatever is in your heart, O hero, speak it — I shall grant it. Setting aside immortality, tell me what is in your mind.'
Then I, with joined palms, my mind fixed on weapons, bowed my head to Śarva and spoke these words.
'If the blessed lord is pleased with me, this is the boon I desire: I wish to learn whatever weapons exist among the gods.' And the blessed Three-eyed Lord said to me: 'I shall give them.'
'The Raudra weapon, which is mine, will attend you, O Pāṇḍava.' And the gracious lord gladly bestowed upon me the Pāśupata weapon.
And Mahādeva said, having given me that ancient weapon: 'This must never be discharged against human beings under any circumstances.
When you are severely pressed, Dhanañjaya, you may powerfully deploy it; and to counter enemy weapons you may always use it.
That weapon, divine and irresistible, which nullifies all other weapons, stands beside me embodied, now that the bull-bannered lord is pleased.'
It is the annihilator of enemies, the destroyer of opposing armies, unapproachable and invincible to gods, demons, and rakshasas alike.
Given leave by him, I sat down right there, and as I watched, the god vanished in that very spot.
Arjuna said: Then, O Bhārata, I spent that night there in joy, by the grace of the god of gods, the great-souled Three-eyed Lord.
Having spent the night and performed my morning rites, I saw again that foremost of twice-born men whom I had seen before.
To him I reported everything that had occurred, exactly as it happened — that I had met the blessed Mahādeva himself, O Bhārata.
That best of twice-born men, filled with delight, said to me, O lord of kings: 'You have seen Mahādeva as none other has seen him.
Meeting with all the world-guardians, beginning with Vivasvat's son, you shall see Devendra, O sinless one, and he will give you weapons.'
Having said this, O king, that brahmin brilliant as the sun embraced me again and again, then departed as he wished.
Then in the afternoon of that same day a holy breeze arose, as if making the world new again, O slayer of enemies.
And divine, freshly fragrant garlands appeared at the foot of the Shaishira mountain, close at hand.
And on all sides were heard celestial instruments of fine resonance, and enchanting hymns of praise joined with Indra's name.
There, hosts of apsaras and gandharvas in front of the god of gods sang songs on every side.
Hosts of Maruts arrived there in divine chariots — the attendants of Mahendra who dwell in the abode of the gods.
Then Marut's lord, drawn by bay steeds splendidly adorned, came there accompanied by Śacī and all the gods.
At that very moment, O king, Kubera, borne by men, revealed himself to me, adorned with supreme splendor.
In the southern direction I beheld Yama stationed; I saw Varuṇa, the king of gods, established each in their proper place.
Those bulls among gods spoke to me, O great king, soothing me: 'O Savyasācin, behold the world-guardians arrayed before you.'
'You have seen Shankara for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose; now receive weapons from us as well, on every side.'
Then, having purified myself and bowed to those bulls among gods, I duly received those great weapons, O lord.
Having received the weapons, I was then dismissed by the gods, O Bhārata; and all the gods departed the way they had come, O subduer of foes.
And Maghavan too, lord of gods, mounting his radiant chariot, spoke these words, the blessed slayer of the enemies of the gods, as if smiling.
'Before this coming of yours I already knew you, Dhanañjaya; henceforth I shall show myself to you further, O bull of the Bhāratas.'
'For you have bathed at the sacred fords again and again in former times, and this austerity you have now performed — you shall go to heaven, O Pāṇḍava.'
'Yet still most severe austerity must be practiced'; and the blessed lord told me everything about the means of that austerity.
'Mātali, by my command, shall bring you to the three heavens; for you are known to the gods and to the great-souled seers.'
Then I said to Śakra: 'Be gracious to me, O blessed lord; I choose you as my teacher for the purpose of learning weapons, O lord of the thirty gods.'
Indra said: 'You will perform a cruel deed as a master of weapons, dear one, O scorcher of foes; whatever the purpose for which you desire those weapons — that wish, O Pāṇḍava, you shall attain.'
Arjuna said: Then I replied: 'I shall not discharge the divine weapons against human beings, O slayer of enemies, except to counter other weapons.'
'Give me those divine weapons, O lord of the wise; and afterwards may I attain the worlds conquered by weapons, O best of gods.'
Indra said: 'This word was spoken to you by me only as a test, Dhanañjaya; your answer befits my own son — well spoken indeed.'
'Go to my abode and learn all weapons, O Bhārata — from Vāyu, from Agni, from the Vasus, from Varuṇa together with the hosts of Maruts.'

'The Sādhya-weapon, the Pitāmaha-weapon, the weapons of the gandharvas, serpents, and rakshasas, all the Vaiṣṇava weapons, and likewise the Nairṛta weapons, and all weapons that abide with me here — learn them all, O chief of the Kurus.'
Arjuna said: Having thus spoken to me, Śakra vanished right there. Then I saw Indra's chariot yoked with bay steeds, divine, fashioned of illusion, sacred, made ready by Mātali, O king.
When the world-guardians had departed, Mātali then spoke to me: 'Śakra, the king of gods, wishes to see you, O greatly brilliant one.'
'You are accomplished, O mighty-armed one — perform this supreme purpose; behold the worlds of those who have done meritorious deeds and go to heaven in your very body.'
Thus addressed by Mātali, I took leave of the Shaishira mountain, circumambulated it clockwise, and mounted that finest of chariots.
Mātali, expert in the science of horses, skilled and expert, then drove the horses whose speed matched that of mind and wind.
Then that charioteer glanced at my face as I stood there while the chariot sped along, O king, and amazed, he spoke these words.
'What strikes me today as exceedingly wonderful and strange is that you have mounted this divine chariot and have not moved a step.'
'For even the king of gods, as I have always observed here, sways at the first surge of the horses, O bull of the Bhāratas.'
'But you remain perfectly steady here as the chariot races on, O foremost of the Kurus — your strength appears to me to surpass even Śakra's.'
Having said this, Mātali entered the sky and showed me, O king, the abodes of the gods and the celestial mansions, O Bhārata.
Mātali, Śakra's charioteer, with affection showed me many forests of the gods — Nandana and others.
Then I saw Śakra's abode, Amarāvatī, adorned with divine wish-fulfilling trees and with jewels throughout.
The sun does not light it — it shines with its own radiance; neither cold nor heat afflicts it, nor weariness; there is no dust, no mud, no darkness there, and no old age, O king.
No sorrow or destitution is seen there, no pallor, O great king, and no languor among the dwellers in heaven, O subduer of foes.
Neither anger nor greed exists there, nor anything inauspicious, O lord of the people; the living beings in the abode of the gods are ever contented and joyful.
The trees there always bear flowers and fruit with ever-green foliage, and there are various lotus-ponds filled with fragrant lotus blossoms.
A cool, fragrant, life-giving, and pure breeze blows there; and the ground is adorned with flowers and variegated with every kind of jewel.
Many lovely deer and birds of sweet voice roam there, and many immortals are seen here moving about in celestial mansions.
Then I beheld the Vasus, the Rudras, the Sādhyas, along with the hosts of Maruts, the Ādityas, and the twin Aśvins — I paid reverence to all of them.
They acknowledged me with regard to valour, fame, radiance, strength, mastery of weapons, and victory in battle.
Entering that beautiful city attended by gods and gandharvas, I stood before the king of the gods, the thousand-eyed Indra, with folded hands.
The gladdened Śakra, foremost among givers, offered me half his seat, and Vāsava touched my limbs out of great respect.
There, O Bhārata, I dwelt in heaven in the company of the gods and gandharvas, richly rewarded, acquiring and practising the weapons.
Citrasena, son of Viśvāvasu, became my friend, O king, and he caused me to learn the entire science of music and dance.
Then, O king, having obtained the weapons and being greatly honoured, I dwelt happily in the abode of Śakra, furnished with every desire.
O scorcher of foes, I heard the sounds of song and the full sounds of instruments, and I watched the foremost apsarases as they danced.
Without slighting any of it, recognising it all as real, O Bhārata, I accepted those gifts with great pleasure and yet remained wholly devoted to the weapons.
Then the thousand-eyed all-powerful Indra was pleased with that resolution of mine. Thus, O king, this period of time passed for me while I dwelt in heaven.
Arjuna said: Then Hari's charioteer, fully trusting that I had mastered the weapons, touched my head with both hands and spoke these words to me.
"You cannot now be conquered in battle even by the hosts of the gods — how much less by unrefined men in the world of humans! Immeasurable, unconquerable, and matchless in battles, you are."
Then the god spoke again, his hair bristling with delight: "In warfare with weapons, O hero, there will be none equal to you."
"You are ever vigilant, skilful, truthful in speech, one who has conquered the senses, devoted to the Brahmins, skilled in weapons, and you are a hero, O best of the Kurus."
"Fifteen weapons have been obtained by you, O Pārtha, through five methods of mastery — there is none equal to you."
"You know, O Dhanaṃjaya, the invocation, withdrawal, repeated application, expiation, and the complete counter of each weapon."
"The time to render service to your teacher has now come, O scorcher of foes. Promise to perform it — thereafter I shall know what further to do."
Then I said to the king of the gods, O king, these words: "If it is within my power to do it, consider it already done."
Then the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra spoke to me with a laugh, O king: "There is nothing in the three worlds that is beyond your power today."
"The dānavas known as the Nivātakavacas, my enemies, dwell in a stronghold sheltered within the depths of the ocean."
"They are said to number thirty million, all equal in form, strength, and splendour. Slay them there, O son of Kuntī — that will be the service to your teacher."
Then he gave me a divine and greatly resplendent chariot yoked to horses whose manes resembled peacock feathers, with Mātali as charioteer.
He also bound on my head this excellent diadem and gave me body ornaments befitting my own nature.
He gave me this impenetrable armour, excellent and pleasant to the touch, and fitted this undecaying bowstring onto the Gāṇḍīva.
Then I set out in that gleaming chariot with which the lord of the gods had formerly conquered Bali, son of Virocana.
All the gods, awakened by that tumult and thinking it was the king of the gods, came together, O lord of the people. And seeing me they asked: "What will you do, O Phalguna?"
I told them truthfully: "Know that I am setting out to battle with the intent of slaying the Nivātakavacas, O greatly fortunate and sinless ones." And they blessed me with auspiciousness.
Pleased, they extolled me as they would the god Puraṃdara: "With this very chariot Maghavan conquered Śambara in battle, and also Namuci, Bala, Vṛtra, Prahlāda, and Naraka."
"And with this chariot Maghavan has conquered in battle many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of daityas."
"You too, O son of Kuntī, shall conquer the Nivātakavacas in battle by your prowess with this chariot, even as the self-controlled Maghavan did of old."
"And this foremost of conches — with it you shall conquer the dānavas. With it the great-souled Śakra himself conquered the worlds."
The conch called Devadatta, born of the waters, given to me by the gods — I accepted it for victory, while being praised by the immortals at that time.
Thus equipped with conch, armour, arrows, and bow in hand, I set out with the desire for battle toward the terrible abode of the dānavas.
Arjuna said: Thus being praised here and there by great sages, I then beheld the terrible, imperishable ocean, the lord of waters.
Waves bearing foam, scattered and assembled, rising high, were seen there moving like mountains; and thousands of ships filled with jewels lay on all sides.
Timiṃgilas, tortoises, and also timitimiṃgilas, and makaras were seen there, submerged in the water like mountains.
Thousands of conches submerged all around in the water were seen like stars at night thinly veiled by clouds.
Similarly, thousands of clusters of gems were floating there, and a terrible wind whirled — it seemed altogether wondrous.
Having crossed that mighty, swiftly moving, supreme receptacle of all waters, I saw at close range that city of the daityas teeming with dānavas.
Right there Mātali swiftly descended to the earth's surface and charged at that city, making it resound with the thundering of the chariot.
Hearing that chariot's thunder as if it were a thunderclap in the sky, the dānavas were alarmed, thinking it was the king of the gods.
All stood with agitated minds, holding bows and arrows, as well as spears, swords, axes, clubs, and pestles in their hands.
Then the dānavas, their hearts struck with fear, shut the gates, having arranged the defence of the city — not one was to be seen outside.
Then, taking up the Devadatta conch of mighty sound and approaching the asura city, I blew it softly.
But that sound, filling the heavens, caused an echo to reverberate — even very great creatures trembled and hid themselves.
Then all the Nivātakavacas on all sides, clad in armour of various kinds, weapons of various kinds in their hands,
with great iron spears, clubs, pestles, battle-axes, swords, and chariot wheels, O Bhārata,
with śataghnīs, bhuśuṇḍīs, and variously adorned swords in hand — the sons of Diti appeared by the thousands.
Then Mātali, having reflected much on the chariot-paths, urged the horses on level ground, O bull among Bhāratas.
By that swift driving of those swift-moving horses goaded forward, I could see nothing then — it seemed to me altogether wondrous.
Then the dānavas there urged on their many battalions of warriors, all of them of deformed voices and shapes, with great vigour.
By that great noise, fish like mountains in the ocean, having lost their senses, leapt up by the hundreds of thousands.
Then the dānavas charged at me with great speed, releasing sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
That tumultuous battle between them and me, O Bhārata, that great and terrible destruction of the Nivātakavacas, commenced.
Then divine sages, groups of sages among the dānavas, brahmarṣis, and siddhas all came together for that great battle.
Those sages, desiring my victory, praised me with fitting and sweet words, just as they had praised Indra in the battle against Tāraka.
Arjuna said: Then all the Nivātakavacas together rushed at me swiftly, O Bhārata, weapons in hand for battle.
Those mighty warriors cut off the path of my chariot, screaming aloud, and surrounding me on all sides poured down showers of arrows.
Then other dānavas of great might, spears and battle-axes in hand, hurled spears and bhuśuṇḍīs at me.
That very great shower of spears, mixed with clubs and śaktis, ceaselessly discharged by them, fell upon my chariot.
Other Nivātakavacas charged at me in battle, terrible strikers bearing sharp weapons and arms, their forms like death itself.
I struck each of them with ten swift, straight-flying arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva in the battle — all of them were turned back by my stone-sharpened arrows.
Then those horses, swiftly urged on by Mātali, swift as the wind, coursed along many chariot-paths; well-controlled by Mātali they crushed the sons of Diti.
Those hundreds upon hundreds of horses yoked to that great chariot moved under Mātali's control as if they were but few.
By the trampling of their hooves, by the sound of the chariot's wheel-rims, and by the fall of my arrows, those asuras were slain by the hundreds.
Others, their lives gone, still clutching their bows, their charioteers slain, were dragged there by their horses.
Those strikers, blocking all directions and intermediate directions, smote with various weapons — and then my mind was distressed.
Then I saw Mātali's most wonderful prowess in the way he effortlessly controlled those swift horses.
Then with swift and varied weapons I cut down those asuras along with their arms in battle, O king, by the hundreds and thousands.
As I moved about thus with all effort, O destroyer of enemies, the heroic Mātali, Śakra's charioteer, became pleased.
Then those who were being slaughtered by the horses and that chariot went toward destruction — some, however, turned back.
The Nivātakavacas, as if competing with us in battle, surrounded me on all sides with great showers of arrows.
Then I swiftly scattered them with swift and varied arrows consecrated with the Brahmā weapon, by the hundreds and thousands.
Then those great asuras, being pressed hard and seized by anger, together tormented me with showers of arrows, spears, and swords.
Then I resorted to the supreme weapon of fierce splendour dear to the king of the gods, named the Mādhava, O Bhārata.
Then by the power of that weapon I cut into a hundred pieces the swords, tridents, and spears by the thousands hurled by them.
Having cut their weapons, I then in anger pierced each and every one of them with ten arrows apiece.
For arrows then issued from the Gāṇḍīva in battle as swarms of bees — Mātali honoured that.
Their arrows too, like locusts in their multitude, powerfully rained down upon me — I scattered them with my arrows.
Then those Nivātakavacas, being slaughtered, again surrounded me on all sides with great showers of arrows.
Cutting down the volleys of arrows with my blazing, supreme, swift arrow-countering weapons, I pierced them by the thousands.
Their severed limbs poured forth blood like mountain peaks drenched by torrential rain in the monsoon season.
Struck by my arrows — swift, straight-flying, and striking like Indra's thunderbolt — those dānavas were thrown into great agitation.
Their bodies and entrails shattered into hundreds of pieces, their weapon-strength exhausted, the Nivātakavacas then fought me with their powers of illusion.
Arjuna said: Then a great shower of rocks burst forth all around — utterly terrifying boulders mountain-sized — and it pressed hard upon me.
I pulverized that shower with my swift arrows charged by Indra's weapon, shattering each rock into a hundred fragments in battle.
As the rock-shower was being ground to powder, fire arose there, and the dust of those crushed stones fell like showers of sparks.
Then, when the rock-shower was destroyed, an even greater rain of water appeared near me, its streams as thick as axle-shafts.
Streams of fierce power poured down from the sky in their thousands, covering the firmament on all sides and in every direction and quarter.
From the crashing of those torrents, the howling of the wind, and the roaring of the daityas, nothing whatsoever could be discerned.
Those streams, linked between heaven and earth on every side, befuddled me there as they fell ceaselessly upon the ground.
There, directed by Indra, I released that blazing, terrible, divine weapon of desiccation, and by it all that water was dried up.
When the rock-shower was destroyed by me and the water-shower dried up, O bestower of honor, the dānavas unleashed their illusion of fire and wind.
Then I extinguished the fire entirely with the water weapon, and with the great mountain-weapon I checked the force of the wind.
But when that illusion was repelled, the dānavas, maddened for battle, simultaneously set loose manifold further illusions, O Bhārata.
Then a great and hair-raising downpour of terrible weapons — of fire, of wind, and of stones — burst forth.
That illusion-wrought downpour afflicted me in battle, and then a dreadful, dense darkness appeared on all sides.
With the world enveloped in that terrible and cruel darkness, the horses turned away, and Mātali himself stumbled.
His golden goad fell from his hand to the ground, and in his fear he called to me again and again: "Where are you?" — O bull of the Bhāratas.
Intense fear seized me as well, and that man, his senses gone, his knowledge fled, trembling, spoke these words to me:
"There was once a great battle between the gods and the asuras fought for the sake of the nectar of immortality, O Pārtha, and I witnessed it, O sinless one.
At the slaying of Śambara too there was a very great battle, and there also I served as charioteer to the king of gods.
Likewise at the slaying of Vṛtra I held the reins, and I witnessed that most terrible battle with the son of Virocana.
I have attended upon all these most dreadful battles, and never before have I lost my senses, O son of Pāṇḍu.
The destruction of all beings has surely been ordained by the Grandfather, for this battle is fit for nothing other than the annihilation of the world."
Hearing those words of his, I steadied myself by my own will, intending to confound the illusion-filled army of the dānavas.
I said to the frightened Mātali: "Behold the strength of my arms, the power of my weapons, and of the bow Gāṇḍīva!
Today with my weapon-illusion I shall destroy this most dreadful illusion of theirs and this fierce darkness. Fear not, charioteer — be steady!"
Having said so, O lord of men, I released the weapon-illusion called the Bewilderer, for the benefit of all enemies and of those who dwell in the three heavens.
As each of their illusions was being afflicted and dispelled, the lords of the asuras, of boundless might, conjured up many further illusions in their place.
Again there was light, then again it was swallowed by darkness; again the world went into invisibility, again it sank under water.
When there was light, Mātali, with the bay horses well in hand, drove the foremost chariot through that hair-raising battle.
Then the fierce Nivātakavacas fell upon me from all sides; seeing an opening, I dispatched them to the abode of Yama.
While that battle — the destruction of the Nivātakavacas — was taking place, I suddenly could not see all those dānavas; they were shrouded in illusion.
Arjuna said: Though invisible, those daityas fought on by means of illusion. I too fought those invisible foes with the power of my weapons.
Arrows released from Gāṇḍīva, properly impelled by weapon-force, severed their heads wherever those daityas happened to be.
Then the Nivātakavacas, being slaughtered by me in battle, suddenly withdrew their illusion and retreated into their own city.
When the daityas had gone away and visibility had returned, I beheld dānavas lying slain there by the hundreds of thousands.
Their weapons, ornaments, limbs, and armor — all shattered and crushed — lay visible there in heaps.
The horses had no space to move a single step; so they suddenly leaped up and stood in the sky, moving through the air.
Then the Nivātakavacas, completely concealing the sky, came on invisibly, hurling masses of boulders.
Other dānavas, dreadful and underground, seized the feet of the horses and the wheels of my chariot, O Bhārata.
Having seized my bay horses and my chariot as I fought, they piled upon me and my chariot from all directions with mountains.
With mountains being heaped up and others falling, the region where we stood became like a cave.
Being covered by mountains and with my horses seized, I fell into the utmost distress. Mātali perceived this.
Perceiving me in fear, he spoke this word: "Arjuna, Arjuna — do not be afraid! Release the vajra weapon!"
Then, hearing his words, I released the vajra weapon — the beloved bolt of the king of gods — O lord of men.
Taking a firm stance, I charged the Gāṇḍīva with the mantra, and released iron-sharp arrows bearing the touch of the thunderbolt.
Then those arrows, impelled by the vajra and having become the vajra itself, penetrated all those illusions and all those Nivātakavacas.
Those dānavas, mountain-like, struck by the force of the vajra, fell to the surface of the earth clinging to one another.
And those dānavas who had seized the chariot-horses underground — the arrows followed them in and sent them to the abode of Yama.
With the Nivātakavacas slain and their mountain-like bodies strewn about, that region was covered as if with scattered mountains.
No harm whatsoever was seen to have befallen the horses, nor the chariot, nor Mātali, nor myself — and that seemed like a wonder.
Then Mātali, smiling, addressed me, O king: "This prowess that is seen in you, Arjuna, is not seen even among the gods."
When the hosts of asuras were slain, their wives wailed throughout that city, like female deer in the autumn season.
Then, together with Mātali, I drove toward that city, terrifying the women of the Nivātakavacas with the thunder of my chariot.
Seeing those ten-thousand horses resembling peacocks and the chariot blazing like the sun, the women fled in groups.
The sound made by their ornaments as they fled in terror was like that of rocks falling upon rocky mountains.
Those terrified women of the daityas then retreated into their own dwellings — richly adorned with many jewels and fashioned of gold.
Seeing that most excellent city of wondrous appearance, superior to the city of the gods, I then questioned Mātali about it.
"Why do the gods not inhabit such a place as this? I perceive that this city surpasses even the city of Purandara."
Mātali said: This city was formerly ours, O Pārtha — it belonged to the king of gods. Then the gods were driven away from here by the Nivātakavacas.
Having performed great and severe austerities and having propitiated the Grandfather, they requested this as their dwelling and immunity from the gods in battle.
Then the blessed Indra, for his own welfare's sake, urged the blessed Self-born One: "Let the Lord ordain here" — meaning their end.
Then Vāsava was told by the blessed one: "It is ordained here — you yourself, O Vṛtrahan, in another body, shall be their end."
Then, for the purpose of their destruction, Śakra gave you those weapons — for those whom you have slain could not be slain by the gods.
By the ripening of time, O Bhārata, you have arrived here as the one who brings their end, and you have done precisely that.
For the destruction of the dānavas, the great Indra caused you, O lord among men, to receive the great power of the great weapons — that supreme gift.
Arjuna said: Then, having entered the city and slain those dānavas, I again departed for the divine abode, together with Mātali.
Arjuna said: As I was returning, I then saw another great city — divine, moving at will, blazing like fire and sun together.
It was inhabited by jeweled, variegated trees with radiant birds, and by the Paulomas and Kālakeys, ever joyful.
Adorned with gateways and towers, with four gates, impregnable, made entirely of precious gems, divine, wondrous to behold, encircled by trees bearing flowers and fruits fashioned of divine jewels.
Filled likewise with divine birds of exquisite beauty, and surrounded on all sides by asuras forever rejoicing, bearing tridents, pikes, pestles, bows, and clubs in their hands, and wearing garlands.
Beholding that city of the daityas, wondrous in appearance, I asked Mātali, O king: "What is this that is seen here?"

Mātali said: A daitya woman named Pulomā and the great asura woman Kālakā practiced supreme austerities for a divine thousand years; at the end of their austerities the Self-born One granted them a boon.
Those two chose as their boon the freedom of their sons from great suffering, and their invulnerability to gods, rākṣasas, and serpents, O king of kings.
This beautiful city, sky-moving, radiant with accumulated merit, replete with all manner of gems, impregnable even by the immortals together with yakshas, gandharvas, serpents, asuras, and rākṣasas —
— furnished with every desired quality, free from sorrow and disease, was made by Brahmā, O best of Bhāratas, for the sake of the Kālakeys.
This divine sky-roaming city, from which the immortals are excluded, is inhabited, O hero, by the Paulomas and the Kālakey dānavas.
This great city is known as Hiraṇyapura — the Golden City — and it is guarded by the Kālakeys and the Paulomas, those mighty asuras.
These beings dwell here ever joyful, invincible to all the gods, O king of kings — free from anxiety and desire; death by a mortal hand was ordained for them by Brahmā of old.
Arjuna said: Learning that they could not be slain by gods or demons, O lord, I joyfully said to Mātali, "Drive straight into that city."
"Until I bring destruction upon the enemies of the lord of the thirty gods with my weapons, these sinful foes of the gods shall surely not escape being slain by me."
Then Mātali swiftly bore me close to Hiraṇyapura in that divine chariot yoked with bay horses.
Seeing me, the Daityas, clad in splendid ornaments and garments, armour-clad, mounted their chariots and rushed forth with great speed.
Then the foremost of Dānavas, fierce in might and enraged, struck me with nālikā arrows, nārācas, bhallaas, śaktis, ṛṣṭis, and tomaras.
I warded off that great shower of weapons with a mighty counter-shower of missiles, O king, drawing on the power of my science of arms.
I bewildered them all as I moved through the battle-field in chariot-manoeuvres; confused, the Dānavas began striking one another down.
While they were thus bewildered and rushing at each other, I severed their heads in hundreds with blazing shafts.
The Daityas, being slaughtered, re-entered that city and rose into the sky with it entire, resorting to their demonic māyā.
Then I checked their path with a great shower of arrows, covering their route and blocking their flight.
That sky-roving, divine, wish-moving city of celestial splendour was sustained at will by the Daityas through the boon they had been granted.
It sank beneath the earth and rose again upward; it moved swiftly sideways and then plunged once more into the waters.
That wish-moving city, resembling Amarāvatī, I countered with many kinds of missiles, O lord of men.
Then with a net of arrows empowered by divine weapons I seized that city together with the Daityas within it, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Pierced through and through by my straight-flying iron arrows, the demonic city crashed shattered to the earth, O king.
Struck by my iron arrows swift as thunderbolts, the asuras reeled about, O king, driven by fate.
Then Mātali too swiftly descended toward the earth as if swooping down, quickly landing with that sun-bright chariot.
Then sixty thousand chariots of those indignant ones, eager to fight with me, wheeled around, O Bhārata.
I pierced them with sharp arrows winged with vulture feathers; they surged back in battle like waves of the ocean.
Reflecting that these could not be overcome by mortal combat alone, I then deployed all my weapons in due order.
Then those thousands of chariots with their variegated warriors began, as it were, to neutralise my divine weapons one by one.
Those great warriors, moving in intricate chariot-paths, appeared in the battle by the hundreds and thousands.
Wearing varied diadems and crowns, varied armour and banners, and varied ornaments, they were, as it were, a delight to my heart.
Yet though I poured showers of weapon-energised arrows upon them in battle, I could not afflict them — while they afflicted me greatly.
Hard pressed by those many skilled warriors trained in arms, I was distressed in that great battle and a great fear came over me.
Then, bowing in battle to Rudra, the god of gods, and uttering "May all beings be well," I invoked the great weapon known as the Raudra — the destroyer of all enemies.
Then I beheld a three-headed person with nine eyes, three faces, six arms, blazing, with hair like the flaming sun, his heads crowned with great serpents whose tongues flickered — the slayer of foes.
Seeing that terrible, ancient Raudra weapon take shape, I was filled with awe; bringing it to the string of Gāṇḍīva, O bull of the Bhāratas —
— bowing to the three-eyed Śarva of boundless radiance, I released it for the defeat of the lords of the Dānavas, O Bhārata.
The moment it was released, thousands of forms appeared — of deer, lions, tigers, O lord of the people, bears, buffaloes, serpents, and cattle —
— of elephants, sṛmaras, śarabhas of every kind, bulls, boars, cats, and likewise wolves, pretas, and bhuruṇḍa birds of every sort —
— of vultures, Garuḍas, makaras, piśācas along with yakṣas, and likewise the enemies of the gods —
— of guhyakas in battle and nairṛtas likewise, great fish, elephant-faced beings, and owls —
— multitudes of fish and tortoises bearing various weapons and swords, and yātudhānas wielding clubs and hammers —
With these and many others assuming various forms, the entire world was pervaded when that weapon was released.
The Dānavas who had assembled were slaughtered again and again by three-headed, four-fanged, four-faced, four-armed forms of many kinds, feeding on flesh, fat, and marrow.
With the blazing energy of the sun, with the radiance of thunderbolts and lightning, with other arrows of iron-hard mountain-stone that rend foes, I slew all the Dānavas in but a moment, O Bhārata.
Seeing them struck down by the Gāṇḍīva-weapon, lifeless and fallen from the sky, I bowed again to the Creator who destroyed Tripura.
Beholding them crushed by the Raudra weapon, still adorned with their divine ornaments, the divine charioteer was filled with the greatest joy.
Seeing that unbearable feat accomplished — difficult even for the gods to achieve — Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, honoured me.

Delighted and joining his palms, he spoke these words: "The deed you have accomplished is unbearable even for gods and demons; not even the lord of the gods would be capable of performing this in battle."
"This great sky-faring city, invincible to gods and demons, has been shattered by you, O hero, through your own strength of valour, weapons, and austerity."
When that city was destroyed and the Dānavas slain, all the women rushed out from the city wailing.
With dishevelled hair, distressed, wretched like osprey-birds, they fell to the earth lamenting their sons, fathers, and brothers.
Weeping with piteous throats, wailing with their lords slain, beating their breasts with their hands, their garlands and ornaments fallen away —
Stricken with grief, stripped of its glory, battered by sorrow and misery, its lustre extinguished and its lords slain, the Dānava city no longer shone.
Like a gandharva city in appearance, like a lake whose great serpent has been slain, like a forest of withered trees, the city became invisible.
But Mātali, his heart overjoyed, quickly brought me — my task accomplished in battle — to the palace of the king of gods.
Having stormed Hiraṇyapura and slain the great asuras and the Nivātakavacas, I then came before Śakra.
And Mātali reported all my deeds in full detail to Indra, lord of the gods, exactly as they had occurred, O greatly splendid one.
The destruction of Hiraṇyapura, the repulsion of the illusions, and the slaying of the mighty Nivātakavacas in battle —
Hearing this, the blessed thousand-eyed Puraṃdara, glorious and accompanied by the Maruts, then said, "Well done, well done!"
Then the king of gods, reassuring me again and again, spoke these very sweet words in the presence of the divine ones.
"This feat performed by you in battle surpasses what gods and asuras could do; a great and weighty service has been rendered to me, O Pārtha, by your slaying of my enemies."
"Always should you be thus — steady in battle, O Dhanaṃjaya; unconfused in applying the weapons, that is what must be done."
"In battle you are invincible to gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, to yakṣas with their asura hosts, gandharvas, winged creatures, and serpents."
"And the earth, O son of Kuntī, conquered by the strength of your arms, will be governed by the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī."
Arjuna said: Then, when I was fully recovered and my arrow-wounds had healed, the king of gods graciously spoke these words to me at the proper time.
"All the divine weapons reside in you, O Bhārata; no mortal on this earth is capable of overpowering you."
"Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Śakuni together with their kings — when you stand on the battlefield, my son, they are not worth a sixteenth part of you."
And the mighty Maghavan, lord of all, bestowed on me this protective covering — a divine impenetrable armour and also a golden garland.
The god also gave me the conch Devadatta with its great sound; and Indra himself placed this divine diadem on my head.
Then Śakra gave me these divine garments and divine ornaments — splendid and magnificent.
Thus honoured, I dwelt happily there, O king, in the sacred palace of Indra, together with the young Gandharvas.
Then Śakra, delighted, spoke to me in the presence of the immortals: "The time has come for you to go, Arjuna — your brothers remember you."
Thus five years were spent by me in the palace of Indra, O Bhārata, O king, all the while remembering the quarrel born of the dice-game.
Then I saw you, surrounded by your brothers, having reached Gandhamādana, on the summit of this very mountain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By good fortune have the weapons been obtained by you, O Dhanaṃjaya, O Bhārata; by good fortune the king, lord and master of the gods, has been propitiated.
By good fortune the blessed Sthāṇu together with the Goddess was directly seen, O scorcher of foes, and pleased by your valiant combat, O sinless one.
By good fortune you have met the world-guardians, O bull of the Bhāratas; by good fortune we all prosper; by good fortune you have returned.
Today I consider this whole divine earth with its garlanded cities to be conquered, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra too to be subdued.
But I desire to see those divine weapons of yours, O Bhārata, with which those mighty Nivātakavacas were slain.
Arjuna said: Tomorrow at dawn you shall see all the divine weapons with which those terrible Nivātakavacas were struck down by me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus narrated his arrival there, Dhanaṃjaya spent that night together with all his brothers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When that night had passed, the dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira rose and performed his necessary duties together with his brothers.
Then he urged Arjuna, the joy of his brothers: "Show the weapons, O son of Kuntī, with which you conquered the Dānavas."
Then Dhanaṃjaya, that Pāṇḍava, O king, displayed those divine weapons bestowed by the gods, O Bhārata.

The greatly radiant Dhanaṃjaya, observing supreme ritual purity in the proper manner, mounting the earthly chariot with its mountain-axle, its tree-staff, its auspicious triple-bamboo triveṇu pole, shone with magnificence.
Then, well-armoured with that resplendent armour, taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow and the conch Devadatta born of the waters —
Resplendent, O son of Kuntī, the mighty-armed one began to display those divine weapons one by one for all to see.
As he was about to discharge those divine weapons, the earth, along with its trees, shook and trembled under his feet.
The rivers were disturbed, the great ocean heaved, the mountains crumbled, and the wind ceased to blow.
The thousand-rayed sun ceased to shine, fire did not burn, and the Vedic hymns no longer came to the minds of the twice-born in any way.
Those living beings that dwelt within the earth, O Janamejaya, rose up in their affliction and surrounded the son of Pāṇḍu.
Trembling, with hands joined in supplication, their faces covered, scorched by those weapons, they all beseeched Dhanañjaya.
Then the brahmarshis, the siddhas, the divine sages, and all mobile creatures stood still.
The foremost royal sages, the dwellers of heaven, the yakshas, rakshasas, gandharvas, and the birds all gathered there likewise.
Then the Grandfather Brahmā, all the guardians of the worlds, and the blessed Mahādeva together with his host came there.
Then the wind, O great king, showered variegated divine garlands of sweet fragrance all around and upon the Pāṇḍavas on every side.
The gandharvas, urged on by the gods, sang various songs, and the hosts of apsaras danced in groups, O king.
In that tumultuous moment, Nārada, sent by the gods, came and spoke these words worthy of hearing to the son of Pṛthā, O king.
"Arjuna, Arjuna, do not discharge the divine weapons, O descendant of Bharata — these are never to be used against a target that does not warrant them.
Nor should one who is not in distress ever use them even against a fitting target, for the improper employment of these weapons brings the gravest of faults, O joy of the Kurus.
If these are guarded in accordance with the rules by which they were received, O Dhanañjaya, they will remain potent and bring happiness — of this there is no doubt.
If not guarded, these weapons bring ruin even to the three worlds, O son of Pāṇḍu. Do not do this again anywhere."
"You, O one without enemies, shall see those weapons employed by the son of Pṛthā in battle for the crushing of foes."
Having thus restrained the son of Pṛthā, all the gods departed as they had come, and so did the others who had assembled there, O bull among men.
When all of them had departed, O descendant of the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas along with Kṛṣṇā dwelt joyfully in that very forest.

Janamejaya said: "After that foremost of chariot-warriors, having mastered the weapons, had returned from the abode of the slayer of Vṛtra, what did the sons of Pṛthā do thereafter, having been reunited with the heroic Dhanañjaya?"

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Those lords of men, those heroes, together with Arjuna who was equal to Indra himself, sported and took their ease in that excellent and beautiful mountain region, journeying to the pleasure-grounds of the lord of wealth."
Beholding those incomparable mansions and the sports near the diverse trees, the diademed archer, that lord among men, ever intent upon his weapons, roamed about in many directions.
Having obtained the dwelling born of the favour of king Vaiśravaṇa, those sons of the lord of men envied no living being, O king, and their time there was auspicious.

Having been reunited with the son of Pṛthā as though it were but a single night, they dwelt there for four years; and those ten years altogether — the six previous and these four — passed auspiciously for the Pāṇḍavas residing in the forests.

Then the swift son of Vāyu, and Jiṣṇu, and the two valiant twins, equal to the king of the gods, seated themselves beside the king in a private place and spoke words that were both beneficial and dear.
"Wishing to fulfil your true vow, O king of the Kurus, and to do what is dear to you, let us leave these forests and follow you to slay Suyodhana along with his followers."
"This is the eleventh year we have dwelt here, deprived of our comforts by Suyodhana. Having deceived that one of base mind and character, let us happily pass our year of incognito."
"Under your command, O king, roaming through the forests without fear, laying aside our pride, those who are tempted by our proximity to them will not recognize us when we are in a remote region."
"Having passed that year in concealment, let us destroy that vilest of men in happiness, exacting our enmity in full — with fruit and flower both — upon that most contemptible of kings and men."
"Then, O king of righteousness, reclaim the earth from Suyodhana surrounded by his followers; roaming this mountain that resembles heaven, the grief of a lord of men can be dispelled."

"Your fame, fragrant with virtue, O descendant of Bharata, would perish in the worlds of the moving and the unmoving; having regained the kingdom of the bull of the Kurus, great deeds can be performed."
"This which you have received from Kubera is ever within reach for you, O lord of men. Make up your mind to slay the enemies and to subdue those who have wronged you, O descendant of Bharata."

"Your fierce energy could not be endured even by the wielder of the thunderbolt himself were he to face you directly, O king; those two would never suffer distress even if they faced the gods themselves, O king of righteousness."

"Both are engaged for the attainment of your purpose — he whose banner bears the Garuḍa eagle, and the grandson of Śini; just as Kṛṣṇa is matchless in strength, so too, O king, is that foremost hero of Śini's line."

"Just as Kṛṣṇa along with those Yādavas is engaged for the achievement of your ends, so too are we, O foremost of lords of men — and the two valiant twins, skilled in action — all of us, whose chief purpose springs from devotion to your cause, will together make the enemies equal to the ground."
Then the great-souled, most excellent son of Dharma, understanding their intention, he who knew the purposes of righteousness and was of the highest valour, circumambulated the abode of Vaiśravaṇa.
The king of righteousness took leave of the mansions, the rivers, the lakes, and all the guardian spirits, looking back along the road by which they had come, and gazing once more at the mountain.

"Having completed my task, together with my friends, having conquered my enemies and recovered my kingdom, I shall return again, O lord of mountains, with steadfast soul devoted to austerity, and see you again" — thus he resolved in his mind.

Accompanied by all his younger brothers and the brahmins, the lord of the Kurus went by that same road; and Ghaṭotkaca likewise carried them all along with their retinues through the mountain torrents.
As they set out, the great seer Lomaśa, with a joyful heart, having instructed them all like a father his sons, departed with a glad mind to the most sacred abode of the celestial beings.
Thus instructed by him and also by Arishthishena, beholding the beautiful holy places, the hermitages, and other great lakes, the foremost of men, the sons of Pṛthā, journeyed onward.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "As they left that excellent mountain endowed with springs and inhabited by the elephants of the directions, kinnara, and birds, those bulls of Bharata's line felt no pleasure in departing from that pleasant abode."
Then great joy arose in them once again as those bulls of Bharata's line beheld Mount Kailāsa, beloved of Kubera, that mountain shining like a mass of clouds.
The heroes beheld the towering peaks, the mountain passes, the mountain plateaus, the chains of mountain bridges, the many waterfalls, and the high and low ground here and there.
Likewise beholding other great forests frequented by deer, birds, and many ascetics, those foremost of men — archers and sword-bearers — advanced with confidence.
Beautiful forests, lakes, rivers, mountain caves, and mountain gorges — these became the ever-changing nightly dwelling places of those bulls among men, as they reached a new one each night.
Having dwelt in many difficult mountain fastnesses and having passed beyond Kailāsa of inconceivable beauty, they reached that most delightful of hermitages, that excellent ashrama of Vṛṣaparvan.
Meeting with the king Vṛṣaparvan and being honoured by him, those who were free from delusion described in detail their auspicious sojourn to Vṛṣaparvan exactly as it had occurred.
Having dwelt happily there for one night in that holy hermitage frequented by gods and great sages, those heroes easily went again to Badarī, that vast and auspicious dwelling place.
Those foremost of men, of great majesty, having arrived at the abode of Nārāyaṇa, dwelt there, free from sorrow, gazing upon the lake beloved of Kubera, frequented by the gods and siddhas.
And having seen that lake, the sons of Pāṇḍu — those foremost of all men — free from sorrow, sported as if they had come to dwell in Nandana, just as the twice-born seers free from fear.
Then those heroic men gradually approached, all together by the very road by which they had come, having sported happily at Badarī for a month, the realm of Subāhu the Kirāta king.

Passing through the lands of the Chinas, Tokharas, Daradas, Darvas, and the gem-rich territories of the Kuṇindas, and crossing the difficult Himālayan regions, those heroic men beheld the city of Subāhu.
Hearing that those sons and grandsons of kings had arrived in his territory altogether, king Subāhu went forth joyfully to meet them; and the bulls of the Kurus welcomed him in return.
Having met with king Subāhu, and with all the bards headed by Viśoka, with Indrasena and the other attendants, and the stewards and those stationed in the royal kitchen —
— having dwelt there happily for one night, taking the charioteers and all the chariots, dismissing Ghaṭotkaca along with his followers, they then proceeded to the king of mountains on the Yamunā.
On that mountain endowed with springs, on its slope reddened by the snow-laden northern winds and whitened in places, those foremost of men arrived at Viśākhayūpa and made their dwelling there.

In that great forest frequented by boars, various deer and birds, shining like the Chaitraratha garden, they passed, devoted chiefly to the hunt and going forth auspiciously, an entire year sporting in that forest.

There, in a mountain gorge, Vṛkodara encountered an exceedingly powerful serpent, tormented by hunger and of a terrible form like Death itself — and his inner soul was afflicted with anguish and bewilderment.

It was there that Yudhiṣṭhira, the most excellent of upholders of righteousness and of boundless energy, became a refuge for Vṛkodara — he who freed him when every limb was coiled about by the serpent.

As the twelfth year was now approaching, the Kurus, blazing with beauty and endowed with austerity, confident in their purpose, prepared to leave that forest which shone like the Chaitraratha garden and to roam in another.
Then, having gone to the edge of the desert, those ever-devoted chiefly to the science of archery, wishing to settle by the Sarasvatī river, went thence to the lake and the Dvaitavana forest.

Seeing them settled in Dvaitavana, those who dwelt there came to them — those endowed with austerity, self-restraint, good conduct, and meditation, who collected grass, water, and vessels, and ground grain with stones.
Plaksha, Akṣa, Rohitaka, Vetasa, Snuhi, Badarī, Khadira, Shirisha, Bilva, Inguda, Pīlu, Shami, and Karira — these grew along the banks of the Sarasvatī.
Roaming joyfully along that Sarasvatī beloved of yakshas, gandharvas, and great sages — like a place of worship for the gods — the sons of the lord of men sported happily.
Janamejaya said: "How did Bhīmasena of mighty strength, whose vitality equals ten thousand elephants, come to experience such intense fear from that python-serpent, O sage?"
"He who in battle challenged Dhanada of the Paulastya lineage, proud of his strength, and made havoc among the excellent yakshas and rakshasas at the Nalinī lake —"
"— you speak of him as seized with fear and fallen into distress, that crusher of enemies. This is what I wish to hear — for my curiosity is very great."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "While those mighty archers were dwelling in that forest of many wonders, O king, having come from the hermitage of the royal sage Vṛṣaparvan —"
"— Vṛkodara, bow in hand, sword girt at his side, wandering by chance, beheld that beautiful forest frequented by gods and gandharvas."
He then beheld the beautiful regions of the Himālaya mountains, frequented by divine sages and siddhas, served by hosts of apsaras.
Resounding here and there with chakoras, chakravakas, jivajivaka birds, kokilas, and bhrinarajas —
— filled with trees that bore perennial flowers and fruits, made soft by the touch of snow, with abundant shade, delighting the mind and eye —
— he gazed upon the mountain rivers with their waters resembling vaidurya gems, cool to the touch with snow, thronged with swans and karandava ducks —
— forests of deodar cedars like snares for clouds, mixed with harichandana trees, and tall kaliyaka trees as well —
— that one of very great strength ranged about, running through the hunt across the level windswept plains, piercing deer with his pure arrows.
He beheld a serpent of enormous body, causing the hair to stand on end, settled in a mountain fastness, its body filling a cavern.
Its body was as massive as a mountain's bulk; its coils were like the orbs of the moon and sun; variegated in markings, with mottled skin, its hue was like that of turmeric.
With its mouth like the entrance of a cave, four-fanged and gleaming silver, with blazing eyes of a deep copper hue, it repeatedly licked the corners of its lips.
It stood there terrifying all living beings, comparable to Death and the end-of-age Yama, as if threatening them with the sound of its hissing and screeching.
That serpent, exceedingly hungry, suddenly rushed at Bhīma and seized him like a great python seizing prey, grasping both his arms with force.
The moment Bhīmasena was touched by it, his consciousness suddenly became confused on account of the boon that had been granted to that serpent.
The strength that ten thousand elephants possess — that very strength dwelt in the arms of Bhīmasena, unequalled by any foe.
That illustrious one, subdued thus by the serpent, shuddered slightly but could not stir — Bhīma was unable to move at all.
He whose vitality equalled ten thousand elephants, with lion-like shoulders and mighty arms, was seized and lost his power, bewildered by the boon.
He made a fierce effort to free himself, but that hero was not able by any means to resist or repel the serpent.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That illustrious Bhīmasena, having thus fallen under the power of the serpent, began to reflect upon the serpent's strength, which was exceedingly wonderful and great.
And he spoke to that great serpent out of curiosity: "Tell me, O snake — who are you, O best among serpents, and what will you do with me?"
"I am Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, second only to the Dharma-king; I whose vitality equals ten thousand elephants — how have you brought me under your power?"
"Lions, tigers, buffaloes, and elephants too — many have come against me and have been slain by me in battle."
"Dānavas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas of great strength have been unable to withstand the speed of my arms, O best of serpents."
"Is it the power of learning, or is it a boon granted to you? Even while I was exerting myself, you have placed me entirely under your control."
"My mind is now firmly convinced that the valour of men is vain — for you, O serpent, have thus checked my great strength."
While the hero Bhīma, the doer of tireless deeds, was speaking thus, the serpent encircled him on all sides with its massive coils.
Having bound that mighty-armed one, and then releasing his stout arms, that serpent spoke these words:
"By good fortune you have been sent today by the gods as food for me who am hungry, O mighty-armed one — for indeed, dear to all embodied beings is life in the face of great time."
"But as to how I have come to be a serpent, O tamer of foes — that I must relate to you today; listen, O best of beings."
"I arrived at this condition through the wrath of the wise; now seeking the end of the serpent's curse, I shall tell you of it."
"The royal sage named Nahuṣa — of whom you have surely heard — I am he, the ancestor of your ancestors, the son of Āyu, founder of your lineage."
"I, having disrespected the Brāhmaṇas and through the curse of Agastya, have fallen into this condition. Behold what fate has done to me."
"Though you are one who should not be slain, coming here so very fair to behold, I shall devour you today — see what my situation is like."
"No one, once seized by me, is released by any means — whether elephant or buffalo — at the sixth meal-time, O best of men."
"You are not seized merely by a common serpent dwelling among animals — this is the boon that is mine, O best of the Kauravas."
"For when I was falling headlong from the summit of my celestial car, fleeing swiftly from Indra's throne, the blessed sage, the best of munis, said to me: 'Bring the curse to its end.'"
"That illustrious one, filled with compassion, spoke to me: 'Your release shall come, O king, through the turn of time in some way.'"
"Then I fell to the earth, and my memory did not leave me; the ancient knowledge that I had acquired remains with me as it was."
"'He who shall knowledgeably answer the questions put to you shall be your liberator from the curse' — thus the sage told me."
"'Of every living creature seized by you, O king, however strong, however great, the loss of vital power will come swiftly to all.'"
"Thus did I hear the words of those compassionate ones who had become tender-hearted toward me — and then those Brāhmaṇas disappeared."
"I, of most wicked deeds, dwell in this impure hell, having attained this serpent-birth, awaiting the right time, O greatly resplendent one."
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena then said to that serpent: "I am not angry with you, O great serpent, nor do I blame myself."
"Because whether a man will or will not experience pleasure and pain — when they come or when they depart, the mind should not be distressed about that."
"Who is able to turn back fate by human effort? I consider fate alone supreme; human effort is without purpose."
"Behold me here today, brought to this condition without cause, though I had recourse to the strength of my arms — through the blow of fate."
"Yet I do not grieve today for myself being thus destroyed as much as for my brothers cast into the forest, dispossessed of their kingdom."
"This Himavat is very difficult to traverse, filled with Yakṣas and Rākṣasas — and they, looking out for me, will fall into distress."
"Or upon hearing of my death they will become disheartened and listless — those virtuous ones who have been oppressed by me who am greedy for the kingdom."
"Surely wise Arjuna will not fall into despondency — he who knows all weapons and is invincible to gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas."
"That mighty-armed one of immense strength is capable, in a single day, of displacing even the king of gods from his throne by his valour."
"How much more then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who cheats at dice, who is hated by all the world, given over to arrogance and greed."
"And I grieve for my pitiable mother, who longs for her sons, who always hopes for our greatness beyond that of rivals."
"How, O serpent, at my death, will all those longings she placed in me become fruitless for that helpless one?"
"Nakula and Sahadeva, the twin brothers who are obedient to their elders — ever relying on the strength of my arms, they always pride themselves as men."
"At my death they will become dispirited, their valour and prowess stripped away, afflicted and sorrowful — so my mind turns."
Thus Vṛkodara lamented greatly in various ways, bound by the serpent's coils and unable to stir.
Meanwhile Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, became uneasy of mind, pondering the dreadful and ill-omened portents he was witnessing.
For a jackal, standing to the south in the blazing quarter, terrified, was uttering a fierce and inauspicious howl near that hermitage.
A quail, hideous to behold, with one wing, one eye, and one foot, was seen vomiting blood toward the sun, crying with ill omens.
A harsh and violent wind blew, dragging gravel along, and all the cries of beasts and birds went in the inauspicious direction.
A black crow behind him cawed again and again "Go, go!" and his right arm throbbed repeatedly.
His heart and left foot twitched, and an inauspicious change came over his left eye.
That wise Dharma-king, suspecting some great calamity, asked Draupadī: "Where is Bhīma?" — O Bhārata.
The Pāñcālī princess told him of Vṛkodara who had gone for a long while; and the mighty-armed king set out accompanied by Dhaumya.
"Draupadī must be guarded" — so he commanded Dhanañjaya, and he instructed Nakula and Sahadeva regarding the Brāhmaṇas.
That lord, tracking his footprints, departing from that very hermitage, saw the earth marked with the signs left by Bhīma.
Of that hero running with the speed of the wind in pursuit of game, trees broken by the blast of his thighs were flung aside along the path.
Following those very signs, he went and beheld in a mountain cave his younger brother, seized by the king of serpents, lying motionless.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yudhiṣṭhira, approaching that beloved heroic brother who was encircled by the serpent's coils, spoke these words:
"O son of Kuntī, how have you fallen into this calamity? And who is this best of serpents, resembling the very coil of a mountain?"
That brother, perceiving the Dharma-king, his elder brother, related to him all that had happened from his seizure onward.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Whether you are a god, a Daitya, or a serpent — if you are willing to speak truly, O snake, Yudhiṣṭhira asks you."
"What, if brought or known, would please you, O serpent? What food shall I offer you? How will you release this one?"
The serpent said: "I was the king named Nahuṣa, your ancestor, O sinless one — the celebrated fifth son descended from Soma through Āyu, O lord of men."
"Through sacrifices, through austerity, through self-study, through self-restraint, and through conquest, I obtained uncontested sovereignty over the three worlds."
"Having obtained that sovereignty, pride overtook me at that time — for a thousand twice-born ones carried my palanquin."
"I, intoxicated with the pride of sovereignty, disrespected the Brāhmaṇas — and by Agastya I was brought to this condition, O lord of the earth."
"Yet my wisdom has not left me even until today — by the grace of that great-souled Agastya himself, O king, O Pāṇḍava."
"This younger brother of yours has come as my food at the sixth meal-time; I shall not release him, and I desire no other."
"But if you shall answer the questions I have propounded, then afterwards I shall release your brother Vṛkodara."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Ask, O serpent, as you please — I shall answer your words, if I am able to bring satisfaction to you, O serpent."
"What a Brāhmaṇa must know here — that you alone know, O king of serpents; having heard it from you, I shall then answer your words."
The serpent said: "Who is a Brāhmaṇa, O king? And what is to be known, O Yudhiṣṭhira? Speak — for we shall judge your great intellect by your words."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Where truth, charity, forbearance, good conduct, non-cruelty, self-restraint, and compassion are seen, O king of serpents — he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa."
"What is to be known, O serpent, is the supreme Brahman — that which is beyond sorrow and beyond joy, going whereto one grieves no more. What is your intent in asking?"

The serpent said: "The four-caste order is the authority, and truth and Brahman as well — and even among Śūdras there is truth, charity, freedom from anger, non-cruelty, non-violence, and compassion also, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
"As for what you said is to be known — that beyond sorrow and beyond joy, O lord of men — I hold that there is no other state inferior to those two, none whatsoever."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "If this mark were found in a Śūdra, and not found in a twice-born — then the Śūdra would not be a Śūdra, and the Brāhmaṇa would not be a Brāhmaṇa."
"Where this conduct is seen, O serpent, he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa; where this is not present, O serpent, that one should be designated as a Śūdra."
"As for what you further said — that there is nothing to be known beyond those two — if indeed there is no state beyond them, going past both,"
"So too is this my view, O serpent — nothing exists inferior to those two; just as between cold and hot there can be neither heat nor coldness."
Indeed such a state exists somewhere, free from both pleasure and pain — this is my view, O serpent; or what does your lordship think?
The serpent said: If, O king, you judge a brahmin by his conduct, then birth is meaningless, O long-lived one — so long as virtuous action is not seen.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Here, O great serpent, O great-minded one, birth in the human world is hard to ascertain, due to the intermixing of all the castes — this is my view.
When all men beget offspring in all women, and speech, sexual union, birth, and death are the same for all human beings —
— and this is the ancient authority too, as in the formula 'we who sacrifice' — therefore those who perceive the truth know that good conduct is of supreme importance.
Before the navel-string ceremony, the birth-rite is prescribed for a man; therein his mother is the Sāvitrī and his teacher is said to be his father.
By occupation he is equal to a shudra until he is born again in the Veda. On this difference of view, Manu the self-born spoke thus:
If the castes, though having performed their duties, do not possess right conduct, then there, O lord of serpents, confusion is seen to be powerful indeed.
Whoever now, O great serpent, possesses refined conduct — him I have previously called a brahmin, O best of serpents.
The serpent said: I have heard your words, O Yudhiṣṭhira, you who know what is to be known. For what reason then should I eat your brother Vṛkodara?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You are such a one in this world, versed in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas — tell me, by performing what action does a person reach the highest state?
The serpent said: By giving to a worthy recipient, by speaking kind words, by speaking truth, O Bhārata, and by being devoted to non-injury — one goes to heaven; this is my view.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Between giving and truth, O serpent, which of these is seen as weightier? And among non-injury and kindly speech, let the relative weight be stated.
The serpent said: Devotion to giving, truth, non-injury, and kindly speech — the relative weight of these is determined by the gravity of the action to be performed.
In some circumstances truth surpasses even the practice of giving, O king of kings; and in some cases giving surpasses truthful speech.
Similarly, O great archer, O lord of earth, non-injury is seen to be weightier than kindly speech, and then kindly speech is deemed superior.
Such is the matter, O king — it depends upon the action at hand. Whatever else you have in mind, ask me while I am speaking to you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How does one go to heaven, O serpent? And how is the sure fruit of actions seen by one who has no body? Tell me about the objects of sense also.
The serpent said: There are indeed three states of existence, O king, determined by one's own actions: humanity, dwelling in heaven, and birth in animal wombs — that is the threefold division.
From the human world, one who is diligent through giving and the like, combined with causes relating to non-injury and truthfulness, attains heaven.
By contrary causes, O king of kings, one becomes human again; or takes birth in animal wombs, dear one — the distinction in this regard will be stated.
One who is possessed of desire and anger, who is accompanied by violence and greed, falls from humanity and is born in an animal womb.
Separate gradations exist even within animal births; in humanity gradations are established; and from among cattle, horses, and the like, even divinity is seen to be attainable.
Thus this being, acting purposefully, traverses all these states, and finally establishes itself in the great eternal, O king.
Born again and again, powerful, the embodied self enjoys; its purpose is fruit, dear one — it remains unattached, experiencing the characteristics of creation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In sound, touch, form, and similarly in taste and smell — tell me clearly the undistracted basis of that self, O serpent, exactly as it is.
Why do you not apprehend the objects of sense simultaneously, O great-minded one? Let this much be explained — and also all that has been said, O best of serpents.
The serpent said: That which is the substance of the self, O long-lived one, connected with the body's dwelling, presided over by the organs of sense — it enjoys objects of experience in due order.
Cognition, intellect, and mind, O bull of the Bhāratas — learn from me about these as the instruments in the experiencing of that self.
Through the mind, dear one, the elemental self — situated at the abode of the sense objects, gone forth from the field — goes to these sense objects one by one in sequence.
Here too, O tiger among men, the mind of a being is determined to be singular; therefore simultaneous apprehension of all objects at once is not possible for it.
That self, O tiger among men, residing between the eyebrows, produces intellect — higher and lower — in relation to various objects.
After the intellect acts, sensation is seen by the wise; this indeed, O tiger among kings, is the process pertaining to the knower of the field.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me the supreme distinguishing mark of both mind and intellect — this is considered the highest task of those who know the inner self.
The serpent said: Intellect follows the self, dear one — it is established through its arising; for the very cognition that depends on it is its regulation in its seeking.
There is no rule of qualities for intellect; but the mind may be qualified. Intellect arises in regard to action, whereas the mind is simply something that arises.
This distinction between mind and intellect has been stated by me, dear one. You too are wise in this matter — or what does your lordship think?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Ah, O best among the wise, auspicious is your intellect! What is to be known is known by you — why do you ask me?
How did delusion enter you, an omniscient one, a dweller in heaven, one of such wondrous deeds? This is my great doubt.
The serpent said: Prosperity deludes a man even if he is very wise and heroic; whoever is presently experiencing happiness does not fully know — this is my view.
I, O Yudhiṣṭhira, was deluded by the intoxication of sovereignty, overcome by pride, and fell; now awakened, I awaken you in turn.
Your task on my behalf has been accomplished, O great king, O scorcher of foes; my curse, hard to bear, has been exhausted by your conversing with me thus virtuously.
For I was formerly traveling in heaven in a divine chariot, intoxicated with pride, and thought of no one else as my equal.
Brahmin-seers, gods, gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas, and kinnaras — all the inhabitants of the three worlds paid tribute to me.
Whichever living being I would look upon with my eye, O lord of the earth, its radiance I would swiftly steal away — for that was the power of my gaze.
Indeed a thousand brahmin seers would bear my palanquin. That arrogance, O king, caused me to fall from my glory.
For there the sage Agastya, while bearing me, was touched by my foot; then, unseen, he spoke to me in anger: 'Fall, become a serpent!'
Then, fallen from the top of that chariot, stripped of my ornaments, as I was tumbling down I became aware of myself transformed into a serpent, falling headlong.
I besought that brahmin, 'Let there be an end to the curse' — saying 'O blessed one, you should forgive one who acted out of ignorance.'
Then, filled with compassion, he spoke to me as I was falling: 'Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-king, will release you from the curse.'
'When the fruit of your terrible pride and power has been exhausted, O lord of men, O great king, you will attain the fruit of your merit.'
Then wonder arose in me, seeing the power of asceticism, and of Brahman, and of brahminhood — by which you, Yudhiṣṭhira, have enlightened me.
Truth, self-restraint, asceticism, yoga, non-injury, and constancy in giving — these are ever the instruments of accomplishment for human beings; not birth, not lineage, O king.
This brother of yours, Bhīma of mighty arms, is unharmed and freed. May it be well with you, O great king — I shall go to heaven again.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus and abandoned the python's body, that king Nahuṣa assumed his divine form and departed to the third heaven.
The virtuous Yudhiṣṭhira too, reunited with his brother Bhīma, accompanied by Dhaumya, glorious as he was, returned to the hermitage.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira the dharma-king related all of that exactly as it had happened to all the assembled twice-born.
Having heard that, all those twice-born, his three brothers, and the illustrious Draupadī were greatly ashamed, O king.
All those foremost twice-born, wishing well for the Pāṇḍavas, said to Bhīma 'Do not do so again,' reproving his recklessness.
But the Pāṇḍavas, seeing the mighty Bhīma freed from danger, rejoiced and sported together filled with delight.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While they were dwelling there, the rainy season arrived — that time which ends the hot season and brings comfort to all beings.
Great roaring dark clouds, covering the sky and all directions, poured rain continuously day and night at that time.
Hundreds and thousands of clouds, heralding the end of the hot season, their nets of solar radiance departed, gleaming brightly with lightning.
The earth, with fresh young grass growing, filled with intoxicated gadflies and crawling creatures, drenched with water, its dust and smoke settled, glowed reddish.
Nothing could be discerned through the water that covered everything equally — neither level ground nor uneven, neither rivers nor stationary objects.
Rivers with their waters churned up, making great noise, flowing swiftly as if breathing hard, adorned the forests at the end of the hot season.
In the depths of the forests, various sounds were heard of boars, deer, and birds being struck by the rain showers.
Wagtails and peacocks, together with groups of male cuckoos, flew about in delight, and frogs too gamboled proudly.
Thus the rainy season, of many diverse forms, resounding with clouds, passed auspiciously for them as they roamed through the forests and deserts.
Autumn arrived, filled with flocks of cranes and geese, with grown-over thickets, forests, and plains, with rivers running clear.
With its pure sky and stars, autumn proved auspicious for those great-souled Pāṇḍavas, filled with deer and birds.
They beheld the nights, dust-free and cool with rain-water, brilliant with groups of planets and stars, and radiant with the moon.
They saw rivers and pools beautifully adorned with night-blooming lotuses and white lotuses, their waters cool, auspicious and bearing cool water.
Joy arose for them as they roamed, seeing the Sarasvatī river with its banks resembling the sky, crowded with kadamba and wild rice, full of holy fords.
Those heroes, those firm bowmen, rejoiced indeed, beholding the Sarasvatī with its clear, auspicious, brimming waters.
For them dwelling there, the most auspicious night was that autumnal Kartika night at the conjunction of the lunar fortnight, O Janamejaya.
Together with ascetics of great souls who had performed meritorious deeds, the Pāṇḍavas, best of the Bhāratas, assembled there and practised the highest yoga.
At the rising of the darkness of that night, the Pāṇḍavas together with Dhaumya, with their charioteers and cooks, departed for the Kāmyaka forest.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having reached Kāmyaka, the sons of Kuntī with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, duly honored as guests by the groups of sages, took their seats together with Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī).
Then many brahmins surrounded from all sides those sons of Pāṇḍu as they dwelt there in full confidence.
Then a certain brahmin, a dear friend of Arjuna, spoke: 'The mighty-armed one, the self-controlled Śauri of noble intellect, will come here.'
For Hari knows that you, the foremost of the Kurus, have arrived here. Hari always longs to see you and ever seeks your welfare.
And Mārkaṇḍeya, the great ascetic who has lived for many thousands of years, absorbed in self-study and austerity, will soon come to meet you.
Even as he spoke those words, Keśava appeared — the best of chariot-warriors — his chariot yoked with Sainya and Sugrīva.
