Like Maghavan accompanied by the daughter of Puloman, the son of Devakī arrived with Satyabhāmā, eager to behold the best of the Kurus.
Descending from the chariot, the wise and joyful Kṛṣṇa greeted Dharmarāja with due ceremony and also Bhīma, the foremost among the strong.
He honored Dhaumya as well; having been greeted by the twins, he embraced Guḍākeśa and then consoled Draupadī.
Seeing the heroic Phalguna, his dear one who had returned after so long, the Dāśārha embraced the subduer of enemies again and again.
Likewise Satyabhāmā, the beloved queen of Kṛṣṇa, embraced Draupadī, the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then all the Pāṇḍavas, together with their wives and their family priest, honored the lotus-eyed one and surrounded him on all sides.
The wise Kṛṣṇa, having united with Pārtha — the terror of demons — shone like the great-souled lord of beings, Bhagavān himself meeting with Guha face to face.
Then the diadem-wearer, having duly related all that had transpired in the forests to the elder brother of Gada, inquired in return: 'How is Subhadrā, and how is Abhimanyu?'
Then the slayer of Madhu, having duly honored the Pārthas, Kṛṣṇā, and the family priest, sat down beside King Yudhiṣṭhira and addressed him with words of praise.

'Dharma is higher than the gaining of a kingdom, O Pāṇḍava; for its sake they speak of austerity alone, O king. Practicing your own dharma with truth and straightforwardness, you have conquered both this world and the next.'

'In the beginning you studied while observing vows; having fully mastered the science of archery and acquired wealth through kṣatriya dharma — all the ancient sacrifices have indeed been accomplished by you.'
'You have no delight in the vulgar duties, O lord of men; you pursue no desires whatsoever, nor do you abandon dharma out of greed for wealth — therefore by your very nature you are Dharmarāja.'
'Charity, truth, austerity, O king — faith, peace, fortitude, and forbearance — having acquired kingdoms, wealth, and pleasures, these are ever your supreme delight, O Pārtha.'
'When the multitude of the Kurujāṅgalas witnessed Kṛṣṇā helpless in the assembly hall — conduct wholly devoid of the practice of dharma — who other than you, O Pāṇḍava, could have endured that?'
'Without doubt, with all desires fulfilled, you will soon rightfully protect your subjects. We are here for the subjugation of the Kurus — if your vow is completed.'
The lion of the Dāśārhas addressed Dhaumya, Kṛṣṇā, Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, and Bhīma: 'By fortune, the diadem-wearer has arrived to your auspicious company — joyful and his weapons mastered.'

The lord of the Dāśārhas also spoke to Kṛṣṇā Yājñasenī, surrounded by his friends: 'O Kṛṣṇe, your sons — devoted chiefly to the science of archery, steadfast in their vows, of good character — ever practice the concentration always cultivated by the virtuous, O Yājñasenī.'
'Though invited with kingdoms and realms by their father and by your brothers, O Kṛṣṇe, your sons do not find delight dwelling in the houses of Yajñasena or of their maternal uncles.'
'With auspicious intent they face Ānarta; your sons, devoted chiefly to the science of archery, having gone and entered the city of the Vṛṣṇis, do not envy even the gods, O Kṛṣṇe.'
'Just as you yourself are worthy of rendering your conduct toward them, and just as the noble Kuntī always tends to them with care — so too does Subhadrā, and even more so.'
'As he is to Aniruddha, as he is to Abhimanyu, as he is to Sunītha, and as he is to Bhānu — so too is the son of Rukmiṇī the guide and protector of your sons, O Kṛṣṇe.'

'He tirelessly and properly trains those heroes in the wielding of maces, swords, and shields, in missile-lore and instruction, and in chariot and horse-riding; and the young Abhimanyu trains them constantly as well.'
'And he too, having properly imparted the training and the weapons to your sons like a teacher, rejoices in the feats of valor of both your sons and Abhimanyu — so says the son of Rukmiṇī.'
'Whenever your sons set out for recreation, O Yājñasenī, chariots, vehicles, and elephants follow behind each and every one of them.'
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke to Dharmarāja: 'The warriors of the Dāśārhas, the Kukuras and the Andhakas — these all observe your command; they stand wherever you wish them to stand, O king.'

'Let the army of the Madhus be set in motion — swept by the wind of bowstring-speed, guided by the grasp of the Ploughshare-wielder — ready for your purposes, O lord of men, with cavalry, infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants.'
'Let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra be sent forth, O Pāṇḍava — Suyodhana, foremost among evildoers — along with his relatives and his multitude of allies, along the path of Saubha and the lord of Saubha.'
'Stay there as long as you wish, O lord of men, according to the agreement you made in the assembly; but let Nāgapura await you with the Dāśārha warriors and their cavalry-fighters.'
'With your anger gone and your sin removed, roam wherever you desire at will; thereafter, free from sorrow and in fullness, you shall first attain Nāgapura together with its realm.'
Then the great-souled Dharmarāja, having understood and duly considered the opinion expressed by the best of men, praised it and with hands folded in reverence spoke to Keśava thus:
'Without doubt, O Keśava, you are the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas; the Pārthas seek shelter in you. When the time arrives, you will accomplish that and more — of this there is no doubt.'
'The time has been spent as pledged; all twelve years in the wilderness have been passed, and after duly completing the year of incognito life, the sons of Pāṇḍu will come to you, O Keśava.'

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the Vṛṣṇi lord and Dharmarāja were thus speaking, O Bhārata, thereafter appeared the righteous-souled Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerity — grown aged by austerity, the bearer of thousands upon thousands of years.
All the brahmins honored that arriving sage, aged with thousands upon thousands of years, and so did Kṛṣṇa together with the Pāṇḍavas.
When that best of sages had been honored and sat at ease, Keśava spoke — in accord with the minds of the brahmins and the Pāṇḍavas.
'These Pāṇḍavas are eager to hear, and the brahmins have assembled; Draupadī, Satyabhāmā, and I likewise — all desire your supreme words.'
'Holy tales of ancient times, the eternal customs of right conduct of kings, women, and sages — O Mārkaṇḍeya, declare these to us.'
While they were seated there, the divine seer Nārada too arrived — of pure soul — to behold the Pāṇḍavas.
All those bulls among men then duly attended that great-souled and wise one as well, with water for the feet and the guest-offering, according to proper rite.
Then the divine seer Nārada, perceiving that they were in an appropriate moment, approved of the discourse that Mārkaṇḍeya was about to deliver.
And that Nārada, knower of the right time, spoke to him with something like a smile: 'O brahmin-seer, let what you desire to say to the Pāṇḍavas be told.'
Thus addressed, Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerity replied: 'Allow an ample moment — much will need to be narrated.'
Thus addressed, the Pāṇḍavas together with those brahmins fell silent for a moment, gazing upon that great sage as one gazes at the midday sun.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Perceiving that great sage ready to speak, the Kuru king, the son of Pāṇḍu, urged him on in order to give rise to the discourse.
'You are the eternal knower of the deeds of gods and demons, of great-souled seers, and of all royal sages.'
'You are worthy of service and veneration in our eyes, long desired by us. And this son of Devakī has arrived to behold us.'
'Indeed my mind becomes troubled when I see myself fallen from happiness and behold the ill-behaved sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra prospering in every way.'
'A person is the doer of his action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, and he reaps the fruit thereof — how then is the agent himself an independent lord?'
'Or, O best among knowers of Brahman, does what is done here follow men in their pleasure and pain into another body, or yet again in this very life?'
'And when the embodied soul abandons the body — pursued by auspicious and inauspicious deeds — how does it become united with them after death, or in this very life, O best of twice-born?'
'Is this pertaining only to this world or also to the next? And where do the deeds of a creature abide after it has died, O descendant of Bhṛgu?'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: 'This supplementary inquiry befits you, O best among speakers. What needs to be known is already known to you; you ask in order to understand the principle rightly.'
'On this I will instruct you — listen here with one-pointed mind — how a person experiences pleasure and pain both in this world and in the next.'
'Prajāpati, born before all others, fashioned the bodies of embodied beings as pure and spotless, bound by the web of dharma.'
'Those ancient, holy men had infallible strength and purpose, were of excellent vows, spoke truth, had become one with Brahman — O joy of the Kurus.'
'All of them would rise with the gods of their own free will into the sky, and they would all come back again, moving freely at will.'
'Men died at will and lived at will; they had little affliction, were free from distress, their purposes accomplished, undisturbed by calamities.'
'They were seers of assemblies of gods and of great-souled sages; all dharmas were direct and manifest to them; they were self-restrained and free from envy.'
'They lived for thousands of years, and likewise had thousands of sons. Then, in another age, they became wanderers on the surface of the earth.'
'Overcome by desire and wrath, living by deceit and fraud, overwhelmed by greed and delusion — those men were then abandoned by the gods.'
'Sinful through inauspicious deeds, destined for animal births and hell, they were cooked again and again in the varied rounds of transmigration.'
'Their desires were vain, their purposes vain, their knowledge vain; they were witless, filled with excessive suspicion, burdened with affliction, and mostly marked by inauspicious deeds.'

'Of base lineage, afflicted by many diseases, evil-souled, causing no remorse to others, they become short-lived sinners bearing the fruit of terrible deeds — seekers of all desires, unbelievers, breakers of sacred bonds.'

'The course of a creature after death is determined by its own deeds here, O son of Kuntī — but where does the storehouse of karma abide, for the wise man and for the man of poor understanding alike?'
'And dwelling where does it experience the merit or the demerit? This is your question — and hear now on that point also the elucidation.'
'This human being, with the primal body created by the gods, accumulates a great store of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds.'
'At the end of life, abandoning this nearly exhausted body, it comes into being simultaneously in the womb — there is no intermediate existence.'
'There its self-wrought karma, ever following it like a shadow, bears fruit; and so it is born worthy of happiness or worthy of suffering.'
'That creature, conjoined with the ordinance of Fate, is perceived — endowed with auspicious or inauspicious marks, without disguise — by those possessed of the eye of knowledge.'
'This then is the course stated for the unintelligent, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Beyond this, understand now the supreme course of those endowed with knowledge.'
'Men who have practiced austerities, devoted to all the sacred scriptures, firm in their vows, intent on truth, delighting in service to the teacher —'
'— of good character, of a pure caste, patient, self-controlled, of excellent splendor, who have passed through a succession of auspicious wombs — mostly bear auspicious marks.'
'Through mastery of the senses they are self-controlled; through their purity they suffer little illness; through having little affliction and fear they are free from calamities.'

'With the eye of knowledge they perceive in every way their own self and the supreme self — departing, being born, and even while in the womb; and having reached this field of action, they return again to the abode of the gods.'
'Men attain things partly through fate, partly through perseverance, and partly through their own deeds, O king — let there be no other consideration in your mind.'
'And understand also this simile regarding this — O best among speakers — what I consider the supreme good in the world of men, O Yudhiṣṭhira.'
Here belongs to one person but not the next world; to another the next world but not this one here. Here and the next world to one; to another neither here nor the next world.

Those who possess abundant wealth and always delight in being adorned with fine ornaments — O slayer of the best of foes, this world is theirs; but that higher world is not for those who are ever devoted to bodily pleasure.

Those who are absorbed in yoga and engaged in austerity, who wear out their bodies in the practice of self-study, who have conquered the senses and are devoted to the welfare of all beings — O slayer of enemies, that higher world is theirs, not this one.
Those who put dharma foremost, who acquire wealth through dharma, and in due time having obtained a wife, perform sacrifices — both this world and the other belong to them.

Those who pursue neither learning, nor austerity, nor charity, who in their delusion make no effort even in procreation, and who, being unfortunate, attain no happiness — neither this world nor the other exists for them.

All of you are possessed of surpassing valour and spirit, endowed with divine energy and excellent bodies; you have descended from that higher world to earth, having studied your learning thoroughly, for the purpose of the gods' work.
Having performed great deeds as heroes, practiced austerity, self-restraint, and right conduct, and having duly satisfied the gods, seers, and all the hosts of the departed with proper rites —

— by your own deeds you shall in due course attain the highest heaven, the abode of the righteous. Let there be no anxiety in you, O lord of the Kauravas, upon seeing this present suffering of yourself — you who deserve happiness.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the sons of Pāṇḍu spoke to the great-souled Mārkaṇḍeya: "We wish to hear of the greatness of the foremost brahmins — please tell us of it."
Thus addressed, the blessed Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerity, of very great splendour and versed in all scriptures, spoke:
A king who established the Haihayas' lineage — a prince endowed with beauty, the conqueror of enemy citadels, mighty — went out hunting.

While ranging through the forest overgrown with grass and shrubs, he saw nearby a sage wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment. That sage was struck down by him in the forest, who mistook him for a deer.
Distressed at having done that deed and with his mind struck by grief, he went to the presence of those Haihaya kings of celebrated spirit.
That prince with lotus-like eyes, O lord of the earth, then related to those kings exactly what had occurred.
Upon hearing of that sage who subsisted on roots and fruits having been killed, and upon seeing it, O dear one, their minds became dejected.
Searching here and there asking "Whose is this man?", all of them went straight to the hermitage of Tarakshya Ariṣṭanemi.
They all saluted that great-souled sage of firm vow and stood before him; the sage then offered them worship.
They said to that great-souled one: "We are not worthy of your honour, O sage, for a brahmin has been killed through our fault."
That seer among brahmins said to them: "How was a brahmin killed among you? Where is he? Tell me all together — behold the power of my austerity."

Having related all of it to him fully and exactly as it happened, they came together to that place searching — but they did not see the sage there as one departed from life; they were ashamed, their minds wandering as if in a dream.
The sage Tarakshya, the conqueror of enemy citadels, spoke to them there: "The brahmin who was destroyed by you — he could be this one; he is my son, O kings, endowed with the power of austerity."
Upon seeing that sage they were filled with the highest astonishment, exclaiming "This is a great wonder indeed!" O lord of the earth.

"This one was dead, yet is seen here alive — how did he attain life again? What is this power of austerity by which he has come back to life? We wish to hear, O seer among brahmins, if it is fit to be heard."
He said to them: "Death has no power over us, O kings. I shall tell you the reason — the connection of causes — briefly."
"We know only truth; we do not set our minds on falsehood; we follow our own dharma — therefore we have no fear of death."
"We speak only of what is good for brahmins; we do not speak of their misconduct — therefore we have no fear of death."
"We satisfy guests with food and drink, servants with abundant food, and we dwell in the abode of the splendorous — therefore we have no fear of death."
"This much only, free of envy, has been told to you. Go all together — you need have no fear on account of sin."
Saying "So be it", all those kings, having honoured the great sage, went back to their own land rejoicing, O bull of the Bhāratas.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen further from me about the greatness of brahmins. Here a royal sage named Vainya was consecrated for the horse sacrifice; Atri undertook to go to him for the purpose of wealth — so we have heard.

But again he was not inclined to it on account of the clear indication of what is right; reflecting upon it, that one of great splendour chose the forest instead. Having summoned his devoted wife and his sons, he spoke thus:
"We shall attain an extremely abundant and untroubled fruit. Let going to the forest quickly be pleasing to you — it is superior in merit."
His wife, devoted to dharma, replied to him thus: "Go to the great-souled Vainya and ask him for much wealth. That royal sage, the sacrificer, will give wealth to one who asks for it."

"Then, O seer among brahmins, having accepted and received the abundant wealth, distributing it among your dependants and sons, go thereafter as you wish. This is declared to be the highest dharma by those who know dharma."
Atri said: "O fortunate one, the great-souled Gautama has told me about Vainya — that he is united with dharma and wealth, and endowed with the vow of truth."
"Yet there are those who hate me dwelling there — brahmins of mine, as Gautama has told me; therefore I am not resolved to go."
"They might pervert the auspicious words I spoke there, the words united with dharma, desire, and wealth — and thus render them fruitless."
"I shall go, O greatly wise one — your words please me; and Vainya will give me cows and an abundant accumulation of wealth."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the great ascetic quickly went to Vainya's sacrifice. Having gone to the sacrificial ground, Atri praised that king:
"O king, O Vainya, you are the lord; you are the foremost ruler upon the earth. The hosts of sages praise you; there is no one other than you who knows dharma."

Then a sage of great austerity spoke angrily to him: "Do not speak thus again, O Atri — your understanding is not collected. In this matter, our foremost authority is Mahendra, who is truly Prajāpati."
Then Atri also addressed Gautama, O lord of kings: "He is indeed the creator just as Indra is Prajāpati. It is you alone who are deluded through delusion; you have no true understanding."
Gautama said: "I know; I am not deluded. You, wishing to speak, are deluded. You will praise him, seeking prosperity, by resorting to his presence."
"You do not know the highest dharma, nor do you understand its purpose. You are childish and foolish — called an elder only by some reason or other."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: As those two were thus disputing in the sight of the sages, those who were assembled at his sacrifice asked: "How are these two —"
"— who gave these two entry into Vainya's assembly? Speaking loudly, for what purpose do they stand here?"
Then Kaśyapa, of supremely righteous soul and versed in all dharma, presented those two disputants as they had arrived.
Then Gautama spoke to those best of sages among the assembly members: "Hear the question stated by us two, O foremost of twice-born. Atri says Vainya is the creator — herein lies our great doubt."
Upon hearing this, those great-souled sages quickly ran to Sanatkumāra, the knower of dharma, in order to resolve the doubt.
Having heard their words, that great ascetic replied to them in accordance with truth, speaking these words joined with dharma and purpose:

Sanatkumāra said: "Brahmā joined with kshatriya power, and kshatriya power joined with brahma — the king is indeed the foremost dharma and lord of subjects. He himself is Śakra, and Śukra, and Dhata, and Bṛhaspati."
"Prajāpati, Virat, Samrat, kshatriya, lord of the earth, ruler — he who is praised by these titles: who would not be worthy of honouring him?"
"Primordial source, victor in battle, fearless, joyous in being, golden-eyed, born-conqueror, tawny one — thus is the king designated."
"True in wrath, living by combat, setter of truth and dharma in motion — when the seers were afraid of adharma, they placed their strength in the kshatriya."
"As the sun among the gods in heaven dispels darkness with its radiance, so too the king upon the earth mightily dispels adharma."
"Therefore the king's pre-eminence is established by the authority of scripture; the latter position is proved, the one by which it is declared 'the king'."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that king, greatly rejoiced with his position established, that high-minded one, spoke with pleasure to Atri who had formerly praised him:
"Since among all men here you declared me to be the greatest, O seer among brahmins, equal to all the gods and the very best — therefore I shall give you various and abundant goods."
"A thousand dark-skinned maidservants adorned with fine garments, ten crores of gold, and likewise ten loads of gold — this I give you, O brahmin; for you are in my view omniscient."
Having righteously accepted all of that, that high-minded, splendorous, great ascetic Atri returned home.
Having joyfully distributed the wealth to his sons, that one of controlled soul, having resolved upon austerity, departed for the forest.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: And here also, O conqueror of enemy citadels, hear what was sung by Sarasvatī when questioned by the wise sage Tarakshya, O hero.

Tarakshya said: "What indeed is highest good for a man in this world, O auspicious one? Acting how does one not fall from one's own dharma? Tell me everything, O one beautiful in all your limbs — instructed by you, may I not fall from my own dharma."
"How should I offer into fire, or how worship? At what time, by what means does dharma not perish? Tell me all this, O fortunate one — so that I may move through the worlds spotless."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus questioned with joy by him, beholding Tarakshya, that brahmin endowed with highest intelligence, devoted to dharma, and well-intentioned, Sarasvatī spoke these words:

Sarasvatī said: "One who knows Brahman according to proper instruction, who is constant in self-study, pure, and vigilant — he will indeed go to the fore of the city of the gods; he will attain union with joy together with the immortals."
"There are lovely, vast, grief-free, richly blossoming sacred lotus-ponds of great merit — free of mud, full of fish, with fine bathing-ghats, surrounded by golden lotuses."
"On the banks of those ponds the doer of meritorious deeds sits, honoured separately by apsaras adorned with most holy fragrances, golden-complexioned — exceedingly joyful."
"Givers of cows attain the highest world; those who give a bull go to the world of the sun. One who gives a garment goes to the world of the moon; one who gives gold attains immortality."
"One who gives a well-behaved cow, good in milking, auspicious, gentle in nature and pace — for as many hairs as she has, for that many years does one enjoy the heavenly world."
"One who gives a bull of good conduct, a bearer of the plough, of boundless vigour, yoke-bearing, powerful, and young — such a person attains ten times the worlds of the cow-giver."

"One who for seven years, O Tarakshya, duly offers oblations into fire, of good vow and virtuous conduct — he purifies by his own deeds seven generations forward and seven generations of his own ancestors."
Tarakshya said: "What is the ancient vow of the agnihotra? Tell me as I ask, O one of beautiful form. Instructed by you I have today the knowledge — but what is the ancient vow of the agnihotra?"

Sarasvatī said: "One who is impure, or one whose hands are unwashed, one ignorant of Brahman, or one without discernment — should not offer; for the gods desire purity and do not accept oblations from one who lacks faith."

"One should not engage one ignorant of the Vedas in the gods' oblation — such a one pours fruitlessly into the beyond; the one ignorant of the Vedas is declared incomplete, O Tarakshya; such a one should not offer the agnihotra."

"Those who offer to fire with faith, who hold the vow of truth and eat the remnants of oblations — having attained the world of cows with its holy fragrance, they behold the Supreme God and Truth itself."

Tarakshya said: "Reflecting upon you — one who has become a knower of the field in the nature of the other world, whose intelligence has deeply entered into the arising of karma, and who bears a divine wisdom, O fortunate one — I ask you: who indeed are you, O one of beautiful form?"

Sarasvatī said: "I have come forth from the agnihotra, to resolve the doubt of the foremost among brahmin seers. Through my meeting with you I have spoken all this — standing in truth, the true meaning exactly as it is."
Tarakshya said: "There is indeed no one equal to you; you shine exceedingly like Śrī herself. Your form is divine and supremely lovely, and you bear a divine wisdom, O fortunate one."

Sarasvatī said: "The finest things which the best of two-footed beings, O learned one, offer at sacrifices — by those very things I grow and flourish; nourished by them I become beautiful in form, O brahmin."
Know this, O learned one: whatever material is used — whether of plant, metal, or earth — it is through divine form and wisdom together that perfection is achieved.
Tārkṣya said: The sages of established repute, considering this the supreme good, strive for it. Tell me of that supreme liberation, free from sorrow, into which the wise enter.

Sarasvatī said: Those who know the Vedas have attained to that supreme state — the ancient one proclaimed as highest among the high. Ascetics enriched by self-study, charity, vows, and meritorious practice are freed from sorrow and liberated.
In the midst of that realm there shines a holy-scented reed with a thousand branches, pure and resplendent; from its roots flow rivers, delightful streams flowing with honey-sweet waters.
Toward branch after branch great rivers flow, their sands fine as grain; there are parched grain and cakes, meat and vegetables, and always currents of milk-pudding flowing like streams of mud.
In that place, O sage, the gods led by Indra, having fire as their mouth, together with the Marut hosts have worshipped with the most excellent sacrificial rites — that is the supreme abode.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the son of Pāṇḍu spoke again to Mārkaṇḍeya: "Tell me here the deeds of Manu, the son of Vivasvat."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The son of Vivasvat, O king, became a great sage, mighty in glory, O tiger among men, with a radiance equal to that of Prajāpati.
In vigor, brilliance, prosperity, and especially in austerity, Manu surpassed his own father and his grandfather as well.
That lord of men, standing on one foot with arms raised in the great expanse of Badarī forest, performed fierce and exceedingly great austerity.
With head bent down and eyes unwinking, firm and steadfast, he then practiced terrible austerity for ten thousand years.
Once, while he was practicing austerity, wearing wet bark garments and matted locks, a fish came to the bank of the Vīriṇī river and spoke to him.
"Blessed one, I am a small fish; I am afraid of the stronger ones, for fishes eat fishes — therefore you, O one of holy vows, should protect me."
"Indeed, the strong ones especially devour the weak fish — such is the eternal law of conduct ordained for us."
"Therefore, as I sink especially beneath this great flood of fear, you should protect me; in return I will render back what you have done for me."
Hearing the fish's words, overwhelmed with compassion, Manu Vaivasvata himself took that fish in his own hands.
Manu Vaivasvata, having brought it to the water's edge, placed that fish — radiant as the rays of the moon — into a jar.
There the fish grew, O king, treated with the utmost care, and Manu developed a particularly fond feeling toward it, as toward a son.
Then, after a long time, that fish grew exceedingly large, and it no longer fit at all in the water of the jar.
Then, seeing Manu, the fish spoke to him again: "Blessed one, please provide me another suitable place today."
Then that blessed sage Manu, having lifted the fish from the jar, brought it to a great pond.
Manu placed it there, O conqueror of enemy cities, and the fish grew again for many more years.
The pond was two yojanas long and one yojana wide; the fish, O lotus-eyed one, could no longer fit in it, O son of Kuntī, O lord of peoples — nor could it move freely in the pond.
Then seeing Manu, the fish spoke to him again: "Lead me, blessed and noble lord, to the Gaṅgā, queen of the ocean — I will dwell there, or as you think best, dear one."
Thus addressed, Manu the self-controlled blessed one brought the fish to the river Gaṅgā and himself placed it there.
The fish grew there for some time, O subduer of foes; then seeing Manu again, the fish spoke these words.
"In the Gaṅgā I am no longer able to move freely, being so large, O lord; take me quickly to the ocean — be gracious, O blessed one."
Lifting the fish from the waters of the Gaṅgā, Manu himself then brought it, O Pārtha, to the ocean and released it there.
Though grown exceedingly large, the fish was then as if drawn by Manu's very mind — delightful to behold, pleasing to touch and smell.
When that fish had been cast into the ocean by Manu, it then spoke these words to him, smiling as it were.
"Blessed one, you have given me complete and exceptional protection; now hear from me what you must do when the time arrives."
"Before long, O blessed and great one, all of this earth — both the moving and the unmoving — will surely go to dissolution."
"The time for the washing away of the worlds has arrived; therefore I alert you today to what is of supreme benefit to you."
"The dreadful time has arrived for all of it — for animals and plants alike, for whatever moves and whatever does not move."
"You must have a strong ship built, equipped with ropes of hemp; together with the seven sages you shall board it, O great sage."
"And you shall board that ship with all the seeds as previously described by me, well preserved in their different categories."
"Standing on the ship, you shall then await me, O dear one to the community of sages; I will come bearing a horn — by that you shall know me, O ascetic."
"This is what you must do; you have been instructed, I go now; and this word of mine should not be doubted overmuch by you, O mighty one."
He replied to the fish: "So shall I do"; and having taken leave of each other as they wished, the two parted.
Then Manu, O great king, just as the fish had instructed, took all the seeds and sailed out on the ocean, O hero, on an auspicious ship upon the vast waves, O subduer of foes.
And Manu meditated upon that fish, O lord of the earth; knowing that thought, the fish — bearing its horn — swiftly came there then, O best of the Bhāratas, O conqueror of enemy cities.
Seeing it, O lord among lords of men, Manu beheld the fish in the ocean — horned and risen like a mountain, exactly in the form foretold.
Then Manu, O tiger among men, placed a noose made of hemp rope on the head of the fish — on that very horn.
Bound by that noose, the fish, O conqueror of enemy cities, drew the ship with great speed across the salt sea.
He crossed the ocean in that ship, O lord of men, the sea as if dancing with its waves and roaring with its waters.
Tossed by mighty winds, the ship whirled about on that great ocean like a fickle, intoxicated woman, O conqueror of enemy cities.
Neither earth nor the directions nor the intermediate directions were visible; all was nothing but water — and sky and heaven, O bull among men.
With the world in such a condition and in confusion, O bull of the Bhāratas, the seven sages, Manu, and the fish alone were visible.
Thus for many years the fish tirelessly pulled that ship, O king, across that expanse of water.
Then the fish pulled the ship to the highest peak of the Himālayas, O bull among men, O joy of the Kurus.
Then the fish gently said with a laugh to those sages: "Bind the ship quickly to this peak of the Himālayas."
It was quickly bound there by those sages, O bull of the Bhāratas, the ship — hearing the words of the fish — to the peak of the Himālayas then.
And that highest peak of the Himālayas, known as Naubandhanam — the Ship's Mooring — is famous even today; know this, O son of Kuntī, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then the unblinking one spoke to those assembled sages: "I am Prajāpati Brahmā; nothing higher than me is attainable. In fish form, by me, you have been saved from this danger."
"And by Manu all beings must be created — gods, asuras, and humans — and all the worlds, both the moving and the unmoving."
"Through the most intense austerity he will shine forth, and by my grace in the work of creation he will not fall into delusion."
Having spoken these words, the fish vanished in a moment. Manu Vaivasvata himself, wishing to create beings, became bewildered at the act of creation and thereafter practiced great austerity.
Armed with great austerity, Manu then proceeded to create all beings directly and properly, O bull of the Bhāratas.
This is the ancient Mātsyaka legend, thus celebrated; this narrative has been recited by me — it removes all sins.
The man who regularly hears from the beginning this account of Manu's deeds shall be happy, successful in all purposes, and shall attain the heavenly world.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira, endowed with humility, questioned the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya again.
"O great sage, you have witnessed the ends of many thousands of yugas, and no one here is equal to your lifespan, save only the great-souled brahmin Parameṣṭhin."
"In this world devoid of sky, bereft of gods and demons, you alone, O brahmin, attend upon Brahmā at the time of dissolution."
"And when dissolution has ended and the Grandfather has awakened, you alone witness the beings being created here."
"O brahmin sage, the four kinds of beings are created properly by Parameṣṭhin, who, having become wind, sets the directions and scatters the waters this way and that."
"By you, O best of the twice-born, the world's teacher, the Grandfather of all the worlds directly, has been worshipped with meditation wholly fixed on him."
"Therefore, O brahmin sage, all-ending death, or old age the destroyer of the body, does not enter into you, by the grace of Parameṣṭhin."
"When there is neither sun nor fire, neither wind nor moon, neither sky nor earth — when nothing whatsoever remains —"
"— in that world become a single ocean, when the moving and the unmoving are destroyed, when the hosts of gods and demons are destroyed, when the great serpents are annihilated —"
"— you alone attend upon the infinite-souled Brahmā lying on a lotus, dwelling in the lotus, the lord of all beings."
"All of this past occurrence was directly witnessed by you, O best of the twice-born. Therefore we wish to hear the narrative that comprehends all causes."
"It has been experienced many times by you alone, O best of the twice-born; there is nothing unknown to you in all the worlds, ever."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Very well, I will tell you — having bowed to the Self-Born, to the Ancient Puruṣa, the Eternal, the Imperishable."
"He who is this one with broad and long eyes, clothed in yellow — Janārdana — he is the maker and the unmake, the creator of all beings and existences."
"He is unthinkable, greatly wondrous, supremely pure, without beginning or end, the universal Being, inexhaustible, imperishable."
"He is the doer but is not done; he is the cause in human affairs. Whoever truly knows this Puruṣa — even the gods do not know him."
"All of this is wondrous indeed, O best of kings, O tiger among men, from the very beginning, at the dissolution of the entire world."
"Four thousand years, they say, is the Kṛta yuga; its twilight is as many hundreds, and after that comes the twilight-portion equally."
"Three thousand years is here called the Tretā yuga; its twilight is as many hundreds, and after that comes the twilight-portion equally."
"Likewise two thousand years is the measure of the Dvāpara; its twilight too is two hundred years, and after that the twilight-portion equally."

One thousand years is declared the Kali age; its twilight is one hundred years, and after that the twilight-fraction likewise — understand that the twilight and the twilight-fraction are equal in measure.
When the Kali age has expired, the Kṛta age commences again. This cycle of twelve thousand years is celebrated as the span of a yuga.

A thousand such cycles constitute what is called one day of Brahmā. The entire universe revolves continuously within Brahmā's abode, O tiger among men; the wise call that the dissolution of the worlds.
When little remains of the age, O bull of the Bhāratas, at the end of the thousand-year cycle, almost all men become speakers of falsehood.
In that era, O Pārtha, substitutes for sacrifice, substitutes for giving, and substitutes for vows prevail everywhere.
Brahmins perform the duties of śūdras; śūdras pursue wealth-earning; and some maintain themselves by the law of warriors — such is the state when the age has passed.
In the Kali age brahmins will abandon sacrifice and Vedic recitation, will neglect the offerings of food and water to ancestors, and will eat everything indiscriminately.
Brahmins will cease to recite mantras, dear one, while śūdras will be devoted to repetition of prayers. When the world is thus inverted, that is the first sign of the final dissolution.
Many mleccha kings will rule the earth, O lord of men — sinful rulers who govern unjustly and are wholly devoted to falsehood.
Āndhra kings, Śakas, Pulindas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Aurṇikas, śūdras, and Ābhīras, O best of men — all will rule as lords of the earth.
Then no brahmin will live by his own dharma, and kṣatriyas and vaiśyas too will be established in wrong livelihood, O lord of men.
Men will be short-lived, of little strength, of scant energy and valour, of puny body and little substance, and sparing in speaking the truth.

When the end of the age arrives, districts will be largely deserted, the regions will be overrun by deer and beasts of prey, the celibate students will be false, śūdras will use the honorific 'bho,' and brahmins will address each other as 'ārya.'

At the end of the age, O tiger among men, many creatures will be born, yet the sense of smell will not register all fragrances as before, O lord of the people, and tastes too will not yield their former sweetness, O tiger among men.
Women will be prolific but small in body, devoid of virtue and good conduct, and bold of face and tongue, O king — such will they be at the decline of the age.
Districts will be marked by watchtower-stakes, crossroads by jackal-stakes, and women by the stake of their hair, O king — so it will be at the decline of the age.
Cows will give little milk, O lord of the people, trees will bear few flowers and fruits, and crows will abound.
Twice-born men will accept gifts from kings who are tainted with the murder of brahmins and who are false accusers, O guardian of the earth.
Overcome by greed and delusion, wrapped in the banner of false dharma, the twice-born will wander the directions in search of alms, O guardian of the earth.
Householders, fearing the burden of taxes, will become plunderers; disguised under the pretence of ascetics' garb, they will make their living by trade.
Men will falsely wear long nails and body hair out of greed for wealth, O tiger among men, and celibate students will live in vain observance.
Those in the hermitages will be of worthless conduct — drunkards, violators of their teacher's bed — and they will seek only worldly gain, the fattening of flesh and blood.
At the decline of the age, O tiger among men, hermitages will be crowded with many heretics who praise the food of others — true hermitages will not exist.
The glorious Indra will not rain seasonably then, O Bhārata; all seeds will not sprout properly; and the fruit of unrighteousness will be exceedingly great in that time, O sinless one.
And in that time, O guardian of the earth, whoever is endowed with dharma is to be considered short-lived — there is no dharma of any kind that avails.
People will sell goods mostly by false weights and measures, and merchants, O tiger among men, will be full of deceit.
The righteous will decline and the sinful will increase; dharma will lose its strength while adharma will wax powerful.
In the decline of the age, those humans who are most righteous will be short-lived and poor, while those who are lawless will be long-lived and prosperous.
People will deal by means of unrighteous stratagems, and even with a small hoard they become wealthy and arrogant.
Men, acting with trickery, will for the most part be determined to steal wealth that has been entrusted to them by others in good faith, O king.
Man-eating creatures, birds and beasts alike, will take their rest in the pleasure-gardens and sacred-tree shrines of cities.
Women of seven or eight years will bear children, O king, and men of ten or twelve years will beget sons.
Men will grow grey at sixteen years of age, and the shortening of human life-span will come about very swiftly.
When the age is in decline, O great king, the young will have the ways of the old, and the conduct proper to the young will appear among the old.
Women, perverse in that time and of vile character, will secretly deceive their husbands and commit adultery even with slaves and animals.
At the end of that thousand-year cycle, when the shortening of life has arrived, a drought lasting many years will arise, O great king.
Then those beings, who are of little substance and racked by hunger, will for the most part perish upon the earth, O guardian of the earth.
Then seven blazing suns will drink up all the water in the oceans and rivers, O lord of men.
Whatever is wood and whatever is grass, dry or wet, O Bhārata — all of it is seen reduced to ash, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then the fire of universal dissolution, together with the wind, O Bhārata, enters the world that was already parched by the suns.
Then, piercing the earth and penetrating into the netherworld, it generates great fear among the gods, demons, and yakṣas.
Burning the realm of the serpents and whatever else exists beneath the earth here, O guardian of the earth, it destroys everything in an instant.
Then that inauspicious wind and that fire of dissolution together consume hundreds of thousands of twenty-yojana expanses.
Then that all-pervading, blazing fire burns the entire world together with gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas.
Then great clouds resembling herds of elephants, adorned with garlands of lightning, rise up in the sky, marvellous to behold.
Some are dark as blue lotuses, some resemble white water-lilies, some look like lotus filaments, and some are yellow cloud-masses.
Some are like turmeric in hue, some resemble the kākāṇḍaka fruit, some have the lustre of lotus petals, and some glow like asafoetida resin.

Some are shaped like great cities, some resemble herds of elephants, some look like collyrium, some are formed like sea-monsters — their limbs wreathed with garlands of lightning, the clouds rise up in hosts.
Terrible in form, O great king, resounding with dreadful thunder, all those rain-bearing clouds then pervade the expanse of the sky.
By them this whole earth, with its mountains, forests, and mines, is filled to overflowing and flooded with torrents of water, O great king.
Then those fearsome roaring clouds, O bull among men, urged on by Brahmā, quickly inundate everything on all sides.
Pouring down mighty waters and filling the earth, they extinguish the most terrible, inauspicious, and fierce fire.
Then for twelve years those clouds, in the great deluge, fill everything with their torrents, urged on by the great soul Brahmā.
Then the ocean overflows its shoreline, O Bhārata, the mountains crumble, and the earth itself disintegrates.
Then those clouds, suddenly scattering in all directions, envelop the sky and vanish, struck down by the force of the wind.
Then the self-born lord, O lord of men, that god whose primal abode is the lotus, drinks up that terrible wind and falls asleep, O Bhārata.
In that terrible single ocean, when all that is moving and unmoving has perished, when the hosts of gods and asuras have perished, with yakṣas and rākṣasas gone —
— with the earth empty of men, O guardian of the earth, devoid of beasts and great trees, with sky uninterrupted, in this world I alone wander with great care.
Wandering in the terrible water of that single ocean, O best of earthly lords, seeing no living beings at all, I fell into the utmost distress.
Then, drifting for a very long time, O lord of men, I grew weary, and though tireless I found shelter nowhere.
Then at a certain moment I beheld in that flood of waters a vast and expansive banyan tree, O guardian of the earth.
On a wide branch of that tree, O lord of men, on a couch spread with a divine coverlet, O guardian of the earth —
— I see a child seated there, O great king, whose face resembles the full moon, whose large eyes are like blooming lotuses, O Bhārata.
Then a very great wonder arose in me, O guardian of the earth: how can this infant be resting when the world has come to its destruction?
Even concentrating my tapas and reflecting upon that infant, I could not discern him, though I know all that has been, all that is, and all that shall be, O lord of men.
He was of the colour of a flax flower, marked with the Śrīvatsa sign — he appeared to me then as a dwelling-place of Śrī herself made manifest.
Then that child, whose eyes resembled lotuses, who bore the Śrīvatsa mark and was radiant, spoke to me words pleasing to the ear.
'I know you are weary and longing for rest, dear one. Sit here, Mārkaṇḍeya, as long as you wish, O descendant of Bhṛgu.'
'Enter within my body, O best of sages, and dwell there — a dwelling has been prepared for you; this grace is done to you by me.'
Then, spoken to thus by that child, I felt at that moment a profound weariness with my long life and with the human condition, O Bhārata.
Then that child suddenly opened his mouth, and I, helpless, was drawn by divine agency into that mouth.
Then, having entered that belly instantly, O lord of men, I see the entire earth crowded with kingdoms and cities.
I see the Gaṅgā, the Śatadru, the Sītā, the Yamunā, the Kauśikī, the Carmaṇvatī, the Vetravatī, the Candrabhāgā, and the Sarasvatī.
And the Sindhu, the Vipāśā, the river Godāvarī, the Vasvokasārā, the Nalinī, and the Narmadā as well, O Bhārata.
The river Tāmrā, the Veṇṇā of holy and auspicious waters, the Suveṇā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Irāmā, the great river Śoṇa, O tiger among men, the Viśalyā, and the Kampu as well.
These and the other rivers of the earth, O best of men, I see as I wander through the belly of that great soul, beholding them as I roam.
Then I see the ocean, frequented by hosts of aquatic creatures, the mine of jewels, O slayer of foes, the great treasury of waters.
Then I see the sky resplendent with moon and sun, blazing with radiances equal to fire and sun. And I see the earth, O king, adorned with forests.
For there brahmins perform sacrifice with abundant oblations, O king, and kṣatriyas apply themselves to the delighting of all the social orders.
Vaiśyas carry on agriculture in the proper manner, O lord of men, and śūdras too are devoted to the service of the twice-born.
Then, O king, flying within the belly of that great soul, I behold the Himavat and also the mountain Hemakūṭa.
I see the Niṣadha and also the Śveta mountain gleaming with silver, and, O lord of the earth, I see the mountain Gandhamādana.
O tiger among men, I see Mandara, and also the great mountain Nīla, and, O great king, I see Meru, the golden mountain.
I see Mahendra and the foremost of mountains the Vindhya, and I also see the Malaya and the mountain Pāriyātra.
These and many other mountains, however many uphold the earth — all of them were seen by me in his belly, adorned with every kind of jewel.
O lord of men, O master of the world — lions, tigers, boars, and serpents, and whatever other creatures exist on the earth — all of these I beheld there as I roamed about at that time.
O tiger among men, having entered his belly and wandering through the directions, I also see Indra and the rest — indeed, all the hosts of gods in their entirety.

O lord of the earth, O master of men — gandharvas, apsarases, yakṣas, and sages as well; the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, the Kāleyas, the sons of Siṃhikā, and whatever other enemies of the gods there are.
Whatever I had seen in the world, moving or unmoving — all of that I now saw within the belly of that great soul, as I wandered about, feeding on fruits, traversing this entire world at that time.
Within his body I dwelt for more than a hundred years, yet nowhere could I find any end of his body.
Constantly running and contemplating, O lord of peoples, O king, I could find no end at all of that great soul.
Then I sought refuge in him alone, that most worthy boon-giving god, with mind and deed, in the proper manner.
Then suddenly, O king, O best of men, I was expelled with the speed of wind from the opened mouth of that great soul.
Then, O lord of peoples, O tiger among men, he sat upon a branch of that very fig tree, having taken up the entire world.
O tiger among men, I see him seated there in that same form of a child, marked with the sign of Śrīvatsa, of immeasurable splendour.
Then, O hero, that child spoke to me, smiling as it were — the bearer of the Śrīvatsa mark, radiant, clad in yellow garments, of great brilliance.
"O best of sages, O Mārkaṇḍeya, have you now dwelt within this body of mine and rested well? Tell me."
After a moment my sight returned anew, by which I saw myself freed and having regained my senses.
His two feet, dear one, with coppery soles, well-planted and beautifully formed, adorned with soft rosy toes —
— with my head, purified, I took hold of them and reverenced them, having seen the boundless power of that one of immeasurable might.
Making a reverent gesture with joined palms and approaching with devotion, I gazed upon that god, the soul of all beings, lotus-eyed.
I, with joined palms, bowed to him and spoke thus: "O god, I wish to know you and this your supreme illusive power."
"O blessed one, having entered through your mouth into your body, I have seen all the worlds in their entirety within your belly."
"O god, within your body dwell gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas; yakṣas, gandharvas, and nāgas; and the world, both moving and unmoving."
"And by your grace, O god, my memory has not failed me, even while running swiftly and constantly within the interior of your body."
"O lotus-eyed one, O blameless one, I wish to know you — having become a child here, why do you remain thus, having drunk in this entire universe? You ought to explain this to me."
"And for what purpose, O sinless one, is the entire world lodged within your body? O subduer of foes, how long must you remain here?"
"O lord of gods, O lotus-petal-eyed one, this I wish to hear from you, O lord, out of the desire of a brahmin — fully and truthfully — for what I have witnessed is great and inconceivable."
Thus addressed by me, that glorious god of gods, of great brilliance, the foremost of speakers, consoling me, spoke these words.
The god said: "O brahmin, even the gods do not truly know me in reality. But out of affection for you, I shall declare how I send forth this world."
"O brahmin-seer, you are devoted to your ancestors and have taken refuge in me; therefore I have appeared to you directly, and your celibate discipline is great."
"The waters are called Nārā — a name I have given as designation; since that is always my resting place, I am called Nārāyaṇa."
"I am named Nārāyaṇa, the origin, eternal, imperishable, the ordainer of all beings, and also their destroyer, O best of twice-born."
"I am Viṣṇu, I am Brahmā, and I am Śakra, lord of the gods; I am king Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama the lord of the departed."
"I am Śiva and Soma, and Kaśyapa the lord of creatures; I am Dhātā and Vidhātā, and I am sacrifice itself, O best of twice-born."
"Fire is my mouth, the earth is my feet, the moon and sun are my two eyes, the sky together with its directions is my body, and wind abides in my mind."
"By me have hundreds of sacrifices been performed with many well-bestowed fees; those who know the Vedas worship me, established in the sacrifice of the gods."
"On earth, lords of kṣatriyas and kings who desire heaven worship me; likewise vaiśyas who seek to win the heavenly world."
"Having become Śeṣa the serpent, I alone uphold this earth, bounded by the four oceans and adorned by Meru and Mandara."
"Having assumed the boar form, this earth, which was sinking in the waters long ago, was lifted up by me through valour, O brahmin."
"O best of twice-born, having become the fire with the mare-mouth, I drink the waters that are stirred up, and then I release them again."
"The brahmin is my face, the kṣatriya my arms; the vaiśyas resort to my thighs; the śūdras worship me through my feet, step by step."
"The Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda, and also the Yajurveda and the Atharvaṇa — these emerge from me and into me alone they return."
"Ascetics whose highest aim is peace, those who restrain their souls and seek liberation, freed from desire, anger, and hatred, unattached, cleansed of impurity —"
"— those brahmins who abide in the quality of sattva, free of ego, ever versed in the knowledge of the self, constantly contemplating me — they worship me."
"I am the fire of dissolution, I am the all-consuming Yama; I am the sun of dissolution, I am the wind of dissolution."
"Those star-forms that are seen in the vault of the sky — know these to be forms of mine, O best of twice-born."
"The oceans, mines of gems, in all four directions — know these to be my garment, my bed, and my abode."
"Desire, anger, joy, fear, and delusion likewise — know all these to be forms of mine, O good one."
"What men, O brahmin, attain through performing meritorious action — truth, charity, severe austerity, and non-violence toward creatures —"
"— those ordained by my ordinance, who dwell in my body, whose understanding is overmastered by me, they act not of their own desire."
"Those twice-born who properly study the Veda, who sacrifice with various rites, whose souls are at peace, and who have conquered anger — they attain me."
"Who, though knowing, cannot be attained by men of evil deeds, by those overcome by greed, by the wretched, the ignoble, the undisciplined of soul —"
"— know that I, of great fruit, am the refuge of those who perform good deeds, difficult to attain for those who are bewildered among brahmins, the path practised by those devoted to yoga."
"Whenever and wherever there is a decline of righteousness, O good one, and a rising up of unrighteousness — then I project myself forth."
"When Daityas addicted to violence, invincible even by the best of gods, and dreadful rākṣasas are about to arise in this world —"
"— then I am born in the houses of those who perform auspicious deeds; entering a human body, I quell everything."
"Having created gods and humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas, and also the stationary beings, I withdraw them all by my own māyā."
"When the time for action comes again, I, meditating upon a body, create; entering a human body for the purpose of establishing the bounds of dharma."
"White is my colour in the Kṛta age, yellow in the Tretā age; attaining the Dvāpara age it is red, and in the Kali age it is black."

"Three parts of unrighteousness arise in that time; and when the time of the end arrives, having become an exceedingly terrible Time, I alone destroy the three worlds entirely, both the moving and the unmoving."
"I am the one of three paths, the soul of all, the bringer of happiness to all worlds; the all-overcoming, all-pervading, infinite, Hṛṣīkeśa, the wide-striding one."
"I alone drive the wheel of time, O brahmin, truly formless — the pacifier of all beings, whose effort encompasses all worlds."
"Thus is my self truly established, O best of sages, O lord of brahmins, in all beings — yet no one knows me."
"And whatever suffering has befallen you, O brahmin — all of that in me leads to the arising of happiness and to your highest good, O sinless one."
"And whatever you have seen in the world, moving or unmoving — in every respect that self is ordained to be mine, O best of sages."
"The grandfather of all worlds is half of my body; I am named Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of conch, discus, and mace."
"For as long as a thousand cycles of yugas revolve, O brahmin-seer, so long do I sleep — I, the soul of the universe, the grandfather of all worlds."
"Thus I abide here through all time, O best of sages — not truly a child, yet in the form of a child — for as long as Brahmā does not awaken."
"And by me, O brahmin, in the form of Brahmā, this boon was granted to you — by me who am repeatedly gratified, O you who are honoured by the hosts of brahmin-seers."
"Having seen the entire world as one ocean, with the moving and unmoving vanished, you were bewildered — I knew this, and therefore I revealed the world to you."
"When you entered the interior of my body and, having seen the entire world, were astonished and could not understand —"
"— then, O brahmin-seer, you were quickly expelled by me from my mouth, and my self was declared to you — that which is difficult to know even by gods and asuras."
"For as long as that blessed Brahmā of great austerity does not awaken, for so long, O brahmin-seer, roam here in confidence and happiness."
"Then when that grandfather of all worlds awakens, I, having become one, shall create again from my body, O best of twice-born."
"Sky, earth, fire, wind, and water — and whatever else remains in the world here — the moving and the unmoving."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, O dear one, that most wondrous god vanished, and I behold these creatures manifold and variously formed.
This was seen by me, O king, when that dissolution of the yuga arrived — this wonder, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O best of all upholders of righteousness.
That god I saw long ago, with eyes like a lotus — that very one, O tiger among men, is your kinsman Janārdana.
By his very grant of a boon, O son of Kuntī, memory does not forsake me, and long life is mine, and also death at my own choosing.
He is this Kṛṣṇa of the Vṛṣṇi clan, the ancient primordial being, all-pervading; Hari of inconceivable nature sits here, mighty-armed, as if at play.
He is the creator, the ordainer, and also the destroyer, the Sātvata lord; Govinda, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark on his chest, the master of all progenitors, the supreme lord.
Having seen this tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, this memory has come back to me — of the primordial god, the unborn Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person clad in yellow garments.
Mādhava is indeed the father and mother of all living beings; go to him for refuge, O bulls of the Kuru clan — he is the worthy refuge.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, those sons of Pṛthā, and the twin heroes, best of men, together with Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, bowed to Janārdana.
And he, tiger among men, consoled them with supremely gracious words of comfort, treating those worthy of honor with due regard as was proper.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, again asked the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya about the future course of the world at the time of universal sovereignty.
O best among speakers, O sage of the Bhṛgu lineage, we have heard from you the wondrous account of what transpired at the beginning of the cosmic cycle — the creation and dissolution.
Yet I have further curiosity about this Kali age as well: when righteousness is thoroughly disrupted, what will remain?
What will be the prowess of men then, what their food and conduct, what their lifespan and clothing at the end of the age?
And having reached what point will the Kṛta age return again? O sage, speak in detail — you speak here of wondrous things.
Thus addressed, that foremost of sages, that great sage, again began to speak, delighting the tiger among the Vṛṣṇis and the Pāṇḍavas.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O bull of the Bhārata line, hear from me the account of all the worlds as it shall be, having reached that turbid time.
In the Kṛta age, the bull of Dharma stood firm on all four feet, complete, free from deceit and false conditions, established fully among men of old.
But pierced by one foot of unrighteousness, Dharma stands in the Tretā on three parts; in the Dvāpara it is said to be mixed, standing on only half.
Unrighteousness occupies the worlds standing on three parts, while Dharma remains present among men on only a quarter of its former measure.
Know from me, O Pāṇḍava, that the lifespan, valor, intelligence, strength, and luster of men progressively diminish through the successive ages.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, kings, brahmanas, vaishyas, and shudras alike will practice righteousness through deceit — men become trappers of Dharma.
Truth will be diminished in the world by men who fancy themselves learned; through the decline of truth, their lifespan will become short.
Due to the wasting of lifespan, they will not be able to acquire learning properly; devoid of learning and wisdom, greed will overwhelm them.
Men, foolish and devoted to greed and anger, addicted to desire, will be bound in enmity, each wishing to kill the other.
Brāhmaṇas, kshatriyas, and vaishyas, intermixing with one another, will become equal to shudras, devoid of austerity and truth.
The lowly will become middling, and the middling will sink to the lowest position — such will the world be when the end of the age draws near.
Hemp will be the finest of garments, millet the best of grains, and men will make their wives their friends at the end of the age.
Men will live on fish and meat, milking goats and sheep when cattle have perished, at the end of the age.
Robbing one another and doing harm, men will be non-reciters of prayers, atheists, and thieves at the end of the age.
They will sow medicinal herbs on riverbanks with hoes, and even those will yield little fruit for them at the end of the age.
Even those men who are ever constant in the observances of shraddha and divine rites will, overcome by greed, consume one another's offerings.
A father will consume what belongs to his son, and a son likewise what belongs to his father — things that should not be consumed will be consumed at the end of the age.
Brāhmaṇas, reviling the Vedas, will not perform their vows; seduced by rationalist arguments, they will not sacrifice or pour oblations.
They will cultivate in lowlands, yoke milch cows to the plough, and men will drive one-year-old calves as draft animals.
A son having slain his father, and a father having slain his son, will speak grandly without remorse and will not incur reproach.
The entire world will become barbarian, without proper rites, devoid of sacrifice, joyless, and without festival.
Men will plunder the wealth of the wretched, of those who have kinsmen, and of widows as well.

Of little valor and strength, arrogant, utterly given to greed and delusion, satisfied with mere talk and gifts, men will accept the company even of the wicked — taking up with those of sinful conduct.
O son of Kuntī, kings of evil minds, intent on slaying one another, foolish yet fancying themselves wise, will at the end of the age be kshatriyas who are thorns to the world.
Failing to protect their subjects, greedy, swollen with pride and arrogance, they will delight only in punishment at the end of the age.
Invading and seizing the wives and wealth of honest men, they will enjoy them without compassion even as those men weep, O Bhārata.
No one will formally seek a bride in marriage, nor will a maiden be properly given; women will seize husbands of their own accord when the end of the age draws near.
Kings too, unsatisfied and dull of mind, coveting others' wealth, will plunder by every means when the end of the age draws near.
The entire world will become barbarian, O Bhārata, and hand will rob hand when the end of the age draws near.
Truth is diminished in the world by men who fancy themselves learned; the old will have the minds of children, and children the understanding of the old.
Cowards will fancy themselves brave, while the truly brave will despair like cowards; no one will trust another when the end of the age draws near.
The entire world will be united in a single object — plunder — established in greed and delusion; great unrighteousness will grow and Dharma will not prevail.
Brāhmaṇas, kshatriyas, and vaishyas will cease to exist, O lord of the people; the world will then be of a single varna at the end of the age.
A father will not forgive his son, nor a son his father; no wife at all will render service to her husband.
Those regions where barley or wheat serves as food — people will resort to those lands when the end of the age draws near.
Men and women will eat whatever they please, O lord of the people, and will not endure one another when the end of the age draws near.
The entire world will become barbarian, O Yudhiṣṭhira; men will not satisfy their ancestors with shraddha offerings.
No one will be anyone's listener, no one anyone's teacher; the world will then be seized by darkness, O lord of men.
The maximum lifespan will then be sixteen years; thereafter men will give up their lives when the end of the age draws near.
A girl will give birth in her fifth or sixth year, and men of seven or eight years will then procreate.
Then, O king, O tiger among kings, a woman will not find satisfaction in her husband, nor a man in his woman, at the end of the age.
People of little substance will bear false marks of distinction, and violence will prevail; no one will be a giver to anyone at the end of the age.
Towns will be marked by gallows, crossroads by poles for jackals, and women too will be marked by disheveled hair at the end of the age.
Men will become barbarians, cruel, eating everything, harsh in all their acts in that final time — of this there is no doubt.
At the time of buying and selling, everyone will deceive everyone else at the end of the age, O foremost of Bhāratas, out of greed for livelihood.
Without properly understanding the sciences, they will perform rites accordingly and will act according to their own whims when the end of the age draws near.
All people will by nature be cruel in their actions and mutually suspicious when the contraction of the age arrives.
They will destroy gardens and trees without remorse; there will be a diminution in the world of the lives of embodied beings.
Overcome by greed, they will roam this earth; and brahmanas will exist who consume the property of other brahmanas.
The twice-born, crying out in lamentation, afflicted by fear, tormented by low-caste men, finding no protector, will wander this earth.
When men will be fierce enders of lives, cruel, harmers of living beings, then the age will contract.
The twice-born, fleeing in terror, will take refuge in rivers, mountains, and rugged places, O upholder of the Kuru lineage.
The foremost twice-born, harassed by bandits like crows, O king, and constantly oppressed by wicked kings with burdens of tribute.
Abandoning courage, O protector of the earth, in the terrible contraction of the age, they will perform forbidden acts as servants of shudras.
Śūdras will expound Dharma while brahmanas attend upon them as devotees, and these will be the established authorities whom people listen to.
This world will be inverted, with low becoming high; they will worship burial mounds and shun the gods; shudras will be attended upon and not the twice-born at the contraction of the age.
In the hermitages of the great sages, in the dwelling places of brahmanas, in temples of the gods, in sacred shrines, and in the abodes of serpents —
— the earth will be marked by burial mounds and not adorned with temples of gods when the age has waned; that is the sign of the end of the age.
When men will always be fierce, devoid of Dharma, meat-eaters and drunkards, then the age will contract.
When, O king, O great king, flower will germinate within flower and fruit within fruit, then the age will contract.
When the age has passed, the rain-cloud will rain out of season; the acts of men will then proceed without order; and the low-caste will enter into conflict with brahmanas.
The earth will soon be overrun by barbarians; out of fear of the burden of tribute, brahmanas will flee to the ten directions.
The districts, undifferentiated and afflicted by rain upon men, will resort to hermitages, living on fruits and roots.
When the world is thus in turmoil, there will be no rule of law; disciples who act disagreeably will not abide by their teacher's instruction.

The teacher's deposit too will be consumed thereafter; friends, connections, and kinsmen will leave for the sake of material interest; and there will be the disappearance of all beings at the end of the age.
All the directions will be ablaze; the stars will be in motion; celestial lights will move adversely; the winds will be turbulent; and there will be many meteor-falls portending great terror.

The sun, accompanied by six others, will blaze with fierce heat; there will be tumultuous roaring sounds and burning of the directions on all sides; and the sun will be hidden by a headless trunk at rising and setting.
The thousand-eyed Indra will rain out of season, and crops will not grow when the end of the age draws near.
Women will constantly speak harshly, be cruel and fond of weeping, and will no longer abide by their husbands' words.
Sons will slay their mothers and fathers at the end of the age; women, relying on their sons, will do away with their husbands.
O great king, at the end of the age Rāhu will seize the sun at an inauspicious time, and fire will blaze up on all sides.
Wayfarers who beg for water and food will find none; turned away, they will sleep on the road.
As the end of the age draws near, elephants, crows, birds together with deer and twice-born will utter harsh, discordant cries.
As the end of the age approaches, men will abandon friends, relatives, and their own dependents.
As the end of the age draws near, people will gradually take refuge in various regions, directions, towns and old cities.
Crying out in terrible voices, 'O father! O son!', people will wander the earth lamenting to one another.
Then, while that tumultuous confusion continues at the end of the age, the world, with the twice-born at its head, will gradually flourish again.
Then, at another turn of time, for the world's increase, fate will again become favourable of its own accord.
When the moon, the sun, and likewise Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati meet in one zodiacal sign, the Kṛta age will come again.

The rain-cloud will rain in season, the constellations will be auspicious, and the planets will move in their proper, clockwise courses; there will be peace, abundance, good health, and freedom from disease.
A twice-born man named Kalki Viṣṇuyaśas, urged on by time, will be born — one of great valour and of great intellectual power and heroism.
Born in an auspicious Brahmin settlement in the village of Śambhala, all conveyances, weapons, warriors, arms, and armour will present themselves to him by a mere act of will.
He will be a king who conquers by righteousness, a world-ruler, and he will bring this troubled world to serenity.
This blazing Brahmin who has arisen, the great-minded one who will put an end to destruction — he is indeed the summary and the turner of the entire age.
Surrounded by Brahmins, that twice-born will then eradicate all the hosts of barbarians who have spread everywhere.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: After exterminating the thieves he will duly assign this earth to the twice-born in the great horse-sacrifice rite.
Having re-established the auspicious boundaries ordained by the Self-born, he of pure and glorious deeds will, when grown old, resort to the forest.
The people dwelling in the world will follow his virtuous conduct, and once the thieves are destroyed by the Brahmins, there will be peace.
Installing black antelope skins, lances, tridents, and various weapons in the conquered lands,
honoured by the lords of Brahmins, respecting the best of twice-born, Kalki will roam the earth, ever intent on slaying brigands.
He will bring to complete destruction those brigands who cry out with such terrible voices: 'O father! O son!'
Then, O Bhārata, when the Kṛta age arrives, there will be the destruction of unrighteousness and the growth of righteousness, and people will be active in their duties.
In the Kṛta age there will be pleasure gardens and sacred trees, lakes and wells, and various sacrificial rites.
Brahmins, good men, sages and ascetics, hermitages together with their communities — all people and subjects will be established in truth.
All seeds that are sown will germinate and grow, O king of kings; in every season, all crops will flourish.

Men will be devoted to charity, vows, and religious observances; Brahmins will be intent on prayer and sacrifice, eager for righteousness, and full of joy; kings will protect this bountiful earth with justice.
In the Kṛta age, Vaiśyas will be devoted to trade; Brahmins will be intent on the six duties; Kṣatriyas will be devoted to protection.
Śūdras will be devoted to service and to the three upper varṇas. This is the dharma in the Kṛta age, in the Tretā, in the Dvāpara, and in the last age — all of this has been declared to you.
O Pāṇḍava, the reckoning of the ages is known to all the world. I have told you all — past and future — recalling the ancient lore spoken by Vāyu and praised by the seers.
Thus the paths of saṃsāra have been seen and experienced by me many times in my long life, and I have told them all to you.
Now hear this further word of mine as well, O steadfast one, together with your brothers, for the purpose of removing doubts about dharma.
You should always unite your soul with dharma, O best of those who uphold dharma, for a king whose soul is righteous rejoices in happiness both here and in the hereafter.
And hear the auspicious word I will speak to you, O sinless one: you must never dishonour a Brahmin, for an enraged Brahmin can burn up whole worlds by his resolve.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, the foremost king of the Kurus, that wise and supremely splendid one, spoke a supreme word.
In what dharma should I remain while protecting my subjects, O sage? And how should I conduct myself so as not to fall away from my own dharma?

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Be compassionate to all beings, friendly, affectionate, and free from envy; be devoted to protecting your subjects as if they were your own children. Walk in dharma, abandon adharma, and honour the ancestors and the gods.
Whatever was done through negligence — conquer that by proper giving. Enough with pride; be always dependent on others (i.e., humble).
Having conquered the whole earth, rejoice and be happy. This dharma for you — past and future — has been proclaimed.
There is nothing past or future on earth that you do not know. Therefore, dear one, do not hold this anguish in your heart.
This is Time, O mighty-armed one — even for all the gods. Creatures become bewildered, dear one, when driven on by Time.
And let there be no doubt in you about what I have told you, O sinless one; for by doubting these words, there would be a falling away from dharma for you.
You were born in the illustrious lineage of the Kurus, O bull of the Bhāratas; fulfil all this in deed, thought, and word.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What you, O best of twice-born, have spoken — words lovely to the ear as scripture — that I will do; I will strive to carry out your command, O lord.
I have no greed, O lord of Brahmins, nor fear, nor envy; I will indeed do everything you have said to me, O master.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of that great-souled Pāṇḍava, O king, the Pāṇḍavas were filled with joy, together with Śārṅga-bowed Kṛṣṇa.
And having heard the auspicious tale told by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, they were filled with wonder at the narration of that ancient lore.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The son of Pāṇḍu said to Mārkaṇḍeya: 'Please speak again on the great good fortune of Brahmins.'
Then Mārkaṇḍeya narrated:
A king named Parīkṣit, born of the Ikṣvāku line in Ayodhyā, went out on a hunt.
While he was pursuing a deer with a single horse, the deer led him far away.
Then, weary from the road, overcome by hunger and thirst, he saw a dark grove in some spot and entered it.
Then in the middle of that grove, seeing an exceedingly beautiful lake, he plunged in together with his horse.
Refreshed, he placed lotus stalks before his horse and sat down on the bank of the lotus-pond.
Then, as he lay there, he heard the sweet sound of singing.
Hearing it, he thought: 'I see no human presence here — whose singing can this be?'
Then he saw a maiden of supremely beautiful appearance, gathering flowers and singing.
Then she walked around close to the king.
The king said to her: 'O lovely one, whose are you?'
She replied: 'I am a maiden.'
The king said to her: 'I desire you.'
Then the maiden said: 'You can win me only on one condition — not otherwise.'
The king asked her what the condition was.
Then the maiden said: 'Water must never be shown to me.'
The king said 'Very well', united with her, and dwelt together with her.
As the king sat there, his army followed step by step; seeing the king, they surrounded him and stood guard.
The king, comforted, went with her in a covered litter, and reaching his own city he lived privately sporting with her alone, seeing nothing else.
Then the chief minister asked the women who attended close to him: 'What purpose is being served here?'
Those women said: 'We observe something unprecedented — no water is brought here.'

Then the minister had a grove made without water, with noble trees bearing many roots, flowers, and fruits, and approaching the king in private said: 'This grove is magnificent and waterless — it is well to take pleasure here.'
At his words, he entered that grove together with the queen. One day, sporting with her in that beautiful grove, he became excessively worn out by hunger and thirst and saw a jasmine bower.
Entering it with his beloved, the king saw a well built with a smooth plaster floor, filled with clear water.
And seeing it, he stood with the queen on its very bank.
Then the king said to the queen: 'Please, descend into the water of the well.'
Hearing his words, she descended and plunged into the well and did not rise again.
The king searched for her but did not find her.
