He even had the well drained, and seeing a frog at the mouth of a rat-hole, furious he commanded: 'Let a slaughter of all frogs be carried out; whoever seeks favour from me should approach me with the gift of dead frogs.'
Then, as the terrible slaughter of frogs was being carried out in all directions, fear seized all the frogs; terrified, they reported the whole event to the king of frogs.
Then the king of frogs, wearing the garb of an ascetic, approached the king.
Approaching him, he said: 'Do not, O king, fall under the sway of anger. Be gracious — you ought not to slay frogs who have committed no offense.'
'Do not seek to kill the frogs; restrain your rage, O Acyuta. And in this regard two verses will be cited for you: the pride of wealth wanes for people who are ignorant.'
'Promise that, even upon encountering them again, you will not loose your anger. You have already done enough wrong — what, indeed, is to be gained by killing the frogs?'

To him speaking thus, the king — his soul overwhelmed with grief for his beloved — replied: 'I cannot forgive this. I will kill them. By these evil-souled creatures my beloved was devoured; the frogs are in every way deserving of death. You should not, O learned one, obstruct me.'

He, hearing that speech, with senses and mind distressed, said: 'Be appeased, O king. I am Āyus, king of the frogs. That daughter of mine is named Suśobhanā. This is her bad conduct — many kings have been deceived by her before.'
The king said to him: 'It is she I desire; let her be given to me.'
Then her father gave her to the king, and said to her: 'Serve this king obediently.'
He said to his daughter: 'Because you have deceived kings, your offspring will be hostile to Brahmins, on account of your untruthfulness.'

The king, having received her, his heart bound by the virtues of their union as if he had obtained sovereignty over the three worlds, with a voice trembling with tears of joy, bowing down and honoring the king of frogs, said: 'I have been blessed.'
And the king of frogs, having taken leave of his son-in-law, departed as he had come.

After some time, three princes were born to that king by her — Śala, Dala, and Bala. Then, in due course, the father consecrated the eldest, Śala, in the kingdom, and with resolute mind departed to the forest for austerities.
Once, Śala went hunting, and having sighted a deer, gave chase in his chariot.
He said to the charioteer: 'Drive me swiftly!'
The charioteer, addressed thus, said to the king: 'Do not pursue it further — this deer cannot be caught by you, even if the two Vāmya horses were yoked to your chariot.'
Then the king said to the charioteer: 'Tell me about these Vāmya horses — or I will kill you!'
So addressed, he, frightened by the king's threat and fearful of Vāmadeva's curse, told the king: 'The two Vāmya horses belong to the sage Vāmadeva — they are swift as thought.'
The king then said to him as he was speaking: 'Go to Vāmadeva's hermitage!'
Going to Vāmadeva's hermitage, he said to the sage: 'Venerable one, a deer I have wounded is fleeing; I would recover it — please grant me the two Vāmya horses.'
The sage said to him: 'I will give you the two Vāmya horses; but once your purpose is accomplished, they must be promptly returned to me.'

He received those two horses, took leave of the sage, and set off with the Vāmya-yoked chariot toward the deer; and as he went, he said to the charioteer: 'These two horse-gems are unfit for Brahmins — they are not to be returned to Vāmadeva.'
Having said this and recovered the deer, he returned to his own city and kept the horses in the inner stables.
Then the sage reflected: 'This young prince, having found a fine pretext, enjoys himself and does not return them to me. Alas, how grievous!'
Having resolved in his mind, after a month had passed he said to his disciple: 'Go, O Ātreya, and tell the king: if it has served your purpose, return the teacher's two Vāmya horses.'
He went and spoke thus to the king.
The king replied to him: 'Such treasures as these are the mount of kings — Brahmins are not worthy of them. Besides, what need do Brahmins have of horses? Let him go away in peace.'
He went and reported thus to the teacher.
Hearing that disagreeable speech, Vāmadeva, his soul overwhelmed with anger, himself went to the king and pressed him for the horses; but the king did not give them.

Vāmadeva said: 'Return my two Vāmya horses, O king — your purpose has been accomplished, which none other could have done. Let not Varuṇa slay you with his terrible nooses, he who stands between the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya orders.'
The king said: 'Two well-behaved and thoroughly tamed bullocks — that is the mount of Brahmins, O Vāmadeva. On them ride wherever you wish, O great sage — Vedic meters carry the likes of you.'

Vāmadeva said: 'Vedic meters do carry the likes of me in that other world, O king — in whatever forms they exist there. But in this world, this is my conveyance, and the conveyance of others like me, O king.'
The king said: 'Let four donkeys carry you, or the finest mules, or yellow horses — on them go wherever you will. This is the mount of a Kṣatriya. Know that my two Vāmya horses are not yours.'

Vāmadeva said: 'They call this the terrible vow of a Brahmin, O king — that one who is maintained here alive by this: let great iron demons of fearful form, with sharp spears, carry you in four directions.'

The king said: 'Those who know you as a Brahmin capable of slaying with word, mind, or deed — let them cast you down here together with your disciples, driven by my command, bearing sharp spears and swords.'

Vāmadeva said: 'No sanctions constrain Brahmins, O king — neither by word, nor by mind, nor by deed. But one who thus pursues Brahmā-knowledge through austerity, knowing it fully, by that he becomes the highest while he lives.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: 'O king, when Vāmadeva had spoken thus, rākṣasas of fearsome form rose up; being struck down by them — spear in hand — that king then cried out these words aloud:
"O Brahmin, whether the Ikṣvākus, or Dala, are subject to me, or even other common folk — I will not release Vāmadeva's two Vāmya horses. Those of dharmic character do not act in such a way."'
Speaking thus, that lord of the earth was slain by the demons and fell quickly to the ground. Then, knowing the king to be slain, the Ikṣvākus consecrated Dala as king.
Then the Brahmin Vāmadeva, going there into the kingdom, spoke these words: 'Dala, O king, what belongs to Brahmins must be given — this is seen as such in all the codes of dharma.'
'If you fear unrighteousness, O lord of men, give me the two Vāmya horses right now today.' Hearing these words of Vāmadeva, that king spoke to his charioteer in fury:
'Bring me at once one of my arrows of peculiar form, smeared with poison and ready to hand — one by which Vāmadeva, when struck, may lie down, mauled by dogs in a pitiful state.'
Vāmadeva said: 'I know, O lord of men, your son ten years of age, born of the queen — named Śyenajit. Him, driven by my command, slay promptly, your own dear one, with dreadful arrows.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: 'O king, addressed thus by Vāmadeva, the arrow, blazing with sharp power, was released and slew the prince in the inner chamber. Hearing this, Dala also spoke these words:
"O Ikṣvākus, behold — I shall do what is dear to you; today I shall smite and kill this Brahmin. Bring me another blazing sharp arrow — O lords of earth, behold my valor today!"'
Vāmadeva said: 'That terrible arrow, smeared with poison, which you are now fitting against me — you will not be able to release that best of arrows or even to nock it, O lord of men.'
The king said: 'O Ikṣvākus, look — I am seized! Truly I cannot release this arrow, nor can I bring myself to destroy it. Let Vāmadeva live long!'
Vāmadeva said: 'Touch the queen with this arrow — from that sin you will be released.'

Mārkaṇḍeya said: 'The king then did as instructed. Then the princess spoke to the sage: "O Vāmadeva, as befits the situation, I, spending each day united with him, have praised him to Brahmins, ever seeking kind words — may I thereby, O Brahmin, attain the world of merit."'

Vāmadeva said: 'You have saved the royal family, O bright-eyed one. Choose a matchless boon — I grant it to you. Rule over your own kindred, O princess — and also over the great and blameless Ikṣvāku kingdom.'

The princess said: 'I choose but one boon, O Lord — let my husband be freed today from his sin. Bless him together with his sons and kinsmen with auspiciousness. This is the boon I have chosen, O foremost of twice-born ones.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: 'Hearing the princess's words, O foremost of Kurus, the sage said, "So be it." Then the king became joyful, and bowing, he gave the two Vāmya horses to him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The sages and the Pāṇḍavas questioned Mārkaṇḍeya: 'Is there anyone elder than yourself?'

He said to them: 'Indeed there was a royal sage named Indradyumna whose merit was exhausted and who fell from the triple heaven with the words: "Your fame has been cut off." He came to me and asked: "Do you, sir, know me?"'
'I said to him: "We are not alchemists who undertake the accomplishment of our purposes through torment of the body."
'"There is on the Himālayas an owl named Prākārakarṇa — if he might know you. The Himālaya is at a great distance; there that one dwells."'
'He, having become a horse, carried me there where the owl was.'
'Then that royal sage questioned him: "Do you know me, sir?"'
'He, meditating for a moment, said to him: "I do not know you, sir."'
'The royal sage Indradyumna, thus addressed, again said to that owl: "Is there anyone elder than yourself?"'
'Addressed thus, he said to him: "Indeed there is a lake called Indradyumna-saras; in it a heron named Nāḍījaṅgha dwells — he is elder than I. Ask him."'
'Then Indradyumna, taking me and the owl, went to that lake where the heron named Nāḍījaṅgha was.'
'He was asked by us: "Do you, sir, know King Indradyumna?"'
'So addressed, he reflected for a moment and said: "I do not know King Indradyumna."'
'Then he was asked by us: "Is there anyone else elder than yourself?"'
'He said to us: "Indeed, in this very lake there lives a tortoise named Akūpāra — he is elder than I. If he could perhaps recognize this king, we should ask that Akūpāra."'
'Then the heron informed the tortoise Akūpāra: "We have a purpose in mind — we wish to ask you something; please come here for a moment."'
'Hearing this, the tortoise rose from that lake and came to where we were standing on the bank of that lake.'
'And when he had come, we asked him: "Do you, sir, know King Indradyumna?"'

'He, meditating for a moment, his eyes filled with tears, his heart agitated, trembling, nearly senseless, with joined palms said: "How could I not know him? For he had previously offered me as a gift a thousand times in fire-altar sacrifices; and this lake was made by the cows given as gifts at his southern rites when they passed over the land; and here I have been living."'
'Then, immediately upon hearing what was spoken by the tortoise, a divine chariot appeared from the world of the gods.'
'And voices were heard addressed to Indradyumna: "Your heaven is ready — occupy the station that befits you. You are glorious. Go without anxiety."'
'The renown of meritorious deeds touches both heaven and earth; as long as that fame endures, so long is a man spoken of.'
'One whose ill-fame is spoken of in the world — whatever being it may be — falls into the lowest realms for as long as that utterance continues to be spoken.'
'Therefore a man should be of virtuous conduct in the world to the utmost degree; abandoning sinful conduct, he should take refuge in dharma alone.'
'Hearing this, the king said: "Wait a moment while I restore these two elders to their proper places."'
'He restored me, Prākārakarṇa, and the owl each to their proper places, and then, his purpose accomplished, took that same vehicle and attained his rightful station.'
'This was experienced and witnessed by me as a long-liver' — so Mārkaṇḍeya said to the Pāṇḍavas.
The Pāṇḍavas, pleased, said: 'Well done — it is excellent that you restored King Indradyumna, who had fallen from the heavenly world, once again to his own place in heaven.'
Then he said to them: 'Moreover, was not the royal sage Nṛga, sinking in hell, rescued from that dire state by Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, and again restored to heaven?'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-king, O bull of the Bhārata lineage, questioned Mārkaṇḍeya — great through austerities, long-lived, and without blemish.

'Known to you, O knower of dharma, are the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas; the various royal lineages and the eternal sages' lineages — nothing in this world is unknown to you, O foremost of the twice-born.'
You know the divine story, O sage, of humans, serpents, and demons. I wish to hear it narrated in truth, O twice-born one.
The unconquered Ikṣvāku known as Kuvalāśva — how did he come to be called Dhundhumāra through that strange reversal of name?
I wish to know this in truth, O best of the Bhārgava line — how the name of the wise Kuvalāśva became thus reversed.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Very well, I shall tell you. Listen, O king Yudhiṣṭhira — hear this most righteous tale of Dhundhumāra.
How that Ikṣvāku king, Kuvalāśva, lord of the earth, came to be called Dhundhumāra — hear that, O lord of the earth.
There was a great sage of fame, O dear one, called Uttaṅka, O Bhārata — his hermitage stood in the pleasant sandy desert wastes, O Kaurava.
Uttaṅka, O great king, practiced severe and arduous austerities for many groups of years, O lord, desiring to propitiate Viṣṇu.
Pleased with him, the blessed Lord came to grant him a vision in person. And the sage, bowing as soon as he saw him, praised him with various hymns.
By you, O god, all creatures together with gods, asuras, and humans, stationary and moving beings likewise, Brahmā, the Vedas, and all that is knowable — all have been created, O greatly radiant one.
Your head is the sky, O god; your two eyes are the moon and sun; your breath is the wind; your splendor is fire, O Acyuta; your arms are all the directions; your belly is the great ocean.
Your thighs are the mountains, O god; the ether is your navel, O Madhusūdana; your feet are the divine earth; your body hair is the herbs and plants.
Indra, Soma, Agni, Varuṇa — gods, asuras, and great serpents — bowing, attend upon you, praising you with various hymns.
All beings are pervaded by you, O lord of the worlds. Great sages with mighty spiritual power, the yogins, praise you.
When you are pleased the world is well; when you are wrathful there is great fear. You alone are the remover of all fears, O supreme Person.
You bring happiness to gods, humans, and all beings. With three strides, O god, you reclaimed the three worlds; and by you the destruction of the prosperous asuras was accomplished.
Through your strides the gods attained supreme liberation, and the lords of the Daityas met their defeat when you were wrathful, O greatly radiant one.
You indeed are the creator and destroyer of all beings here in every way. Having propitiated you, the gods prosper in happiness on every side.
Thus praised, O Hrishikesha, by the great-souled Uttaṅka, Viṣṇu said to Uttaṅka: "I am pleased — choose a boon."
Uttaṅka said: This itself is boon enough for me, that I have seen Hari — the eternal, divine Person, the creator and lord of the universe.
Viṣṇu said: I am pleased with your freedom from greed and your devotion, O best of twice-born ones. You must certainly receive a boon from me, O brahmin, O twice-born one.
Being thus urged to choose a boon by Hari, Uttaṅka then, with joined palms, requested a boon, O best of the Bhārata line.

"If you are pleased with me, O blessed one whose eyes resemble lotuses, may my mind ever abide in dharma, truth, and self-restraint; and may there be constant devotional practice toward you, O great lord."

Viṣṇu said: All this shall indeed come to pass for you by my grace, O twice-born one. A yoga power shall be revealed to you by which, once yoked to it, you shall accomplish a great task for the three worlds of the celestials.
A great demon named Dhundhu is performing terrible austerities for the destruction of the worlds. Hear now who will slay him.
A lord of the earth shall arise, known as Bṛhadaśva. His son, pure and self-controlled, is known as Kuvalāśva.
That best of kings, relying on my yogic power and at your command, O sage among brahmins, shall become Dhundhumāra — the slayer of Dhundhu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having thus spoken to Uttaṅka, Viṣṇu disappeared.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When Ikṣvāku passed away, O king, Shasada obtained this earth — a man of supreme righteousness, he became king in Ayodhyā.
Shasada's heir was the mighty Kākutstha. Kākutstha's son was Anenas, and Pṛthu was the son of Anenas.
Vishvagashva was the son of Pṛthu; from him was born Ardra. Yuvanāśva was Ardra's son, and Shravasta was his own son.
King Shravastaka was born, by whom the city of Shravasti was built. The heir of Shravasta was the greatly powerful Bṛhadaśva. Bṛhadaśva's son in turn is known as Kuvalāśva.
Kuvalāśva had twenty-one thousand sons — all of them deeply versed in the sciences, powerful, and difficult to approach in battle.
Kuvalāśva surpassed his father in virtues. In due time, therefore, Bṛhadaśva consecrated him to the kingdom, O great king — that heroic and supremely righteous Kuvalāśva.
Having transferred royal sovereignty to his son, the wise lord of the earth Bṛhadaśva, destroyer of foes, departed to a forest grove for ascetic practice.
Then Uttaṅka the foremost of twice-born ones heard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, O king, that the royal sage Bṛhadaśva was setting forth to the forest.
The great-spirited Uttaṅka, of immense soul and vast splendor, met that best of men — the best of all who know weapons — and stopped him.
Uttaṅka said: You must still perform the duty of protection. Please do so. By your grace, O king, may we dwell free from distress.
For the earth, O king, protected by you, great-souled one, will be free from distress. You should not go to the forest.
For great dharma is seen in the protection of subjects here in this world — it is not seen in that manner in the forest. Let not such a thought arise in you.

Such dharma as this — of protecting subjects, which was formerly practiced by royal sages — is not found anywhere else, O lord of kings. Subjects must be protected by the king; you should protect them.
For I am unable to practice austerities free from distress, O king, near my hermitage in the level sandy desert wastes.
There is a sea filled with sand, known as Ujjānaka — vast in extent across many yojanas and long across many yojanas.
There dwells a terrible lord of demons, of mighty valor and prowess — the son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, known as Dhundhu — dreadfully fierce.
He dwells inside the earth, O king, of immeasurable might. Having slain him, O great king, you may then go to the forest.
He lies in austerity, practicing terrible penance for the destruction of the worlds, for the ruin of the thirty gods and of the worlds, O king.
He is invulnerable to gods, to Daityas, to Rākṣasas, to serpents, to Yakṣas, and to Gandharvas on every side, O king — having obtained a boon from the grandfather of all the worlds.
Destroy him — good fortune to you! Let your mind not be otherwise. You shall attain great, eternal, imperishable, and enduring fame.
As that fierce one lies sleeping, hidden within the sand, at the end of each year his breath begins to move — and then the earth shakes along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
By the wind of his breath, a great cloud of dust is hurled up, covering the path of the sun. For seven days the earth quakes, with sparks flying, with flames and smoke — most terrible.
Because of that, O king, I cannot remain in my own hermitage. Destroy him, O king of kings, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds. Let the worlds be at peace this day, once that demon is slain.
You alone are capable of his destruction — this is my conviction. And Viṣṇu shall augment your splendor with his own splendor.
And a boon was given to me by Viṣṇu formerly in regard to his slaying: that the Vaiṣṇava splendor shall enter that lord of the earth who will slay that fierce and mighty demon, difficult to approach.
Absorbing that splendor — hard to bear on earth — O king of kings, slay that evil Daitya of fierce prowess.
For the greatly splendid Dhundhu cannot be consumed with little splendor, O protector of the earth — not even in a hundred years.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: That royal sage, the unconquered one, thus addressed by Uttaṅka, then spoke to Uttaṅka with joined palms, O best of the Kauravas.
"Your coming to me, O brahmin, shall not be in vain. This son of mine, O blessed one, known as Kuvalāśva —
"— steadfast and swift in action, unequaled in valor on earth — he shall surely do all that you desire. There is no doubt."
"Send me forth, O brahmin, surrounded as I am by all my heroic sons with arms like iron clubs. I have now laid down my weapons."
Told "So be it" by the sage of immeasurable splendor, the royal sage directed his son to serve the great-souled Uttaṅka with the words "Let it be done," and departed to the excellent forest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who is this demon, O blessed one, of great valor, O wealth of austerities? Whose son is he, or whose grandson? I wish to know this.
Such a mighty demon — I have not heard of him, O wealth of austerities. I wish to know this fully in truth, O blessed one, O greatly wise one, O wealth of austerities, in detail.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hear all this, O king, exactly as it occurred, O lord of men. At that time, in the terrible universal ocean, when stationary and moving things had perished, when all beings had disappeared, O bull of the Bhārata line —
— the eternal, imperishable Person, the source of all beings, the blessed Viṣṇu slept alone upon a bed of water, on the great coils of the serpent Śeṣa of immeasurable splendor.
The blessed Acyuta Hari, maker of the worlds and greatly fortunate one, embraced this earth with the great coils of the serpent.

From the navel of that sleeping god there issued forth a lotus brilliant as the sun, and therein was born the Grandfather himself — Brahmā, teacher of the worlds — on that lotus resplendent as sun and moon.
He of four Vedas, four forms, and likewise four faces — unapproachable through his own power, of great strength and valor.
Then after some time, two demons of exceeding valor — Madhu and Kaiṭabha — beheld Lord Hari.
Lying on a divine couch, on the serpent's coils, greatly resplendent, extending across many yojanas in breadth and many yojanas in length.
Wearing a crown and the Kaustubha gem, clad in yellow silk garments, blazing with beauty, splendor, and form, O king — equal to a thousand suns, wonderful and beyond comparison to behold.
There was great astonishment in Madhu and Kaiṭabha at that time, seeing also the Grandfather on the lotus, he whose eyes resemble lotuses.
Then those two began to terrify Brahmā of immeasurable energy. As the greatly famous Brahmā was being terrified repeatedly by those two, he shook the lotus stalk — and thereby Keśava awakened.
Then Govinda saw the two demons of exceeding valor. Seeing those two, the god said: "Welcome to you both, O mighty ones. I shall grant you both a choice boon, for delight arises in me."
Those two great demons of mighty valor laughed and replied together to Hrishikesha, O great king — to Madhusūdana.
"You choose a boon from us, O god — we are boon-givers, O best of gods. We grant a boon to you — speak it without hesitation."
The blessed one said: "I accept the boon, O heroes, and the desired boon from me is this: you two are endowed with valor — there is no man equal to you two.
"Let you two, truly valorous, submit to being slain by me. This is the wish I desire to fulfill, for the welfare of the worlds."
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said: "We have never spoken an untruth before — certainly not in casual matters; how then otherwise? Know us to be devoted to truth and dharma, O supreme Person.
"In strength, beauty, valor, and equanimity — there is no one equal to us two; nor in dharma, austerity, giving, or in character, courage, and self-control.
"A great flood is approaching us, O Keśava. Fulfill what was spoken — for time is difficult to transgress.
"We desire this of you, O god — let one thing be done by you, O lord: let our slaying take place in this unobstructed open sky, O best among the gods."
We shall both become your sons, O beautiful-eyed one. This is the boon chosen, O God; know it thus, O best among the gods.
The Lord said: So be it. I shall do exactly this; all of it shall come to pass.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Govinda, the slayer of Madhu, reflected and found no unoccupied spot — neither on earth nor in heaven.
Then, O king, the best of gods, the greatly glorious Madhusūdana, seeing his own thighs unsubmerged, severed the heads of Madhu and Kaiṭabha there with his sharp-edged discus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The son of those two was Dhundhu by name, of great energy and great splendour. He performed great austerities, possessed of mighty valour and prowess.
He stood on one foot, emaciated, his veins protruding. Brahmā, pleased, gave him a boon, and he asked for a boon, O lord.
"May I be invincible to gods, dānavas, yakṣas, serpents, gandharvas, and rākṣasas — this is the boon I have chosen."
"So be it; go," said the Grandfather to him. Thus addressed, he touched the Grandfather's feet with his head and departed.
Then Dhundhu, of mighty valour and prowess, having obtained the boon, remembering the slaying of his fathers, attacked Viṣṇu.
The wrathful Dhundhu, having conquered the gods together with the gandharvas, again and again oppressed all the gods and Viṣṇu greatly.
That ocean filled with sand is known as Ujjānaka. Coming to that region, O bull of the Bhāratas, the evil-souled one oppressed with utmost force the hermitage of Uttaṅka, O lord.
There, having gone underground and concealed within the sand, Dhundhu, son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, of terrible prowess,
lay sleeping, sustained by the power of his austerities, for the destruction of the worlds, near the hermitage of Uttaṅka, breathing out flames of fire.
At this very time, King Kuvalāśva, accompanied by his retinue, army, and conveyances, attended by thousands of mighty warriors,
twenty-one thousand sons, the crusher of foes, went together with Uttaṅka to the abode of that Dhundhu.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu entered him with his radiance, at Uttaṅka's bidding, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds.
When that invincible one set forth, a great sound arose in heaven: "This glorious prince shall become Dhundhumāra."
The gods showered him on all sides with divine flowers, and the celestial kettledrums sounded of their own accord.
A cool wind blew at the departure of that wise one, purifying the earth, and the lord of the gods rained down.
In the sky, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the celestial chariots of the gods became visible right there where the great asura Dhundhu was.
The great sages, filled with eagerness to see the battle of Kuvalāśva and Dhundhu, together with the gods and gandharvas, watched.
Invigorated by the energy of Nārāyaṇa, O descendant of the Kurus, that king quickly went in all directions with those sons.
King Kuvalāśva caused the sandy ocean to be dug; and indeed in that ocean of sand, by the sons of Kuvalāśva,
after digging for seven days, the mighty Dhundhu was seen. His body, vast and terrible, concealed within the sand, blazed like the sun in its energy, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then, O great king, O tiger among kings, Dhundhu lay sleeping, turned toward the western quarter, blazing like the fire of universal dissolution.
Surrounded on all sides by the sons of Kuvalāśva, he was rushed upon and struck with sharp arrows, clubs, pestles, halberds, iron bars, javelins, and bright sharp swords.
Struck thus, the mighty one arose in great fury, and in his rage consumed their various weapons.
Vomiting fire from his mouth comparable to the fire of the end of time, he burned all the king's sons with his own energy.

With the fire born from his mouth, enraged, as if overturning the worlds, O tiger among kings, in an instant — just as Kapila the lord had in former times burned the sons of Sagara in his fury — that too seemed like a wonder.
When they were burned by the fire of his wrath, O best of the Bhāratas, the greatly energetic King Kuvalāśva approached that awakened great-souled one, who was like another Kumbhakarṇa.
From his body, O great king, much water flowed abundantly; then the king, that yogi, absorbed that fiery energy made of water, O king, and by yoga extinguished the fire with water.
Then the king burned the demon of cruel valour with the Brahmā-weapon, O best of the Bhāratas, for the sake of fearlessness for all the worlds.

Having burned that great demon, the enemy of the gods, with his weapon, the royal sage Kuvalāśva, slayer of foes, like another lord of the three worlds, thenceforth became known by the name Dhundhumāra — "slayer of Dhundhu."
Then, told "choose a boon" by all the delighted gods together with the great sages, he stood with joined palms, bowed down, exceedingly joyful, O king, and spoke these words:

"May I give wealth to the foremost brahmins, and may I be unconquerable by enemies; may friendship with Viṣṇu be mine, and non-injury to all beings; may there be constant delight in righteousness, and an eternal dwelling in heaven."
"So be it" — thus was that king told by the delighted gods, by the sages together with the gandharvas, and by the wise Uttaṅka.
Having honoured that king with various blessings, the gods and the great sages then departed to their own abodes.
Three of his sons remained surviving, O Yudhiṣṭhira: Dṛḍhāśva, Kapilāśva, and Candrāśva, O Bhārata. From them, O king, descended in succession the great-souled Ikṣvāku kings.
Thus was Dhundhu the daitya, of great valour, son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, slain by that Kuvalāśva, O excellent one.
And King Kuvalāśva became known as Dhundhumāra, endowed with that name along with its qualities from that time forth.
All of this that you asked me has been narrated — the celebrated tale of Dhundhumāra, famous by reason of his deeds.
This holy narrative, which is also a glorification of Viṣṇu — whoever hears it shall be righteous-souled and shall have sons.
He becomes long-lived and steadfast upon hearing it at the sacred days; nor does he encounter any fear of disease, freed from fever.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of the Bhāratas, asked Mārkaṇḍeya of great brilliance a question on dharma most difficult to answer.
"I desire to hear, O Lord, the supreme greatness of women as narrated by you, O brahmin, and the subtle dharma as it truly is."
"For directly visible, O brahmin-sage, O excellent one, are the gods — the sun and moon, wind, earth, and fire."
"Father and mother, O Lord, and cows too, O excellent one, and whatever else is ordained — all that too, O joy of the Bhṛgu line."
"I regard all of these as like a teacher; and devoted wives — the service of chaste women to their husbands seems difficult to me."

"Pray tell us the greatness of chaste wives, O lord, O sinless one — those who, restraining the entire host of the senses, controlling the mind, and regarding their husband as a god, remain steadfast."
"O Lord, this seems difficult to me, O master: the service of women toward their fathers and mothers, and toward their husbands, O brahmin."

"Indeed I see nothing more difficult than the most severe dharma of women — what women of good conduct, O brahmin, perform with constant reverence. Alas, both fathers and mothers perform what is difficult."
"And those women who are faithful to one husband, who speak the truth, who carry a child in the womb for ten months — women who, brought together in time, what is more wonderful than that?"
"Facing the greatest peril and unequalled pain, women bring forth sons with great suffering, O lord, and nourish them too with great love, O best of brahmins."
"And those who, engaged in all the harsh duties, blameless, always perform their own duty — that too I consider difficult."
"Tell me truly also the practice of the kṣatriya dharma, O brahmin. Dharma is very difficult to attain, O brahmin, by the cruel-natured and evil-souled."
"This I desire, O Lord, O best among those who know questions, to hear from the best of the Bhṛgu lineage. I am eager to attend upon you, O one of good vows."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Well then, I shall narrate all of this question most difficult to answer, truly, O best of the Bhāratas. Listen to me as I speak.
"Some regard the mother as equal to, dear child, and others regard fathers; the mother does what is hard, she who nurtures offspring."
"Through austerities, worship of the gods, salutation, forbearance, and by rites and means, fathers strive for sons."
"Thus, having with great hardship obtained a son so difficult to get, they always think, O hero: 'How will this one turn out?'"
"Both father and mother hope from their sons, O Bhārata, for glory, fame, prosperity, offspring, and dharma as well."
"He who fulfils that hope of theirs is truly the knower of dharma. He whose father and mother are always pleased — both here and hereafter his glory and dharma are eternal."
"There is no sacrifice for women, nor any śrāddha, nor any fast. But she who renders service to her husband — by that she attains heaven."
"Regarding this topic, O king Yudhiṣṭhira, listen attentively to the fixed dharma of devoted wives."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: There was a certain excellent brahmin, a student of the Vedas, rich in austerity, an ascetic, virtuous in conduct, named Kauśika, O Bhārata.
That best of brahmins studied the Vedas together with their limbs and Upaniṣads. He stood at the foot of a certain tree, reciting the Vedas aloud.
A crane settled in the tree above him, and it dropped its excrement upon the brahmin.
Looking up at it, the brahmin became angry and glared at it. Utterly overcome by wrath, he stared at that crane.
Cursed by the brahmin's angry gaze, it fell to the ground. Seeing the crane fallen, drained of life, unconscious, the brahmin was filled with compassion and lamented for it.
"I have done a wrongful deed, overcome by the force of passion and hatred" — saying this repeatedly, the learned one went to the village to beg alms.
Moving through the respectable households of the village, O bull of the Bhāratas, he entered the very household where he had formerly begged.
Saying "Give!" and begging, he was told "Wait" by a woman there, while the housewife was performing the cleansing of her vessels.
In the meantime, O king, O best of the Bhāratas, her husband suddenly arrived, greatly afflicted by hunger.
But that virtuous woman, seeing her husband, set aside that brahmin and gave water for washing feet, water for sipping, and a seat to her husband.
The dark-eyed one bowed reverently and served her husband with food, eatables, and very sweet words.
She always ate the remnants of her husband's meal, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and she regarded her husband as a god, ever following the mind of her husband.
Neither in deed nor in mind did she transgress him; she neither overate nor drank excessively; devoted to him with all her heart, she was intent on serving her husband.
Of good conduct, pure, capable, devoted to the welfare of the household — whatever was the welfare of her husband, she constantly pursued that.
Always intent on serving gods, guests, servants, and likewise mother-in-law and father-in-law, with senses ever restrained.
Then she, the bright-eyed one, while engaged in serving her husband, saw the brahmin standing there waiting for alms, and remembered him.
Ashamed, that noble and glorious woman, O best of the Bhāratas, took alms and went out to the brahmin.
The brahmin said: What is this, O beautiful lady? You told me to wait, and having kept me waiting, you have not dismissed me. Why?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Seeing the brahmin burning with anger, blazing as it were with his own fiery energy, that virtuous woman, O lord of men, spoke conciliatory words.
"Please forgive me, O brahmin. My husband is my great deity; he came weary and hungry and I attended to him."
The brahmin said: Are brahmins not greater? You have made your husband greater than brahmins! Though living in the householder's dharma, you disrespect brahmins.

Even Indra bows to them — how much more so ordinary mortals on earth! You are haughty; you do not know, you have not heard the words of the elders. Brahmins, like fire, could burn even the earth itself.
The woman said: I do not disrespect brahmins, those wise ones who are equal to the gods. Forgive me this offence, O brahmin, O sinless one.
I know the power of brahmins and the great fortune of those wise ones. The ocean, once undrinkable, was made saline in anger by one of them.
Likewise the fire of wrath of those sages of blazing austerities and purified souls — that fire does not cool even today in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Because of contempt for brahmins, the wicked and cruel great asura Vātāpi was digested upon encountering the sage Agastya.
Many such feats of those who speak of Brahman are heard of, O brahmin. Both the wrath and the grace of great souls are immeasurably vast.
Yet in this transgression, O sinless brahmin, you should forgive me. The dharma of serving one's husband — that is what appeals to me, O twice-born.
Among all deities, my husband is my supreme deity. Without discrimination I shall perform my duty toward him, O best of twice-born.
See, O brahmin, what fruit comes from devoted service to one's husband — for I know that you burnt the crane in rage.
Anger is the enemy dwelling within the body of men, O best of twice-born. The gods know as a true brahmin the one who abandons anger and delusion.
The one who speaks truth here, who satisfies his teacher, who does not injure though injured — him the gods know as a brahmin.
The one who has conquered the senses, is devoted to dharma, is intent on self-study, is pure, and has desire and anger under control — him the gods know as a brahmin.
The one who regards all the world as equal to himself, who knows dharma, who is wise, and who is devoted to all dharmas — him the gods know as a brahmin.
The one who teaches, studies, sacrifices, officiates at sacrifice, and gives according to his ability — him the gods know as a brahmin.
The twice-born who lives as a student of the Vedas, who studies them and is diligent in self-study — him the gods know as a brahmin.
One should proclaim the good of brahmins and speak truth among them; the mind of those who speak thus takes no delight in falsehood.

The wealth of a brahmin, they say, is self-study, self-restraint, uprightness, and the eternal subduing of the senses, O best of twice-born. Those who know dharma declare truth and uprightness to be the highest dharma.
The eternal dharma is hard to know, yet it is established in truth. Dharma has scripture as its authority — such is the teaching of the elders.

Dharma is seen in many forms and is indeed subtle, O best of twice-born. You too are a knower of dharma, devoted to self-study and pure — yet in my opinion, O venerable one, you do not truly know dharmas in their essence.

A hunter who serves his mother and father, speaks truth, and has his senses under control lives in Mithilā — he will teach you the dharmas. Go there; may it be well with you and may you go as you please, O best of twice-born.
You should forgive whatever excess I may have said, O blameless one, for women are inviolable to all those who know dharma.

The brahmin said: I am pleased with you; may it be well with you, O beautiful one, and my anger is gone. The reproach you gave me is my supreme good. May you be blessed. I shall go and accomplish this, O radiant one.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Dismissed by her, that brahmin Kauśika went out and returned to his own dwelling, blaming himself, O best of men.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having reflected on that wonder and on all the woman had said, that brahmin, blaming himself, appeared as one who had committed a fault.
Reflecting on the subtle course of dharma he then said: "One must have faith. I shall go to Mithilā."
"In that city dwells a hunter who is self-realized and a knower of dharma, they say — a man rich in austerity. I shall go to him this very day to ask about dharma."
Thus having resolved in his mind, faithful to the woman's words, convinced by the incident of the crane and by her righteous and auspicious words, he set out for Mithilā filled with eager curiosity.
Passing through forests, villages, and cities, he then came to Mithilā, well protected by Janaka.
It was filled with embankments of dharma, filled with sacrifices and festivals, beautiful, graced with towers and gateways, adorned with houses and enclosing walls.
Entering that delightful city surrounded by many mansions, well-stocked with many commodities, and with broad well-laid-out streets,
Filled with horses, chariots, elephants, and many vehicles, thronged with cheerful and well-fed people, always bustling with festivity,
That brahmin, passing through and seeing all its varied affairs, asked after the righteous hunter, and he was pointed out to him by the brahmins there.
Going there he saw that austere man stationed in the midst of a meat-market, selling venison and buffalo flesh. Because of the crowd of buyers, the brahmin stood apart to one side.
But the hunter, knowing that the brahmin had arrived, rose up quickly with respect and came to where the brahmin was seated alone.
The hunter said: I salute you, O venerable one. Welcome to you, O best of twice-born. I am the hunter — may it be well with you. What shall I do? Command me.
"I know all of it — that you were told by the devoted wife to go to Mithilā, and the purpose for which you have come here."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hearing those words of his, that brahmin was greatly delighted. The twice-born reflected: "This is the second wonder."
"This place is not a fitting place for you," the hunter told the brahmin. "Let us go home, O venerable one, if it pleases you, O sinless one."
"Very well," the brahmin replied with great joy. Placing the brahmin ahead of him, the hunter went toward his home.
And entering the pleasant house, the best of twice-born was honored with a seat, and received water for his feet and for rinsing his mouth.
Then, seated comfortably, he spoke to the hunter: "This occupation does not seem fitting for you, it appears to me. I am deeply grieved, dear friend, by your dreadful occupation."
The hunter said: This is the work appropriate to my lineage, inherited from my fathers and forefathers. I live in my own dharma. Do not be angry with me, O twice-born.
I maintain the occupation ordained by the Creator from the beginning. And I serve with care my parents, the two elders, O best of twice-born.
I speak truth, I do not slander, I give according to my ability, and I live on what remains after providing for gods, guests, and servants.
I do not revile anything, I do not blame the more powerful. The deed done pursues the doer — that is karma from the past, O best of twice-born.
Agriculture, cattle-keeping, and trade are the livelihood of people in this world; also the science of governance and the threefold knowledge of the Vedas — by these the worlds exist.
Service is prescribed for the shudra, agriculture for the vaishya, battle for the kshatriya; celibacy, austerity, sacred chants, and truth always for the brahmin.
The king governs his subjects in accordance with dharma; those who are devoted to their own duties — and those who transgress their proper duties — he sets back on their own occupations.
One should always fear kings, for they are lords of their subjects. They slay those who transgress their duties, as hunters with arrows slay their prey.
In Janaka's realm, O brahmin-sage, there is no one transgressing his duty; all four castes are devoted to their own dharmas, O best of twice-born.
This king Janaka places even a misbehaving son under punishment if he deserves it, and likewise does not neglect the virtuous man.
The king whose conduct is well ordered sees all things through dharma. Prosperity, sovereignty, and the rod of justice belong to kshatriyas, O best of twice-born.
For kings through their own dharma seek abundant prosperity, and the king indeed becomes the protector of all the castes.
O brahmin, I do not myself slay the boars and buffaloes — they are killed by others, O brahmin-sage. I only sell them always.
I do not eat meat; I approach my wife only in her season. I am always fasting and I eat only at night, O twice-born.
Even a man who has been of bad character can become virtuous; and even one addicted to harming living beings can again become righteous.
Through the transgressions of kings, great dharma becomes confused, adharma increases, and likewise the subjects intermingle.
Dwarfs, hunchbacks, those with large heads, eunuchs, the blind, the deaf, and those with hanging ears are born — from the unrighteousness of kings the decline of subjects always follows.
This king Janaka sees all things through dharma, always favoring his subjects who are each devoted to their own dharma.
Both those who praise me and those who blame me — I satisfy all people through well-measured conduct.
Those who live by their own dharma and those kings who enjoy accordingly — those who are capable and diligent do not depend on anyone for their livelihood.

Constant giving of food according to one's ability, forbearance, steadfastness in dharma, honor given as befits each person, and compassion toward all beings — virtues of mortals rest nowhere in a person except through generosity.
One should shun false speech, should do what is pleasing without being asked, and should not abandon dharma out of desire, anger, or hatred.
One should not be excessively overjoyed at the pleasant nor burn in distress at the unpleasant; one should not be bewildered in financial difficulties, nor should one abandon dharma.
If there is some other better course of action, one should not practice what is different from it. Whatever is auspicious — on that should one fix oneself.
One should not be wicked in return for wickedness; one should always be a good person. The wicked one who wishes to do evil is slain by his own self.
This is the conduct of the wicked, of sinners acting wickedly — those who think there is no dharma and who mock the pure. Those without faith in dharma perish — there is no doubt.
The wicked man is always puffed up like a great inflated water-skin; the speech of the foolish and arrogant is without substance. He reveals his inner self like the sun reveals its form by day.
A fool does not shine in the world by self-praise alone; even one who is without physical grace but has acquired learning shines forth.
Not speaking ill of anyone, not lauding oneself — no one who is endowed with virtues is seen to be prominently visible on the earth.
One who is tormented by wrongful action is freed from sin; resolving "I will not do this again," one is freed from the second offence.
By whatever action one is freed here from sin, O best of twice-born — thus, O brahmin, this teaching is seen throughout the dharma scriptures.
Sins formerly committed here in ignorance — one of virtuous character destroys them afterward. O brahmin, dharma drives away from men that which they do in sin and negligence here.
Having done wrong, a person should think "I am not that self" and should only desire to do good, being faithful and free from malice.

He who exposes the faults of the virtuous as one exposes the holes in a garment — if such a person, having done evil, turns toward the good, he is freed from all sins, as the moon is freed from great clouds.
Just as the sun rising dispels all darkness, so one who abides in virtue is freed from all sins.

Know that greed alone is the seat of all sins, O best of twice-born. The greedy and the poorly learned commit sin; those who follow unrighteousness under the guise of righteousness are like wells covered with grass.
For them, self-restraint and purifications are mere talk cloaked in dharma; everything may be found in them, yet the conduct of the righteous is exceedingly rare.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that brahmin, most learned, asked the Dharma-Hunter: 'How may I know the conduct of the righteous, O best of men? Tell me truly, O hunter of great wisdom, exactly as it is.'
The hunter said: Sacrifice, charity, austerity, the Vedas, and truth, O best of twice-born — these five are always the purifications found in the conduct of the righteous.
Those who have subdued desire and anger, who have renounced pretense, greed, and dishonesty, who are satisfied with dharma alone — they are the righteous, honored by the righteous.
For those devoted to sacrifice and self-study there is no transgression; and observance of right conduct is indeed the second mark of the righteous.
Service to the teacher, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and charity — these four, O brahmin, are always present in the conduct of the righteous.
Fixing one's mind on righteous conduct and establishing oneself therein in every way, the satisfaction one obtains cannot be had by any other means.
The secret teaching of the Veda is truth; the secret teaching of truth is self-restraint; the secret teaching of restraint is renunciation — these are always present in the conduct of the righteous.
Those persons deluded in intellect who revile dharma travel the wrong path; even one who follows such people is harmed.
But those who are righteous, well-controlled, devoted to the knowledge of scripture and renunciation, who have mounted the path of dharma and are devoted to truth and righteousness —
— such persons endowed with righteous conduct restrain the highest intellect; established in the teaching of their preceptors, steadfast, they perceive dharma and its true purpose.
Abandon atheists, those who transgress boundaries, the cruel, and those fixed in sinful thought; taking refuge in wisdom, associate instead with the righteous.
Making fortitude your boat, cross the river of the five senses crowded with the demons of desire and greed, and traverse the difficult passages of existence.
Dharma accumulated gradually through the yoga of wisdom becomes great; attachment to righteous conduct in the virtuous is like whiteness in a garment.

Non-violence, truthful speech, and the highest good of all beings — non-violence is the supreme dharma, and it is established in truth; when one establishes oneself in truth, all one's activities proceed rightly.
Truth alone is most weighty when practiced in the conduct of the righteous; the conduct of the good is indeed dharma, and the good are known by their conduct.
Whatever is the nature of a creature, it experiences that very nature; the sinful soul, lacking self-mastery, incurs the faults of anger, desire, and the like.
Whatever undertaking is joined with justice is remembered as dharma; misconduct indeed is adharma — this is the teaching of the righteous.
Those who do not become angry, who do not envy, who are free from ego and jealousy, who are upright and endowed with tranquility — they possess the conduct of the righteous.
Those accomplished in the three Vedas, the pure, those of good character, the high-minded, those devoted to serving their teachers, the self-controlled — they too possess righteous conduct.
Of those of undepressed spirit who practice difficult austerities and are honored by their own deeds, even the harshness of their deeds completely disappears.
Seeing that wondrous, ancient, eternal, and immovable good conduct as dharma through dharma, the wise attain heaven.
Those who are believers, free from pride, who honor the twice-born community, who are endowed with learning and good conduct — such righteous ones are bound for heaven.
The supreme dharma declared in the Vedas, the other in the law-treatises, and that practiced by the righteous — these are the threefold marks of dharma.
Mastery of the sciences, immersion in sacred fords, forbearance, truthfulness, straightforwardness, and purity — these are demonstrations of righteous conduct.
Those who are compassionate toward all beings, always devoted to non-violence, who never speak harshly — such good people are always dear to the twice-born.
Those who know the ripening of the accumulated fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds — they are the righteous, honored by the righteous.
Endowed with justice and virtue, desiring the good of all worlds, the pure good ones who have conquered heaven are established on the true path.
Those who give, who share equitably, who show grace to the wretched, who are compassionate toward all beings — they are the righteous, honored by the righteous.
Those worthy of universal honor, rich in learning, and also the ascetics who are ever given to charity — they attain pleasant worlds and prosperity here as well.
Even at cost of hardship to their spouse and dependents, the good who gather with the good give beyond their means.
Seeing the way of the world, dharma, and what is beneficial for the self, the good who live in this manner flourish for endless years.
Non-violence, truthful speech, gentleness, uprightness, absence of malice, freedom from excessive pride, modesty, forbearance, self-restraint, and tranquility —
— those who are wise and steadfast, compassionate toward all beings, free from desire and hatred — they are the good ones, honored by the world.
They declare only three steps to be the unsurpassed conduct of the good: do no harm to anyone, always give, and always speak the truth.

The good who are compassionate everywhere, who know compassion, who go along here fully contented on the righteous, supreme path — great-souled ones of righteous conduct whose dharma is firmly established.
Freedom from envy, forbearance, peace, contentment, pleasant speech, and the abandonment of desire and anger — these are the practice of righteous conduct.
Those endowed with learning through action, who tirelessly follow dharma, always practice the unsurpassed path of the good, which is righteous conduct.

Ascending the palace of wisdom and observing great masses of deluded people, and beholding the various activities of the world, O best of twice-born — the very sinful deeds among those are exceedingly meritorious, O best of the twice-born.
All this has been told to you, O brahmin, to the best of my wisdom and learning, placing foremost the virtues of righteous conduct, O bull among twice-born.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the Dharma-Hunter spoke to the brahmin, O Yudhiṣṭhira: 'That I indeed perform a terrible occupation — of this there is no doubt.'

'But fate is powerful, O brahmin; what was done in a former life is hard to overcome; this fault of action arises from sin committed in a former life. And in overcoming this fault, O brahmin, I am indeed striving.'
'What has been ordained by fate in a former life — a killer may become the mere occasion for it; we are indeed only the occasion for this action, O best of twice-born.'
'The flesh of those we slay and sell, O brahmin — dharma may arise even for them through its enjoyment and consumption, through the honoring of gods, guests, servants, and ancestors.'
'Herbs, plants, cattle, deer, and birds have become food and the like for the world — this too is heard in the Vedic teaching.'
'By offering his own flesh, the forbearing king Śibi, son of Uśīnara, attained the very rare heaven, O best of twice-born.'
'In the royal kitchen of Rantideva in former times, O brahmin, two thousand animals were slaughtered daily.'
'Because Rantideva always gave food with meat, incomparable fame accrued to that king, O best of twice-born; at the four-monthly festivals animals were always slaughtered.'

'"The sacred fires too desire meat" — this also is heard in Vedic teaching. In sacrifices, O brahmin, animals are always slaughtered by twice-born; consecrated by mantras, those animals too are said to attain heaven.'
'If the sacred fires had never desired meat in former times, O brahmin, flesh would not have been food for anyone at all, O best of twice-born.'

'Even here the rule has been stated by sages regarding the eating of meat: one who always eats after offering to gods and ancestors, duly and with faith according to the rule, is not defiled by that eating.'
'"One becomes a non-meat-eater in this way" — this also is heard in Vedic teaching; a brahmin who approaches his wife only in the fertile season is a celibate student.'
'Having considered truth and untruth, a rule is stated here as well: in former times, human flesh was eaten by king Saudāsa who was overwhelmed by a curse. What do you think of that here, O brahmin?'
'Considering this my own duty, I do not abandon it, O best of twice-born; knowing it as what was determined in a former life, I live by this occupation.'
'For one who abandons his own duty, adharma is seen here; but one who is devoted to his own duty — that is dharma, this is the certainty.'
'The action ordained in a former life does not release the embodied being; this rule of the Creator has been seen in many ways in the determination of karma.'
'A wise person engaged in cruel occupation must consider: how may I perform auspicious deeds? How may I be freed from defeat? The determination of that terrible karma may arise in many ways.'

'In charity, in truthful speech, in service to my teacher, and in honoring the twice-born — I am always devoted to dharma; from excessive speech and excessive pride I have withdrawn, O best of twice-born.'

'People think agriculture is good, yet great violence is considered inherent in it — those who plow with plows kill many creatures dwelling in the earth and many other living beings. What do you think of that here?'
'The grain seeds they speak of — rice and the rest, O best of twice-born — all these are living beings. What do you think of that here?'
'Humans attack and kill cattle too and eat them; and they also cut down trees and plants, O brahmin.'
'Many living beings are found in trees and fruits as well, and many also in water — what do you think of that here?'
'All this universe, O brahmin, is pervaded with living beings sustained by life; fish devour fish — what do you think of that here?'
'Beings live upon beings in many ways, O best of twice-born; living creatures eat one another — what do you think of that here?'
'While walking about, humans kill many living beings dwelling on the ground with their feet, O brahmin — what do you think of that here?'
'Even sitting and lying down they kill living beings in many ways, and so do those possessed of knowledge and science — what do you think of that here?'
'All this — sky and earth alike — is possessed by living beings; and out of ignorance they harm one another — what do you think of that here?'

'What was declared as non-violence by astonished men in former times — who, while living in this world, does not do harm, O best of twice-born? Considering much, there is truly no one in this world who is non-violent.'
'The ascetics devoted to non-violence, O best of twice-born, do commit harm; but through effort theirs becomes ever less.'
'Invisible persons born in good families, endowed with great virtues, after performing very terrible deeds, truly feel no shame.'
'Friends do not see other friends rightly, nor do enemies see enemies rightly; they do not rightly observe those who behave properly.'
'Kinsmen do not rejoice with kinsmen in prosperity; and the foolish who fancy themselves learned even revile their teachers.'
'Much in the world is seen to be inverted, O best of twice-born — unrighteousness mingled with righteousness — what do you think of that here?'
'Much of various kinds can be said about deeds in the realm of dharma and adharma; but one who is devoted to his own duty shall attain great fame.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The Dharma-Hunter then spoke skillfully once more, O Yudhiṣṭhira — that best among all upholders of dharma spoke thus to the foremost of brahmins:
'It has been said by elders that dharma has the Vedas as its authority; the course of dharma is subtle, with many branches and of unbounded scope.'
'In a life-threatening situation and at a wedding, an untruth may be spoken; and an untruth may become truth, and truth itself may become untruth.'
'What is supremely beneficial to beings — that is held to be truth; what produces the contrary is adharma. Observe the subtlety of dharma.'
Whatever inauspicious or auspicious action a man performs, O best of twice-born, he must inevitably reap that fruit — there is no doubt in this matter.
When he falls into adversity, the fool bitterly reviles the gods; he does not recognize that the faults in his own actions are to blame.
The deluded man, deceitful and fickle, O best of twice-born — when the reversal of pleasure and pain overtakes him, neither wisdom nor good conduct nor even manliness can save him.
If the fruit of a man's actions depended on no one else, then whatever desire he harbored he would attain that very desire exactly as he wished.
Yet men who are self-restrained, capable, and intelligent are seen to be fruitless, cast aside despite all their efforts.
Another man, ever engaged in harming creatures and deceiving the world, lives here in comfort with ease.
Prosperity approaches one man who sits doing nothing; another who works tirelessly never attains what he seeks.
After worshipping the gods and performing austerities, miserly men greedy for sons see born from their wombs — carried ten months — children who disgrace the family.
Others are born into abundant wealth, grain, and enjoyments accumulated by their ancestors, having obtained those very auspicious blessings.
The diseases of human beings are indeed born of their actions — there is no doubt here. They are afflicted by mental anguish and bodily ailments just as small animals are hunted by hunters.
And yet those diseases are warded off by skillful physicians skilled in compounding medicines — just as animals are held at bay by hunters, O twice-born.
There are those who have the means to enjoy but, afflicted by digestive disorders, cannot eat — behold this, O best among upholders of dharma.
Others, possessed of great physical strength, struggle greatly, and only with difficulty do they obtain their food, O best of twice-born.
Thus this world, overwhelmed by delusion and sorrow, is again and again swept away like a current and carried off by something more powerful.
If sovereign mastery were truly within reach, none would die, none would grow old, all would fulfill every desire, and none would ever face what is unwished.
Everyone strives to rise higher and higher in the world and exerts himself according to his capacity — yet things do not turn out that way.
Many are seen who share the same birth-star and auspicious signs, yet great inequality of result is observed at the junctures of their actions.
No one is master of seizing things by his own will alone, O brahmin, O best of good men — the fulfillment of ordinary actions is seen to depend on something else.
As this scriptural teaching holds, O brahmin: the self is indeed eternal, while the body in this world is impermanent for all living beings.
When the body is destroyed, the body perishes indeed; but the self migrates elsewhere, bound by the bonds of its accumulated karma.
The brahmin said: How is the self eternal, O best among upholders of dharma? I wish to know this truth — tell me, O best among those who speak truthfully.

The hunter said: There is no destruction of the self when the body dissolves; the fools who say 'it dies' speak falsely. The self departs, having passed through the body; the dissolution of the body is as nothing compared to the self.

For another does not eat the fruit of an action that has been done; the very doer himself experiences pleasure and pain. Whatever action has been done by him, he reaps that — there is no destruction of what has been done.
Those of sinful disposition may become meritorious, and best among men may become sinners — a man here is accompanied by his own actions, and is reborn shaped by them.
The brahmin said: How does conception in the womb occur? How do merit and demerit operate? How does one go to auspicious or inauspicious births, O good one?
The hunter said: This action connected with the planting of the embryo is observed here — I will explain it to you briefly and quickly, O best of twice-born.
Just as one who has accumulated provisions is born again, the doer of good is born in auspicious wombs, and the doer of evil in evil wombs.
By auspicious conduct one attains divinity; by mixed actions one becomes human; by deluding means one goes to lower births; and by sinful deeds one descends further.
Constantly assailed by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, and cooked in the cycle of existence by the faults he himself has made, man wanders on.
Having passed through thousands of animal births and through hell itself, souls revolve in this cycle, bound by the bonds of karma.
The creature, suffering after death on account of its own various actions, obtains a low birth for the purpose of counteracting that suffering.
Then again it undertakes new and manifold actions, and is cooked anew by them — just as a sick man who eats harmful food suffers again.

Perpetually tormented yet calling itself free from pain and naming its state 'happiness,' and because its bondage never ceases even with the rise of new actions, it wanders through samsara like a wheel, experiencing many sufferings.
But if one has dissolved its bonds and is purified in its actions, it attains the worlds of the meritorious — having gone there, it grieves no more.
One who commits evil and lives evilly never reaches the end of sin; therefore one should strive to perform meritorious deeds and shun transgression.
One who is free from envy and grateful cultivates only the auspicious; such a man attains happiness, dharma, wealth, and heaven.
For the man of culture, self-controlled, disciplined, with mastered soul and wise — his sustenance is unobstructed, both in this world and the next.
One should live by the dharma of the good, conduct one's actions as the learned do, and seek one's livelihood without causing distress to the world, O twice-born.
For there are learned men, well-versed in scripture, who have attained wisdom; by living according to one's own dharma, action in the world remains without confusion.
The wise man delights in dharma and lives by dharma; with the wealth obtained through dharma, O best of twice-born, he waters its very root and perceives the virtues therein.
In this way he becomes righteous of soul and his mind grows serene; content among kindly people, he rejoices both here and hereafter.
Sound, touch, form, desired fragrances, and lordly power — all these he obtains; the wise know this to be the fruit of dharma, O good man.
Having obtained the fruit of dharma, he is not satisfied, O great twice-born; and in that dissatisfaction he takes up dispassion with the eye of knowledge.
The man whose eye is wisdom does not here conform to any fault; he becomes dispassionate as he wishes, yet does not abandon dharma.
Having seen the world to be of a perishing nature, he strives toward the renunciation of all things; then he strives toward liberation — not by indirect means but by the direct path.
Thus he takes up dispassion, abandons sinful action, becomes righteous, and attains supreme liberation.
Austerity is the highest good for a living being; its root is tranquility and self-restraint. By that one attains all the desires that the mind wishes for.
By the restraint of the senses, by truth, and by self-control, one attains the supreme state of Brahman, O best of twice-born.
The brahmin said: What are those that are called the senses, O you of firm vows? How is their restraint to be practiced, and what is the fruit of that restraint?
And how does one attain the fruit thereof, O best among upholders of dharma? I desire to know this dharma in truth, O you who are deeply righteous.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed by the brahmin, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-hunter replied to the brahmin accordingly — hear that, O lord of men.
The hunter said: For the purpose of knowing, the mind of human beings first sets itself in motion; having obtained its object, it then indulges in desire and anger, O best of twice-born.
Then for that very purpose it strives and undertakes great action; it constantly pursues the habituation of desired forms and fragrances.
From that arises passion, and immediately after it hatred; from that arises greed, and immediately after it delusion.
Of one overwhelmed by greed and struck down by passion and hatred, the intellect does not arise toward dharma; he performs dharma only through pretense.

He practices dharma by pretense, he takes pleasure in wealth by pretense; when wealth is acquired through pretense, O best of twice-born, the intellect delights in that very thing and then desires to commit sin.
Even when restrained by friends and by learned men, O best of twice-born, he speaks a reply connected to scripture, invoking scripture to justify himself.
Adharma in three forms grows in him out of the fault of passion: he thinks sin, speaks sin, and commits sin.
For one who has turned toward adharma, good virtues perish; and those who are of like character come to enjoy his friendship — those who commit evil actions.
By this he obtains misery and is struck down in the hereafter — thus one becomes of sinful soul. Now hear from me the gaining of dharma.

But he who by wisdom foresees these very faults from the outset, who is skilled in pleasure and pain and frequents the company of the virtuous — through association with good beginnings, his intellect is born toward the ways of dharma.
The brahmin said: You speak dharma that is true and pleasant — there is no other speaker of it like you. Of divine splendor and exceeding greatness, you seem to me truly a sage.
The hunter said: Brahmins are indeed the most fortunate; they are the forefathers who partake first always. A wise man should with all his soul do what pleases them in the world.
What pleases them I will tell you, O best of twice-born — having paid homage to the brahmins, learn from me the knowledge born of Brahman.
This entire universe, wholly unconquerable in every respect, O brahmin, has the great elements as its soul; there is nothing higher than this.
The great elements are: space, wind, fire, water, and earth — and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities.
All of their qualities operate mutually on one another; each carries forward the qualities of the one preceding it — all in succession among the three modes of being.
The sixth is named consciousness — it is called the mind; the seventh is the intellect; and after that comes the ego-sense.
And the five senses, along with rajas, sattva, and tamas — this is the group of seventeen known by the name of the unmanifest.

Perfectly enveloped by all the objects of the senses here, both manifest and unmanifest, this is the twenty-fourth — the principle composed of both manifest and unmanifest. All this has been declared to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed by the dharma-hunter, O Bhārata, that brahmin then spoke once more a discourse that increases the joy of the mind.
The brahmin said: O best among those who know dharma, those five great elements of which they speak — tell me properly the qualities of each of the five individually.
The hunter said: Earth, water, fire, wind, and space — all have qualities exceeding one another; I will tell you their qualities.
Earth has five qualities, O brahmin, and water has four; fire has three qualities, and space and wind each have two — or rather three between them.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth — these five qualities of earth are richest in qualities compared to all others.
Sound, touch, form, and taste — O best of twice-born, O brahmin, O you of excellent vows, these are proclaimed to be the qualities of water.
Sound, touch, and form — these three are the qualities of fire. In wind there are sound and touch; in space, sound alone.

These fifteen qualities, O brahmin, abide in the five elements — they are present in all beings, in whom the worlds are grounded. They do not transgress one another, and their conjunction brings well-being, O twice-born.
But when the moving and unmoving beings enter into a state of imbalance, then the embodied soul in the course of time mounts another body.

In succession they perish, and in succession they are born; here and there the elements composed of the five great ones are seen — by which this entire world, of moving and unmoving things, is enveloped.
Whatever is produced by the senses is known as the manifest; that which is beyond the grasp of the senses and is apprehended only through its marks is to be understood as the unmanifest.
These senses each grasp their respective objects — sound and the rest — and when the embodied being supports them here, he undergoes austerity.
He sees the Self spread through the world and the world within the Self; the knower of the near and far, though engaged, sees all beings.
For one who sees all beings in all conditions at all times, who has become Brahman, no association with the inauspicious can arise.
For one who has transcended the affliction rooted in knowledge and born of delusion, the world is seen by the light of the intellect on the path of what is to be known.

The wise Lord declared: the living being is without beginning or end, self-originated, eternally imperishable, incomparable, and formless — all this that you, O brahmin, ask me about has its root in austerity.
The senses are indeed everything — both heaven and hell; when restrained they lead to heaven, when let loose they lead to hell.
The entire discipline of yoga consists in the restraint of the senses; this is indeed the root of all austerity and likewise the root of all hell.
Through indulgence of the senses one falls into fault without doubt; by restraining those same senses, one thereafter attains perfection.
One who achieves mastery over the six ever-present senses within the self — that conqueror of the senses is not bound by sins, still less by misfortunes.

The body of a person is seen as a chariot; they say the Self is the driver and the senses are the horses — the skilled one, vigilant with well-trained and disciplined horses, travels comfortably like a wise charioteer.
The steadfast one who holds the reins of the six ever-present and turbulent senses within the self would be the supreme charioteer.
For senses let loose on their tracks like horses, one should exercise steadiness in charioteering; by steadiness one will certainly conquer them.
When the mind follows along with the roving senses, it carries away one's intellect as the wind carries away a boat upon the waters.
One who is resolute and studious in those six matters wherein people go astray from delusion when fruits arrive — that one obtains the fruit born of meditation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Bhārata, when the Dharma-Hunter had thus spoken on subtle matters, that brahmin, with concentrated mind, asked once more about something subtle.
The brahmin said: Tell me accurately and in truth about the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas as they truly are, explaining them correctly to me as I ask here.
The hunter said: Come, I shall tell you what you ask of me — know the qualities of these separately as I speak.
Among these, tamas is characterized by delusion and rajas by agitation; sattva, because it is abundant in luminosity, is called the highest here.
Abounding in ignorance, bewildered, prone to sleep, unconscious, dim-sighted, overwhelmed by darkness, wrathful, and slothful — such is the tamasic person.
One who is verbose, scheming, attached, envious, inquisitive, O seer among brahmins, arrogant and proud — such is the rajasic person.
Abounding in luminosity, steadfast, without excessive curiosity, free from envy, not given to anger, wise and self-restrained — such a person is sattvic.
But when the sattvic person, being fully awakened, is troubled by worldly conduct and comes to understand what is to be understood, he turns away in disgust from worldly behavior.
For the form of dispassion arises first; the ego-sense becomes soft, and whatever straightforwardness there is becomes serene.
Thereafter all the pairs of opposites within him mutually subside; and no restraint whatsoever is needed for him anywhere.
For one born in the womb of a shudra who abides in good qualities, O brahmin, the state of a vaishya arises, and likewise the state of a kshatriya.
For one who lives in straightforwardness, brahminhood arises. All those qualities have been described — what more do you wish to hear?
The brahmin said: When the bodily fire meets the earthly element, how does it exist? And how does the wind function through the particular cavities of the body?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, this question raised by the brahmin — the hunter expounded it to that great-souled brahmin.

The hunter said: The fire, taking up residence in the head, protects the body; the vital breath, operating in both the head and the fire, stirs into action — all that has been, all that is, and all that shall be is established in the vital breath.

That very one is the best among beings — we worship the light of Brahman; that living being is the Self of all beings, the eternal Person; mind, intellect, ego-sense, and the objects of beings — he is all that.
Thus here he is everywhere sustained by the vital breath; behind it, the equalized breath, each taking up its own course.
At the base of the bladder and in the rectum, the fire takes up residence; the downward breath, carrying urine and feces, moves in rotation.
That one breath which operates in the three — in effort, action, and strength — those who know the inner self call it the udana breath.
The breath lodged in every joint throughout the body of human beings is designated the vyana breath.
The fire spread through the bodily elements, stirred by the wind, runs throughout, processing the essences, the elements, and the humors.
Through the confluence of the vital breaths, their joint action arises; the heat, which is to be known as the fire, digests the food of the embodied beings.
The prana and vyana breaths, concentrated between the apana and udana, together with them at their station, cause the fire to digest properly.
And its extent reaches to the anus, which is thus called the guda; from that arise the channels in all the vital breaths of the embodied.
The vital breath that carries the force of fire is repelled at the end of the rectum; coming upward again, it once more projects the fire upward.
The stomach of cooked food lies below the navel; above it stands the stomach of raw food; in the center of the navel, all the vital breaths are established.
All ten channels, flowing from the heart sideways, upward, and downward, carry the essences of food, impelled by the vital breaths.

This is the path of yogins by which they reach the Supreme — the steadfast ones who have mastered the posture of exhaustion place the Self in the crown of the head. Thus the prana and apana breaths are spread through all embodied beings.
Know that which has eleven modifications as its nature and is assembled from an accumulation of fractions — know it as the embodied one, eternally characterized by a self won through action.
The fire that is ever established in that one, placed as if in a cooking vessel — know that Self as eternally characterized by a self won through yoga.
