'The dead man does not conquer enemies; the living man sees prosperity. Where is prosperity for the dead, O son of Kuru — where is victory? Today is no time for despondency, for fear, or for death.'

The mighty-armed one embraced him with both arms and said: 'Arise, O king — why do you lie there? Why do you grieve, O slayer of enemies? You who have scorched your foes with your valor — how can you wish to die?'
'Or if fear has arisen in you upon seeing Arjuna's valor, I swear to you truly: I will slay Arjuna in battle.'
'When the thirteenth year has passed, I take up my weapon in earnest — I will bring the Pārthas under your dominion, O lord of the people.'
Thus addressed by Karṇa, and likewise by the words of the Daityas and the prostrations of others, Suyodhana rose up; having heard the words of the Daityas, he fixed a firm resolve in his heart.
Then that tiger among men marshaled his army — dense with chariots, elephants, and horses, and thronging with infantry.
That great army set forth, O king, resembling the flood of the Gaṅgā, gleaming with white parasols, banners, and bright white fly-whisks.
Exceedingly crowded with chariots, elephants, and foot-soldiers, it shone brilliantly — like the autumnal sky, indistinct yet clear, when the thick clouds have passed away.
Praised with victory-blessings by the foremost Brahmins as though he were a paramount sovereign, and receiving garlands of joined palms, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the people —
— Suyodhana marched at the fore, blazing with supreme splendor, together with Karṇa and Saubala the gambler, O lord of kings.
And all his brothers headed by Duḥśāsana, and Bhūriśravas, Somadatta, and the great king Bāhlika —
— the foremost of Kurus followed that lion among kings as he marched, in chariots of varied forms, with horses and excellent elephants; and in a short time, O king, they all entered their own city.
Janamejaya said: While the great-souled Pārthas were dwelling in that forest, what did the Dhārtarāṣṭras, those great bowmen, do, O virtuous one?
Karṇa Vaikartana, the mighty Śakuni, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa — please relate all of this to me.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: After the Pārthas had gone away thus, and Suyodhana had been released and arrived at Hāstinapura, freed by the sons of Pāṇḍu, Bhīṣma spoke these words to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great king.
'It was said by me before, dear child, when you were setting out for the forest-hermitage — that expedition did not please me; yet you did not do as I said.'
'Then, O hero, you suffered capture by your enemies by force; and you were released by the Pāṇḍavas who know dharma — and yet you feel no shame.'

'It was witnessed by you yourself, O scion of Gāndhāra, O lord of the people, that the charioteer's son fled in fear from the battle against the Gandharvas while you, O lord of kings, O son of a king, were crying out for help along with your army.'
'The valor of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas has been seen by you, O mighty-armed one, as well as that of Karṇa the charioteer's son of wicked mind.'
'Nor is Karṇa worthy to be even at the feet of the Pāṇḍavas, O best of kings — not in archery, not in valor, not in dharma, O you who love dharma.'
'For this reason I consider it proper for you to make peace with those great-souled Pāṇḍavas, O best of those who know the art of reconciliation, for the prosperity of this lineage.'
Thus addressed by Bhīṣma, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the people, suddenly laughed and departed with Saubala, O king.
Knowing him to have set forth, Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the others — great bowmen — followed behind the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing them depart thus, Bhīṣma the grandsire of the Kurus, ashamed and abashed, O king, went to his own quarters.
After Bhīṣma had departed, O great king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the people, returned to that place and consulted with his ministers.
'What would be to our benefit? What task remains to be done? How might something well accomplished come about?' — thus he took counsel, O Bhārata.
Karṇa said: Duryodhana, hear this that I shall tell you, O Kaurava; and having heard it, you ought to do exactly all of it, O subduer of foes.
'Today the earth is yours without rival, O hero, O best of kings; rule it as Indra, the great-minded slayer of his enemies, rules his realm.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Karṇa, the king again spoke to Karṇa: 'Nothing is unattainable for him who has you, O bull among men.'
'You are my ally, devoted to me, and ever ready for my sake. But I have a certain desire — hear it truly as it is.'
'Having witnessed the Pāṇḍava's Rājasūya sacrifice, that chief of rituals, a longing arose in me then — fulfill it, O son of a charioteer.'
Thus addressed, Karṇa then said this to the king: 'Today all the guardians of the earth are subject to you, O best of kings.'
'Let the foremost Brahmins be summoned; let the materials be gathered properly; let the implements of sacrifice be assembled, O best of Kurus.'
'And let the officiating priests be called together — those versed in the Vedas as prescribed — let them perform the rites for you, O king, according to scripture, O subduer of foes.'
'Let a great sacrifice, furnished with abundant food and drink, endowed with fully flourishing qualities, be undertaken for you as well, O bull of the Bhāratas.'
Thus addressed by Karṇa, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O lord of the people, summoned his household priest and spoke these words.
'Conduct the Rājasūya, the foremost of sacrifices, complete with its excellent fees, for my sake, in proper order and due sequence.'
Thus addressed, that foremost of twice-born men said to the king: 'That foremost of sacrifices cannot be conducted while Yudhiṣṭhira lives, O best of Kauravas, O best of kings in your lineage.'
'Moreover, your father Dhṛtarāṣṭra lives and is long-lived; and for that reason too this sacrifice is barred to you, O best of kings.'
'There is, however, another great sacrifice equal to the Rājasūya, O lord; with that, do you sacrifice, O king of kings — and hear this word of mine.'
'Let these guardians of the earth who are your tributaries, O king, present their tributes and gold both wrought and unwrought.'
'With that, let a plough be made for you today, O best of kings; and let the ground of your sacrificial enclosure be tilled with it, O Bhārata.'
'There, O best of kings, let a sacrifice well performed, abundantly stocked with food, proceed in proper order, unobstructed from all sides.'
'This is called the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice for you — fit for righteous men; none but ancient Viṣṇu has ever performed this.'

'This great sacrifice rivals the Rājasūya, the foremost of rites; it is pleasing to us and will be to your benefit, O Bhārata; and it will proceed without obstacle, so that your desire may bear fruit.'
Thus addressed by those Brahmins, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth, then spoke these words to Karṇa, Saubala, and his brothers.
My entire speech pleases the Brāhmaṇas — of this there is no doubt. If it pleases you as well, then tell me so without delay.
Thus addressed, all of them said to the lord of men, "So be it." The king then gave orders to those stationed at their duties, each in proper sequence.
All the craftsmen were also instructed regarding the fashioning of the plough, and, O best of kings, everything was done just as ordered, in proper sequence.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all the craftsmen, together with the foremost ministers, reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, and the greatly wise Vidura announced it.
"O king, O Bhārata, the foremost sacrifice is ready; the proper time has come; and the divine golden plough, of immense wealth, has been fashioned."
Hearing this, O lord of the people, the best of kings, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, commanded that the king of sacrifices be commenced.
Then the sacrifice commenced — with abundant food, well-performed — and Gāndhārī too was consecrated for initiation according to scripture and in proper order.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was overjoyed, as was the greatly renowned Vidura, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the illustrious Gāndhārī.
He also dispatched swift messengers to invite kings and Brāhmaṇas alike, O king of kings; those envoys with swift mounts departed to their assigned destinations.
Then Duḥśāsana addressed one of the departing envoys: "Go quickly to the Dvaita forest; invite the sinful Pāṇḍavas in the proper manner, as well as the Brāhmaṇas in that great forest."
That messenger went to the dwelling of the Pāṇḍavas, bowed to them, and said, "O great king, Duryodhana, the best of kings, is performing a sacrifice."
"Having acquired great wealth by his own valour, the joy of the Kurus is holding it; kings and Brāhmaṇas are coming from all directions to attend."

"I have been sent, O king, by the great-souled Kaurava; the king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the people, invites you — you should come to witness that sacrifice which is the king's heart's desire."
Then king Yudhiṣṭhira, tiger among kings, having heard what the envoy said, replied: "By good fortune king Suyodhana performs the foremost of sacrifices, he who enhances the glory of his ancestors."
"We too shall come, but not now, under any circumstances — our pledge must be kept until thirteen years have passed."
Having heard this, Bhīma then spoke these words: "Indeed, king Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira will go —
— when that lord of men, in the fire blazing with weapons and missiles, will cast him into it at a war-sacrifice after thirteen years have elapsed.
When the Pāṇḍava releases the oblation of his wrath upon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — then you should tell that Suyodhana: 'They will come.'"
The remaining Pāṇḍavas, O king, spoke nothing disagreeable. And the envoy reported the whole matter as it had transpired to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then came the best of men, lords of various kingdoms, and greatly blessed Brāhmaṇas, all heading toward the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.
They were honored according to scripture, according to their station, and in proper order, with the greatest joy and affection, O lord of men.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra too, O king of kings, surrounded by all the Kauravas, filled with great delight, spoke to Vidura:
"See to it at once, O Kṣattā, that all the people be happy and well-provided with food, and that they be satisfied in the hall of sacrifice."
Thus commanded, Vidura, O crusher of foes, the wise knower of dharma, honored all the social orders in due measure.
He supplied them with things to eat and drink, food and beverages, with fragrant garlands, and with garments of many kinds — all with a joyful heart.

After the hero duly performed the concluding ablution according to scripture and in proper order, the king of kings, having consoled them and given them various riches, dismissed the kings and Brāhmaṇas in their thousands.
Having dismissed the kings, he entered Hāstinapura surrounded by his brothers, together with Karṇa and the son of Subala.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As he entered, O great king, bards praised the unshakeable one; the people too praised that great archer, the best of kings.
Strewing parched rice and sandalwood powder upon him, the people then said: "By good fortune this sacrifice of yours has been completed without obstacle, O king."
But others among the gossipers there spoke to that lord of the earth: "This sacrifice is not equal to Yudhiṣṭhira's sacrifice — it does not merit even a sixteenth part of that one."
Thus did some gossips speak there to that lord of men; but his friends said there: "This sacrifice surpasses all."
"Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Māndhātā, and Bharata — all were purified by performing this sacrifice and went to heaven."
Hearing these auspicious words of his friends, O bull of the Bhāratas, the lord of men entered the city joyfully and then his own palace.
Then, O lord of the people, he bowed at the feet of his mother and father, and also of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the wise Vidura.
Greeted by his younger brothers, that affectionate elder brother took his seat on the foremost throne, surrounded by his brothers.
Rising before him, O great king, the son of the charioteer spoke these words: "By good fortune, O best of the Bhāratas, this great sacrifice of yours has been completed."
"When the sons of Pṛthā have been slain in battle, and the Rājasūya has been performed by you, I shall honour you again, O best of men."
The greatly renowned great king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, said to him: "What you say is true, O hero, regarding those wicked-souled Pāṇḍavas."
"When they have been slain, O best of men, and when the great Rājasūya sacrifice has been obtained, you will exalt me again, O hero."
Having spoken thus, the greatly wise Kaurava embraced Karṇa, O Bhārata, and began to contemplate the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices.
He also spoke to his friends standing nearby, that best of kings: "When shall I, O Kauravas, slay all the Pāṇḍavas and perform that foremost sacrifice, the great Rājasūya, of immense wealth?"
Then Karṇa said to him: "Hear me, O elephant among kings — I shall not wash my feet until Arjuna has been slain."

Then there arose shouts of acclaim from the great bowmen, the great chariot-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons; when Karṇa had pledged the slaying of Phalguna in battle, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra considered the Pāṇḍavas already vanquished.

Duryodhana too, O king of kings, dismissing those bull-like men, the glorious lord entered his home like the lord entering the Chaitraratha forest. And all those great bowmen also went to their dwellings, O Bhārata.
And the Pāṇḍavas, those great bowmen, stirred up by the envoy's words, thinking on that very matter, found no peace anywhere.
And again through spies, O king of kings, news was brought of the pledge of the charioteer's son regarding the slaying of Vijaya.
Hearing this, the son of Dharma was deeply agitated, O lord of men; considering Karṇa with his impenetrable armour to be of wondrous valour, and remembering his own sufferings, he found no peace.
In his mind oppressed by anxiety, the thought arose in that great soul to leave the Dvaita forest, teeming with many snakes and wild beasts.
The king, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, for his part, ruled the earth together with his heroic brothers and with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa.

Meeting with the son of the charioteer, Karṇa, who was resplendent in battle, Duryodhana the lord of the earth, ever abiding in what was dear to him, honoured the foremost Brāhmaṇas with sacrifices bearing lavish sacrificial fees.
He also did what was pleasing to his brothers, O king, that scourge of enemies; the hero, having resolved in his mind, distributed wealth the fruit of which was giving and enjoyment.
Janamejaya said: After freeing Duryodhana, what did the mighty sons of Pāṇḍu do in that forest? Please tell me this.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then at night in the Dvaita forest, the deer appeared to the sleeping son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, at the end of a dream, their voices choked with tears.
That king of kings said to them, trembling with hands joined in supplication: "Speak what you wish to say. Who are you? What is desired?"
Thus addressed by the glorious Pāṇḍava, the son of Kuntī, the deer — the survivors of the slaughter — spoke there to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"We are the deer of the Dvaita forest, O Bhārata, the survivors of the killing. Let us not perish utterly, O great king — let there be a change of dwelling."
"You brothers are heroes, all of you skilled in weapons, and you have reduced the families of forest dwellers to only a few survivors."
"We who remain are but seed-animals, O great-minded one; through your grace, O king of kings, O Yudhiṣṭhira, may we multiply again."
Seeing those deer trembling, terrified, only seed-animals left in number, king Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was deeply pained.
The king who was devoted to the welfare of all beings said to them: "So be it. What you say is true, and I shall do exactly that."
Thus having awakened at the end of the night, that best of kings, filled with compassion for the deer, spoke to his brothers assembled together:
"I have been spoken to at night by the deer, those who remain after the killing, at the end of a dream: 'We have become few; blessings on you — show compassion to us.'"
"They speak the truth; we must show compassion to the forest creatures — for we have been consuming them for nearly eight months now throughout the year."

"Let us go again to Kāmyaka, that delightful forest with many deer, the best of forests, famed as the head of the desert land, toward the lake of Tṛṇabindu — let us dwell in those abodes that remain and take pleasure roaming there."
Then those Pāṇḍavas, versed in dharma, quickly departed together with the Brāhmaṇas, O king, and those who had dwelt there with them, and followed by servants headed by Indrasena.
Traveling along well-trodden paths with good food and pure water, they beheld the holy Kāmyaka hermitage filled with ascetics.
Those descendants of Kuru, O best of the Bhāratas, surrounded by foremost Brāhmaṇas, entered that forest like the virtuous entering heaven.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: For those great-souled Pāṇḍavas dwelling in the forest, eleven years passed in hardship, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Subsisting on fruits and roots, those best of men, though worthy of happiness, endured the greatest suffering, meditating on the time that had yet to come.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the royal sage, long-armed, reflected on the supreme suffering of his brothers, born of his own actions and transgressions.
The king slept not happily, his heart as if pierced by arrows, beholding that wickedness which had arisen from the dice-game at that fateful time.
Recalling the harsh words of the charioteer's son, the Pāṇḍava, wretched, breathing heavy sighs, bore within him a great poison of wrath.
Arjuna, the twin brothers, the illustrious Draupadī, and Bhīma of great energy, the mightiest of all — looking to Yudhiṣṭhira, they endured unparalleled suffering.
Those bulls among men, considering that only a little time remained, bore themselves as if in a different body through the exertions of zeal and indignation.
Then after some time, Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, the great yogin, came to visit the Pāṇḍavas.
Seeing him arrive, Kuntī's son Yudhiṣṭhira went forth to meet that great soul and received him with due ceremony.
Sitting near him once he was seated, the son who was the joy of the Pāṇḍavas attended on Vyāsa with disciplined senses, pleasing him with obeisance.
Seeing those emaciated grandsons living in the forest on forest fare, the great seer, out of compassion, spoke with a voice choked by tears:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, long-armed, O best of those who uphold dharma, hear me — those who have not undergone austerity, my son, do not attain great happiness."
"For a man experiences happiness and suffering in alternation; no one endures absolute unhappiness forever, O bull among men."
A person who is truly wise, endowed with the highest understanding, who knows the rising and setting of things — he neither grieves nor exults.
He should enjoy happiness when it comes and endure suffering when it arrives; he should attend to what the season brings, just as a farmer tends to crops.
There is nothing higher than austerity; through austerity one attains great things. Nothing is unattainable by austerity — understand this, O descendant of Bharata.

Truth, straightforwardness, freedom from anger, sharing, self-restraint, tranquility, freedom from envy, non-violence, purity, and control of the senses — these, O great king, are the means of meritorious conduct for men.
Those foolish persons who delight in unrighteousness, destined for inferior births, having attained a miserable womb, find no happiness.
Whatever deed is done here is experienced in the hereafter; therefore one should employ the body in austerity and observance of vows.
One should give according to one's ability, having honoured and reverenced the worthy recipient, at the right time and to the right person, with a joyful heart, O king, free from envy.
A speaker of truth gains long life; a straightforward person gains it without effort; one free from anger and free from envy attains the highest peace.
One who is self-controlled and ever devoted to tranquility does not encounter affliction; nor does the self-controlled soul grieve upon seeing another's prosperity.
A man who shares and gives enjoys pleasures and happiness; one who is non-violent attains supreme health.
One who honours those worthy of honour is born in a noble family; one who has conquered the senses does not fall into the company of vices.
One whose mind tends toward auspicious reflection, united with the law of time, manifests through that union — he is truly a person of noble understanding.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: O blessed one, O great sage, among the virtues of giving, the virtues of dharma, or the practice of austerity, which is said to yield the most fruit after death, or which is said to be the most difficult?
Vyāsa said: There is nothing more difficult than giving on this earth, for the craving for wealth is immense, and wealth itself is obtained only through hardship.
For the sake of wealth, valiant men enter great battles, leaving behind their dear lives; they venture into the ocean and into forests.
Some men resort to agriculture and cattle-rearing; others who desire wealth go out as servants seeking their fortunes.
To give up wealth thus earned with such suffering is extremely difficult; therefore there is nothing more difficult than giving — that is my view.
Yet a distinction must be understood here: wealth righteously earned should be given to worthy persons, in the right place and at the right time.
The dharma of giving performed with wealth unjustly acquired does not protect its doer from great fear.
Even a small gift given to a worthy recipient at the right time, O Yudhiṣṭhira, with a perfectly pure mind, is remembered as yielding infinite fruit after death.
On this subject they also cite this ancient story — the fruit that Mudgala obtained by giving away a measure of rice.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was that measure of rice given up by that great soul? To whom was it given, O blessed one, and by what rite? Tell me this.
You, O blessed one, are one who sees dharma directly. I consider fruitful the birth of that practitioner of true dharma whose actions have pleased you.
Vyāsa said: O king, there was Mudgala, a man of righteous soul and sharpened vows, who lived by gleaning grain from the fields; he dwelt in Kurukṣetra, a speaker of truth, free from envy.
Devoted to the vow of hospitality and active in rites, he had adopted the pigeon's way of living; the great ascetic performed the sacrifice known as Ishtikrita.
The sage, together with his sons and wife, ate only once a fortnight; living by the pigeon's gleaning, he gathered a measure of rice over a fortnight.
Performing the new-moon and full-moon rites, free from envy, he sustained his body on what remained after the gods and guests had been served.
Indra himself, together with the gods, the lord of the three worlds in person, would receive his portion at each lunar observance, O great king.
Having completed the sacred occasion with a sage's conduct, he gave food to guests with a heart overflowing with joy.
On that day, as the great-souled one gave out food from his measure of rice, the remainder — of one who was free from envy — increased at the sight of each guest.
Even hundreds of wise brahmins would eat of it; through the purity of the sage's renunciation, that food kept multiplying.
Then Durvasa — the sky-clad sage, O king — heard of that most righteous Mudgala of sharpened vow, and came to him.
The sage wore an irregular garb, O Pāṇḍava; he appeared like a madman, his hair dishevelled, uttering various harsh words.
Approaching that brahmin, the great sage said: Know me, O best of sages, as one who has come seeking food.
"You are welcome" — so Mudgala addressed the sage, and offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and then the finest food.
He who was pledged to hospitality, steadfast in his vow, gave to the hungry and seemingly mad guest that food earned through austerity, with supreme faith.
Then that mad one, filled with hunger, ate all of that savory food himself; and Mudgala gave it entirely to him.
Having eaten all the food, he then smeared his own body with the leavings, and departed just as he had come.
In this same manner, when the second lunar observance arrived, that wise one came again and ate all the food of the one who lived by gleaning.
The sage, left without food, would go out gleaning again; and hunger was unable to bring any agitation in Mudgala.
Neither anger, nor envy, nor contempt, nor confusion entered that best of twice-born ones as he gleaned with his sons and wife.
In this same way, Durvasa, that foremost of sages, with firm resolve, tested that practitioner of the gleaning-dharma six times at the proper occasion.
The sage found not the slightest perturbation in his mind; he saw the pure, stainless mind of one whose nature was wholly pure.
Then that sage, filled with joy, spoke to Mudgala: "There is no giver in this world equal to you, who is utterly free from envy."
Hunger drives away the awareness of dharma and takes away even steadiness; the tongue, following sense-objects, drags one toward tastes.
The vital breaths are sustained by food; the mind is difficult to restrain and restless; and the one-pointed concentration of the mind and senses — that is truly what is meant by austerity.
To give up with a pure heart what has been earned with such effort and pain — all that has been perfectly accomplished by you, O virtuous one.
We are pleased and feel honoured to have met with you; the conquest of the senses, steadiness, sharing, self-restraint, and tranquility —
— compassion, truth, and dharma — all these are established in you. The worlds have been won by your deeds; you have attained the supreme destination.
Ah, how greatly your act of giving is proclaimed by the dwellers of heaven! You, O one of noble vow, shall ascend to heaven in your own body.
While sage Durvasa was saying these very words, a divine messenger arrived before Mudgala in a celestial chariot.
It was yoked with swans and cranes, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, moving at will, wondrous in its beauty, fragrant with divine scents.
He spoke to that brahmin-sage: "This celestial chariot has been won by your deeds — ascend it. You have attained the highest perfection, O sage."
The sage spoke to that divine messenger who had spoken thus: "I wish to hear from you the qualities of those who dwell in heaven."
"What are the virtues of those who dwell there? What is the austerity, what the resolve? What is the happiness of heaven? And what, O divine messenger, are its faults?"
"The virtuous, those established in a noble lineage, say that seven steps together make a friendship. Honouring that friendship, I ask you, O lord."
"Whatever is true and beneficial in this matter, speak it without hesitation; having heard, I shall act accordingly by the resolution your words inspire."
The divine messenger said: O great sage, you are acting without discernment — like an ignorant person, you are deliberating over the supreme happiness of heaven that has been placed before you.
That world above, known by the name Svarga — heaven — is the ever-upward path, the good path, eternally traversed by the way of the gods, O sage.
Those who have not heated themselves with austerity, those who have not performed great sacrifices, the dishonest and the faithless — they do not go there, O Mudgala.
Those whose souls are righteous, who have conquered themselves, who are peaceful and self-controlled and free from envy, who delight in the dharma of giving, who are heroes bearing auspicious marks —
— they go there, having performed the highest deeds of restraint and self-control, to those worlds of the meritorious, O brahmin, frequented by virtuous men.
The gods, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts along with the great sages, the Yamas, the Dhamas, O Mudgala, and the Gandharvas and Apsaras —
— for each of these groups of gods there are many separate worlds, radiant, fulfilling all desires, made of light, auspicious.
Meru, the king of mountains, golden, thirty-three thousand yojanas in extent — there the divine gardens are found, O Mudgala.
Nandana and other sacred groves, the pleasure-grounds of those of meritorious deeds — there is no hunger, no thirst, no weariness, no fear of cold or heat.
Nothing disgusting or inauspicious, no diseases of any kind — on all sides are charming fragrances, and pleasant sensations everywhere.
Sounds that delight both the ear and the mind are everywhere there, O sage. There is no grief, no old age, no toil, no lamentation.
Such is that world, O sage, caused by the fruit of one's own deeds; men of good deeds come to be there by their own actions.
The bodies acquired by those who go there, O Mudgala, are made of light and born of karma alone — not of mother and father.
There is no sweat, no foul odour, no excrement, no urine for those beings there, O sage; dust does not soil their garments.
Their garlands of divine, mind-delighting fragrance do not wilt; they are surrounded by celestial chariots — such indeed are those beings, O brahmin.
Free from envy, grief, and exhaustion, bereft of delusion and jealousy, those who have won heaven live there in happiness, O great sage.
Above those worlds of such beings, O bull among sages, are the worlds of Śakra, endowed with divine qualities, layer upon layer.
Before Brahmā there are those luminous, auspicious worlds where the sages go, O brahmin, purified by their own meritorious deeds.
There are others known as the Ribhus — gods even among gods; their worlds are beyond those others, and the gods themselves worship them here.
Those worlds are self-luminous, radiant, and yield all desires; for those beings there is no torment caused by women, no jealousy over the lordship of worlds.
They do not sustain themselves through oblations, nor do they feed on ambrosia; likewise they possess divine bodies and are not embodied in forms that conflict with one another.
Those eternal gods of gods do not even desire happiness in happiness; they do not revolve through the cycles of cosmic ages as others do.
Where would old age or death be for them? There is no elation, no joy, no pleasure — and no sorrow, no happiness either. Where would attachment and aversion be, O sage?
O Maudgalya, even the gods desire that supreme goal; the highest perfection is hard to attain and lies beyond the reach of those governed by desires.
These thirty-three worlds — the remaining worlds are reached by the wise through excellent disciplines or through gifts given according to proper rite.
This prosperity, earned by your gift, has been attained here and brings joy; enjoy it, O one whose radiance is kindled by austerity — it was won by meritorious deeds.
Such is the bliss of heaven, O brahmin; such are the many kinds of worlds, and the virtues of heaven have been told to you — now hear from me its faults as well.
There in heaven the fruit of deeds already done is enjoyed; no new karma is created — one consumes entirely, down to the root.
This I regard as a fault in it: the fall at its end, O Mudgala — and the fall of those whose minds are wholly absorbed in pleasure.
Discontent and anguish arise in those stationed at a lower place when they behold the more resplendent glories — that too is hard to bear.
There is confusion of mind in those who fall, the assault of rajas, and when the garlands begin to wilt, the dread of impending descent.
These terrible flaws extend even to the abode of Brahmā, O Maudgalya; yet in the imperishable world the virtues of the meritorious are ten-thousandfold for men.
This, however, is another surpassing virtue for those who fall from heaven, O sage: through the connection of auspicious residual merit they are reborn among humans.
There too one is born greatly fortunate and partakes of happiness; but if one does not attain awakening there, one descends further to a lower state.
Whatever karma is performed here is enjoyed in the beyond; this world is held to be the field of action, O brahmin, and that world is held to be the field of fruit.
All this that you asked me, O Mudgala, has been told to you out of compassion; now, O virtuous one, let us go — delay no longer.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words, Maudgalya reflected with his mind; and having reflected, that foremost of sages thus addressed the divine messenger.
O divine messenger, homage to you — go, dear one, as you please; I have no business with something so greatly flawed, nor with heaven or its pleasures.
That great fall is misery, the anguish is truly terrible; those who partake of heaven fall back here — therefore I do not desire heaven.
That place where, having gone, one neither grieves nor trembles nor wavers — I shall seek that state alone, absolutely and without exception.
Having spoken these words, that sage dismissed the divine messenger and, abandoning the gleaning-of-grain livelihood, he established himself in the highest tranquility.
Becoming equal toward blame and praise, treating clods, stones, and gold alike, through pure union with knowledge he became perpetually absorbed in meditation.
Having gained strength through the yoga of meditation and attained the unsurpassable power, he reached eternal and supreme perfection, marked by nirvana.
Therefore you too, O son of Kuntī, ought not to grieve; though fallen from a flourishing kingdom, you shall recover it through austerity.
After happiness comes sorrow, and after sorrow comes happiness; they revolve in turn upon a man as spokes upon a wheel's rim.
O one of immeasurable valor, you shall recover the ancestral kingdom after thirteen years are past — let the fever of grief depart from your mind.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, that blessed Vyāsa, the wise one, left the son of the Pāṇḍavas and went back once more to his hermitage for austerity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: In that forest teeming with deer, the great warriors, the foremost among the Bhāratas, sported in the Kāmyaka forest like the immortals.
Surveying on all sides the many kinds of forest regions and the rows of trees beautifully flowering as befitted each season,
the Pāṇḍavas, fond of the hunt, roaming through that great forest, sported for a time — those tamers of foes, peers of Indra.
Then all of them, those tigers among men, those scorchers of foes, went out simultaneously in the four directions for the hunt, for the sake of a brahmin.
Having left Draupadī in the hermitage, with the permission of the great seer Tṛṇabindu of blazing austerity and of the priest Dhaumya,
at that time the king of the Sindhus, Vṛddhakṣatra's son, the greatly renowned one, was traveling toward the Shalveyas with desire for marriage.
Surrounded by great pomp fit for a king, along with many kings, he came to the Kāmyaka forest.
There he saw the beloved and renowned wife of the Pāṇḍavas, Draupadī, standing at the hermitage gate in the lonely forest.
Blazing with beauty, bearing a surpassing form, illuminating that forest region like lightning against a dark cloud —
"An apsara, or a daughter of the gods, or an illusion fashioned by the gods?" — thinking thus, all of them, joining their palms, gazed at that blameless one.
Then that king of the Sindhus, Vṛddhakṣatra's son Jayadratha, was astonished upon seeing that woman of blameless limbs, and his mind grew bold with desire.
Bewildered by desire, he spoke to King Kotikashya: "Whose is this woman of faultless limbs — or is she perhaps not even human?"
"Having seen this exceedingly beautiful one, I have no interest in any other for marriage — I shall take this very one and go to my own home."
"Go and find out about her, O gentle one — whose wife is she, who is she, where does she come from, and why has this fair-browed lady come to this thorny forest?"
"O may this woman of noble hips, a beauty of the world, with long sidelong eyes, fine teeth, and slender waist, choose me today."
"Might I have my desire fulfilled by winning this noble woman? Go and find out who is her lord — thus, O Koṭika."
Kotikashya, hearing that, leapt down from his chariot, his earrings swaying, and approached her; then he questioned her as a jackal might question a tigress.
Kotikashya said: Who are you who, bending a branch of the kadamba tree, stand radiant in this hermitage, blazing like a flame in the night, swaying in the breeze, O fair-browed one?
You are endowed with surpassing beauty, and yet you have no fear in these forests — are you a goddess, a yakshi, a danaví, a foremost apsara, or the finest consort of the daityas?
A shapely serpent-king's daughter, a forest-dweller, a woman who walks by night, or perhaps the queen of King Varuṇa, of Yama, of Soma, or of Kubera the lord of wealth?
Have you come forth from the abode of Dhata, Vidhātā, the Sun, the Lord, or Indra? For you do not ask us who we are, nor do we know your lord here.
We ask you, O fortunate one, in order to honor you — tell us truly your origin and your lord; reveal your kinsmen, your husband, your lineage, and whatever business brings you here.

I am the son of King Suratha, known among men as Kotikashya. And he who stands in the golden-bodied chariot, like fire in an altar, is the Trigarta king — O lotus-eyed one, that hero is named Kshemankara.
Beyond him is this mighty archer, the foremost son of the lord of the Kuṇindas; he gazes at you with broad, long shoulders, greatly astonished — he is one who always dwells in the mountains.
And that dark youth who stands near the lotus pool, so handsome to behold, is the son of the Ikṣvāku king Subala — he, O one of fair limbs, is the slayer of enemies.
In whose retinue march twelve Sauvīra princes bearing banners, all in chariots yoked with reddish horses, blazing like sacrificial fires at a great rite —
Angara, Kunjaraputaka, Shatrunjaya, Sañjaya and Supravriddha, Prabhankara, Bhamara, Ravi, Śūra, Pratapa, and Kuhara by name —
whom six thousand charioteers follow, along with elephants, horses, and foot soldiers — if you have heard of Jayadratha, O fortunate one, that is he, the king of the Sauvīras.
His other brothers of undaunted spirit, experts in shattering armies of Balāhaka horses — foremost Sauvīra warriors, young and strong — these mighty ones follow the king.
The king advances with these companions, guarded like Indra by the hosts of Maruts — O beautiful-haired one, make yourself known to us who do not know: whose wife are you, and whose daughter?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the royal princess Draupadī, questioned by that foremost of the Śibis, slowly looked about, released the branch, and drawing up her silk upper garment, spoke.
"I know you by intelligence, O son of a lord of men; a woman such as I is not fit to address you — and you have no words to say to me here, nor has any other man or woman."
"For I am alone here, and I speak to you only briefly; mark this well, O gentle one — how could I who am devoted to my own dharma address you alone, here alone in the forest?"
"I know you as the son of Suratha, whom men know as Kotikashya; therefore, O Śaibya, I shall likewise tell you about my kinsmen — hear this well."
"I am the offspring of King Drupada; men know me as Kṛṣṇā, O Śaibya. I have chosen five men as husbands — those who went to Khāṇḍavaprastha, of whom you have heard."
"Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the two heroic sons of Mādrī — having settled me here, the Pārthas divided the four directions and have gone to the hunt."
"The king went east, Bhīmasena south, Jaya west, the twin sons of Yama north — I believe the time for those finest of chariot-warriors to return here has all but arrived."
"Honored by them you shall depart as you wish; unharness your horses and let them drink — the great-souled son of Dharma, who loves guests, will be pleased to see you."
Having said thus much, that moon-faced daughter of Drupada, the confident one, entered that excellent leaf-hut, reflecting on the dharma of hosting guests on their behalf.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O Bhārata, when all those kings were seated and had heard Kotikashya's words, the Sauvīra king spoke to Śaibya.
"When she was speaking, my mind delighted in this foremost among parted-hair women — how then can you turn back?"
"Having seen her, O mighty-armed one, other women appear to me like she-monkeys — I tell you this truly."
"For by merely seeing her, my mind has been wholly stolen away by her; tell me about that auspicious one, O Śaibya — is she human?"
Kotikashya said: "This is indeed Draupadī, the dark princess, the renowned one, held in the highest esteem as the queen consort of the five sons of Pāṇḍu."
"Dear and highly esteemed by all the Pārthas, she is a woman of virtue — O Sauvīra, go meet with her, then proceed happily among great heroes."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Jayadratha, lord of the Sauvīras and Sindhus, wicked-hearted, replied: "We shall see Draupadī."
He entered the empty hermitage like a wolf entering a lion's lair, himself the seventh, and spoke these words to Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī).
"Are you well, O noble-hipped one? Are your husbands also free from ailment? Those for whose welfare you care — are they too free from illness?"
Draupadī said: "The Kaurava king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, is well; I am well, his brothers are well — and those others you ask after too."
"Accept this water for your feet, and a seat as well, O son of a king; and five hundred deer — I offer you a morning meal."
"Black antelope, spotted deer, nyankus, hariṇas, sharabhas, hares, rishyas, rurus, shambaras, gavyas, and many other deer —"
"— boars and buffalo, and whatever other kinds of game there are — Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, will himself give to you."
Jayadratha said: "Enough of a morning meal — all due honor has been rendered to me; come, mount my chariot, and enjoy happiness alone."
"The Pārthas have lost their glory, fallen from their kingdom, pitiable, broken in spirit, dwelling in the forest — you ought not to bind yourself to them."
"Wise women do not attach themselves to a husband bereft of fortune; one should attach oneself to a husband who is active and prospering — one should not dwell where prosperity has dried up."
"Deprived of fortune and of their kingdom, destroyed for years without end — enough of this trouble of devotion to the sons of Pāṇḍu."
"Become my wife, O fair-hipped one; abandon these men and enjoy happiness. Come with me and obtain all the lands of the Sindhu and the Sauvīras."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the king of Sindhu with words that made the heart tremble, Kṛṣṇā moved away from that spot with furrowed brows.
Scorning his words and rebuking him, the slender-waisted Kṛṣṇā said to the king of Sindhu, "Do not do this — be ashamed!"
She, the blameless one, longing for the arrival of her husbands, tried to dissuade him further by joining her words of rebuke with words of persuasion.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With a lovely face flushed with anger and passion, with eyes reddened and brows knit high and low, turning her face fully toward the lord of the Sauvīra realm, the daughter of Drupada then spoke again.
"Reviling those illustrious great warriors, sharp as venom, equal to Mahendra, devoted to their own duties, who stand firm even among hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas — how, O fool, are you not ashamed?"
"Dogs speak so even of praiseworthy men — whether a forest-dweller, a householder, or an ascetic fully accomplished in learning. They bark without praising anything good, O king of the Sauvīras."
"I think there is no one among such an assembly of kṣatriyas who could today seize your falling hand as you tumble toward the mouth of hell and pull you back."
"You, who aspire to conquer Dharmarāja, are like one who tries to drive away with a stick a maddened elephant, mountain-like, roaming the Himālayan slopes from its herd."
"You pluck the eyelashes from the mouth of a mighty sleeping lion — and then you flee on foot. When you see Bhīmasena in his wrath, what will become of you?"
"You strike with your toe-tip a terrible, fully-grown, mighty lion born in mountain caves while it sleeps — you who would dare to approach the fierce and enraged Jiṣṇu."
"You recklessly tread upon the tails of two sharp-fanged, dark cobras with keen venom — you who would fight with the two younger-born among the Pāṇḍavas, those best of men."

"Just as the bamboo, the plantain, and the reed bear fruit only for their own destruction and not for their flourishing, so you will seize me who am protected by them — and it will bring about your end, like the womb of a she-crab."
Jayadratha said: "I know it, Kṛṣṇā, I know well what manner of men are these sons of the god-king. Yet we cannot be frightened today by you with this boasting and threatening."
"We, O Kṛṣṇā, are all born in seventeen illustrious clans. We consider the sons of Pāṇḍu, O Draupadī, inferior to us in six virtues and more."
"So quickly mount an elephant or a chariot — we cannot be stopped by words alone. Or beg piteously and seek once more the grace of the king of the Sauvīras."
Draupadī said: "Though mighty, shall I appear weak here? Shall I, who am known for my valor, beg piteously of the king of the Sauvīras? Am I so regarded by the king of the Sauvīras?"
"She in whose steps Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna — allies seated together on one chariot — would follow: even Indra could not carry her away; how then any mere mortal, let alone this wretch?"
"When Kirīṭī, the slayer of enemy heroes, standing in his chariot and crushing the hearts of foes, enters your army to find me — like fire burning through dry grass in summer heat —"
"— all the Vṛṣṇi heroes who follow Janārdana, the great bowmen and the Kekaya warriors too — all these princes of mine would joyfully follow his track."
"The terrible arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, loosed from the bowstring with the roar of thunder, of exceeding swiftness, strike Dhanañjaya's hand and roar with a sound most dreadful."

"The mighty torrents of arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, swift as swarms of locusts — when the Gāṇḍīva-bearer, blowing his conch and sounding his palm-guard, repeatedly pours those arrows upon your chest, what then will become of your spirit?"
"Seeing Bhīma rushing at you with mace in hand, the two sons of Mādrī flying at you from all directions, spewing the venom of their indignant rage — you will suffer long torment, O wretch."
"And just as I would never transgress in any way my most worthy husbands — not even in my mind — by that truth I shall today see you subdued and dragged away by the Pārthas."
"I shall not flee in confusion though dragged away by you, O cruel one. For I have come together with the foremost heroes of the Kuru line and have returned to the Kāmyaka forest."

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The wide-eyed one glanced at them as they reached out to seize her, rebuking them; frightened, she cried out "Touch me not! Touch me not!" and called loudly to Dhaumya, the family priest.
Jayadratha seized her by the hem of her upper garment; she wrenched herself away — and that sinful one, his body jerked by her, fell like a tree with its roots cut through.
Yet seized with great force, the royal daughter Kṛṣṇā heaved repeated sighs; dragged along, she was made to mount the chariot — though not before she bowed at the feet of Dhaumya.
Dhaumya said: "She cannot be taken by you without first conquering those great warriors. Reflect on the ancient duty of the kṣatriya order, Jayadratha."
"Having committed this base act, you will without doubt reap a sinful fruit when you encounter those heroic Pāṇḍavas led by Dharmarāja."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Dhaumya then followed that illustrious royal princess as she was being carried away, walking in the midst of the foot-soldiers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the Pārthas, having ranged in all directions — those foremost bowmen on earth — slaying deer, boars, and buffaloes while roaming separately, came together again.
Then, in that great forest thronging with deer and snakes and echoing with the cries of birds, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed those brothers, having heard the voices of the deer calling out.
"Turning toward the direction lit by the sun, the deer and birds speak harshly, foretelling a terrible ordeal — a great battle with enemies, or an insult suffered."
"Turn back quickly — enough of hunting for us. My mind is pained and burning; anger has overwhelmed my reason, and the lord of life is stirred and churned within my body."

"The Kāmyaka forest appears to me like a lake whose serpents have been carried off by Garuḍa, like a kingdom stripped of its king and bereft of prosperity, like a jar whose liquor has been drunk by drunkards."
Then those heroic men, borne by great swift horses of the Sindhu breed, swift as a gust of wind, harnessed to large and fine chariots, turned their faces toward the hermitage.
Then a jackal, clamorous with no small noise, approached the left flank of those who were returning and howled. Having reflected on this, the king spoke to Bhīma and Dhanañjaya.
"As this low-born jackal howls, approaching our left flank — it is quite clear that sinful men have committed a violent assault upon us, overpowering us, the Kurus."
Thus speaking, as they entered the forest — having hunted in that great wilderness — they then saw, weeping, the young nurse-maid and attendant of their beloved wife.
Indrasena, hastening toward her, leaped from the chariot and ran to her; O lord of men, he spoke to that nurse-maid these words, greatly distressed at that moment.

"Why do you weep, fallen on the ground? Why does your face wither with a wretched hue? Surely Draupadī, the royal princess, of blameless form and very wide eyes, who equals the very bodies of the foremost Kurus — has she not been violated by those sinful and most cruel men?"
"Even if the goddess has entered the earth, or gone to heaven, or plunged into the ocean — the Pārthas will follow her track; for Dharmarāja burns with grief."

"For who, among such enemies of foes, enduring hardship, unconquered — who would wish to steal one who is dearer to them than their own lives? That hero who is devoted to them is my husband Nakula, the swordsman of light and wondrous hand, and great wise Sahadeva, without equal."

"Whose body will those dreadful sharp and foremost arrows pierce today before entering the earth? Do not grieve regarding her, O timid one — know that Kṛṣṇā will return today. The Pārthas will come with the daughter of Yajña after slaying all their enemies to the last man."
Then the nurse-maid, wiping her lovely face, said to the charioteer Indrasena: "Kṛṣṇā has been carried off by Jayadratha, who violently overpowered and dishonored those five men equal to Indra."
"The tracks are fresh and clear; even the broken trees have not yet wilted. Turn around and follow quickly — the royal princess has not gone far at all."
"All of you, O Indra-like ones, don your great and fine armor; take up your mighty bows and arrows and quickly follow the track."

"For before long she — bewildered by threat and force, her mind in confusion, her face withering — may give her body to one who does not deserve it, like a ladle full of choice ghee poured into ashes."

"Before the offering is poured as if into a fire of husks; before the garland is cast away as if in a cremation ground; before the soma, moving through the ritual, is lapped up by a dog while the assembly is deluded — go now! Before the jackal wallows in the lotus lake, having hunted in the great forest."

"Let no evildoer touch the beautiful, fine-nosed, fine-eyed, moon-bright, serene face of your beloved — as a dog would devour the sacrificial cake. Follow these tracks quickly; let not the moment swiftly pass you by."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Good woman, be silent and restrain your speech — do not say harsh things in our presence. Kings and princes drunk on power meet with their undoing."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said just that much, they went forth swiftly, following those very tracks, again and again hissing like serpents and plucking the bowstrings of their great bows.
Then they saw the dust of that army, whirled up and driven by the hooves of horses, and Dhaumya in the midst of the foot-soldiers, crying out, "Bhīma! Rush forward!"
Consoling the deeply distressed Dhaumya with the words "May you go in peace" — those princes then rushed at that army with speed, like hawks when prey is in sight.
The wrath of those men of valor equal to great Indra blazed up, inflamed by the insult to the daughter of Yajña, and at the sight of Jayadratha and their beloved standing on his chariot.
Vṛkodara, Dhanañjaya, the twin brothers, and the king — all those great wielders of bows — cried out at the king of Sindhu; and then the directions became bewildered for the enemies.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, in the forest, a most dreadful uproar arose among those kṣatriyas filled with rage upon seeing Bhīmasena and Arjuna.
Seeing the banner-tops of those foremost Kurus, the evil-souled King Jayadratha himself — his power now broken — said to the daughter of Yajña, Bhānumatī, standing on his chariot:
"These five great chariots are approaching; I believe these are your husbands, O Kṛṣṇā. You who know them — tell us, O beautiful-haired one, who stands highest on each chariot among the Pāṇḍavas."

Draupadī said: "What use to you, O fool, is knowing those great wielders of bows, having committed this most heinous and life-destroying act? These heroes, my husbands, have come together — not one of you shall remain alive in this battle."

"Yet it is my duty to tell everything when asked, even to one doomed to die — that is the dharma for me. I have no anguish nor any fear of you, now that I see Dharmarāja together with his younger brothers."

"He on whose banner-top the two sweet and well-matched drums, Nanda and Upananda, resound — this one who is expert in determining what is right in duty and purpose — him men always follow when they have matters of importance."
"He who is pure gold-bright in complexion, with a fierce nose, slender build, and long eyes — he whom they call the foremost of all the Kurus: that is Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, my husband."
"Even for an enemy who comes seeking refuge would this righteous hero give his life. Approach him quickly, O fool, for your own welfare — hands folded, weapons laid aside."
"And him you see standing on his chariot — long-armed, tall as a great śāla tree, biting his lip, his brows knit in a frown — that is Vṛkodara, my husband."
"Thoroughbred, strong, well-trained horses of great power carry this hero along. His deeds are superhuman — the name Bhīma has spread across the earth on his account."
"Those who have wronged him do not survive here; nor does he ever forget an enmity. He brings about the end of a feud — but he does not become excessively calm afterward."
"Gentle, generous, steadfast, illustrious, master of his senses, devoted to his elders — this heroic man, both brother and pupil of Yudhiṣṭhira: that is Dhanañjaya, my husband."

"He who would not abandon dharma out of desire, or fear, or greed — and would do no cruelty: he, the son of Kuntī, is of blazing splendor equal to Vaiśvānara fire, capable of enduring enemies, and a destroyer of foes."

"He who is expert in determining all matters of duty and purpose, the remover of fear for those afflicted by fear, the wise one — whose form they call the finest on earth, whom all the Pāṇḍavas guard closely —"

"— who is dearer to them than their own lives and who is wholly devoted to them: that hero is Nakula, my husband. And he who is a sword-fighter of light and wondrous hand, the great and wise Sahadeva, without equal —"

"— whose deeds you will witness today, O dull-witted one, as if Śatakratu himself were fighting in the armies of the daityas: a hero, skilled in arms, intelligent, wise, and beloved of King Dharmasuta —"

"— he who is of splendor equal to the moon and sun, the youngest-born of the Pāṇḍavas and dearly loved, whose equal in intelligence no man is to be found, and who is likewise a speaker and expert in determining truth among the good —"

"— that hero, ever wrathful and spirited, wise and prudent: that is Sahadeva, my husband. He would give up his life, enter the fire — but he would never speak what is contrary to dharma. Always high-minded, devoted to the duty of the warrior, the most beloved of Kuntī's sons among men."
"You will see this army of yours — all its warriors slain — tossed and churned by the sons of Pāṇḍu, like a treasure-laden ship crumbling at the ocean's edge on the back of a sea-monster."

"Thus have the sons of Pāṇḍu been described to you — whom you, in your delusion, dared to dishonor. If you escape from them with your body unharmed, you will be born again — you will have gained a second life."

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then those five Pārthas, equal to five Indras, bypassing the terrified foot-soldiers with their folded hands, in their rage overwhelmed and enveloped the chariot-host from all sides in a darkness of arrow-rain.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Stand firm! Strike quickly! Charge in all directions!" — thus the king of Sindhu urged on those princes.
Then a most dreadful uproar arose in the battle at that time, among the soldiers, upon seeing Bhīma, Arjuna, the twin brothers, and Yudhiṣṭhira together.
Despondency arose among the Śibis, Sindhus, and Trigartans when they saw those tiger-like men — fierce in strength like tigers indeed.
Bhīma seized his mace — all of sharpened iron, adorned with golden designs, tall and splendid — and charged at the Sindhava king, driven as if by Death itself.
Meanwhile, Koṭikāśya wheeled around and attacked, surrounding Vṛkodara with a great array of chariots.
Though showered by javelins, lances, and iron arrows hurled by the arms of heroes, Bhīma did not tremble.
In the vanguard of the Sindhava army, Bhīma slew with his mace an elephant along with its rider, and fourteen foot-soldiers as well.
Pārtha, eager to protect the Sauvīra, slew five hundred mountain heroes and great chariot-warriors at the forefront of that army.
The king himself slew a hundred of the foremost, most valiant, hard-striking Suvīras in that battle in the space of a mere blink.
Nakula was seen there, leaping down from his chariot with sword in hand, repeatedly scattering the heads of the foot-guards like seeds sown broadcast.
Sahadeva, advancing with his chariot against elephant-fighters, brought them down with iron arrows as peacocks are knocked from trees.
Then a Trigarta warrior, bow in hand, descended from his great chariot and with his mace slew four horses of that king.
When that warrior came close on foot, the righteous king, son of Kuntī, pierced him in the chest with a crescent-headed arrow.
His heart split open, that hero vomited blood from his mouth and fell forward facing Pārtha, like a tree uprooted at its base.
The righteous king, his horses slain, leapt from his chariot along with Indrasena and took refuge on Sahadeva's great chariot.
Kṣemaṃkara and Mahāmukha, targeting Nakula, both rained showers of sharp arrows on him from either side.
Those two, pouring down arrows like monsoon clouds, were each slain with a single decisive shot by Mādrī's son.
Then Suratha, king of the Trigartans, expert in elephant warfare, charged from the chariot's pole and caused his chariot to crash by means of an elephant.
Nakula, fearless, leapt from that chariot with shield and sword in hand, took up a commanding position, and stood immovable as a mountain.
Suratha then furiously urged that great elephant — its trunk raised — toward Nakula for the kill.
As that elephant came close upon him, Nakula severed its trunk at the root with his sword — the trunk complete with its tusk.
That elephant, adorned with anklet ornaments, let out a great roar and fell headlong to the ground, crushing its riders beneath it.
Having accomplished that great feat, the heroic son of Mādrī, that great chariot-warrior, found safety by reaching Bhīmasena's chariot.
In the battle, as king Koṭikāśya bore down, Bhīma severed with a razor-headed arrow the head of that king's charioteer as he urged the horses on.
The king did not realize his charioteer had been slain by that mighty-armed one; his horses, driverless, bolted in all directions across the battlefield.
Bhīma, the foremost striker, the Pāṇḍava, advanced and slew that king — turned away and driverless — with a palm-strengthened javelin.
Dhanaṃjaya cut off, with sharp broad-headed arrows, both the bows and the heads of all twelve of the Sauvīra warriors.
That superb chariot-warrior slew in battle the Śibis, the foremost of the Ikṣvākus, the Trigartans, and the Sindhavans as they came within range of his arrows.
Many were laid low by Savyasācī — elephants with their banners still flying, great chariot-warriors with their standards still raised.
Headless trunks and detached heads lay strewn across the whole field of battle, covering the earth.
Dogs, vultures, herons, crows, kites, jackals, and ravens feasted insatiably there on the flesh and blood of the slain heroes.
With those heroes slain, Jayadratha the king of Sindhu, terror-stricken, released Kṛṣṇā and devoted himself entirely to flight.
That lowest of men, intent on saving his own life, set Draupadī down amid that chaotic army and fled toward the forest.
Yudhiṣṭhira the righteous king, seeing Draupadī with Dhaumya at her side, had the heroic son of Mādrī place her upon a chariot.
Then, with Jayadratha gone, Vṛkodara struck that fleeing army again and again, targeting them with iron arrows.
But Savyasācī, seeing Jayadratha fleeing, restrained Bhīma who was slaughtering the Sindhava soldiers.
Arjuna said: The one through whose offense this intolerable suffering has come upon us — I do not see that Jayadratha anywhere on this battlefield.
Seek him out — blessings be on you. What purpose is served by felling these soldiers? How do you regard this fruitless work?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the wise Guḍākeśa, the eloquent Bhīmasena glanced toward Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke these words.
The enemies' champions are slain; they have largely scattered in all directions. Taking Draupadī with you, O king, let Your Majesty turn back from here.
Together with the twin brothers and with the great-souled Dhaumya, return to the hermitage, O king of kings, and console Draupadī.
That foolish Sindhava king shall not escape me with his life — even if he shelters in the depths of Pātāla and Indra himself acts as his charioteer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That Sindhava must not be slain, O mighty-armed one, even wicked though he is — remember Duḥśalā and the glorious Gāndhārī.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that, Draupadī — distraught, furious, yet modest and wise — spoke to Bhīma, addressing both her husbands Bhīma and Arjuna.
If you truly wish to do what is dear to me, then that vile wretch must be killed — that outcast of the Sindhava line, that wicked, evil-minded stain upon his family.
One who abducts another's wife, who without any quarrel robs an enemy of his kingdom — such a man does not deserve to live even if he begs for mercy in battle.
Addressed thus, those two tiger-like men went to where the Sindhava had fled; the king meanwhile turned back, taking Kṛṣṇā with him along with the family priest.
Entering the hermitage, he found it — its rush-mat seats overturned and scattered — thronged with brāhmaṇas headed by Mārkaṇḍeya.
The greatly wise king, surrounded by his brothers and with his wife beside him, rejoined those assembled brāhmaṇas who were lamenting over Draupadī.
They rejoiced to see the king returned once more, having defeated the Sindhus and Sauvīras and having recovered Draupadī.
The king, surrounded by them, sat down right there; and the spirited Kṛṣṇā entered the hermitage together with the twin brothers.
Bhīma and Arjuna, hearing that the enemy had gone only a kośa away, themselves goaded their horses and charged after him at full speed.
Herein Arjuna performed a feat most wonderful: he slew the horses of the Sindhava who had gone but a single kośa away.
Endowed with divine weapons, unagitated even in moments of crisis, he accomplished that difficult feat with arrows charged with sacred weapon-spells.
Then both heroes, Bhīma and Dhanaṃjaya, charged toward the Sindhava — his horses slain, alone, frightened, his mind in turmoil.
The Sindhava, deeply distressed to see his horses slain and beholding the feats of valor that Dhanaṃjaya was performing, mustered his resolve for flight and ran toward the forest.
Watching the Sindhava stride away in flight, the mighty-armed Phalguna gave chase and called out these words.
With this much valor you dared seize a woman by force? Turn back, O prince — flight does not befit you. How can you flee abandoning your followers in the midst of the enemy?

Thus addressed by Pārtha, the Sindhava did not turn back. "Stand! Stand!" — with that cry the mighty Bhīma suddenly charged at him, while the compassionate Pārtha called out to him: "Do not kill him!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Jayadratha, seeing both brothers with weapons raised, ran swiftly — composed on the surface but deeply distressed, eager for his life.
Bhīmasena, mighty and furious beyond measure, leapt from his chariot, gave chase, and seized him by the hair.
Lifting him up in rage, he dashed the king to the ground, seized him by the throat, and beat him repeatedly.
As the king revived and tried again to leap up, the mighty-armed Bhīma kicked him in the head as he was wailing.
Bhīma drove his knee into him and struck him with his elbow; overwhelmed by the force of those blows, the king fell into unconsciousness.
Then Phalguna restrained the enraged Bhīmasena, saying: "O Kaurava, remember what the king said — spare him for Duḥśalā's sake."
Bhīmasena said: This one of wicked conduct does not deserve to live at my hands — this lowest of men who tormented Draupadī, who was entirely undeserving of such treatment.
What can I do, since the king is always merciful, and you too with your childish reasoning forever hinder us?
Having spoken thus, Vṛkodara shaved five locks of hair from the king's head with a crescent-headed arrow, while he lay speechless.
Having thus dishonored the king, Vṛkodara then said to him: "If you wish to live, you fool, listen to the terms I am about to state."
"You must declare 'I am a slave' in all assemblies and gatherings. If you do this, I shall grant you your life — this is the rule of the battle-won."
"So be it" — with these words the barely-breathing king Jayadratha spoke to Bhīma, that tiger among men, who shone magnificently in battle.
Then the Pārtha Vṛkodara bound the writhing, senseless, dust-covered king and placed him upon his chariot.
Then Bhīma, mounting that chariot and following Pārtha, drove to the center of the hermitage and approached Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bhīma then displayed Jayadratha in that wretched condition; the king laughed on seeing him and said: "Let him be released."
Bhīma also told the king: "Let it be reported to Draupadī — this evil-minded one has entered the state of a slave to the Pāṇḍavas."
Then the eldest brother spoke to him with affectionate words: "Release this man of base conduct — if we are of any authority to you."
Draupadī too, glancing at Yudhiṣṭhira, told Bhīma: "Let this slave be freed — you have already given him five tufts of hair by the king's grace."
Freed, that trembling king came forward, paid his respects to Yudhiṣṭhira, and then bowed before all the sages assembled there.
The merciful king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, then spoke to him — seeing Jayadratha in that state, caught by Savyasācī.

"You are no slave — go, you are freed. Never do this again anywhere. Shame on you, you wretch, lusting after women, low-born with base associates. Who else but you, lowest of men, would have done such a deed?"
Knowing that the doer of this evil had lost his spirit — the best of the Bhāratas, that lord among kings, looked upon him and felt compassion.
"May your understanding grow in righteousness and may you not set your mind on unrighteousness. Go in peace, Jayadratha, with your horses, chariot, and foot-soldiers."
Thus addressed, O Bhārata, the king went away in shame, silent, his face slightly downcast, grieved, toward the Gate of the Ganges.
Going for refuge to the god Virūpākṣa, the lord of Umā, he performed intense austerities; and Vṛṣadhvaja (Śiva) was pleased with him.
The three-eyed god himself, well pleased, received his oblation and granted him a boon; hear what he chose.
"May I conquer in battle all five Pāṇḍavas along with their chariots" — so the king said to the god; but the god replied, "No."
"You will be able to check them in battle — those who are unconquerable and unslayable — all except the mighty-armed Arjuna, who is difficult to approach even by the gods."
"He whom they call the unvanquished god who bears conch, discus, and mace — that foremost among weapon-masters, Kṛṣṇa, protects him."
Thus addressed, the king returned to his own abode, while the Pāṇḍavas continued to dwell in the Kāmyaka forest.
Janamejaya said: After Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) had been abducted and the greatest distress had been suffered, what did those tiger-men, the Pāṇḍavas, do thereafter?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus freed Kṛṣṇā and thoroughly defeated Jayadratha, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira sat in the company of the hosts of sages.
In the midst of those great sages who were listening and lamenting with him, the son of Pāṇḍu spoke these words to Mārkaṇḍeya.
"I believe that Time is mighty, and so is Fate ordained by providence — and the inevitable destiny of beings which none can transgress.
"For how could such a calamity touch our wife, who knows and practises dharma, who is pure — like theft touching what is false?
"For Draupadī has never done any sinful act or blameworthy deed anywhere; on the contrary, she has always observed great dharma toward the brāhmaṇas.
"Yet the dull-witted king Jayadratha abducted her by force; for that abduction he received the shaving of his head, and along with his allies he was fully defeated in battle.
"She has been recovered by us after slaughtering that Saindhava army, yet this abduction of our wife was something we never anticipated.

"Painful is this forest life, and our livelihood through hunting; painful is the killing of animals by those who dwell in the forest among other forest dwellers; and painful is this banishment from our kinsmen through the machinations of the wicked.
"Surely there must be some man more unfortunate than I — have you, venerable one, ever seen or heard of such a one?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O bull of the Bhāratas, Rāma suffered incomparable sorrow — his wife Jānakī was carried off by a mighty demon.
From his hermitage, the lord of rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, taking to the sky and resorting to magic, swiftly killed the vulture Jaṭāyus and carried her away.
Rāma recovered her, relying on the forces of Sugrīva, building a bridge across the ocean and burning Laṅkā with his sharp arrows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In what lineage was Rāma born? What was his prowess, what his valour? Whose son was Rāvaṇa? And what was the enmity between them?
All this, O venerable one, you should narrate to me properly; I wish to hear the story of Rāma of untiring deeds.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: There was a great king named Aja, born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku; his son was Daśaratha, ever devoted to sacred study and pure of conduct.
He had four sons skilled in dharma and statecraft: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and the mighty Bharata.
Kausalyā was Rāma's mother; Kaikeyī was Bharata's; the two scorchers of foes, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, were sons of Sumitrā.
Janaka was king of Videha; Sītā was his daughter, O lord — whom Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned as the beloved queen of Rāma.
Thus the birth of Rāma and of Sītā has been related to you; now I shall also explain the birth of Rāvaṇa, O lord of men.
Rāvaṇa's grandfather was no less than the god Prajāpati, the Self-existent, lord and creator of all the worlds, of great austerity.
Pulastya by name was his beloved mind-born son; Pulastya had a son named Vaiśravaṇa, born of a cow, who became a lord.
He abandoned his father and attended upon his grandfather; in anger at this, his father, O king, created another self from himself.
That one was born as the twice-born Viśravā, made from half of himself, wrathful, as a countermeasure against Vaiśravaṇa.
But the grandfather, pleased in heart, granted Vaiśravaṇa immortality, lordship of wealth, and the rank of world-guardian.
And also friendship with Īśāna (Śiva), a son named Nalakūbara, and the city of Laṅkā, filled with hosts of rākṣasas, as his capital.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The sage who had been born as a half-body from Pulastya's wrath — that wrathful one named Viśravā — he looked upon Vaiśravaṇa.
The lord of rākṣasas, Kubera, recognized his father as wrathful, O king, and ever strove to propitiate him.
That king of kings, Naravāhana (Kubera), dwelling in Laṅkā, gave three rākṣasī women to his father as attendants.
Those women, skilled in song and dance, then strove to please that great-souled sage, O tiger of the Bhāratas.
Puṣpotkaṭā and Rākā and Mālinī — O lord of men, O king — those slender-waisted ones, eager for the best, vied with one another.
Pleased with them, that blessed great-souled one granted boons to each of them — sons comparable to world-guardians, as each desired.
In Puṣpotkaṭā were born two sons who became lords of rākṣasas — Kumbhakarṇa and Daśagrīva — matchless in strength on earth.
Mālinī gave birth to one son, Vibhīṣaṇa; in Rākā were born twins — Khara and Śūrpaṇakhā.
Vibhīṣaṇa surpassed all others in beauty; he became greatly blessed, a guardian of dharma, devoted to righteous acts.
Daśagrīva was the eldest of all, the foremost among rākṣasas, of great energy, great heroism, great strength and valour.
Kumbhakarṇa surpassed all others in physical strength at that time; he was a master of illusion, keen in battle, fierce, and a night-wanderer.
Khara was valiant with the bow, a hater of brāhmaṇas, a flesh-eater; and Śūrpaṇakhā too was fierce, one who creates obstacles for the virtuous.
All of them were learned in the Vedas, all were heroes, all observed excellent vows; devoted to their father, they lived on Mount Gandhamādana.
Then there they saw Vaiśravaṇa, the bearer of human conveyance (Kubera), seated together with their father, endowed with supreme prosperity.
Rivalry having arisen in them, they resolved upon asceticism and pleased Brahmā with fierce austerities.
Daśagrīva stood on one foot for a thousand years, subsisting on air, practising the five-fire penance, perfectly concentrated.
Kumbhakarṇa lay face-downward, disciplined in food and vows; Vibhīṣaṇa subsisted on a single fallen leaf.
Devoted to fasting, wise, ever intent on recitation of mantras, that noble-minded one maintained that same intense austerity throughout the entire period.
Khara and Śūrpaṇakhā, with joyful hearts, attended upon and guarded the others as they performed their austerities.
When a thousand years were complete, the irresistible ten-headed one cut off his head and offered it in fire; by this the lord of the universe was pleased.
Then Brahmā himself went there, stopped them from their austerities, and enticed each of them separately with the granting of boons.
Brahmā said: I am pleased with you; desist, dear sons, and choose boons — whatever is desired, save one thing: immortality — let that be so.
"All those heads of yours that were offered in the fire with great desire — even so, all of them shall exist on your body as you wish."
"And your body shall bear no deformity; you will be able to assume any form at will, and you will be victorious over your enemies in battle — of this there is no doubt."
Rāvaṇa said: From gandharvas, gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents, kiṃnaras, and spirits — may I never suffer defeat.
Brahmā said: From all those you have mentioned, there shall be no fear for you — except from a human. Be well; so has it been ordained by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed, Daśagrīva became satisfied at that time; for that evil-minded man-eater despised human beings.
Then the great-grandfather spoke similarly to Kumbhakarṇa; but his mind being seized by delusion, he chose great sleep.
Saying "So shall it be," he then spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa: "Choose a boon, my son" — repeatedly saying "I am pleased with you."
Vibhīṣaṇa said: Even when fallen into the greatest adversity, may my mind never turn to adharma; and O blessed one, may the Brahmāstra manifest to me though untaught.
Brahmā said: Because, though born in the rākṣasa womb, O scorcher of foes, your mind takes no pleasure in adharma — I grant you immortality.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having obtained the boon, O lord of men, Daśagrīva the rākṣasa expelled the lord of wealth from Laṅkā after defeating him in battle.
The blessed Kubera abandoned Laṅkā and retired to Gandhamādana, accompanied by gandharvas and yakṣas along with rākṣasas and kiṃpuruṣas.
Rāvaṇa seized and carried off his aerial chariot Puṣpaka; Vaiśravaṇa cursed him: "This shall no longer carry you."
"This shall carry him who kills you in battle; having dishonoured your elder and me, you shall swiftly cease to be."
But Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, ever mindful of the dharma of the virtuous, followed Kubera, O great king, endowed with supreme prosperity.
Pleased with him, that blessed lord of wealth, the wise brother, gave his brother the commandership of both the yakṣa and rākṣasa armies.
The rākṣasas, man-eaters, and the mighty piśācas — all assembled and consecrated Daśānana as king.
Daśagrīva, excelling in power over daityas and gods alike, moving through the sky and assuming any form at will, seized and carried off their treasures.
Because he made the worlds cry out in terror, Daśagrīva is therefore called Rāvaṇa; powerful as he willed, he instilled fear in the gods.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the brahmarṣis, the siddhas, and the divine royal sages, placing Agni (the fire-carrier) before them, sought refuge with Brahmā.
Agni said: That son of Viśravā, Daśagrīva the mighty, has been made unkillable in times past by the blessed one's boon.
The mighty one oppresses all creatures with his outrages; therefore, O blessed one, protect us — for no other protector exists.
Brahmā said: O Fire, he cannot be conquered in battle by gods or asuras; yet what needs to be done for his destruction has been arranged all around.
"For this very purpose, the four-armed Viṣṇu, the foremost among those who strike, has descended at my command; he shall accomplish this deed."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The Grandfather then spoke this word in the presence of all those assembled, together with all the hosts of gods: "Be born on the earth."
"Beget valiant sons as helpers of Viṣṇu, everywhere among the she-bears and female monkeys — sons endowed with strength and the power to assume any form."
Then, by their respective portions and allotments, the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas all descended to the earth and filled it with delight straightway.
In their presence the boon-granting god commanded a gandharva woman named Dundubhī, for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose.
Hearing the word of the Grandfather, the gandharva woman Dundubhī then became Mantharā, a hunchback, in the human world.
And Indra and all those foremost gods begat sons upon the noblest she-monkeys and she-bears; those sons all followed in their fathers' footsteps in both glory and strength.
They were breakers of mountain peaks, armed with śāla-trees, palm-trees, and rocks; all of them had frames hard as the thunderbolt, and all possessed power like a rushing torrent.

All were endowed with valor and prowess at will, all were skilled in battle; their vital breath equaled ten thousand elephants, their speed equaled the wind. Some among these forest-dwellers could live wherever they wished.
