Mārkaṇḍeya said: His father spoke to him again, greatly delighted, O lord of men: 'Go to Ayodhyā and rule it, O Rāma of red-cornered eyes.'
Then, having bowed to the gods and been celebrated by his friends, he was reunited with his wife, even as Mahendra with Paulomī.
Then the scorcher of foes granted a boon to Avindhya, and he appointed the Rākṣasī Trijaṭā, who had been sought for her virtuous service, to tend Sītā.
Then Brahmā, surrounded by the gods headed by Indra, spoke to him: 'O son of Kausalyā, what boons do you desire? I grant them to you today.'
Rāma chose steadfastness in dharma, invincibility against enemies, and the revival of the monkeys who had been slain by the Rākṣasas.
Then, O great king, when Brahmā had spoken those words 'so be it,' the monkeys rose up, their consciousness restored.
The greatly blessed Sītā too granted a boon to Hanūmān: 'Your life, my son, shall be equal to the fame of Rāma.'
'And divine pleasures, granted by my favor, shall always be present for you, O Hanūmān' — so she spoke, O monkey-eyed one.
Then, as those men of effortless deeds looked on, all the gods headed by Indra vanished from sight.
But Mātali, charioteer of Indra, seeing Rāma reunited with Jānakī, was filled with the greatest joy and spoke these words in the midst of the friends:
'The suffering of gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, humans, Asuras, and Bhogins has been removed by you, O true hero of real valor.'
'The worlds — gods, Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and serpents — shall sing of you for as long as the earth endures.'
Having thus spoken and taken leave of Rāma, best of weapon-bearers, and having duly honored him, Mātali departed in that chariot blazing like the sun.
Then Rāma, placing Sītā at his side, together with Saumitri and all the monkeys headed by Sugrīva,
having arranged the protection of Laṅkā with Vibhīṣaṇa at the fore, crossed again over the sea — the abode of sea-monsters — by that same bridge.
Accompanied by his chief ministers as was fitting, the self-controlled one traveled in the Puṣpaka celestial vehicle, that sky-farer blazing with splendor, that goes wherever one wishes.
Then at the shore of the ocean, at the very place where that king had rested before, the righteous-souled one halted together with all the monkeys.
Then, in due time, Rāghava summoned them, honored them, satisfied them thoroughly with jewels, and dismissed them.
When the monkey-lords and the bear-tailed bears had departed, Rāma together with Sugrīva returned once more to Kiṣkindhā.
Accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa and together with Sugrīva, he showed Vaidehī the forests from the Puṣpaka celestial vehicle.
Having arrived at Kiṣkindhā, Rāma, best of warriors, consecrated Aṅgada — who had distinguished himself in battle — as crown prince.
Then Rāma, together with those same companions and with Saumitri, set out toward his own city by the same way they had come.
Having approached the city of Ayodhyā, the lord of the realm then dispatched Hanūmān as a messenger to Bharata.
Having read all of Bharata's signals and reported the glad tidings to him, when the son of Vāyu returned, Rāma went to Nandigrāma.
There he saw Bharata, his body smeared with grime, clad in bark garments, seated upon a seat with the sandals placed before him.
Having met with Bharata and with Śatrughna, O bull among Bhāratas, the valiant Rāghava rejoiced together with Saumitri.
Likewise Bharata and Śatrughna, reunited with their elder, were filled with great joy at the sight of Vaidehī.
Bharata, suffused with supreme delight, restored to the returning hero that kingdom which had been held as a trust for him and had been properly honored.
Then Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva together consecrated that hero on an auspicious day under a Vaiṣṇava asterism.
Once consecrated, he gave leave to Sugrīva, best of monkeys, together with his companions, and to Vibhīṣaṇa of the line of Pulastya, to return to their homes.
Having honored them with various gems, and both filled with love and joy, having made all proper arrangements, he dismissed them with a sorrowful heart.
And that Puṣpaka celestial vehicle — having reverently honored it, that son of Raghu, that Rāghava, joyfully returned it to Vaiśravaṇa himself.
Then, accompanied by divine sages along the river Gomatī, he performed ten unimpeded Aśvamedha sacrifices of the Jārūthya type.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O mighty-armed one, thus did Rāma of boundless splendor in former times endure that most severe affliction born of forest-exile.
Do not grieve, O tiger among men; you are a warrior, O scorcher of foes. You travel a path supported by the strength of your arms, a path of blazing resolution.
Not even the slightest fault is visible in you. Upon this path, even gods and demons together with Indra would despair.
Vṛtra was slain in battle by the Maruts and Indra the thunderbolt-wielder; so too was the invincible Namuci and the demoness Dīrghajihvā.
All purposes are fully achieved when one has allies. What indeed could be unconquered in battle for one whose brother is Dhanaṃjaya?
And here is Bhīma, best among the mighty, of terrifying valor; and the two young great archers, the twins sons of Mādrī. With such allies, O scorcher of foes, why do you grieve?

These men who could conquer even the army of Indra together with the Maruts — with these great bowmen as allies, gods in form, you too shall vanquish all your enemies in battle, O bull of the Bhārata line.
Furthermore, consider this: Draupadī was carried off by the wicked, powerful, and pride-maddened Jayadratha of Sindhu, yet these great-souled ones brought her back.
Kṛṣṇā Draupadī was recovered after that most difficult feat was accomplished, and King Jayadratha himself was conquered and brought under control.
By Rāma, fighting virtually alone, Vaidehī was recovered after slaying in battle the ten-headed demon Rāvaṇa of terrifying valor.
His allies were monkeys, bears, and the Kālamukhas — beings of a different species entirely. Reflect on this with your mind, O king.
Therefore, O tiger among the Kurus, do not grieve, O bull of the Bhārata line. Great-souled men like you do not grieve, O scorcher of foes.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus consoled by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, the king, casting off his sorrow, undepressed in spirit, spoke again as follows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I do not grieve for myself, O great sage, nor for these brothers, nor even for the loss of the kingdom, as much as I grieve for this daughter of Drupada.
Tormented by wicked men at the dice game, we were yet saved by Kṛṣṇā; and now she has again been forcibly carried off from the forest by Jayadratha.
Has any woman ever been seen or heard of — any woman with a parting, devoted to her husband, of great good fortune — who is the equal of this daughter of Drupada?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hear, O king Yudhiṣṭhira, of the great good fortune of nobly born women — all of this as it was attained by Sāvitrī, the princess.
There was among the Madras a righteous king, supremely virtuous, devoted to Brahmins, a refuge for all, true to his word, and master of his senses.
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, skillful, beloved of the townspeople and the countryside — that king was named Aśvapati, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Endowed with forbearance, yet childless, truthful in speech, master of his senses — as his years advanced he was seized by sorrow.
For the purpose of begetting offspring he undertook a severe austerity: eating only a measured portion at the proper time, practicing celibacy, subduing his senses.
Offering a hundred thousand oblations to Sāvitrī, O best of kings, he subsisted every sixth mealtime on scanty food.
By this practice he continued for exactly eighteen years; when the eighteenth year was completed, Sāvitrī was pleased and, O king, appeared to that monarch in her own form.
Rising from the sacrificial fire, filled with great joy, the boon-giver spoke these words to that king.
"By your pure celibacy, self-restraint, and discipline, and by your whole-hearted devotion to me, I am pleased with you, O king."
"Choose a boon, O Aśvapati, king of the Madras, whatever you desire. And you must never be negligent in matters of righteousness under any circumstances."
Aśvapati said: "This undertaking was begun by me out of desire for offspring, with longing for righteousness. May I have many sons, O goddess, who will uphold our lineage."
"If you are pleased with me, O goddess, this is the boon I choose. The twice-born tell me that progeny is the highest righteousness."
Sāvitrī said: "O king, knowing already this intention of yours, the Grandfather was already addressed on your behalf beforehand, for the sake of sons."
"And by his grace, as ordained by the Self-Born, a radiant daughter will come to you on earth very soon, O gentle one."
"You should say nothing further about this under any circumstance. I am pleased with the Grandfather's decree — this is what I tell you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having agreed with "So be it" to Sāvitrī's words, the king beseeched her again: "May it be so quickly."
When Sāvitrī disappeared, the king returned to his own home; he dwelt in his own kingdom with joy, ruling his subjects by righteousness.
Then, as some time passed, that king, firm in his vows, begot a child upon his eldest queen, a righteous woman.
That embryo in the Mālavī princess grew, O bull of the Bhārata line, like the lord of stars in the bright fortnight of the sky.
When the time came she gave birth to a lotus-eyed daughter; and the king joyfully performed the rites for her.
She was given as a gift by a pleased Sāvitrī, born of oblations offered to Sāvitrī — so the Brahmins and her father gave her the name Sāvitrī.
That princess grew like the goddess Śrī incarnate; and in time that maiden reached the bloom of youth.
Seeing her with slender waist and broad hips, like a golden image, people thought: "Surely this must be a celestial maiden descended here."
Yet no one sought her in marriage — she whose eyes were like lotus petals and who blazed with radiance — for they were repelled by her splendor.
Then, having fasted and bathed her head, having approached the divinities and offered into the fire according to rite, she had Brahmins recite on the holy day.
Then, taking the remaining flowers as blessed offerings from those great-souled ones, she went before her father like the goddess Śrī in human form.
She paid homage to her father's feet, first presented the remaining offerings, stood with joined palms, that noble-hipped woman, at the king's side.
Seeing his own daughter, goddess-like in form, arrived at the bloom of youth yet unsought by suitors, the king was grieved.
The king said: "Daughter, your time for being given in marriage has come, yet no one seeks me. Yourself seek out a husband equal to you in virtues."
"Whatever man you desire, tell him to me; I shall reflect and bestow you. Choose as you wish."
"For I have heard this recited by twice-born men from the textbook of righteousness — and you too, O auspicious one, hear my words as I speak them."
"A father who does not bestow her is blameworthy; a husband who does not love her is blameworthy; a son who does not protect his mother after the husband's death is blameworthy."
"Having heard these words of mine, hasten to seek a husband; act in such a way that the gods will not have cause to blame me."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having thus spoken to his daughter, the king also instructed the elder counselors and urged the escort party: "Let them go."
She paid homage to her father's feet and, proud-spirited yet seemingly abashed, having received her father's command, departed without hesitation.
She mounted a golden chariot and, surrounded by elder counselors, she visited the delightful forest-hermitages of the royal sages.
Paying homage at the feet of the revered elders there, she visited all the forests in order, my son.
Thus, distributing wealth at all the sacred fords, the princess went from place to place among the chief twice-born.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the king, lord of the Madras, was met by Nārada and sat together with him in the midst of the assembly hall in conversation, O Bhārata.
Then, having visited all the sacred fords and the hermitages as well, Sāvitrī returned to her father's house together with the counselors.
The auspicious one, seeing her father seated with Nārada, bowed her head and paid homage at the feet of both.
Nārada said: "Where had this daughter of yours gone, O king, and from where has she now returned? Why do you not bestow this young woman on a husband?"
Aśvapati said: "It is for this very purpose that she was sent out, and she has just now returned. Hear, O divine sage, about the husband she has chosen."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Urged by her father with "Speak fully about it," the auspicious Sāvitrī, receiving his word as if it were a divine command, spoke thus.
"There was among the Śālvas a righteous Kṣatriya, lord of the earth, known as Dyumatsena; he later became blind."
"When he lost his sight, his kingdom was seized while his son was still young — a wise king — by a former enemy who exploited this vulnerability."
"He went to the forest together with his wife, who still cared for him like a child; entering the great forest, he practiced austerities of great vows."
"His son, born in the city but grown up in the hermitage, Satyavān — fitting to be my husband — I have chosen in my heart."
Nārada said: "Ah, what a great wrong has been done unknowingly by Sāvitrī, O king — that she has chosen this virtuous Satyavān!"
"His father speaks truth, his mother speaks truth — therefore the Brahmins gave him this name: Satyavān, 'the truthful one.'"
"As a child he loved horses; he used to make clay horses and drew horses in pictures — so he is also called Citrāśva, 'the one of painted horses.'"
The king said: "Is he then radiant, wise, that son of a king? Is Satyavān, who delights his father, also patient and valiant?"
Nārada said: "He is radiant as Vivasvān, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, valiant as great Indra, and endowed with patience like the earth."
Aśvapati said: "Is Satyavān, the prince, also a giver, devoted to Brahmins, handsome, noble-spirited, or of pleasant appearance?"
Nārada said: "In giving, according to his ability, he equals Rantideva of Saṅkṛti's line; devoted to Brahmins and truthful in speech like Śibi of Uśīnara's line."
"Noble as Yayāti, of pleasant appearance like the Moon — in beauty, Dyumatsena's powerful son is unsurpassed, a match for the Aśvins."
"He is self-restrained, gentle, and brave; truthful and master of his senses; friendly and free from envy; modest and steadfast."
"In him there is ever directness, and his steadfastness is unwavering. In brief, this is what is said of him by those venerable in austerity and those venerable in character."
Aśvapati said: "You describe him to me as endowed with all virtues, O blessed one. Tell me also of his faults, if there are any here."
Nārada said: "He has one flaw and no other: Satyavān, from this very day, will exhaust his lifespan and lay down his body within a year."
The king said: "Come, Sāvitrī, go and choose another, O lovely one. His one great flaw overshadows and overcomes all his virtues."
"As the blessed Nārada, honored by the gods, has told me: within a year that short-lived one will lay down his body."
Sāvitrī said: "A lot falls but once; a daughter is given but once; and one says 'I give' but once — these three things happen only once, each only once."
Whether long-lived or short-lived, whether endowed with virtues or lacking them — a husband once chosen by me, I shall not choose a second time.
A resolve formed first in the mind is then declared in speech, and afterward carried out in deed; the mind is therefore my authority.
Nārada said: The understanding of Sāvitrī, your daughter, O best of men, is firm; she cannot by any means be turned away from this dharma.
The qualities that Satyavān possesses are not found in any other man. Therefore the giving away of your daughter pleases me.
The king said: What has been spoken by the blessed one is true and beyond deliberation; I shall do exactly this, for you, O blessed one, are my guru.
Nārada said: May the giving of your daughter Sāvitrī be free of obstacles. We shall accomplish it. May good befall all of you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Nārada soared into the sky and departed to heaven. The king too made all the wedding preparations for his daughter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, reflecting on that very matter of giving away his daughter, the king assembled all the requisite goods for the wedding.
Then, having summoned all the elder twice-born, the officiating priests, and the family chaplain, he set out with his daughter on an auspicious day.
Arriving at the sacred forest, the king proceeded on foot together with the brahmins and approached the hermitage of Dyumatsena, that royal sage.
There they saw the greatly fortunate blind king sitting on a cushion of kuśa grass, leaning against a śāla tree.
That king paid homage to the royal sage as was fitting and, restraining his speech carefully, introduced himself.
That knower of dharma offered him the arghya, a seat, and a cow, and then the king asked the other king: "What is the purpose of your coming?"
He disclosed to him his entire intention and the entire course of action to be done, directing it all toward Satyavān.
Aśvapati said: O royal sage, this lovely daughter of mine is named Sāvitrī. O knower of dharma, receive her from me according to proper rite as a daughter-in-law.

Dyumatsena said: We have been deprived of our kingdom and have taken to forest life; we practice dharma with discipline as ascetics. How shall your daughter, who is undeserving of such hardship, endure this toil in the hermitage?
Aśvapati said: When my daughter and I both understand that joy and sorrow are of the nature of coming and going, such words do not befit one like me. I have come to you with firm resolve, O king.
You ought not to destroy my hope out of friendship and affection; you should not refuse one who has come to you from all sides with love.
We are indeed well-matched for this union — you for me and I for you. Accept my daughter as a daughter-in-law, as a wife for Satyavān.
Dyumatsena said: This alliance with you was desired by me even before, but I was deprived of my kingdom, and so I held back from it.
But let that desire of mine, which was longed for even before, be fulfilled this very day; for you are a guest I have desired.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having assembled all the brahmins dwelling in the hermitage, the two kings had the marriage performed according to rite.
After giving his daughter and a suitable dowry of possessions, Aśvapati returned to his own home filled with the highest joy.
Satyavān too rejoiced upon obtaining that wife endowed with every virtue, and she rejoiced upon obtaining him as the husband she had desired in her heart.
After her father departed, she put aside all her ornaments and took up only the bark garments and the ochre-colored cloth.
By her service, her virtues, her modesty and self-restraint, and by fulfilling every desire, she won the satisfaction of all.
She pleased her mother-in-law with all the attentions to her body and with clothing and such things, and her father-in-law with the performance of divine rites and with restraint of speech.
Likewise, she completely pleased her husband with pleasant speech, with skillfulness, with tranquility, and with attendance upon him in private.
Thus, O Bhārata, some time passed for those virtuous people as they dwelt in that hermitage engaged in their ascetic practices.
But for Sāvitrī, whether lying down or standing, day and night, that speech spoken by Nārada ever remained in her mind.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, after much time had elapsed, there arrived, O king, that moment when Satyavān was to die.
And as Sāvitrī counted each passing day, that word spoken by Nārada rested perpetually in her heart.
Reflecting that death was to come on the fourth day, the beautiful woman undertook a three-night vow and stood still both day and night.
Hearing of his daughter-in-law's painful vow, the king rose, afflicted with sorrow, and spoke words to Sāvitrī to comfort her.
This undertaking you have begun is exceedingly severe, O princess; standing for three full days and nights is supremely difficult.
Sāvitrī said: You should not be distressed, father. I shall complete the vow; this is done by firm resolve, and resolve is the cause.
Dyumatsena said: I am in no way able to tell you to break the vow; one such as I should say only the proper word: "Complete it."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the noble-minded Dyumatsena fell silent, and Sāvitrī as she stood appeared like a wooden post.
On the eve of her husband's death, O bull of the Bhāratas, that night passed for Sāvitrī as she stood, afflicted with grief.
"Today is that day" — having offered oblations into the blazing fire, when the sun had risen a yoke's height, and having performed the morning rites,
she then saluted in due order all the elder twice-born, her mother-in-law, and her father-in-law, and stood with folded hands, composed.
All the ascetics dwelling in the ascetic forest then spoke auspicious blessings of non-widowhood for Sāvitrī's sake.
"So be it" — Sāvitrī, wholly intent on meditative absorption, accepted all those words of the ascetics with her mind.
Awaiting that time and that moment, the princess thought on the words of Nārada just as he had spoken them, deeply distressed.
Then her mother-in-law and father-in-law, O foremost of the Bhāratas, spoke these words with affection to the princess who stood apart.
The parents-in-law said: This vow, as it was prescribed, has been properly completed by you. The time for eating has arrived; do now what comes next.
Sāvitrī said: I shall eat after the sun has set, when my wish has been fulfilled. This is the resolve in my heart and the pledge I have made.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: While Sāvitrī was thus speaking about food, Satyavān took his axe upon his shoulder and set out for the forest.
But Sāvitrī said to her husband: "You should not go alone. I shall go with you; I cannot bear to be separated from you."
Satyavān said: You have not gone to the forest before, and the path is difficult, O beautiful one; weakened as you are by vow and fast, how will you walk on foot?
Sāvitrī said: I feel no fatigue from the fast, nor any weariness. I have resolved to go; you should not prevent me.
Satyavān said: If you are resolved on going, I shall do what pleases you; but first take leave of my elders, so that no fault may touch me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: She who had taken the great vow approached and spoke to her mother-in-law and father-in-law: "My husband is going to the great forest for fruits."
"I desire to be permitted by the noble lady and by my father-in-law to go out with him; separation from him is not bearable for me."
"Your son is going out for the sake of the sacred fire and the guru; he cannot be stopped. He might be stopped if he were going to the forest otherwise."
"For nearly a year I have not gone outside the hermitage; I have a great longing to see the forest in bloom."
Dyumatsena said: Ever since Sāvitrī was given to me as a daughter-in-law by her father, I do not recall that she has ever made an improper request.
Let this daughter-in-law then obtain the wish she desires. But care must be taken, my daughter, on the path alongside Satyavān.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Permitted by both, the illustrious Sāvitrī went forth with her husband, appearing to smile while her heart was torn with anguish.
The wide-eyed woman beheld the varied and delightful forests all around, resounding with the calls of peacocks.
The holy-flowing rivers and the blossoming trees — Satyavān kept saying to Sāvitrī in sweet words: "Look at this!"
The blameless woman, watching her husband in all his moods, already regarded him as dead, recalling in that moment the sage's words.
Yet following her husband, she walked with gentle gait, as if her heart were split in two, all the while watching for that moment.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that valiant man, with his wife as his companion, gathered fruits and filled his basket, and afterward split firewood.
As he split the wood, sweat broke out upon him, and from the exertion he felt a pain arise in his head.
Approaching his dear wife, he said, tormented by fatigue: "From this exertion of mine a pain has arisen in my head."
"And all my limbs and my heart seem to burn, O Sāvitrī, O you of measured speech; I perceive that I am unwell."
"I perceive that my head is pierced as if by spears; I wish to sleep, O auspicious one — I have no strength to stand."
Then Sāvitrī approached, embraced her husband, placed his head in her lap, and sat down upon the ground.
Then that ascetic woman, reflecting on Nārada's words, reckoned that moment, that instant, that hour, and that day together.
And within a moment she saw a man clad in yellow garments, with a bound diadem, magnificent in form, with radiance equal to the sun's.
Dark-complexioned and fair, with red eyes, a noose in his hand, inspiring dread, he stood at Satyavān's side, gazing intently at him.
Seeing him, she quickly rose, gently laid her husband's head down, stood with folded hands, and spoke, distressed, her heart trembling.
"I recognize you as a divine being, for this form is superhuman. Tell me of your own will, O god — who are you, and what do you intend to do?"
Yama said: "You are a devoted wife, Sāvitrī, and likewise endowed with ascetic power; therefore I address you directly. Know me, O auspicious one — I am Yama."
"This Satyavān, your husband, the son of a king, has exhausted his lifespan; I shall bind him and lead him away — know this to be my intention."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the blessed lord of the fathers began to explain fully his entire intention for her sake, wishing to please her.
"For this man is endowed with righteousness, handsome, an ocean of virtues; he is not fit to be led away by my messengers — therefore I have come myself."
Then Yama forcibly drew from the body of Satyavān the thumb-sized person bound with a noose, come under his sway.
Then that body, its life-breath extracted, its breath gone, its lustre lost, motionless — became a pitiable sight to behold.
Yama, having thus bound him, departed facing southward; and Sāvitrī too, tormented by grief, followed Yama himself — she who was perfected in vows and observances, the greatly blessed devoted wife.
Yama said: Turn back, go, Sāvitrī; perform the post-mortem rites for him. Your debt to your husband has been paid; you have gone as far as one may go.
Sāvitrī said: Where my husband is led, or where he himself goes, I too must go there — this is the eternal law.
Through austerity, devoted service to the teacher, love for my husband, and through vows, and by your own grace, my path is not obstructed.
The wise who perceive the truth of things declare that seven steps together make a friendship; honouring that friendship, I shall say something — listen to it.
Those of various natures wander in the forest, enduring dharma, dwelling, and hardship; the wise declare dharma through understanding; therefore the good say dharma is paramount.
By the dharma of the one, by the conviction of the good, all of us enter that path; let no one desire a second or a third; therefore the good say dharma is paramount.
Yama said: Turn back — I am pleased by this speech of yours, composed of excellent syllables, letters, and logic; choose a boon here, excepting this one's life; I grant you any boon, blameless one.

Sāvitrī said: My father-in-law, fallen from his own kingdom and dwelling in the forest, his eyes destroyed, lives in the hermitage; may he by your grace regain his sight, becoming a powerful king, blazing like fire and sun.
Yama said: I grant you all of this boon, blameless one; it shall be as you have said. I perceive what seems like weariness in your path; turn back, go — let there be no fatigue for you.

Sāvitrī said: How can there be weariness for me near my husband? For where my husband is, that is my certain course; wherever you will lead my lord, there is my path. O lord of the gods, hear yet another word from me.

A single meeting with the good is supremely desired; beyond that, it is called true friendship; association with a virtuous person is never fruitless; therefore one should dwell in the company of the good.

Yama said: You have spoken to me words pleasing to the mind, increasing the wisdom of the wise, conducive to welfare — again excepting the life of this Satyavān; choose a second boon, passionate lady.

Sāvitrī said: The kingdom of my wise father-in-law was stolen of old; may that king regain his own realm, and may my venerable father-in-law never abandon his own dharma — this second boon I ask of you.

Yama said: He shall soon regain his own kingdom; the king shall not be separated from his own dharma — this wish is granted by me, O daughter of a king; turn back, go, let there be no fatigue for you.

Sāvitrī said: These creatures are restrained by you through law; having restrained them you lead them, not from desire — thus your lordship as Yama, O god, is renowned; hear also this word spoken by me.
Non-malice toward all beings in deed, thought, and speech, along with benevolence and giving — this is the eternal dharma of the good.
Such indeed is this world — human beings are delicate in their power; yet even the good show compassion toward enemies when they are in distress.
Yama said: As water is to one who thirsts, so has this speech been uttered by you; again excepting the life of this Satyavān, choose here whatever boon you wish, auspicious one.
Sāvitrī said: My father, the lord of the earth, is without offspring; may there be a hundred sons born of my father himself, continuing the lineage of his family — this third boon I ask of you.

Yama said: A hundred sons of your father, continuing the lineage, of great splendour — may they be yours, auspicious one; this wish is granted, O daughter of a king; turn back — you have come a long way.
Sāvitrī said: This is not far for me when near my husband; for my mind races even farther ahead; thus even as you walk, listen once more to the words I am ready to speak.
You are the glorious son of Vivasvat; therefore the wise call you Vaivasvata; the creatures are won over by your peace and dharma — hence, O lord, you hold here the kingship of dharma.
Even in oneself there is not as much trust as there is in the good; therefore everyone especially desires affection from the good.
From the goodwill of all beings, trust is born; therefore people especially place their trust in the good.

Yama said: The words you have uttered, O slender-waisted, auspicious one — such have not been heard by me from any other; by these I am pleased; excepting this one's life, choose a fourth boon and go.
Sāvitrī said: May there be born sons of my own body from Satyavān, a hundred sons bearing strength and valour, upholding both our families here — this fourth boon I ask of you.
Yama said: A hundred sons bearing strength and valour shall be born to your delight, gentle one; let there be no weariness for you, O daughter of a king; turn back — you have come a long way.
Sāvitrī said: The conduct in dharma of the good is always eternal; the good neither sink nor tremble; association with the good is never fruitless; the good do not follow fear from the good.
For the good guide the sun by truth; the good uphold the earth through austerity; the good are the course of the past and the future, O king; among the good, the good do not sink.
Knowing this conduct to be eternal, honoured by the noble, the good, acting for the sake of others, do not look for any return.
Grace bestowed upon the virtuous is never wasted; neither wealth nor honour is lost; because this is certain and constant among the good — therefore the good become protectors.

Yama said: The more you speak words combined with dharma, pleasing to the mind, well-formed and full of great meaning, the more my supreme devotion grows toward you; choose an incomparable boon, O lady of firm vows.

Sāvitrī said: Your release from meritorious action does not happen without being granted, O giver of honour, as in the other boons; I choose this boon: let this Satyavān live — for without my husband I am as if dead.
I do not desire happiness bereft of my husband; I do not desire heaven bereft of my husband; I do not desire prosperity bereft of my husband; I do not resolve to live as one without a husband.
The grant of the boon — my having a hundred sons — was given by you yourself, yet my husband is being taken away; I choose the boon: let this Satyavān live; thus your own word will be true.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having said "So be it" and releasing those bonds, Yama Vaivasvata, the king of dharma, his soul filled with joy, spoke these words to Sāvitrī:
"This husband of yours, auspicious one, delighter of your family, has been released by me; free from disease, he will lead you and his purposes shall be fulfilled."
"He shall attain a lifespan of four hundred years together with you; having performed sacrifices with dharma, he shall gain renown in the world."
"Satyavān shall beget on you a hundred sons; all of them shall be kings, warriors, with sons and grandsons, renowned and bearing your name — they shall be eternal here."

"And a hundred sons shall be born to your father by your mother, of the Mālava lineage — Mālavas by name, eternal, with sons and grandsons; they shall be your brothers, warriors equal to the thirty gods."
Having thus granted the boons to her, the glorious king of dharma, turning Sāvitrī back, went to his own abode.
And Sāvitrī too, when Yama had departed and she had recovered her husband, went to where the lifeless body of her husband lay.
Seeing her husband on the ground, she approached and embraced him, and placing his head in her lap, she sat down on the earth.
And Satyavān, having regained consciousness, spoke to Sāvitrī; gazing at her again and again with affection, as if returned from a journey.
Satyavān said: "Alas, I have slept very long — why was I not awakened? And where is that dark man who was dragging me away?"
Sāvitrī said: "Alas, you have slept very long on my lap, O bull among men; that blessed god who restrains the creatures, Yama, has gone."
"You are rested, O greatly fortunate one, and free from sleep, O son of a king; if you are able, rise up and behold the deep night."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having regained his senses, he rose as if from a pleasant sleep; gazing at all the directions and the edges of the forest, Satyavān spoke:
"I went out to gather fruits with you, O slender-waisted one; then, while splitting wood, a pain arose in my head."
"Scorched by the burning heat in my head, unable to stand for long, I fell asleep in your lap — all this I remember, auspicious one."
"And while being embraced by you, my mind was carried away by sleep; then I saw terrible darkness and a man of great radiance."
"If you know what that was, tell me, O slender-waisted one — whether it was a dream I saw, or whether it was real indeed."
Then Sāvitrī said to him: "The night is deepening; tomorrow, O son of a king, I shall tell you everything exactly as it occurred."
"Rise up, rise up — may good come to you; see your parents, O one of pure vows; this night is deep and the day-maker has departed."
"These night-wanderers roam about, joyful and uttering fierce cries; the sounds of leaves and of animals roaming in the forest are heard."
"These jackals, with their terrible cries, taking up the south-western direction, howl fiercely, shaking my heart."
Satyavān said: "The forest appears terrifying, wrapped in dense darkness; you will not be able to discern the path, and you will not be able to go."
Sāvitrī said: "In this forest that was burned today, a dry tree stands blazing; fanned by the wind, fire is visible here and there."
"Then, having brought fire here, I shall kindle it on all sides; there is wood here — cast off the anguish of your heart."
"If you are not able to go, I observe that you are in pain; and you will not know the path in the forest covered by darkness."
"Tomorrow at dawn, when the forest is visible, we shall go with your consent; let us stay here this night, if it pleases you, O sinless one."
Satyavān said: "The pain in my head has subsided; I perceive my limbs to be well; I wish to meet my mother and father — and this meeting is born of your grace."
"Never before have I gone to the hermitage at an improper time; my mother stops me whenever the evening has not yet come."
"Even when I go out during the day, both my venerable parents are distressed; my father searches for me together with the hermitage-dwellers."
"By my mother and father, greatly afflicted, I have often been reproached in the past: 'You have come back late.'"
"What is their condition today on my account, I think; when I am unseen by them, great sorrow will befall them."
"They used to speak to me before as well, not tearful in the night, greatly afflicted, the two elders, many times full of affection:"
"'Without you we cannot live even for a moment, my son; as long as you shall live, my son, for that long our life is certain.'"
"'You are the staff of two old blind people; in you the lineage is established; in you rest our funeral offerings, our renown, and our continuity.'"
"My mother is old, my father is old, and I am their staff; not seeing me this night, what condition will those two come to?"
"And I am angry at sleep, on account of which my father and my innocent mother have come to uncertainty because of me."
"And I myself have come to uncertainty, fallen into terrible danger; for without my mother and father I do not resolve to live."
"Clearly my father, whose sight is wisdom, with an agitated mind, at this very hour questions each hermitage-dweller one by one."
"I do not grieve for myself as much as I grieve for my father, O auspicious one, and for my mother who has followed her husband and is utterly frail."

"For on my account the two of them shall today reach the greatest anguish; as long as they live I live after them — they are to be supported by me; thinking 'I must do what is dear to them,' I too live."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled one, devoted to his elders and dear to them, raised his arms and, tormented by grief, wept aloud.
Then, seeing her husband thus emaciated by grief, Sāvitrī the dharma-walking one, wiping the tears from his eyes, spoke:
"If austerity has been practiced by me, if gifts have been given, if oblations have been offered — may this night be auspicious for my mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband."
"I do not recall having ever spoken an untruth even in casual matters; by that truth, may both my parents-in-law be sustained today."

Satyavān said: I long to see my parents — go at once, Sāvitrī, do not delay. If I were to see any affliction of my mother or father, I could not live, O fair-limbed one; I swear this on my own soul by truth.
If your mind is set on dharma, and if you wish me to live, and if you desire to do what pleases me, then go now — leave at once for the hermitage nearby.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Sāvitrī rose, bound up her hair, and that devoted woman raised her husband, clasping him firmly with both arms.
Satyavān rose, wiped his limbs with his hand, surveyed all the directions, and then fixed his gaze upon the firewood bundle.
Then Sāvitrī said to him: You shall carry the fruits tomorrow; for your welfare and support I will carry the axe for you now.
Having placed the bundle of firewood hanging upon a tree branch, she took up the axe and came again to her husband's side.
The slender-thighed one laid her husband's arm upon her left shoulder, clasped him with her right arm, and walked on with gentle steps.
Satyavān said: O timid one, the paths are familiar to me from frequent travel; and by the moonlight filtering through the trees I can also make them out clearly.
Yesterday we came by a certain path and gathered fruits along it — O auspicious one, go back by the same road; do not waver from the path.
In this grove of palāśa trees the path forks in two; take the northern branch and hurry along it — I am well, I am strong, and I am eager to see both my parents.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Saying this and urging haste, he set out toward the hermitage.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: At that very moment, Dyumatsena, in the great forest, had regained his sight; with a serene mind and clear vision he beheld all things around him.
He went through all the hermitages with his wife Śaibyā, and in his distress on account of his son he was overwhelmed with grief, O bull among men.
The husband and wife wandered through hermitage after hermitage, river after river, forest after forest, and lake after lake, searching each region in turn.
Hearing any sound at all and lifting their faces in hope that it was their son, they ran toward it — and indeed Satyavān approached together with Sāvitrī.
With feet torn and rough, wounded and stained with blood, their bodies pierced by sharp kuśa grass and thorns, they ran like people driven mad.
Then all those brāhmaṇas dwelling in the hermitage came forward, surrounded the couple, comforted them, and brought them back to their own hermitage.
There, accompanied by his wife and surrounded by aged ascetics rich in penance, he was consoled with varied accounts drawing on the stories of kings of old.
Then those two old ones, somewhat comforted yet longing to see their son, recalled the deeds of their son in childhood and were overcome with deep sorrow.
Uttering pitiful words again, worn away by grief, they wept — "Alas, my son! Alas, virtuous daughter-in-law! Where are you, where are you?"
Suvarcas said: As Sāvitrī, his wife, is endowed with austerity, self-restraint, and righteous conduct, so surely Satyavān lives.
Gautama said: I have studied the Vedas with all their auxiliary branches, I have accumulated great austerity, I observed celibacy from boyhood, and I have satisfied my teachers and the sacred fire.
With concentrated mind I have observed all the vows, fasted living on air alone, and practised all the purifying disciplines that are mine.
By this ascetic power I know all that has been done and all that is about to occur — know this for truth: Satyavān lives.
The pupil said: As the word has gone forth from my teacher's mouth, it shall never prove false — thus Satyavān lives.
The sages said: As his wife Sāvitrī is endowed with all auspicious marks that ward off widowhood, so Satyavān lives.
Bhāradvāja said: As his wife Sāvitrī is endowed with austerity, self-restraint, and righteous conduct, so Satyavān lives.
Dālbhya said: As your sight has been restored to you, and as Sāvitrī's vow holds — she who went without food — so Satyavān lives.
Māṇḍavya said: As the beasts and birds speak out in the peaceful direction, and as the earthly omens in your case are favourable, so Satyavān lives.
Dhaumya said: As your son is endowed with all virtues, beloved of the people, long-lived, and bearing auspicious marks — so Satyavān lives.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus consoled by those truth-speaking ascetics, the king set aside anxiety after anxiety and became steady, as it were.
Then after a short time Sāvitrī together with her husband Satyavān arrived, and at night she entered the hermitage full of joy.
The brāhmaṇas said: Having today seen you reunited with your son and having beheld you with sight restored, we all ask for your continued prosperity, O lord of the earth.
By reunion with your son, by the sight of Sāvitrī, and by the recovery of your own eyes — by these three blessings you have fortunately prospered.
What was said by all of us has come to pass — there is no doubt of it; and yet further and further prosperity shall quickly come to you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then those twice-born ones, kindling the sacred fire there, all paid homage to Dyumatsena, the great king, O Pārtha.
Śaibyā, Satyavān, and Sāvitrī, having been granted permission by all of them, sat down together, free from sorrow.
Then all those forest-dwellers, seated with the king and seized with curiosity, questioned the son of the king, O Pārtha.
Why did you not come earlier with your wife, O lord? And why did you come in the dead of night? What was the sequence of events for you?
Your father, your mother, and all of us were tormented with grief, O son of the king — we know this did not happen without cause; please tell us everything.
Satyavān said: I was given leave by my father and went accompanied by Sāvitrī; then, while I was splitting wood in the forest, a pain arose in my head.
I lay down overcome by the pain and, as I reckon it, I slept for a long time — never before had I slept so long.
I thought: may none of you all be made to suffer on my account — that is why I returned in the dead of night; there is no other reason for it.
Gautama said: The recovery of sight by Dyumatsena your father was not without cause; you do not know the reason — Sāvitrī should speak of it.
I wish to hear it, Sāvitrī — for you know the higher and the lower truth; I recognise you, Sāvitrī, as one equal in radiance to Sāvitrī herself.
You know the cause of all this — therefore let the truth be declared. If there is nothing secret in this, speak to us about it.
Sāvitrī said: It is exactly as you suppose — your conviction is not otherwise. Nor is there anything secret on my part; hear what is true in this matter.
The death of my husband was foretold to me by the great-souled Nārada, and that very day had arrived — therefore I did not leave him.
While he lay asleep, Yama himself came in person with his servants, bound him, and led him away toward the quarter frequented by the ancestors.
I praised that all-pervading god with truthful words, and by him five boons were granted to me — hear them from me.
The restoration of sight and sovereignty — these two boons were for my father-in-law; for my father a hundred sons were obtained; and a hundred sons for myself.
My husband Satyavān was obtained with a life of four hundred years; and it was for the life of my husband that I steadfastly observed the firm vow.
I have thus told you truly and in full the cause of all this — how this great sorrow of mine, as it unfolded, leads to happiness in the end.

The sages said: The family of the king, which was sinking and beset by misfortunes, plunged in a dark lake of affliction, has been rescued by you, O woman of noble conduct, who hold to the merit of dharma — rescued once more by one who is truly of noble lineage.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having thus praised and honoured that excellent woman, the assembled sages took proper leave of the king together with his son, and departed joyfully to their own dwellings by an auspicious road.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When that night had passed and the sun's orb had risen, all those ascetics rich in penance gathered together, having completed their morning rites.
Those great sages could not get their fill of narrating again and again to Dyumatsena all the great good fortune that had come through Sāvitrī.
Then all the subjects who had come from the Śālva territories announced to the king that the king there had been slain by his own minister.
They reported truthfully that the minister had killed him along with his allies and kinsmen, and that the hostile army had been scattered and put to flight.
And they declared the unanimous will of all the people toward the king: "Whether he has sight or no sight, let him be our king."
"With this resolve we have been sent here, O king; these conveyances have arrived, and your fourfold army stands ready."
"Go forth, O king — blessings to you! Victory has been proclaimed in the city. Occupy for long years the ancestral throne inherited from your fathers and grandfathers."
Beholding the king now with sight restored and possessed of his former handsome form, they all fell at his feet with wide eyes blooming in wonder.
Then, having reverenced those elder twice-born dwellers of the hermitage, and having been honoured by all of them in return, he set out toward the city.
Śaibyā too set out together with Sāvitrī, upon a well-spread and richly decked conveyance drawn by men, surrounded by the army.
Then the royal chaplains joyfully consecrated Dyumatsena, and they consecrated his great-souled son in the position of crown prince.
Then, in the course of time, that hundred sons who would enhance the fame of Sāvitrī were born — heroes who never turned back in battle.
And likewise there were born to Aśvapati, lord of the Madras, a hundred brothers of the same mother — of great might — from a Mālavī woman.
Thus her own self, her father, her mother, her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, and the family of her husband — all were rescued from peril by Sāvitrī.
Even so shall this auspicious Draupadī, honoured for her character, like Sāvitrī a noble woman of her lineage, rescue all of you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus consoled by that great-souled one, the Pāṇḍava, free from grief and fever, dwelt at that time in Kāmyaka, O king.
Janamejaya said: What was the word that Lomaśa then spoke, O great brahmin, coming at Indra's bidding to Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu —
"— and regarding that intense fear of yours which you disclose nowhere: 'that too I shall remove when the Left-handed Archer comes here' —
— what was that great fear regarding Karṇa, O best of the learned? And why did that righteous-souled one not speak of it to anyone?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: I shall tell you this tale, O tiger among kings, since you ask — O best of the Bhāratas, be attentive to my words.
When the twelfth year had passed and the thirteenth arrived, Śakra, acting for the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, set out to beg from Karṇa.
Then, having learned of Mahendra's intention, O great king, Vibhāvasu — the sun — approached Karṇa regarding the matter of the earrings.
The hero lay on a most precious bed covered with a matchless spread, resting unsuspecting — devoted to the brahmins and ever truthful in speech.
At the end of a dream, in the night, O lord of kings, the radiant sun revealed himself, filled with the deepest compassion and moved by a father's love, O Bhārata.
The sun, taking the form of a brahmin versed in the Vedas and possessed of a handsome form by his yogic power, spoke these soothing words to Karṇa for his benefit.
O Karṇa, dear son, hear my word — O best among those who uphold truth, O mighty-armed one — for today I speak to you, out of deep friendship, that which is supremely beneficial.
O Karṇa, Śakra will come to you, desiring the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, disguised in the form of a brahmin, wishing to steal your earrings.
Your character is known to him, as it is to the whole world — that when asked by worthy men you give freely and never refuse.
For you, dear son, always give to brahmins when they ask — wealth and whatever else they may name — you never refuse at any time.
Knowing you to be of such a nature, Pākaśāsana himself — Indra — will come to beg for your earrings and also your armour.
To him who comes begging, you must not give the earrings; he should be appeased to the utmost of your ability — this is indeed the highest good for you.
Dear son, he who comes speaking of the earrings must be turned away again and again by you with many arguments and with wealth of many kinds offered instead.
With jewels, women, pleasures, wealth of many varieties, and with many inducements — Purandara, who desires your earrings, should be redirected.
If you give away, O Karṇa, those auspicious earrings born with you, your life will waste away and you will come under the power of death.
O giver of honour, know my words to be true — protected by your armour and both earrings, you are invincible to your enemies on the battlefield.
For both of these — the armour and earrings — arose from ambrosia, born of precious substances. Therefore, O Karṇa, guard them, if your life is dear to you.
Karṇa said: Who are you, O revered one, who speak to me thus, revealing supreme friendship? Kindly tell me, O blessed one — who are you, wearing the guise of a brahmin?
The brahmin said: I am, dear son, Sahasrāṃśu — the thousand-rayed sun — and out of friendship I advise you. Do as I say; this is indeed the highest good for you.
Karṇa said: It is indeed the highest good for me whose lord and master, the lord of cattle — the sun — speaks today seeking my welfare. Now hear this word of mine.
I propitiate you, O granter of boons, and speak out of affection: I cannot be turned away from this vow, if I am truly dear to you.
O Vibhāvasu, this entire world knows my vow — that I would surely give even my life to the foremost among brahmins.
O best among sky-dwellers, if Śakra comes to me covered in the disguise of a brahmin to beg, for the welfare of the sons of Pāṇḍu —
— I will give, O best of the wise, both the earrings and the finest armour, so that my fame, renowned in all three worlds, does not perish.
For one like me, preserving life at the cost of dishonour is not proper; what is proper is what accords with glory — a death honoured by the world is proper.
Thus I will give to Indra both the earrings and the armour, if the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra comes to me with the purpose of begging.
For him to beg my earrings for the welfare of the sons of Pāṇḍu — that will bring glory to me in the world, while disgrace will fall upon him.
I choose fame in the world even over life, O sun-god; the man of fame attains heaven, while one stripped of fame perishes.
Fame indeed revives a man in the world like a mother; dishonour destroys life even while the embodied one still breathes.
This is an ancient verse sung by the Creator himself, O Vibhāvasu, O lord of the worlds: fame is the very life-span of a man.
In the other world, fame alone is the supreme refuge of a man; and in this world, pure fame prolongs life.
Thus, by giving what was born with my body, I will attain eternal fame; and having given as a gift in due order to the brahmins according to proper rite —
— having offered up my body in battle, having performed deeds most difficult to do, or having conquered enemies in the fight, I will attain glory alone.
Having given safety to the frightened and those who seek life on the battlefield, having freed the aged, children, and brahmins from great danger —
— I will attain the highest glory in the world, O slayer of Svarbhānu. Fame is to be guarded even at the cost of life — know that to be my vow.
Thus I, having given this unsurpassed gift to Maghavat — to Indra disguised as a brahmin — O god, will attain the highest state in the world.
The Sun said: O Karṇa, do not do harm to yourself, nor to your friends, your sons, your wives, your mother, and your father.
O best among the living, O bearer of life, attainment of glory and lasting fame in the three worlds is desired without injury to the body.
You who seek eternal fame through the destruction of your life — that fame will depart taking your life with it; there is no doubt of this.

O bull among men, O tiger among men, know this through reason: it is for those who live that father, mother, sons, and whatever other kinsmen there may be in this world — and kings — perform their duties.

O greatly resplendent one, the good fame of a man exists while he lives; what use is fame to the dead, to an embodied being reduced to ash? The dead man does not know his fame; it is the living man who enjoys fame.
The fame of a dead mortal is like a garland upon one whose life is gone. I tell you this because you are my devotee and I desire your welfare.
My devotees are to be protected — for this reason too, since you are devoted to me with the highest devotion, O mighty-armed one, affection has arisen in me as well; therefore, do as I say.
There is also a certain higher spiritual matter here, ordained by the gods; and for this reason too I tell you this — let it be done without doubt.
O bull among men, the divine secret cannot be known by you; therefore I do not reveal the secret to you — in due time you will come to know it.
I will say again what has been said: O son of Rādhā, understand this — do not give your earrings to the one who begs, to Vajrapāṇi.
O greatly resplendent one, you shine with those beautiful earrings like the spotless moon in the sky between the Viśākhā stars.
Know this: good fame belongs to a man who lives; therefore, dear son, Purandara should be refused by you when he comes for the earrings.
O sinless one, the desire of the king of gods for your earrings can be thwarted by you with many kinds of arguments supported by reasoning, again and again.
O Karṇa, drive away this intention of Purandara with words adorned by sweetness and grounded in well-reasoned meaning.
You, O tiger among men, always rival Savyasācin; that hero Savyasācī will indeed meet you in battle.
Arjuna would not be able to defeat you in battle while you are possessed of both earrings, even if Indra himself were to become his arrow.
Therefore these auspicious earrings must not be given to Śakra, O Karṇa, if you desire to defeat Arjuna in battle.
Karṇa said: O lord of cattle, O sun of supreme fierce rays, I am devoted to you as you know me to be — I am devoted to no other god in any way.
Neither my wife, nor my sons, nor my own self, nor my friends — none are as dear to me always in devotion as you are, O lord of cattle.
Great souls perform beloved deeds for their beloved devotees — there is no doubt of this; and you know this too, O Bhāskara.
Thinking 'Karṇa is my beloved devotee and worships no other deity in heaven,' the blessed lord spoke for my welfare — knowing this.
And again I beg with bowed head, propitiating you again and again — this is what I say, O fierce-rayed one; you should pardon me.
I do not fear death as much as I fear falsehood — especially towards all brahmins and the righteous at all times; in the matter of giving even my life there is no deliberation for me.
And as for what you told me, O god, regarding Phalguna the Pāṇḍava — let the sorrow born of anguish leave your mind, O Bhāskara, regarding Arjuna and me: I will defeat Arjuna in battle.
O god, you too know my great power of weapons — what I received from Jāmadagni, and likewise from the great-souled Droṇa.
O best of the gods, approve this vow of mine: I would give even my own life to Vajrin when he comes begging.
The Sun said: If, dear son, you give those auspicious earrings to Vajrin, then you too should speak to him for the sake of victory, O greatly powerful one.
You should give the earrings to Śatakratu conditionally; for equipped with those earrings you are invincible to all beings.
For the slayer of demons — Indra — desiring your destruction through Arjuna in battle, wishes to steal your earrings, my son.
Therefore you too should propitiate him with kind and true words again and again, and beseech Purandara, the lord of the gods, for a purpose that will not go in vain.
'Give me the unfailing Śakti-weapon that destroys enemies — I will give you, O thousand-eyed one, the earrings and also the finest armour.'
With this condition you should give the earrings to Śakra; with that weapon, O Karṇa, you will slay your enemies on the battlefield.
O mighty-armed one, that Śakti of the king of gods, having slain the enemies, does not return to his hand — it has done so hundreds and thousands of times.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Sahasrāṃśu — the sun — suddenly disappeared. Then, at the end of his prayers to the sun, Karṇa reported the dream.
Exactly as he had seen it, exactly as it had truly been, exactly as both had spoken in the night — all of it Vṛṣa (Karṇa) narrated to him in proper sequence.
Having heard that, the blessed god Bhānu — the slayer of Svarbhānu — spoke thus to Karṇa, the sun smiling as it were.
Then Rādheya — the slayer of enemy heroes — knowing this to be the truth, desiring only the Śakti-weapon, waited for Vāsava.
Janamejaya said: What was that secret which the hot-rayed sun did not reveal to Karṇa here? And what were those earrings like? And what was the armour like?
And from where did he get the armour and the earrings, O best of men? I wish to hear this — tell me that, O treasure of asceticism.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O king, I will tell you what that secret of Vibhāvasu was, and what those earrings were like, and what the armour was like.
O king, long ago a brahmin came to Kuntibhoja — fierce in radiance, tall and majestic, bearing a staff-beard and matted locks.
He was handsome, of faultless limbs, blazing as it were with splendour, of a honey-amber hue, sweet of speech, and adorned with asceticism and sacred study.
He of great asceticism spoke to king Kuntibhoja: 'O one without jealousy, I wish to take my meals in your house as a guest.'
'No offense must be done to me by you or by your attendants; on these terms I will dwell in your house, if it pleases you, O sinless one.'
'And I should be able to come and go as I please; and as to my bed and seat, O king, no one should give offense to me.'
Kuntibhoja spoke to him these affectionate words: 'So be it, and even more so,' and then spoke to him again.
'O great brahmin, I have a daughter named Pṛthā, a glorious maiden, endowed with good character and conduct, virtuous, disciplined, and free of arrogance.'
'She will attend upon you, honouring you without contempt; and you will find satisfaction in her character and conduct.'
Having spoken thus to the brahmin and honoured him in the proper manner, he then went to his daughter and spoke to Pṛthā of large eyes.
'My dear child, this highly fortunate brahmin wishes to reside in my house, and I have given him my word, saying: so be it.'
On you, my child, rests the honour of serving this brahmin, the support of our life. That word of mine you must never make false at any time.
This ascetic lord, this twice-born devoted to his studies, this man of great splendour — whatever he asks, all of it must be given ungrudgingly.
Brahmins are the highest splendour; brahmins are the highest austerity. It is by obeisance to brahmins that the sun shines in the sky.
For Vātāpi the great demon, who dishonoured those worthy of honour, was slain by the staff of brahmic power — and Tālajaṅgha likewise.
This great burden, my child, has now been placed upon you. You must always, with self-restraint, perform the honouring of this brahmin.
I know your devotion since childhood, my dear daughter, toward all brahmins and toward teachers and kinsmen alike.
Likewise toward all servants, toward friends, relations, and mothers, and toward me as well — you have always conducted yourself with full respect.
There is no dissatisfied person in this city or in the inner apartments with regard to you, O blameless one, and not even among your servants, owing to your proper conduct.
Yet I think I must instruct you regarding this irascible twice-born, O Pṛthā — bearing in mind that you are young and that you are my daughter.
You were born in the clan of the Vṛṣṇis, the beloved daughter of Śūra; as a child you were given to me long ago by your father himself out of affection.
Sister of Vāsudeva, foremost among children — your father having pledged his first child at the outset, you became my daughter.
Born in such a lineage and raised in such a lineage, you have moved from comfort to comfort, as if passing from one lake to another.
Women who have come from inferior families and by some chance risen to prosperity generally misbehave in their youth, O fair one.
But you, Pṛthā, were born in a royal family, and your beauty is marvellous to behold — endowed with all of these, you are well-graced, O passionate one.
Therefore, O spirited one, abandoning pride, deceit, and arrogance, serve this brahmin who grants boons, and you shall be yoked to prosperity, O Pṛthā.
In this way you will surely attain good fortune, O auspicious and sinless one. But if this best of twice-born is angered, my entire lineage could be consumed.
Kuntī said: Bound by duty, O king, I shall attend upon the brahmin with reverence as promised, O lord of kings — I do not speak falsely.
This is moreover my own nature — to honour the twice-born. And this is what is dear to you and what is my highest good.
Whether he comes in the evening, in the morning, or at night, or even at midnight — the reverend one shall not find cause to be angry with me.
This is my own gain, O lord of kings, that by honouring brahmins while abiding in your command, I shall be doing what is beneficial — O best of men.
Be at ease, O lord of kings — the best of twice-born shall find no offence while dwelling in your house. I tell you this truly.
Whatever is pleasing and beneficial to this brahmin and to you, O sinless one, I shall strive for — O king, let the fever of your mind pass.
For brahmins of great fortune, when honoured, O lord of the earth, are capable of causing liberation — but in the opposite case, of causing destruction.
Knowing this, I shall satisfy this best of twice-born. You shall suffer no distress on my account from this best of brahmins, O king.
For when kings transgress, brahmins bring misfortune, O lord of kings — as Cyavana did in the matter of Sukanyā in former times.
With the utmost restraint I shall attend upon this best of twice-born, exactly as you, O best of lords of men, have spoken concerning the brahmin.
The king said: This is indeed what you must do, my good daughter, without hesitation — for my welfare, for the welfare of the family, and for your own welfare, O delightful one.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to that maiden, the greatly renowned Kuntibhoja, tender toward his daughter, entrusted Pṛthā to that brahmin.
This, O brahmin, is my daughter, a child raised in comfort. Whatever small offence she might commit — you must not take it to heart.
Twice-born of great fortune are generally free of anger toward the aged, children, and ascetics — even toward those who have wronged them — always.
Even for very great offences, forbearance is appropriate for the twice-born. And the honour given according to ability and eagerness should be accepted, O best of twice-born.
When the brahmin said "So be it," the king, his mind rejoiced, assigned to him a house white as a swan and as the moon's rays.
There in the fire-room, a bright seat was arranged for him, and all provisions of food and the rest were also made ready accordingly.
The princess, casting off all lethargy and pride, devoted herself with the utmost care to the service and honour of the brahmin.
Going there to the brahmin, Pṛthā, chaste and devoted to purity, attended upon him who was worthy of service and gratified him according to the proper rites, as if he were a god.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That maiden, O great king, steadfast in her vows, gratified the brahmin who was firm in his vows, with a pure mind.
Sometimes the best of twice-born, having said he would come in the morning, would then arrive in the evening, or again at night, O lord of kings.
And at all these hours she, the maiden, would honour him with food, drink, and hospitality, ever increasing in her service, always.
The proper provision of food and other things, and the arrangement of his bed and seat — day by day these only grew and were never diminished.
Even when rebuked or blamed, or spoken to with unpleasant words by the brahmin, Pṛthā did nothing displeasing to him at that time, O king.
At inconvenient times the twice-born would arrive or often not arrive at all, and he would say, "Provide even what is hard to obtain."
And all of that Pṛthā accomplished and presented to him — with full composure, like a student, like a daughter, like a sister.
According to his pleasure, O lord of kings, that blameless maiden produced delight in the best of twice-born through her diligent efforts.
The best of brahmins was satisfied by her conduct and character, and with attentiveness he thereafter made even greater effort on her behalf.
Her father would ask her morning and evening, O descendant of Bharata: "Is the brahmin pleased with your service, my daughter?"
She, the renowned one, would always reply to him "Greatly so," and thereupon Kuntibhoja of great spirit attained supreme joy.
Then, when a full year had passed, that best of those who recite sacred texts, devoted to friendship with her, saw not a single fault in Pṛthā.
Then, his mind rejoiced, the brahmin said to her: "I am supremely delighted by your service to me, O auspicious and gentle one."
"Choose boons, O fortunate one — boons difficult for humans to obtain — by which you shall surpass all women of noble families in glory."
Kuntī said: All things have been accomplished for me since you are pleased with me, O best knower of the Vedas. And by your boons my father's purpose is fulfilled, O brahmin.
The brahmin said: If you do not wish a boon from me, O gentle and bright-smiling one, then take this mantra for the summoning of the gods.
"Whichever god you summon with this mantra, O gentle one, that very god shall be obliged to be under your command."
"Whether willing or unwilling, that divine being, calmed by the mantra's power, shall not escape your control but shall bow to your word like a servant."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: She, the blameless one, was unable to refuse again that best of twice-born — out of fear of a curse, O king.
Then the brahmin caused that woman of flawless limbs to receive that whole collection of mantras, O king, as heard in the Atharvāṅgiras.
Having given it, O lord of kings, he spoke to Kuntibhoja: "I have dwelt happily, O king, fully satisfied by your daughter."
"Well provided for in your house, always well honoured — we shall now proceed with our purpose." Having said this, he vanished.
The king, seeing that brahmin vanish right there and then, was filled with wonder, and he honoured Pṛthā deeply.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: After that best of twice-born had departed, at some point in the course of time, the maiden began to reflect on the power of the collection of mantras.
"What is this collection of mantras given to me by that great-souled one? I shall come to know its power before too long."
While thinking thus, she happened by chance to observe the season; abashed, the young girl, still in her maidenhood, became a woman in her menses.
Then Pṛthā beheld the blazing sun with its thousand rays as it rose, and she could not be satisfied with the form of the sun as it rested in the twilight.
Her sight became divine and she saw a divine vision — the god wearing his armour and adorned with his earrings.
Curiosity arose in her regarding the mantra, O lord of men, and the spirited woman then made the invocation of that god.
Having sipped the breath, she invoked the maker of day; and then, O king, the maker of day came swiftly.
Honey-golden, great-armed, with a throat like a conch, appearing to smile, wearing armlets and with a bound crown, blazing the directions as if on fire.
Having divided himself in two through his yogic power, he came and blazed, and then addressed Kuntī with a voice supremely sweet and gentle.
"I have come under your power, O gentle one, compelled by the force of your mantra. What shall I do, O queen? Having no choice, tell me — I shall do it for you."
Kuntī said: Go, O reverend one, back to where you came from. You were summoned out of mere curiosity. Be gracious, O reverend one.
The Sun said: I shall go as you say, O slender-waisted one. But it is not proper to summon a god and then dismiss him in vain.
"Your intent, O fortunate one, is this: 'May there be a son from the Sun' — one unmatched in valour in the world, bearing armour and earrings."
"Therefore, O woman with the gait of an elephant, give yourself over; for a son shall be born to you, O fair courtyard-dwelling one, exactly as you intended."
"But if I go, O gentle and bright-smiling one, without uniting with you, I shall curse you in my anger, and your brahmin father as well."
"On your account I shall burn them all — without doubt — including your foolish father who does not understand the impropriety you have done."
"And that brahmin who gave you the mantra without knowing your character and conduct — I shall today impart supreme punishment to him."
"For all these gods in heaven, led by Indra, behold you mocking them as it were, O passionate one, and they are smiling."
"Look at these hosts of gods — this divine eye is yours, given by me even before; it is by means of this that you saw me."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king's daughter saw the thirty gods, all of them stationed in their places in the sky, and the great luminous sun shining just as the Āditya shines.
Seeing them, the young woman, the goddess, abashed and afraid, spoke to the Sun: "Go to your own chariot, O lord of cattle. This solicitation is a hardship for one still a maiden."

"Father, mother, and teachers, and whatever others have authority over the giving of this body — I shall not transgress dharma in the world. The conduct of women is honoured as the protection of their body."
O Vibhāvasu, you were summoned by me to test the power of my mantra. Having treated it as a childish act, saying it was mere child's play, you ought to forgive me for that, O mighty one.

Sūrya said: Accepting your plea that it was a childish act, I grant you this concession — no other concession shall be obtained. Give yourself to me, O daughter of Kuntī; only thus will you find peace, O timid one.

Moreover, it is not fitting that I should depart having been summoned falsely. If I go now, O blameless-limbed one, I shall become a laughingstock in the world, and all the gods will have reason to mock me, O auspicious one.
Therefore, unite with me; you shall obtain a son equal to me, and you shall become distinguished in all the worlds, O beautiful one.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But that high-minded maiden, speaking sweet words in many ways, was unable to appease the thousand-rayed one.
When the young girl was unable to refuse the dispeller of darkness, frightened of a curse, O king, she then reflected for a long time.
A curse from an innocent father and likewise from a brahmin — how could I not incur such a curse on account of myself from this wrathful Vibhāvasu?
Even by a child, even in confusion, even with the most vehement denials, the fierce energy and austerities of the mighty should not be provoked excessively.
I am now greatly frightened and my hand is firmly seized — yet how can I perform this improper act of surrendering myself on my own?
She, thus terrified of the curse, thinking over many things, her limbs overcome with confusion, smiling again and again—
— addressed that god, frightened for her kinsmen, O best of kings, with voice trembling in shame, terrified of the curse, O lord of the people.
Kuntī said: O god, my father lives, as does my mother and other kinsmen. While they are alive, this transgression of custom should not occur.
O god, if union with you were to take place outside of proper rites, then on my account the fame of this family would be destroyed in the world.
Or if you, O foremost among the radiant ones, consider this to be righteous even without the gift of myself by my kinsmen, then I shall fulfill your desire.
Having surrendered myself to you as a chaste woman, O invincible one, may righteousness, fame, glory, and the life-span of embodied beings rest in you.
Sūrya said: Neither your father, nor your mother, nor your teachers have authority over you, O bright-smiling one, O one of beautiful hips. May good come to you — hear my words.

Because the root 'kan' and the verbal root from which 'kanya' is derived signifies desiring from all, O beautiful one, therefore a maiden here, O lovely-hipped one, O one of excellent complexion, is independent.
No unrighteousness whatsoever would be committed by you, O beautiful one. How could I, who am desired by the worlds, ever practice unrighteousness?
All women and men are naturally free and unrestrained, O one of excellent complexion — this is the natural order of the worlds; anything else is considered a distortion.
After uniting with me, you shall again become a virgin, and the son born to you shall be mighty-armed and of great renown.
Kuntī said: If a son should be born to me from you, O dispeller of all darkness — one who is adorned with earrings, clad in armor, a hero, mighty-armed, and of great strength—
Sūrya said: He shall be mighty-armed, adorned with earrings, and bearing divine armor; both of these, O auspicious one, shall be made of ambrosia.
Kuntī said: If the earrings and the excellent armor of my son, whom you shall beget from yourself upon me, are indeed made of ambrosia—
— then let union with me take place, O god, as you have declared, O blessed one; and may that son be endowed with righteousness, with your valor, beauty, essence, and energy.
Sūrya said: O queen, the earrings were given to me by Aditi, shining with intoxicating splendor; I shall give both these and this excellent armor to your son, O timid one.
Pṛthu said: By all means, O blessed god, I shall unite with you, if a son shall be born as you have described, O lord of rays.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Saying 'so be it,' the sky-traveler, the enemy of Svarbhānu, whose essence is yoga, entered Kuntī and touched her at the navel.
Then that maiden became overwhelmed by the radiance of Sūrya; that divine girl fell upon the bed, her mind bewildered.
Sūrya said: I shall bring it about, O lovely-hipped one — you shall give birth to a son, the foremost among all who bear weapons, and you shall remain a virgin.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then that ashamed young girl spoke to Sūrya as he was departing, O king of kings, saying 'so be it' to the one of great splendor.
Thus addressed, that daughter of the king Kuntī, having beseeched Vivasvat with shame, fell upon that sacred bed, overcome with stupor, like a creeper being broken.
The sharp-rayed one, having stupefied her with his radiance, entered her through yoga and established himself within her; yet the sun did not defile her. The young girl then regained consciousness.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then a child was conceived within Pṛthā, O lord of the earth, in the tenth month of the bright fortnight, like the moon-lord in the sky.
That young girl, lovely-hipped, concealing the embryo out of fear of her kinsmen, bore it within herself; no one became aware of her.
Indeed, no other woman knew of her, except the nurse who was skilled in guarding secrets, residing in the women's quarters.
Then in time that one of excellent complexion gave birth to the child, still a virgin, by the grace of that god — a child of divine brilliance.
And just so — clad in natural armor, adorned with golden gleaming earrings, with tawny eyes and the shoulders of a bull, just like his father.
As soon as the child was born, that beautiful woman, after consulting with the nurse, placed him in a box that was well-lined on all sides.
In that box coated with beeswax, comfortable, smooth, well-covered — weeping — she set it afloat on the Aśva river.
Knowing full well that bearing a child while an unwed maiden was improper, yet out of love for her son, O king of kings, she lamented piteously.
As she was releasing the box into the waters of the Aśva river, weeping, Kuntī spoke these words — hear them.
May you be blessed by the beings of the atmosphere, by those of the earth, O my little son; and by the divine beings and those who move through water.
May your paths be auspicious and free from adversaries; and may those you encounter, O son, be of benevolent hearts.
May King Varuṇa, the lord of waters, protect you in the water; may Pavana, who dwells in the atmosphere and moves everywhere, protect you in the sky.
May your father, the sun, the foremost among the radiant ones, protect you everywhere — by whom you were given to me, O son, truly by a divine ordinance.
